abstract: Simard, LeCun & Denker (1993) showed that the performance of nearest-neighbor classification schemes for handwritten character recognition can be improved by incorporating invariance to spe(cid:173) the so cific transformations in the underlying distance metric - called tangent distance. The resulting classifier, however, can be prohibitively slow and memory intensive due to the large amount of prototypes that need to be stored and used in the distance compar(cid:173) isons. In this paper we develop rich models for representing large subsets of the prototypes. These models are either used singly per class, or as basic building blocks in conjunction with the K-means clustering algorithm. *This work was performed while Trevor Hastie was a member of the Statistics and Data Analysis Research Group, AT&T Bell Laboratories, Murray Hill, NJ 07974.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the computational cost of recognizing handwritten characters with tangent distance. This distance measure incorporates invariance to selected transformations, allowing nearest-neighbor classification to account for changes that should preserve character identity. The difficulty is that a classifier may need to store and compare against a very large collection of prototypes.

The authors develop richer models that each represent substantial subsets of those prototypes. The aim is to replace many individual reference examples with representations that capture their shared structure. This shifts attention from the distance calculation alone to the way the classifier organizes and represents its reference collection.

The proposed models can be used in two ways: as one model per class or as building blocks combined with k-means clustering. These options allow representation at either the whole-class level or through multiple groups within a class. The contribution is a modeling strategy aimed at the time and memory burden of tangent-distance classification while retaining its emphasis on transformation-aware comparisons.
summary.tldr: Rich prototype models represent groups of handwritten examples to address the storage and comparison costs of tangent-distance classification.

title: Learning Prototype Models for Tangent Distance
High-Performance Job-Shop Scheduling With A Time-Delay TD(λ) Network

abstract: We present a new algorithm for associative reinforcement learn(cid:173) ing. The algorithm is based upon the idea of matching a network's output probability with a probability distribution derived from the environment's reward signal. This Probability Matching algorithm is shown to perform faster and be less susceptible to local minima than previously existing algorithms. We use Probability Match(cid:173) ing to train mixture of experts networks, an architecture for which other reinforcement learning rules fail to converge reliably on even simple problems. This architecture is particularly well suited for our algorithm as it can compute arbitrarily complex functions yet calculation of the output probability is simple.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Probability Matching, an algorithm for associative reinforcement learning. Its central idea is to derive a probability distribution from the environment's reward signal and train a network so that its output probabilities match that distribution. Reward feedback thus becomes the basis for a probabilistic learning target.

The authors report that the algorithm learns faster and is less susceptible to local minima than previously existing algorithms. Local minima matter because training can settle into a solution that is hard to improve through nearby changes. The stated comparison suggests that the probability-matching formulation improves both learning speed and the reliability of finding useful solutions.

The method is also used to train mixtures of experts, an architecture for which other reinforcement learning rules reportedly fail to converge reliably even on simple problems. This architecture is a useful fit because it can represent complex functions while keeping output-probability calculation simple. The paper connects that computational convenience directly to the quantity its learning rule needs to match.
summary.tldr: Probability Matching trains network output probabilities against reward-derived distributions, improving learning and enabling reliable mixture-of-experts training.

title: Reinforcement Learning by Probability Matching

abstract: We previously proposed a quantitative model of early visual pro(cid:173) cessing in primates, based on non-linearly interacting visual filters and statistically efficient decision. We now use this model to inter(cid:173) pret the observed modulation of a range of human psychophysical thresholds with and without focal visual attention. Our model - calibrated by an automatic fitting procedure - simultaneously re(cid:173) produces thresholds for four classical pattern discrimination tasks, performed while attention was engaged by another concurrent task. Our model then predicts that the seemingly complex improvements of certain thresholds, which we observed when attention was fully available for the discrimination tasks, can best be explained by a strengthening of competition among early visual filters.

paragraphs: This paper uses a quantitative model of early vision to explain how attention changes people's ability to distinguish visual patterns. The model combines visual filters that interact nonlinearly with a statistically efficient decision process. Its target is discrimination thresholds: the levels at which differences between patterns become distinguishable in the tested tasks.

The authors automatically fit the model to observations from four classical discrimination tasks performed while another task occupied attention. A single modeling framework reproduces the thresholds across all four tasks simultaneously. This gives the analysis a shared starting point for examining what changes when attention becomes fully available for visual discrimination.

The model then attributes the observed, seemingly complicated improvements in certain thresholds to stronger competition among early visual filters. This matters because several behavioral changes can be interpreted through a common adjustment to the interactions within the model. The result is a model-based explanation of attention's effects, with strengthened filter competition identified as the best explanation within the reported analysis.
summary.tldr: A quantitative vision model explains attention-related improvements in pattern discrimination through stronger competition among early visual filters.

title: Attentional Modulation of Human Pattern Discrimination Psychophysics Reproduced by a Quantitative Model

abstract: We present three simple approximations for the calculation of the posterior mean in Gaussian Process classification. The first two methods are related to mean field ideas known in Statistical Physics. The third approach is based on Bayesian online approach which was motivated by recent results in the Statistical Mechanics of Neural Networks. We present simulation results showing: 1. that the mean field Bayesian evidence may be used for hyperparameter tuning and 2. that the online approach may achieve a low training error fast.

paragraphs: This paper proposes three simple approximations for computing the posterior mean in Gaussian-process classification. The posterior mean summarizes the model after incorporating observed training data. The focus is on practical ways to calculate this quantity approximately, giving Gaussian-process classifiers alternative computational routes for learning from examples.

Two approaches draw on mean-field ideas from statistical physics. The third uses a Bayesian online approach motivated by results from the statistical mechanics of neural networks. These provide different approximations within the same classification setting, and the paper examines useful consequences of both the mean-field and online perspectives.

The simulations suggest that Bayesian evidence computed through the mean-field approach may help tune hyperparameters, the settings that govern the model. They also suggest that the online approach may reach low training error quickly. These are distinct findings: one concerns selecting model settings, while the other concerns speed of fitting the training examples. The latter claim specifically addresses training error, preserving the scope of the reported result.
summary.tldr: Three Gaussian-process classification approximations show potential for evidence-based hyperparameter tuning and rapid reduction of training error.

title: Efficient Approaches to Gaussian Process Classification

abstract: Low-dimensional representations are key to solving problems in high(cid:173) level vision, such as face compression and recognition. Factorial coding strategies for reducing the redundancy present in natural images on the basis of their second-order statistics have been successful in account(cid:173) ing for both psychophysical and neurophysiological properties of early vision. Class-specific representations are presumably formed later, at the higher-level stages of cortical processing. Here we show that when retinotopic factorial codes are derived for ensembles of natural objects, such as human faces, not only redundancy, but also dimensionality is re(cid:173) duced. We also show that objects are built from parts in a non-Gaussian fashion which allows these local-feature codes to have dimensionalities that are substantially lower than the respective Nyquist sampling rates.

paragraphs: Compact visual representations are important for tasks such as face compression and recognition. The paper starts from factorial coding strategies that reduce redundancy in natural images using second-order statistics. Such strategies had helped account for properties of early vision, while representations specific to object classes were presumed to emerge later in cortical processing.

The authors derive retinotopic factorial codes for collections of natural objects, including human faces. They show that these codes reduce dimensionality as well as redundancy. Those outcomes are related but distinct: reducing repeated information also produces a representation that needs fewer dimensions for the object ensembles studied.

The paper further shows that the way objects are assembled from parts is non-Gaussian. This structure allows local-feature representations to have dimensionalities substantially below the corresponding Nyquist sampling rates. The finding connects statistical structure in natural objects to compact representations of their parts. It suggests why coding approaches grounded in local features can offer dimensionality reduction relevant to higher-level visual tasks, alongside their role in removing redundancy.
summary.tldr: Local-feature factorial codes reduce both redundancy and dimensionality by exploiting non-Gaussian structure in natural objects.

title: Redundancy and Dimensionality Reduction in Sparse-Distributed Representations of Natural Objects in Terms of Their Local Features

abstract: A serious problem in learning probabilistic models is the presence of hid(cid:173) den variables. These variables are not observed, yet interact with several of the observed variables. As such, they induce seemingly complex de(cid:173) pendencies among the latter. In recent years, much attention has been devoted to the development of algorithms for learning parameters, and in some cases structure, in the presence of hidden variables. In this pa(cid:173) per, we address the related problem of detecting hidden variables that interact with the observed variables. This problem is of interest both for improving our understanding of the domain and as a preliminary step that guides the learning procedure towards promising models. A very natural approach is to search for "structural signatures" of hidden variables - substructures in the learned network that tend to suggest the presence of a hidden variable. We make this basic idea concrete, and show how to integrate it with structure-search algorithms. We evaluate this method on several synthetic and real-life datasets, and show that it performs surpris(cid:173) ingly well.

paragraphs: An unobserved variable can influence several observed variables and make their relationships appear complicated. This paper addresses how to detect such hidden variables when learning a probabilistic model. Identifying their possible presence can improve understanding of the domain and guide the search toward models that explain the observed dependencies more naturally.

The proposed approach looks for structural signatures: patterns within a learned network that tend to suggest an underlying hidden variable. The authors turn this idea into a concrete method and integrate it with algorithms that search over network structures. Detection therefore becomes part of the model-search process, using the structure already learned from observations to suggest promising additions.

The paper evaluates the method on several synthetic and real-world datasets and reports strong performance. Its interpretation remains suggestive rather than definitive: the network patterns are evidence pointing toward hidden variables, not a claim that every such pattern uniquely establishes one. The contribution is a structural route to discovering useful hidden-variable candidates and directing subsequent model learning.
summary.tldr: Patterns in learned network structures help identify candidate hidden variables and guide probabilistic model search.

title: Discovering Hidden Variables: A Structure-Based Approach

abstract: A cortical model for motion-in-depth selectivity of complex cells in the visual cortex is proposed. The model is based on a time ex(cid:173) tension of the phase-based techniques for disparity estimation. We consider the computation of the total temporal derivative of the time-varying disparity through the combination of the responses of disparity energy units. To take into account the physiological plau(cid:173) sibility, the model is based on the combinations of binocular cells characterized by different ocular dominance indices. The resulting cortical units of the model show a sharp selectivity for motion-in(cid:173) depth that has been compared with that reported in the literature for real cortical cells.

We consider the computation of the total temporal derivative of the time-varying disparity through the combination of the responses of disparity energy units. To take into account the physiological plau(cid:173) sibility, the model is based on the combinations of binocular cells characterized by different ocular dominance indices. The resulting cortical units of the model show a sharp selectivity for motion-in(cid:173) depth that has been compared with that reported in the literature for real cortical cells.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a cortical model for detecting motion in depth from binocular information. Its target is the selectivity of complex cells in visual cortex: how a modeled cell can respond strongly to particular motion toward or away from the observer, using information supplied by the two eyes.

The approach extends phase-based disparity estimation into time. Disparity describes a difference between the two eyes' views, and the model combines responses from disparity energy units to compute the total temporal derivative of changing disparity. This connects a representation of binocular differences to a representation of how those differences evolve.

To address physiological plausibility, the model combines binocular cells with different ocular dominance indices, meaning different relative contributions from the eyes. The resulting cortical units exhibit sharp selectivity for motion in depth, which the authors compare with published observations of real cortical cells. The stated result supports this hierarchy as a candidate computational account of motion-in-depth selectivity.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical binocular model combines disparity responses over time to produce sharply motion-in-depth-selective cortical units.

title: A Hierarchical Model of Complex Cells in Visual Cortex for the Binocular Perception of Motion-in-Depth

abstract: We present a geometric approach to statistical shape analysis of closed curves in images. The basic idea is to specify a space of closed curves satisfying given constraints, and exploit the differential geometry of this space to solve optimization and inference problems. We demonstrate this approach by: (i) deﬁning and computing statistics of observed shapes, (ii) deﬁning and learning a parametric probability model on shape space, and (iii) designing a binary hypothesis test on this space.

paragraphs: This paper treats the analysis of closed image curves as a problem in geometry and statistics. Its starting point is to define a space whose elements are curves satisfying specified constraints. A shape is therefore an object in a structured space, and the constraints determine which shapes belong to that space.

The authors use the differential geometry of this curve space to formulate optimization and inference problems. This matters because statistical operations can then be defined in relation to the geometry of the allowed shapes. The approach connects the representation of admissible curves with the mathematical machinery used to analyze observations of them.

Three demonstrations show the range of the framework. The paper defines and computes statistics of observed shapes, defines and learns a parametric probability model on shape space, and constructs a binary hypothesis test there. Together, these contributions extend the geometric viewpoint from describing shape collections to learning their distribution and making a statistical decision between two hypotheses.
summary.tldr: The paper uses the geometry of constrained closed-curve spaces to compute shape statistics, learn probability models, and construct a binary hypothesis test.

title: Geometric Analysis of Constrained Curves

abstract: We present a probabilistic generative model of entity relationships and their attributes that simultaneously discovers groups among the entities and topics among the corresponding textual attributes. Block-models of relationship data have been studied in social network analysis for some time. Here we simultaneously cluster in several modalities at once, incor- porating the attributes (here, words) associated with certain relationships. Signiﬁcantly, joint inference allows the discovery of topics to be guided by the emerging groups, and vice-versa. We present experimental results on two large data sets: sixteen years of bills put before the U.S. Sen- ate, comprising their corresponding text and voting records, and thirteen years of similar data from the United Nations. We show that in compari- son with traditional, separate latent-variable models for words, or Block- structures for votes, the Group-Topic model’s joint inference discovers more cohesive groups and improved topics.

paragraphs: The paper develops a model that discovers groups of entities and topics in associated text at the same time. Relationship data reveal patterns among entities, while textual attributes provide information about what those relationships concern. The model brings both sources into a shared probabilistic account instead of analyzing them independently.

Its key feature is joint inference. Emerging groups help guide the topics the model discovers, and emerging topics help guide the groups. This extends the block-model approach to relationship data by incorporating words associated with relationships. The two kinds of hidden structure can therefore inform one another throughout the analysis.

The authors evaluate the Group-Topic model using sixteen years of U.S. Senate bills and voting records and thirteen years of comparable United Nations data. Compared with separate latent-variable models for words or block structures for votes, joint inference finds more cohesive groups and improved topics. The results support combining relational and textual evidence when both describe different aspects of the same underlying activity.
summary.tldr: Jointly modeling relationships and their text yields more cohesive groups and improved topics than separate models on legislative datasets.

title: Group and Topic Discovery from Relations and Their Attributes

abstract: The performance of EEG-based Brain-Computer-Interfaces (BCIs) critically depends on the extraction of features from the EEG carrying information relevant for the classification of different mental states. For BCIs employing imaginary movements of different limbs, the method of Common Spatial Patterns (CSP) has been shown to achieve excellent classification results. The CSP-algorithm however suffers from a lack of robustness, requiring training data without artifacts for good performance. To overcome this lack of robustness, we propose an adaptive spatial filter that replaces the training data in the CSP approach by a-priori information. More specifically, we design an adaptive spatial filter that maximizes the ratio of the variance of the electric field originating in a predefined region of interest (ROI) and the overall variance of the measured EEG. Since it is known that the component of the EEG used for discriminating imaginary movements originates in the motor cortex, we design two adaptive spatial filters with the ROIs centered in the hand areas of the left and right motor cortex. We then use these to classify EEG data recorded during imaginary movements of the right and left hand of three subjects, and show that the adaptive spatial filters outperform the CSP-algorithm, enabling classification rates of up to 94.7 % without artifact rejection.

paragraphs: EEG brain-computer interfaces need features that distinguish mental states despite interference in the recordings. Common Spatial Patterns, or CSP, can classify imagined limb movements well, but the paper identifies its dependence on artifact-free training data as a robustness problem. The proposed alternative uses prior knowledge about where the relevant brain activity originates.

The adaptive filter maximizes the variance attributed to a predefined brain region relative to the total variance in the measured EEG. This directs the filter toward a chosen source region. For imagined hand movements, the authors use the known involvement of the motor cortex and construct separate filters centered on its left and right hand areas.

The filters are evaluated on recordings from three subjects imagining right- and left-hand movements. They outperform CSP in that evaluation and achieve classification rates up to 94.7% without rejecting artifacts. The result demonstrates how anatomical prior information can support useful classification in recordings where the usual requirement for clean training data is problematic.
summary.tldr: Spatial filters guided by motor-cortex locations outperform CSP on three subjects' imagined-hand-movement EEG without artifact rejection.

title: Adaptive Spatial Filters with predefined Region of Interest for EEG based Brain-Computer-Interfaces

abstract: We introduce two methods to improve convergence of the Kernel Hebbian Algorithm (KHA) for iterative kernel PCA. KHA has a scalar gain parameter which is either held constant or decreased as 1/t, leading to slow convergence. Our KHA/et algorithm accelerates KHA by incorporating the reciprocal of the current estimated eigenvalues as a gain vector. We then derive and apply Stochastic MetaDescent (SMD) to KHA/et; this further speeds convergence by performing gain adaptation in RKHS. Experimental results for kernel PCA and spectral clustering of USPS digits as well as motion capture and image de-noising problems confirm that our methods converge substantially faster than conventional KHA.
originalAbstract: We introduce two methods to improve convergence of the Kernel Hebbian Algorithm (KHA) for iterative kernel PCA. KHA has a scalar gain parameter which is either held constant or decreased as 1/t, leading to slow convergence. Our KHA/et algorithm accelerates KHA by incorporating the reciprocal of the current estimated eigenvalues as a gain vector. We then derive and apply Stochastic MetaDescent (SMD) to KHA/et; this further speeds convergence by performing gain adaptation in RKHS. Experimental results for kernel PCA and spectral clustering of USPS digits as well as motion capture and image de-noising problems confirm that our methods converge substantially faster than conventional KHA.

paragraphs: Kernel principal component analysis can be computed iteratively using the Kernel Hebbian Algorithm, or KHA. The paper identifies its gain parameter, which controls update sizes, as a source of slow convergence. Conventional KHA uses a single gain that either remains constant or decreases according to a fixed schedule.

The first proposed improvement, KHA/et, replaces that scalar with a gain vector based on reciprocals of the currently estimated eigenvalues. This makes update scaling depend on the components being learned. The second improvement derives and applies Stochastic MetaDescent to KHA/et, adapting gains in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space in which the kernel method operates.

Experiments cover kernel PCA and spectral clustering of USPS digits, along with motion capture and image denoising problems. The authors report substantially faster convergence than conventional KHA, with the additional adaptation further accelerating the first improvement. The contribution concerns how efficiently the iterative procedure approaches its solution: adaptive update sizes make better use of the evolving estimates than the conventional scalar gain choices.
summary.tldr: Eigenvalue-based gains and further gain adaptation substantially accelerate iterative kernel PCA in the reported experiments.

title: Fast Iterative Kernel PCA

abstract: We describe a neurobiologically plausible model to implement dynamic routing using the concept of neuronal communication through neuronal coherence. The model has a three-tier architecture: a raw input tier, a routing control tier, and an invariant output tier. The correct mapping between input and output tiers is realized by an appropriate alignment of the phases of their respective background oscillations by the routing control units. We present an example architecture, implemented on a neuromorphic chip, that is able to achieve circular-shift invariance. A simple extension to our model can accomplish circular-shift dynamic routing with only O(N ) connections, compared to O(N 2 ) connections required by traditional models.

paragraphs: Dynamic routing concerns how a neural system changes which inputs communicate with which outputs. This paper proposes a neurobiologically plausible model in which that routing depends on neuronal coherence. The key idea is to control the timing relationship between background oscillations so that the appropriate input and output units communicate.

The architecture separates three roles: receiving raw input, controlling routing, and producing an invariant output. Units in the middle tier align the oscillation phases of the input and output tiers to establish the desired mapping. This makes phase coordination an explicit mechanism for selecting communication paths within the model.

An example implemented on a neuromorphic chip achieves circular-shift invariance, meaning that circularly shifting the input can preserve its output representation. The authors also describe a simple extension that can perform circular-shift dynamic routing with O(N) connections, compared with O(N²) for traditional models. The demonstrated invariance and proposed connection savings concern this specific routing setting, supporting a concrete computational role for neuronal coherence.
summary.tldr: A neural routing model uses oscillation-phase alignment to achieve circular-shift invariance, with an extension requiring only linearly many connections.

title: An in-silico Neural Model of Dynamic Routing through Neuronal Coherence

abstract: We propose a new approach to value function approximation which combines linear temporal difference reinforcement learning with subspace identification. In practical applications, reinforcement learning (RL) is complicated by the fact that state is either high-dimensional or partially observable. Therefore, RL methods are designed to work with features of state rather than state itself, and the success or failure of learning is often determined by the suitability of the selected features. By comparison, subspace identification (SSID) methods are designed to select a feature set which preserves as much information as possible about state. In this paper we connect the two approaches, looking at the problem of reinforcement learning with a large set of features, each of which may only be marginally useful for value function approximation. We introduce a new algorithm for this situation, called Predictive State Temporal Difference (PSTD) learning. As in SSID for predictive state representations, PSTD finds a linear compression operator that projects a large set of features down to a small set that preserves the maximum amount of predictive information. As in RL, PSTD then uses a Bellman recursion to estimate a value function. We discuss the connection between PSTD and prior approaches in RL and SSID. We prove that PSTD is statistically consistent, perform several experiments that illustrate its properties, and demonstrate its potential on a difficult optimal stopping problem.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes difficult when the underlying state is high-dimensional or only partly observable. Methods then depend on features, and their success can hinge on whether those features preserve useful information. This paper considers a large collection of features whose individual contributions to estimating future value may each be limited.

Predictive State Temporal Difference learning, or PSTD, combines linear temporal-difference learning with subspace identification. It finds a linear compression that reduces the large feature set to a smaller one while preserving the maximum amount of predictive information. It then uses a Bellman recursion to estimate a value function from that representation, connecting predictive feature selection with reinforcement-learning estimation.

The authors prove statistical consistency, use experiments to illustrate the algorithm's properties, and demonstrate its potential on a difficult optimal-stopping problem. They also relate PSTD to earlier reinforcement-learning and subspace-identification approaches. The contribution is a coordinated way to compress abundant features and use the retained predictive information for value estimation.
summary.tldr: PSTD compresses large feature sets to preserve predictive information, then uses temporal-difference learning for statistically consistent value estimation.

title: Predictive State Temporal Difference Learning

abstract: Hashing-based methods provide a very promising approach to large-scale similarity search. To obtain compact hash codes, a recent trend seeks to learn the hash functions from data automatically. In this paper, we study hash function learning in the context of multimodal data. We propose a novel multimodal hash function learning method, called Co-Regularized Hashing (CRH), based on a boosted co-regularization framework. The hash functions for each bit of the hash codes are learned by solving DC (difference of convex functions) programs, while the learning for multiple bits proceeds via a boosting procedure so that the bias introduced by the hash functions can be sequentially minimized. We empirically compare CRH with two state-of-the-art multimodal hash function learning methods on two publicly available data sets.

We propose a novel multimodal hash function learning method, called Co-Regularized Hashing (CRH), based on a boosted co-regularization framework. The hash functions for each bit of the hash codes are learned by solving DC (difference of convex functions) programs, while the learning for multiple bits proceeds via a boosting procedure so that the bias introduced by the hash functions can be sequentially minimized. paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn compact hash codes for data with multiple modalities. Such codes support large-scale similarity search by representing data in a compact form. The problem is to learn the hash functions from the available data while taking the multimodal setting into account, rather than choosing the functions independently of the learning task.

The proposed method, Co-Regularized Hashing, combines co-regularization with boosting. Learning the hash functions for an individual bit is formulated as a difference-of-convex optimization problem. Learning a complete code then proceeds across multiple bits through a boosting procedure, which sequentially reduces the bias introduced by the hash functions.

This separates the construction into two connected levels: optimizing individual bits and coordinating how additional bits contribute to the representation. The authors compare the method empirically with two leading multimodal hashing approaches on two public datasets. The stated contribution is the learning framework and its evaluation; the abstract reports the comparison without specifying a performance advantage or its magnitude.
summary.tldr: Co-Regularized Hashing learns multimodal binary codes through per-bit optimization and a boosting procedure across bits.

title: Co-Regularized Hashing for Multimodal Data

abstract: Numerical integration is an key component of many problems in scientific computing, statistical modelling, and machine learning. Bayesian Quadrature is a model-based method for numerical integration which, relative to standard Monte Carlo methods, offers increased sample efficiency and a more robust estimate of the uncertainty in the estimated integral. We propose a novel Bayesian Quadrature approach for numerical integration when the integrand is non-negative, such as the case of computing the marginal likelihood, predictive distribution, or normalising constant of a probabilistic model. Our approach approximately marginalises the quadrature model's hyperparameters in closed form, and introduces an active learning scheme to optimally select function evaluations, as opposed to using Monte Carlo samples. We demonstrate our method on both a number of synthetic benchmarks and a real scientific problem from astronomy.

paragraphs: Many probabilistic calculations require integrating a function, including computing model evidence, predictive distributions, and normalizing constants. This paper develops a Bayesian quadrature method for cases where that function is nonnegative. Bayesian quadrature treats integration as a modeling problem, using a model of the function to estimate both the integral and uncertainty about its value.

The approach addresses two decisions within this process. It approximately averages over the quadrature model's hyperparameters in closed form, accounting for uncertainty in those settings. It also introduces an active learning procedure that chooses where to evaluate the function, instead of relying on Monte Carlo samples to supply evaluation locations.

This matters because each function evaluation contributes information toward the integral, and selecting evaluations deliberately can make that information more useful. The abstract motivates Bayesian quadrature through improved sample efficiency and more robust uncertainty estimates relative to standard Monte Carlo methods. The proposed approach is demonstrated on synthetic benchmarks and an astronomy problem, showing its use in both controlled examples and scientific inference.
summary.tldr: An active Bayesian quadrature method selects informative evaluations to estimate integrals of nonnegative functions.

title: Active Learning of Model Evidence Using Bayesian Quadrature

abstract: Many applications require the analysis of complex interactions between time series. These interactions can be non-linear and involve vector valued as well as complex data structures such as graphs or strings. Here we provide a general framework for the statistical analysis of these interactions when random variables are sampled from stationary time-series of arbitrary objects. To achieve this goal we analyze the properties of the kernel cross-spectral density operator induced by positive definite kernels on arbitrary input domains. This framework enables us to develop an independence test between time series as well as a similarity measure to compare different types of coupling. The performance of our test is compared to the HSIC test using i.i.d. assumptions, showing improvement in terms of detection errors as well as the suitability of this approach for testing dependency in complex dynamical systems. Finally, we use this approach to characterize complex interactions in electrophysiological neural time series.

paragraphs: Interactions between time series can be nonlinear, and each observation may itself be a vector, graph, or string. This paper develops a statistical framework for analyzing such interactions when observations come from stationary time series. That setting retains temporal structure while allowing a broad range of data types.

The framework uses a kernel cross-spectral density operator built from positive definite kernels. Kernels allow the analysis to work across arbitrary input domains, while the operator provides a basis for studying coupling between sequences. The authors use it to construct both an independence test and a similarity measure for comparing different forms of coupling.

The independence test is evaluated against an HSIC test using independent-and-identically-distributed assumptions. The reported comparison shows improved detection errors and supports the approach's suitability for complex dynamical systems. The authors also apply it to electrophysiological neural time series. The contribution is a unified way to test and compare temporal interactions in complex data, with stationarity defining the stated setting for the analysis.
summary.tldr: Kernel cross-spectral operators support dependence testing and coupling comparisons for stationary time series of complex observations.

title: Statistical analysis of coupled time series with Kernel Cross-Spectral Density operators.

abstract: We present a method for training recurrent neural networks to act as near-optimal feedback controllers. It is able to generate stable and realistic behaviors for a range of dynamical systems and tasks -- swimming, flying, biped and quadruped walking with different body morphologies. It does not require motion capture or task-specific features or state machines. The controller is a neural network, having a large number of feed-forward units that learn elaborate state-action mappings, and a small number of recurrent units that implement memory states beyond the physical system state. The action generated by the network is defined as velocity. Thus the network is not learning a control policy, but rather the dynamics under an implicit policy. Essential features of the method include interleaving supervised learning with trajectory optimization, injecting noise during training, training for unexpected changes in the task specification, and using the trajectory optimizer to obtain optimal feedback gains in addition to optimal actions.

paragraphs: This paper presents a way to train recurrent neural networks as near-optimal feedback controllers for diverse moving characters. It generates stable, realistic swimming, flying, and walking behaviors across different body shapes, including bipeds and quadrupeds. The method does not require motion capture, task-specific features, or manually specified state machines.

The network combines many feed-forward units, which learn elaborate relationships between states and actions, with a smaller set of recurrent units that maintain memory beyond the physical system's state. Its outputs are velocities. The authors therefore describe it as learning dynamics under an implicit policy, a distinction that clarifies what the network is being trained to represent.

Training alternates supervised learning with trajectory optimization. It also injects noise and includes unexpected changes in task specifications. The trajectory optimizer supplies optimal feedback gains as well as optimal actions, contributing information about responses to deviations. These elements form a training method that supports the reported range of stable behaviors without requiring a separate hand-built control structure for each task.
summary.tldr: Recurrent controllers trained with trajectory optimization generate stable, realistic movement across diverse bodies and tasks.

title: Interactive Control of Diverse Complex Characters with Neural Networks

abstract: To improve the efficiency of Monte Carlo estimation, practitioners are turning to biased Markov chain Monte Carlo procedures that trade off asymptotic exactness for computational speed. The reasoning is sound: a reduction in variance due to more rapid sampling can outweigh the bias introduced. However, the inexactness creates new challenges for sampler and parameter selection, since standard measures of sample quality like effective sample size do not account for asymptotic bias. To address these challenges, we introduce a new computable quality measure based on Stein's method that bounds the discrepancy between sample and target expectations over a large class of test functions. We use our tool to compare exact, biased, and deterministic sample sequences and illustrate applications to hyperparameter selection, convergence rate assessment, and quantifying bias-variance tradeoffs in posterior inference.

paragraphs: Faster approximate Monte Carlo methods can produce more samples while introducing bias. That tradeoff can be worthwhile when the reduction in variance outweighs the bias, but it complicates evaluation. Measures such as effective sample size do not account for asymptotic bias, so they cannot by themselves assess this aspect of sample quality.

The paper introduces a computable quality measure based on Stein’s method. It bounds differences between expectations estimated from samples and expectations under the target distribution across a large class of test functions. This directly connects the assessment of a sample sequence to the accuracy of quantities one might estimate with it.

The authors use the measure to compare exact, biased, and deterministic sample sequences. They illustrate its use in choosing hyperparameters, assessing convergence rates, and quantifying bias-versus-variance tradeoffs in posterior inference. The contribution is a shared way to evaluate sampling outputs that includes the discrepancy approximate methods can retain even when they generate samples rapidly.
summary.tldr: A computable Stein-based measure assesses sample quality by bounding expectation errors, including discrepancies missed by effective sample size.

title: Measuring Sample Quality with Stein's Method

abstract: We introduce a neural network with a recurrent attention model over a possibly large external memory. The architecture is a form of Memory Network (Weston et al., 2015) but unlike the model in that work, it is trained end-to-end, and hence requires significantly less supervision during training, making it more generally applicable in realistic settings. It can also be seen as an extension of RNNsearch to the case where multiple computational steps (hops) are performed per output symbol. The flexibility of the model allows us to apply it to tasks as diverse as (synthetic) question answering and to language modeling. For the former our approach is competitive with Memory Networks, but with less supervision. For the latter, on the Penn TreeBank and Text8 datasets our approach demonstrates comparable performance to RNNs and LSTMs. In both cases we show that the key concept of multiple computational hops yields improved results.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a neural network that repeatedly directs attention over an external memory, which may be large. The model can perform several computational steps, called hops, before producing each output symbol. These repeated memory-access steps are a central architectural feature rather than a single lookup attached to an otherwise unchanged prediction process.

The network is trained end to end. Compared with the earlier Memory Network described in the abstract, this substantially reduces the supervision required during training. That reduction matters for applicability: the architecture can be trained with less instructional information while retaining the ability to make multiple passes over its memory.

The authors evaluate the model on synthetic question answering and language modeling. For question answering, it is competitive with Memory Networks while using less supervision. On Penn TreeBank and Text8, its language-modeling performance is comparable to recurrent neural networks and LSTMs. In both task categories, multiple hops improve results. The findings support repeated attention-based computation as a useful component across these distinct applications.
summary.tldr: End-to-end Memory Networks repeatedly attend to external memory, reducing supervision needs and improving results through multiple computational hops.

title: End-To-End Memory Networks

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the differences between two causal directed acyclic graph (DAG) models with a shared topological order given i.i.d. samples from each model. This is of interest for example in genomics, where changes in the structure or edge weights of the underlying causal graphs reflect alterations in the gene regulatory networks. We here provide the first provably consistent method for directly estimating the differences in a pair of causal DAGs without separately learning two possibly large and dense DAG models and computing their difference. Our two-step algorithm first uses invariance tests between regression coefficients of the two data sets to estimate the skeleton of the difference graph and then orients some of the edges using invariance tests between regression residual variances. We demonstrate the properties of our method through a simulation study and apply it to the analysis of gene expression data from ovarian cancer and during T-cell activation.

paragraphs: Sometimes the important question is how a causal system changes between two conditions. Learning a complete graph for each condition can be an unnecessarily large intermediate task, especially when both graphs are dense. This paper directly estimates their differences, motivated in part by changes in gene regulatory networks.

The setting assumes independent, identically distributed samples from each of two causal directed acyclic graph models that share a topological order. The algorithm first tests whether regression coefficients remain invariant across the datasets to identify the connections in the difference graph without directions. It then tests invariance of regression residual variances to orient some of those connections.

The authors provide a provably consistent method for estimating differences directly, avoiding separate reconstruction of the two full graphs. The shared ordering is part of the stated problem, and the orientation step identifies directions for some edges rather than promising a fully directed answer. Simulations and applications to ovarian cancer gene expression and T-cell activation demonstrate the method's properties and its use in studying changing biological relationships.
summary.tldr: For two causal DAGs sharing a topological order, invariance tests estimate graph differences directly and orient some changed connections.

title: Direct Estimation of Differences in Causal Graphs

abstract: Incentive mechanisms for crowdsourcing are designed to incentivize financially self-interested workers to generate and report high-quality labels. Existing mechanisms are often developed as one-shot static solutions, assuming a certain level of knowledge about worker models (expertise levels, costs for exerting efforts, etc.). In this paper, we propose a novel inference aided reinforcement mechanism that acquires data sequentially and requires no such prior assumptions. Specifically, we first design a Gibbs sampling augmented Bayesian inference algorithm to estimate workers' labeling strategies from the collected labels at each step. Then we propose a reinforcement incentive learning (RIL) method, building on top of the above estimates, to uncover how workers respond to different payments. RIL dynamically determines the payment without accessing any ground-truth labels. We theoretically prove that RIL is able to incentivize rational workers to provide high-quality labels both at each step and in the long run. Empirical results show that our mechanism performs consistently well under both rational and non-fully rational (adaptive learning) worker models. Besides, the payments offered by RIL are more robust and have lower variances compared to existing one-shot mechanisms.

Static incentive mechanisms often assume prior knowledge of worker expertise or effort costs. This paper introduces a sequential mechanism that learns from collected labels without requiring that prior worker-model knowledge, allowing payment decisions to respond to evidence gathered over time.

A Bayesian inference algorithm augmented with Gibbs sampling first estimates workers' labeling strategies. Reinforcement incentive learning then uses these estimates to learn how workers respond to different payments. The mechanism adjusts payments dynamically without access to ground-truth labels, joining inference about worker behavior with learning how incentives influence that behavior.

The authors prove that the mechanism can encourage rational workers to supply high-quality labels both at individual steps and over the long run. Experiments also report consistently good performance for rational workers and workers modeled through adaptive learning. Compared with existing one-shot mechanisms, the offered payments are more robust and have lower variance. The theoretical rational-worker result and the broader empirical findings provide distinct forms of support.
summary.tldr: Bayesian worker inference and reinforcement learning jointly adapt crowdsourcing payments without requiring ground-truth labels or prior worker-model knowledge.

title: Inference Aided Reinforcement Learning for Incentive Mechanism Design in Crowdsourcing

abstract: Directed exploration strategies for reinforcement learning are critical for learning an optimal policy in a minimal number of interactions with the environment. Many algorithms use optimism to direct exploration, either through visitation estimates or upper confidence bounds, as opposed to data-inefficient strategies like e-greedy that use random, undirected exploration. Most data-efficient exploration methods require significant computation, typically relying on a learned model to guide exploration. Least-squares methods have the potential to provide some of the data-efficiency benefits of model-based approaches—because they summarize past interactions—with the computation closer to that of model-free approaches. In this work, we provide a novel, computationally efficient, incremental exploration strategy, leveraging this property of least-squares temporal difference learning (LSTD). We derive upper confidence bounds on the action-values learned by LSTD, with context-dependent (or state-dependent) noise variance. Such context-dependent noise focuses exploration on a subset of variable states, and allows for reduced exploration in other states. We empirically demonstrate that our algorithm can converge more quickly than other incremental exploration strategies using confidence estimates on action-values.

paragraphs: Efficient reinforcement learning requires choosing which actions to explore, rather than relying entirely on random exploration. Optimistic methods use uncertainty to direct these choices, but many require substantial computation. This paper builds on least-squares temporal difference learning, whose summaries of past interactions offer a way to support informed exploration with incremental computation.

The authors derive upper confidence bounds for the action values learned by this method. A central feature is that the noise variance can depend on the state. Consequently, the exploration signal can distinguish between states with different levels of variability, concentrating exploration on some states while reducing it in others.

The resulting strategy is described as computationally efficient and incremental. It aims to capture some of the data-efficiency benefits associated with model-based methods while keeping computation closer to model-free approaches. Experiments show that it can converge faster than other incremental strategies that also use confidence estimates on action values. This is an empirical comparison supporting the value of accounting for state-dependent noise.
summary.tldr: State-dependent confidence bounds guide reinforcement-learning exploration toward variable states while supporting efficient incremental updates.

title: Context-dependent upper-confidence bounds for directed exploration

abstract: Modeling uncertainty in deep neural networks, despite recent important advances, is still an open problem. Bayesian neural networks are a powerful solution, where the prior over network weights is a design choice, often a normal distribution or other distribution encouraging sparsity. However, this prior is agnostic to the generative process of the input data, which might lead to unwarranted generalization for out-of-distribution tested data. We suggest the presence of a confounder for the relation between the input data and the discriminative function given the target label. We propose an approach for modeling this confounder by sharing neural connectivity patterns between the generative and discriminative networks. This approach leads to a new deep architecture, where networks are sampled from the posterior of local causal structures, and coupled into a compact hierarchy. We demonstrate that sampling networks from this hierarchy, proportionally to their posterior, is efficient and enables estimating various types of uncertainties. Empirical evaluations of our method demonstrate significant improvement compared to state-of-the-art calibration and out-of-distribution detection methods.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty through distributions over network weights, but their weight priors are often chosen without reference to how input data are generated. This paper argues that such a disconnect might encourage unwarranted generalization on out-of-distribution inputs. It proposes linking uncertainty modeling more directly to the relationship between data generation and prediction.

The authors suggest a confounder affecting the relationship between inputs and the discriminative function, conditional on the target label. They model this proposed confounder by sharing connectivity patterns between generative and discriminative networks. The resulting architecture organizes networks sampled from a posterior over local causal structures into a compact hierarchy.

Sampling networks from that hierarchy in proportion to their posterior is shown to be efficient and to support estimation of different types of uncertainty. These results support the proposed architecture as an uncertainty-estimation approach, while the suggested confounder remains part of the paper's modeling rationale.
summary.tldr: Sharing generative and discriminative connectivity in a hierarchy of sampled networks improves uncertainty calibration and out-of-distribution detection empirically.

title: Modeling Uncertainty by Learning a Hierarchy of Deep Neural Connections

abstract: Stochastic Proximal Gradient (SPG) methods have been widely used for solving optimization problems with a simple (possibly non-smooth) regularizer in machine learning and statistics. However, to the best of our knowledge no non-asymptotic convergence analysis of SPG exists for non-convex optimization with a non-smooth and non-convex regularizer. All existing non-asymptotic analysis of SPG for solving non-smooth non-convex problems require the non-smooth regularizer to be a convex function, and hence are not applicable to a non-smooth non-convex regularized problem. This work initiates the analysis to bridge this gap and opens the door to non-asymptotic convergence analysis of non-smooth non-convex regularized problems. We analyze several variants of mini-batch SPG methods for minimizing a non-convex objective that consists of a smooth non-convex loss and a non-smooth non-convex regularizer. Our contributions are two-fold: (i) we show that they enjoy the same complexities as their counterparts for solving convex regularized non-convex problems in terms of finding an approximate stationary point; (ii) we develop more practical variants using dynamic mini-batch size instead of a fixed mini-batch size without requiring the target accuracy level of solution. The significance of our results is that they improve upon the-state-of-art results for solving non-smooth non-convex regularized problems. We also empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of the considered SPG methods in comparison with other peer stochastic methods.

Existing finite-time analyses for nonsmooth nonconvex problems generally required that regularizer itself to be convex. This paper addresses a smooth nonconvex loss combined with a regularizer that can be both nonsmooth and nonconvex.

The authors analyze several minibatch stochastic proximal-gradient variants. Their complexity for reaching an approximate stationary point matches the corresponding methods for convex-regularized nonconvex problems. They also develop variants that adjust minibatch sizes dynamically without requiring a target solution accuracy in advance.

Experiments compare the methods with other stochastic approaches and demonstrate their effectiveness. The theoretical target is approximate stationarity, not finding a global optimum of an arbitrary nonconvex objective. The abstract provides no particular complexity formulas or numerical results, but identifies both an expanded analysis regime and a practical adaptation that reduces dependence on advance tuning.
summary.tldr: Stochastic proximal-gradient methods gain finite-time guarantees with nonconvex, nonsmooth regularizers.

title: Non-asymptotic Analysis of Stochastic Methods for Non-Smooth Non-Convex Regularized Problems

abstract: Recent work has shown that CNN-based depth and ego-motion estimators can be learned using unlabelled monocular videos. However, the performance is limited by unidentified moving objects that violate the underlying static scene assumption in geometric image reconstruction. More significantly, due to lack of proper constraints, networks output scale-inconsistent results over different samples, i.e., the ego-motion network cannot provide full camera trajectories over a long video sequence because of the per-frame scale ambiguity. This paper tackles these challenges by proposing a geometry consistency loss for scale-consistent predictions and an induced self-discovered mask for handling moving objects and occlusions. Since we do not leverage multi-task learning like recent works, our framework is much simpler and more efficient. Comprehensive evaluation results demonstrate that our depth estimator achieves the state-of-the-art performance on the KITTI dataset. Moreover, we show that our ego-motion network is able to predict a globally scale-consistent camera trajectory for long video sequences, and the resulting visual odometry accuracy is competitive with the recent model that is trained using stereo videos. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to show that deep networks trained using unlabelled monocular videos can predict globally scale-consistent camera trajectories over a long video sequence.

Moving objects violate the static-scene assumption used in geometric image reconstruction. Separately, predictions can use inconsistent scales across frames, preventing individual camera-motion estimates from forming a coherent trajectory over a long video.

The paper introduces a geometry-consistency loss to encourage predictions to share a consistent scale. It also derives a self-discovered mask that handles moving objects and occlusions. These components address consistency and unreliable reconstruction regions within one framework. The authors describe the approach as simpler and more efficient because it avoids the multi-task learning used by recent alternatives.

Evaluation reports state-of-the-art depth-estimation performance on KITTI and globally scale-consistent camera trajectories over long video sequences. Visual-odometry accuracy is competitive with a recent model trained on stereo video. The trajectory result concerns agreement of scale throughout a sequence: it addresses the frame-to-frame inconsistency identified in the paper. The authors present it as, to their knowledge, the first such demonstration using unlabeled monocular training.
summary.tldr: Geometry consistency and a learned mask improve monocular depth estimation and enable globally scale-consistent camera trajectories from unlabeled video.

title: Unsupervised Scale-consistent Depth and Ego-motion Learning from Monocular Video

abstract: In barter exchanges, participants swap goods with one another without exchanging money; these exchanges are often facilitated by a central clearinghouse, with the goal of maximizing the aggregate quality (or number) of swaps. Barter exchanges are subject to many forms of uncertainty--in participant preferences, the feasibility and quality of various swaps, and so on. Our work is motivated by kidney exchange, a real-world barter market in which patients in need of a kidney transplant swap their willing living donors, in order to find a better match. Modern exchanges include 2- and 3-way swaps, making the kidney exchange clearing problem NP-hard. Planned transplants often \emph{fail} for a variety of reasons--if the donor organ is rejected by the recipient's medical team, or if the donor and recipient are found to be medically incompatible. Due to 2- and 3-way swaps, failed transplants can ``cascade'' through an exchange; one US-based exchange estimated that about $85\%$ of planned transplants failed in 2019. Many optimization-based approaches have been designed to avoid these failures; however most exchanges cannot implement these methods, due to legal and policy constraints. Instead, we consider a setting where exchanges can \emph{query} the preferences of certain donors and recipients--asking whether they would accept a particular transplant. We characterize this as a two-stage decision problem, in which the exchange program (a) queries a small number of transplants before committing to a matching, and (b) constructs a matching according to fixed policy. We show that selecting these edges is a challenging combinatorial problem, which is non-monotonic and non-submodular, in addition to being NP-hard. We propose both a greedy heuristic and a Monte Carlo tree search, which outperforms previous approaches, using experiments on both synthetic data and real kidney exchange data from the United Network for Organ Sharing.

title: Improving Policy-Constrained Kidney Exchange via Pre-Screening

abstract: Invertible neural networks based on coupling flows (CF-INNs) have various machine learning applications such as image synthesis and representation learning. However, their desirable characteristics such as analytic invertibility come at the cost of restricting the functional forms. This poses a question on their representation power: are CF-INNs universal approximators for invertible functions? Without a universality, there could be a well-behaved invertible transformation that the CF-INN can never approximate, hence it would render the model class unreliable. We answer this question by showing a convenient criterion: a CF-INN is universal if its layers contain affine coupling and invertible linear functions as special cases. As its corollary, we can affirmatively resolve a previously unsolved problem: whether normalizing flow models based on affine coupling can be universal distributional approximators. In the course of proving the universality, we prove a general theorem to show the equivalence of the universality for certain diffeomorphism classes, a theoretical insight that is of interest by itself.

paragraphs: Coupling-based invertible neural networks use restricted transformations to make inversion analytically possible. Those restrictions raise an expressiveness question: could a well-behaved invertible transformation remain beyond the model's approximation capabilities? This paper addresses that question theoretically, examining universality for diffeomorphisms, or smooth invertible transformations, in these network families.

The authors establish a sufficient criterion for universality. A coupling-based invertible network is universal if its layers include affine coupling and invertible linear functions as special cases. This gives a concrete condition on the available transformations under which the architecture retains broad approximation power. It resolves the concern for networks satisfying the criterion without asserting that every invertible architecture is universal.

A consequence is an affirmative answer to whether normalizing flows based on affine coupling can universally approximate distributions. The proof also establishes an equivalence between universality for certain classes of diffeomorphisms. These results clarify the representational capacity of the model family: the contribution concerns what it can approximate, with the layer criterion identifying a sufficient architectural foundation.
summary.tldr: Coupling-based invertible networks are universal diffeomorphism approximators when their layers include affine coupling and invertible linear transformations.

title: Coupling-based Invertible Neural Networks Are Universal Diffeomorphism Approximators

abstract: Several sampling algorithms with variance reduction have been proposed for accelerating the training of Graph Convolution Networks (GCNs). However, due to the intractable computation of optimal sampling distribution, these sampling algorithms are suboptimal for GCNs and are not applicable to more general graph neural networks (GNNs) where the message aggregator contains learned weights rather than fixed weights, such as Graph Attention Networks (GAT). The fundamental reason is that the embeddings of the neighbors or learned weights involved in the optimal sampling distribution are \emph{changing} during the training and \emph{not known a priori}, but only \emph{partially observed} when sampled, thus making the derivation of an optimal variance reduced samplers non-trivial. In this paper, we formulate the optimization of the sampling variance as an adversary bandit problem, where the rewards are related to the node embeddings and learned weights, and can vary constantly. Thus a good sampler needs to acquire variance information about more neighbors (exploration) while at the same time optimizing the immediate sampling variance (exploit). We theoretically show that our algorithm asymptotically approaches the optimal variance within a factor of 3. We show the efficiency and effectiveness of our approach on multiple datasets.

paragraphs: Training a graph neural network often involves sampling neighbors instead of processing every connection. The quality of that sampling affects the variance of the information used during training. Choosing the best sampling distribution is difficult because neighbor representations and learned aggregation weights change as training proceeds, and their current values are observed only when those neighbors are sampled.

The paper treats this decision as an adversarial bandit problem. A sampler must balance exploring neighbors to learn about their contribution to variance with exploiting its current knowledge to reduce variance immediately. This formulation accommodates changing rewards tied to node representations and learned weights, addressing a difficulty that also arises in graph attention networks.

The authors prove that their algorithm asymptotically approaches the optimal sampling variance within a factor of three. This is a qualified approximation guarantee, rather than exact optimality. Experiments across multiple datasets also support the approach's efficiency and effectiveness, connecting the theoretical sampling objective to practical graph neural network training.
summary.tldr: An adaptive bandit sampler handles changing graph representations and provably approaches optimal sampling variance within a factor of three asymptotically.

title: Bandit Samplers for Training Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Clustering is a ubiquitous task in data science. Compared to the commonly used k-means clustering, k-medoids clustering requires the cluster centers to be actual data points and supports arbitrary distance metrics, which permits greater interpretability and the clustering of structured objects. Current state-of-the-art k-medoids clustering algorithms, such as Partitioning Around Medoids (PAM), are iterative and are quadratic in the dataset size n for each iteration, being prohibitively expensive for large datasets. We propose BanditPAM, a randomized algorithm inspired by techniques from multi-armed bandits, that reduces the complexity of each PAM iteration from O(n^2) to O(nlogn) and returns the same results with high probability, under assumptions on the data that often hold in practice. As such, BanditPAM matches state-of-the-art clustering loss while reaching solutions much faster. We empirically validate our results on several large real-world datasets, including a coding exercise submissions dataset from Code.org, the 10x Genomics 68k PBMC single-cell RNA sequencing dataset, and the MNIST handwritten digits dataset. In these experiments, we observe that BanditPAM returns the same results as state-of-the-art PAM-like algorithms up to 4x faster while performing up to 200x fewer distance computations. The improvements demonstrated by BanditPAM enable k-medoids clustering on a wide range of applications, including identifying cell types in large-scale single-cell data and providing scalable feedback for students learning computer science online. We also release highly optimized Python and C++ implementations of our algorithm.

This supports interpretable representatives and arbitrary distance measures, making the approach useful for structured objects. Both the assumptions and the probability qualification matter: the claim is not unconditional equivalence on every run.

The findings show how reducing distance computations can make representative-based clustering practical on larger datasets while preserving the clustering quality of the compared PAM-like methods.
summary.tldr: BanditPAM reduces PAM’s per-iteration complexity to O(n log n), preserving its results with high probability under stated data assumptions.

title: BanditPAM: Almost Linear Time k-Medoids Clustering via Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: Recent works have shown that gradient descent can find a global minimum for over-parameterized neural networks where the widths of all the hidden layers scale polynomially with N (N being the number of training samples). In this paper, we prove that, for deep networks, a single layer of width N following the input layer suffices to ensure a similar guarantee. In particular, all the remaining layers are allowed to have constant widths, and form a pyramidal topology. We show an application of our result to the widely used LeCun's initialization and obtain an over-parameterization requirement for the single wide layer of order N^2.

In this paper, we prove that, for deep networks, a single layer of width N following the input layer suffices to ensure a similar guarantee. In particular, all the remaining layers are allowed to have constant widths, and form a pyramidal topology. We show an application of our result to the widely used LeCun's initialization and obtain an over-parameterization requirement for the single wide layer of order N^2.

paragraphs: The paper studies when gradient descent can reach a global minimum in a deep neural network. Earlier guarantees described in the abstract require every hidden layer to have a width that grows polynomially with the number of training examples. The authors investigate whether a comparable guarantee can hold when substantial width is concentrated near the input.

Their theorem shows that a layer immediately following the input, with width equal to the number of training samples, is sufficient for a similar convergence guarantee in the setting analyzed. Subsequent layers may have constant widths and form a pyramidal topology. This changes the architectural requirement: the guarantee does not demand that every hidden layer expand with the dataset.

The authors also apply their result to LeCun initialization. For that application, the over-parameterization requirement for the single wide layer is of order the square of the sample count. These are distinct statements: the general sufficient-width result and its initialization-specific application have different width requirements. The contribution clarifies how the placement of width can support global-convergence theory.
summary.tldr: A convergence theorem concentrates sufficient network width in one early layer, allowing later layers to remain narrow.

title: Global Convergence of Deep Networks with One Wide Layer Followed by Pyramidal Topology

abstract: Real-world timeseries have complex underlying temporal dynamics and the detection of anomalies is challenging. In this paper, we propose the Temporal Hierarchical One-Class (THOC) network, a temporal one-class classification model for timeseries anomaly detection. It captures temporal dynamics in multiple scales by using a dilated recurrent neural network with skip connections. Using multiple hyperspheres obtained with a hierarchical clustering process, a one-class objective called Multiscale Vector Data Description is defined. This allows the temporal dynamics to be well captured by a set of multi-resolution temporal clusters. To further facilitate representation learning, the hypersphere centers are encouraged to be orthogonal to each other, and a self-supervision task in the temporal domain is added. The whole model can be trained end-to-end. Extensive empirical studies on various real-world timeseries demonstrate that the proposed THOC network outperforms recent strong deep learning baselines on timeseries anomaly detection.

paragraphs: Time-series anomalies can be difficult to detect because temporal behavior has structure at multiple scales. The Temporal Hierarchical One-Class network, or THOC, addresses this by learning a representation of temporal patterns at several resolutions. Its one-class formulation organizes the behavior used to identify departures from those patterns.

A dilated recurrent neural network with skip connections captures dynamics across scales. Hierarchical clustering produces multiple hyperspheres, which define a Multiscale Vector Data Description objective. These hyperspheres represent temporal clusters at different resolutions. The model also encourages their centers to be orthogonal and adds a temporal self-supervision task to support representation learning.

All these components are trained end-to-end, bringing the temporal representation and one-class objective into a single learning process. Experiments on various real-world time series show better anomaly-detection performance than recent strong deep-learning baselines. The findings support representing temporal behavior through multiple hierarchical clusters, allowing the detector to account for more than one scale of dynamics in the evaluated data.
summary.tldr: THOC combines multiscale temporal representations with hierarchical one-class clustering to improve anomaly detection on evaluated real-world time series.

title: Timeseries Anomaly Detection using Temporal Hierarchical One-Class Network

abstract: Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) data is crucial for robust machine learning systems. Normalizing flows are flexible deep generative models that often surprisingly fail to distinguish between in- and out-of-distribution data: a flow trained on pictures of clothing assigns higher likelihood to handwritten digits. We investigate why normalizing flows perform poorly for OOD detection. We demonstrate that flows learn local pixel correlations and generic image-to-latent-space transformations which are not specific to the target image datasets, focusing on flows based on coupling layers. We show that by modifying the architecture of flow coupling layers we can bias the flow towards learning the semantic structure of the target data, improving OOD detection. Our investigation reveals that properties that enable flows to generate high-fidelity images can have a detrimental effect on OOD detection.
