We demonstrate that flows learn local pixel correlations and generic image-to-latent-space transformations which are not specific to the target image datasets, focusing on flows based on coupling layers. We show that by modifying the architecture of flow coupling layers we can bias the flow towards learning the semantic structure of the target data, improving OOD detection. Our investigation reveals that properties that enable flows to generate high-fidelity images can have a detrimental effect on OOD detection.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows assign likelihoods to images, but those likelihoods can be misleading indicators of whether an image belongs to the training distribution. The paper highlights a striking example: a flow trained on clothing images can assign higher likelihood to handwritten digits. It investigates the mechanisms behind this behavior, focusing on flows built with coupling layers.

The authors demonstrate that these models learn local pixel correlations and broadly applicable transformations from images into latent space. Such patterns and transformations need not be specific to the intended image dataset. Consequently, an unfamiliar image can fit properties the flow has learned even when its semantic content differs from the training data.

By changing the architecture of coupling layers, the authors bias the model toward learning semantic structure specific to the target data and improve out-of-distribution detection. Their investigation also shows that properties supporting high-fidelity image generation can harm detection. The findings explain why a flow's ability to model or generate images does not by itself establish that its likelihood reliably identifies unfamiliar inputs.
summary.tldr: Coupling-layer flows can favor generic image statistics over dataset semantics, and architectural changes that encourage semantics improve out-of-distribution detection.

title: Why Normalizing Flows Fail to Detect Out-of-Distribution Data

abstract: Iterative solvers are widely used to accurately simulate physical systems. These solvers require initial guesses to generate a sequence of improving approximate solutions. In this contribution, we introduce a novel method to accelerate iterative solvers for rod dynamics with graph networks (GNs) by predicting the initial guesses to reduce the number of iterations. Unlike existing methods that aim to learn physical systems in an end-to-end manner, our approach guarantees long-term stability and therefore leads to more accurate solutions. Furthermore, our method improves the run time performance of traditional iterative solvers for rod dynamics. To explore our method we make use of position-based dynamics (PBD) as a common solver for physical systems and evaluate it by simulating the dynamics of elastic rods. Our approach is able to generalize across different initial conditions, discretizations, and realistic material properties. We demonstrate that it also performs well when taking discontinuous effects into account such as collisions between individual rods. Finally, to illustrate the scalability of our approach, we simulate complex 3D tree models composed of over a thousand individual branch segments swaying in wind fields.

paragraphs: Simulating flexible rods accurately often involves an iterative solver: a procedure that starts with an approximate answer and repeatedly improves it. This paper uses a graph network to predict a better starting point for that procedure. The learned component therefore helps the solver reach its answer with fewer iterations, accelerating a calculation that still uses the physical solver.

The authors study this approach with position-based dynamics and simulations of elastic rods. They report improved runtime and describe their method as guaranteeing long-term stability, leading to more accurate solutions than approaches that learn the physical evolution entirely end to end. The central contribution is the placement of learning inside the simulation process: it supplies initial guesses for subsequent refinement.

The evaluations show generalization across initial conditions, discretizations, and realistic material properties. They also include collisions between rods, demonstrating performance when motion involves discontinuous effects. To illustrate scalability, the authors simulate three-dimensional trees with more than a thousand branch segments moving in wind fields.
summary.tldr: A graph network accelerates rod simulation by predicting better initial guesses for an iterative physical solver.

title: Accurately Solving Rod Dynamics with Graph Learning

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have shown to perform very well on large scale object recognition problems and lead to widespread use for real-world applications, including situations where DNN are implemented as “black boxes”. A promising approach to secure their use is to accept decisions that are likely to be correct while discarding the others. In this work, we propose DOCTOR, a simple method that aims to identify whether the prediction of a DNN classifier should (or should not) be trusted so that, consequently, it would be possible to accept it or to reject it. Two scenarios are investigated: Totally Black Box (TBB) where only the soft-predictions are available and Partially Black Box (PBB) where gradient-propagation to perform input pre-processing is allowed. Empirically, we show that DOCTOR outperforms all state-of-the-art methods on various well-known images and sentiment analysis datasets. In particular, we observe a reduction of up to 4% of the false rejection rate (FRR) in the PBB scenario. DOCTOR can be applied to any pre-trained model, it does not require prior information about the underlying dataset and is as simple as the simplest available methods in the literature.

paragraphs: DOCTOR addresses the decision of whether to accept a classifier's prediction or reject it as potentially incorrect. This is useful when a neural network is already trained and may be available only through restricted access. The method aims to detect likely misclassifications so that trust can be assessed separately for each prediction.

The authors study two access settings. In the totally black-box setting, only the model's soft predictions are available. In the partially black-box setting, gradients can also be propagated to support input preprocessing. DOCTOR can be applied to any pretrained model and does not require prior information about the dataset underlying it.

Across the evaluated image and sentiment-analysis datasets, the authors report better empirical performance than the state-of-the-art methods they compare against. In the partially black-box setting, they observe a reduction of up to 4% in false rejection rate. This indicates fewer rejected correct predictions in those experiments, while retaining a method described as comparable in simplicity to the simplest existing approaches.
summary.tldr: DOCTOR assesses whether pretrained classifiers' predictions should be accepted, using either soft predictions alone or additional gradient access.

title: DOCTOR: A Simple Method for Detecting Misclassification Errors

abstract: Ensembles of machine learning models yield improved system performance as well as robust and interpretable uncertainty estimates; however, their inference costs can be prohibitively high. Ensemble Distribution Distillation (EnD$^2$) is an approach that allows a single model to efficiently capture both the predictive performance and uncertainty estimates of an ensemble. For classification, this is achieved by training a Dirichlet distribution over the ensemble members' output distributions via the maximum likelihood criterion. Although theoretically principled, this work shows that the criterion exhibits poor convergence when applied to large-scale tasks where the number of classes is very high. Specifically, we show that for the Dirichlet log-likelihood criterion classes with low probability induce larger gradients than high-probability classes. Hence during training the model focuses on the distribution of the ensemble tail-class probabilities rather than the probability of the correct and closely related classes. We propose a new training objective which minimizes the reverse KL-divergence to a \emph{Proxy-Dirichlet} target derived from the ensemble. This loss resolves the gradient issues of EnD$^2$, as we demonstrate both theoretically and empirically on the ImageNet, LibriSpeech, and WMT17 En-De datasets containing 1000, 5000, and 40,000 classes, respectively.

paragraphs: An ensemble can improve predictions and uncertainty estimates, but running all its models is expensive. Ensemble distribution distillation aims to transfer both benefits into one model. For classification, the approach studied here learns a Dirichlet distribution over the class-probability outputs of ensemble members, preserving more than a single averaged prediction.

The paper identifies a problem with training that distribution by maximum likelihood when there are many classes. Low-probability classes generate larger gradients than high-probability classes. Training consequently emphasizes the ensemble's low-probability tail instead of concentrating appropriately on the correct class and closely related alternatives. This gradient imbalance leads to poor convergence on large classification tasks.

The authors replace the objective with reverse KL divergence to an ensemble-derived Proxy-Dirichlet target. They demonstrate theoretically and empirically that the new loss resolves the identified gradient issue. Evaluations cover ImageNet, LibriSpeech, and WMT17 English–German, with 1,000, 5,000, and 40,000 classes respectively. The contribution addresses how to train an uncertainty-preserving distilled model effectively as the output space becomes large.
summary.tldr: A Proxy-Dirichlet training target fixes gradient imbalance that hinders ensemble distribution distillation when classification has many classes.

title: Scaling Ensemble Distribution Distillation to Many Classes with Proxy Targets

abstract: The Text-to-SQL task, aiming to translate the natural language of the questions into SQL queries, has drawn much attention recently. One of the most challenging problems of Text-to-SQL is how to generalize the trained model to the unseen database schemas, also known as the cross-domain Text-to-SQL task. The key lies in the generalizability of (i) the encoding method to model the question and the database schema and (ii) the question-schema linking method to learn the mapping between words in the question and tables/columns in the database schema. Focusing on the above two key issues, we propose a \emph{Structure-Aware Dual Graph Aggregation Network} (SADGA) for cross-domain Text-to-SQL. In SADGA, we adopt the graph structure to provide a unified encoding model for both the natural language question and database schema. Based on the proposed unified modeling, we further devise a structure-aware aggregation method to learn the mapping between the question-graph and schema-graph. The structure-aware aggregation method is featured with \emph{Global Graph Linking}, \emph{Local Graph Linking} and \emph{Dual-Graph Aggregation Mechanism}. We not only study the performance of our proposal empirically but also achieved 3rd place on the challenging Text-to-SQL benchmark Spider at the time of writing.

SADGA focuses on both representing the question and schema and learning the links between them.

The proposed linking machinery includes global graph linking, local graph linking, and a dual-graph aggregation mechanism, bringing information from both graphs into the question-schema mapping.

That result provides evidence for the approach on the reported benchmark, while the methodological contribution is a shared graph-based representation coupled with explicit structural linking.
summary.tldr: SADGA links graph representations of questions and database schemas to improve text-to-SQL generalization to unseen schemas.

abstract: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) are a family of generative models which allows for the computation of exact likelihoods and marginals of its probability distributions. PCs are both expressive and tractable, and serve as popular choices for discrete density estimation tasks. However, large PCs are susceptible to overfitting, and only a few regularization strategies (e.g., dropout, weight-decay) have been explored. We propose HyperSPNs: a new paradigm of generating the mixture weights of large PCs using a small-scale neural network. Our framework can be viewed as a soft weight-sharing strategy, which combines the greater expressiveness of large models with the better generalization and memory-footprint properties of small models. We show the merits of our regularization strategy on two state-of-the-art PC families introduced in recent literature -- RAT-SPNs and EiNETs -- and demonstrate generalization improvements in both models on a suite of density estimation benchmarks in both discrete and continuous domains.

They combine expressive modeling with tractable probability calculations, but large circuits can overfit. The paper addresses how to retain the capacity of a large circuit while controlling the flexibility of its learned parameters.

HyperSPNs use a small neural network to generate the mixture weights of a larger probabilistic circuit. The authors interpret this as soft weight sharing: the circuit's weights are linked through a common generator. This arrangement combines the expressive structure of the large model with generalization and memory-footprint properties associated with a smaller parameterization.

The authors apply the approach to two probabilistic circuit families, RAT-SPNs and EiNETs. Across density-estimation benchmarks containing both discrete and continuous data, they report improved generalization for both families. The contribution is therefore a regularization strategy that works within existing circuit models, using a compact weight-generating network to improve how their expressive capacity translates to performance on unseen data.
summary.tldr: HyperSPNs generate large probabilistic circuits' mixture weights with a small neural network, improving generalization through soft weight sharing.

title: HyperSPNs: Compact and Expressive Probabilistic Circuits

abstract: We develop an algorithm to address unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) in continual learning (CL) settings. The goal is to update a model continually to learn distributional shifts across sequentially arriving tasks with unlabeled data while retaining the knowledge about the past learned tasks. Existing UDA algorithms address the challenge of domain shift, but they require simultaneous access to the datasets of the source and the target domains. On the other hand, existing works on CL can handle tasks with labeled data. Our solution is based on consolidating the learned internal distribution for improved model generalization on new domains and benefitting from experience replay to overcome catastrophic forgetting.

paragraphs: This paper considers a model that encounters a sequence of changing data distributions and must keep adapting. New tasks arrive without labels, while knowledge from earlier tasks should remain useful. The setting combines unsupervised domain adaptation, which addresses distribution shifts, with continual learning, which addresses learning over time without losing earlier capabilities.

The authors identify a mismatch between the existing approaches they discuss and this combined setting. Domain adaptation methods require simultaneous access to source and target datasets, whereas continual learning methods handle labeled tasks. The proposed algorithm instead centers on consolidating the model's learned internal distribution so that accumulated knowledge can support generalization to newly arriving domains.

The method also uses experience replay to address catastrophic forgetting. These two components serve complementary purposes: the consolidated distribution supports adaptation, and replay helps retain knowledge of past tasks. The contribution is an algorithm organized around both requirements within one learning process. The abstract describes this mechanism and its intended benefits without reporting a numerical performance comparison or a formal guarantee of complete retention.
summary.tldr: The proposed algorithm combines internal-distribution consolidation and experience replay to adapt continually to unlabeled domains while retaining past knowledge.

title: Lifelong Domain Adaptation via Consolidated Internal Distribution

abstract: We consider the problem of minimizing a convex function that is evolving in time according to unknown and possibly stochastic dynamics. Such problems abound in the machine learning and signal processing literature, under the names of concept drift and stochastic tracking. We provide novel non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for stochastic algorithms with iterate averaging, focusing on bounds valid both in expectation and with high probability. Notably, we show that the tracking efficiency of the proximal stochastic gradient method depends only logarithmically on the initialization quality when equipped with a step-decay schedule.

paragraphs: Optimization becomes a tracking problem when the function being minimized changes over time. This paper considers evolving convex objectives whose dynamics are unknown and may themselves be random. Such a setting captures the need to keep adapting as the target changes, as in concept drift and stochastic tracking.

The authors establish non-asymptotic guarantees for stochastic algorithms that average their iterates, meaning that the analysis concerns finite stages of optimization rather than only eventual behavior. They provide bounds both in expectation and with high probability. These two forms describe average performance and probabilistic control of deviations, offering different ways to characterize the reliability of tracking.

A highlighted result concerns the proximal stochastic gradient method with a step-decay schedule. Under that schedule, tracking efficiency depends only logarithmically on initialization quality. This gives a quantified account of how the starting point affects tracking, with a relatively mild dependence. The contribution is theoretical guidance on averaging and step-size scheduling when the objective continues to move and the algorithm must follow it.
summary.tldr: Finite-time guarantees explain how stochastic methods track changing convex objectives, including mild initialization dependence under step decay.

title: Stochastic optimization under time drift: iterate averaging, step-decay schedules, and high probability guarantees

abstract: Partition-based methods are increasingly-used in extreme multi-label classification (XMC) problems due to their scalability to large output spaces (e.g., millions or more). However, existing methods partition the large label space into mutually exclusive clusters, which is sub-optimal when labels have multi-modality and rich semantics. For instance, the label “Apple” can be the fruit or the brand name, which leads to the following research question: can we disentangle these multi-modal labels with non-exclusive clustering tailored for downstream XMC tasks? In this paper, we show that the label assignment problem in partition-based XMC can be formulated as an optimization problem, with the objective of maximizing precision rates. This leads to an efficient algorithm to form flexible and overlapped label clusters, and a method that can alternatively optimizes the cluster assignments and the model parameters for partition-based XMC. Experimental results on synthetic and real datasets show that our method can successfully disentangle multi-modal labels, leading to state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on four XMC benchmarks.

paragraphs: Extreme multilabel classification must handle very large sets of possible labels, potentially numbering in the millions. Partitioning labels into clusters helps make this manageable, but assigning every label to exactly one cluster can be restrictive. A label may carry multiple meanings, as with Apple referring to either a fruit or a brand.

This paper treats label assignment as an optimization problem aimed at maximizing precision. The resulting algorithm permits flexible, overlapping clusters, allowing a label to participate in more than one grouping. The authors also propose alternating between updating cluster assignments and updating model parameters, so the organization of labels can adapt alongside the classifier.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the method can separate the different modes of ambiguous labels. The authors report state-of-the-art results on four extreme multilabel classification benchmarks. These findings support making the partition structure responsive to the downstream prediction objective: scalability need not depend on forcing every label into a single mutually exclusive semantic group.
summary.tldr: Optimizing overlapping label clusters helps disentangle ambiguous labels and improves extreme multilabel classification on four benchmarks.

title: Label Disentanglement in Partition-based Extreme Multilabel Classification

abstract: The firing of neural populations is coordinated across cells, in time, and across experimentalconditions or repeated experimental trials; and so a full understanding of the computationalsignificance of neural responses must be based on a separation of these different contributions tostructured activity.Tensor decomposition is an approach to untangling the influence of multiple factors in data that iscommon in many fields. However, despite some recent interest in neuroscience, wider applicabilityof the approach is hampered by the lack of a full probabilistic treatment allowing principledinference of a decomposition from non-Gaussian spike-count data.Here, we extend the Pólya-Gamma (PG) augmentation, previously used in sampling-based Bayesianinference, to implement scalable variational inference in non-conjugate spike-count models.Using this new approach, we develop techniques related to automatic relevance determination to inferthe most appropriate tensor rank, as well as to incorporate priors based on known brain anatomy suchas the segregation of cell response properties by brain area.We apply the model to neural recordings taken under conditions of visual-vestibular sensoryintegration, revealing how the encoding of self- and visual-motion signals is modulated by thesensory information available to the animal.

paragraphs: Neural activity has structure across cells, time, and experimental conditions or repeated trials. Tensor decomposition aims to separate these contributions, helping researchers understand coordinated population responses. This paper addresses a barrier to using that approach with neural recordings: spike counts require a probabilistic treatment that accommodates their non-Gaussian character.

The authors extend Pólya-Gamma augmentation, previously used for sampling-based Bayesian inference, to support scalable variational inference in non-conjugate spike-count models. Within this framework, they develop methods related to automatic relevance determination to infer an appropriate tensor rank, or number of components. They also allow anatomical knowledge to enter as prior information, such as differences in cell response properties across brain areas.

The model is applied to recordings collected during visual and vestibular sensory integration. The analysis reveals how the encoding of self-motion and visual-motion signals changes with the sensory information available to the animal. The contribution connects a probabilistic decomposition suited to spike-count observations with tools for selecting model complexity and incorporating known biological organization.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic tensor model separates structured neural spike activity while inferring model complexity and incorporating anatomical prior information.

title: Probabilistic Tensor Decomposition of Neural Population Spiking Activity

abstract: Many sequential decision making problems are high-stakes and require off-policy evaluation (OPE) of a new policy using historical data collected using some other policy. One of the most common OPE techniques that provides unbiased estimates is trajectory based importance sampling (IS). However, due to the high variance of trajectory IS estimates, importance sampling methods based on state-action visitation distributions (SIS) have recently been adopted. Unfortunately, while SIS often provides lower variance estimates for long horizons, estimating the state-action distribution ratios can be challenging and lead to biased estimates. In this paper, we present a new perspective on this bias-variance trade-off and show the existence of a spectrum of estimators whose endpoints are SIS and IS. Additionally, we also establish a spectrum for doubly-robust and weighted version of these estimators. We provide empirical evidence that estimators in this spectrum can be used to trade-off between the bias and variance of IS and SIS and can achieve lower mean-squared error than both IS and SIS.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a new policy would perform using data collected by another policy. Trajectory importance sampling can provide unbiased estimates, but its variance can be high. Methods based on state-action visitation distributions often reduce variance over long horizons, yet estimating their distribution ratios can introduce bias.

SOPE places these two approaches at opposite ends of a spectrum of estimators. This gives a new way to understand and adjust their bias-variance tradeoff. The paper also establishes corresponding spectra for weighted estimators and doubly robust estimators, extending the perspective beyond the basic importance-sampling formulations.

The empirical results show that intermediate estimators can achieve lower mean-squared error than either endpoint. This means that accepting some of one method’s weaknesses in exchange for reducing the other’s can improve overall estimation accuracy. The finding supports considering a range of estimators when evaluating a policy from historical data. It does not assert that a particular intermediate choice always dominates both endpoints across all problems.
summary.tldr: SOPE connects trajectory and visitation-distribution importance sampling through estimator families that can improve the bias-variance tradeoff.

title: SOPE: Spectrum of Off-Policy Estimators

abstract: Evaluating adversarial robustness amounts to finding the minimum perturbation needed to have an input sample misclassified. The inherent complexity of the underlying optimization requires current gradient-based attacks to be carefully tuned, initialized, and possibly executed for many computationally-demanding iterations, even if specialized to a given perturbation model.In this work, we overcome these limitations by proposing a fast minimum-norm (FMN) attack that works with different $\ell_p$-norm perturbation models ($p=0, 1, 2, \infty$), is robust to hyperparameter choices, does not require adversarial starting points, and converges within few lightweight steps. It works by iteratively finding the sample misclassified with maximum confidence within an $\ell_p$-norm constraint of size $\epsilon$, while adapting $\epsilon$ to minimize the distance of the current sample to the decision boundary.Extensive experiments show that FMN significantly outperforms existing $\ell_0$, $\ell_1$, and $\ell_\infty$-norm attacks in terms of perturbation size, convergence speed and computation time, while reporting comparable performances with state-of-the-art $\ell_2$-norm attacks. Our open-source code is available at: https://github.com/pralab/Fast-Minimum-Norm-FMN-Attack.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness evaluation asks how small an input change can make a model misclassify a sample. Finding such changes is an optimization problem, and existing gradient-based attacks can demand careful tuning, special starting points, or many expensive iterations.

The proposed fast minimum-norm attack, FMN, adapts the permitted perturbation size during optimization. Within the current constraint, it searches for a sample that is misclassified with high confidence. It then adjusts the constraint to reduce the sample's distance to the decision boundary.

FMN supports perturbation models based on the l0, l1, l2, and infinity norms. The authors report robustness to hyperparameter choices, no requirement for an already adversarial starting point, and convergence in a small number of lightweight steps. These properties target both setup effort and computation.

Extensive experiments show improvements over existing l0, l1, and infinity-norm attacks in perturbation size, convergence speed, and computation time. Performance is comparable to leading l2 attacks. The findings therefore differ by perturbation model, with the strongest reported advantages outside the l2 case.
summary.tldr: FMN efficiently searches for small adversarial perturbations by adapting its norm constraint across several perturbation models.

title: Fast Minimum-norm Adversarial Attacks through Adaptive Norm Constraints

abstract: We consider the task of learning latent community structure from multiple correlated networks. First, we study the problem of learning the latent vertex correspondence between two edge-correlated stochastic block models, focusing on the regime where the average degree is logarithmic in the number of vertices. We derive the precise information-theoretic threshold for exact recovery: above the threshold there exists an estimator that outputs the true correspondence with probability close to 1, while below it no estimator can recover the true correspondence with probability bounded away from 0. As an application of our results, we show how one can exactly recover the latent communities using \emph{multiple} correlated graphs in parameter regimes where it is information-theoretically impossible to do so using just a single graph.

First, we study the problem of learning the latent vertex correspondence between two edge-correlated stochastic block models, focusing on the regime where the average degree is logarithmic in the number of vertices. We derive the precise information-theoretic threshold for exact recovery: above the threshold there exists an estimator that outputs the true correspondence with probability close to 1, while below it no estimator can recover the true correspondence with probability bounded away from 0. paragraphs: The paper investigates how multiple related networks can reveal hidden communities. Before information from two networks can be combined, it may be necessary to determine which vertex in one corresponds to which vertex in the other. The authors study this matching problem for two edge-correlated stochastic block models, focusing on average degrees that grow logarithmically with the vertex count.

They derive a precise information-theoretic threshold for recovering the entire correspondence. Above the threshold, an estimator exists that finds the true matching with probability approaching one. Below it, no estimator can recover the true matching with a success probability that stays bounded away from zero. This distinguishes a shortage of statistical information from a failure of a particular method.

The matching result also enables exact community recovery from multiple correlated graphs in some parameter regimes where a single graph cannot provide enough information. The benefit is therefore stronger than merely improving an existing estimate: additional related networks can make exact recovery possible. These are information-theoretic statements about recoverability within the studied graph models.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies an exact graph-matching threshold and shows how correlated networks can enable otherwise impossible community recovery.

title: Correlated Stochastic Block Models: Exact Graph Matching with Applications to Recovering Communities

abstract: A common pain point in differentially private machine learning is the significant runtime overhead incurred when executing Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DPSGD), which may be as large as two orders of magnitude. We thoroughly demonstrate that by exploiting powerful language primitives, including vectorization, just-in-time compilation, and static graph optimization, one can dramatically reduce these overheads, in many cases nearly matching the best non-private running times. These gains are realized in two frameworks: one is JAX, which provides rich support for these primitives through the XLA compiler. We also rebuild core parts of TensorFlow Privacy, integrating more effective vectorization as well as XLA compilation, granting significant memory and runtime improvements over previous release versions. Our proposed approaches allow us to achieve up to 50x speedups compared to the best alternatives. Our code is available at https://github.com/TheSalon/fast-dpsgd.

paragraphs: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent can impose a substantial runtime cost, sometimes reaching two orders of magnitude above ordinary training. This paper studies how much of that overhead can be reduced through implementation choices. Its focus is on executing private training efficiently using capabilities already available in machine-learning frameworks.

The approach combines vectorization, just-in-time compilation, and static graph optimization. These mechanisms let the software express and optimize computation more effectively. The authors implement the approach in JAX using its support for the XLA compiler. They also rebuild core components of TensorFlow Privacy, introducing more effective vectorization and XLA compilation into that framework.

The paper reports substantial runtime and memory improvements over previous TensorFlow Privacy releases and speedups of up to 50 times compared with the best alternatives. In many evaluated cases, runtime nearly matches the best non-private training times. These findings show that implementation overhead can account for a large, reducible part of the cost of private training, making compiler and framework design practically important.
summary.tldr: Vectorization and compiler optimizations greatly accelerate private SGD, in many cases bringing runtime close to non-private training.

title: Enabling Fast Differentially Private SGD via Just-in-Time Compilation and Vectorization

abstract: Neurons in the dorsal visual pathway of the mammalian brain are selective for motion stimuli, with the complexity of stimulus representations increasing along the hierarchy. This progression is similar to that of the ventral visual pathway, which is well characterized by artificial neural networks (ANNs) optimized for object recognition. In contrast, there are no image-computable models of the dorsal stream with comparable explanatory power. We hypothesized that the properties of dorsal stream neurons could be explained by a simple learning objective: the need for an organism to orient itself during self-motion. To test this hypothesis, we trained a 3D ResNet to predict an agent's self-motion parameters from visual stimuli in a simulated environment. We found that the responses in this network accounted well for the selectivity of neurons in a large database of single-neuron recordings from the dorsal visual stream of non-human primates. In contrast, ANNs trained on an action recognition dataset through supervised or self-supervised learning could not explain responses in the dorsal stream, despite also being trained on naturalistic videos with moving objects. These results demonstrate that an ecologically relevant cost function can account for dorsal stream properties in the primate brain.

paragraphs: The brain's dorsal visual pathway responds to motion with increasingly complex representations along its hierarchy. This paper asks whether those responses can be explained by a practical behavioral objective: helping an organism orient itself while moving. The hypothesis connects neural selectivity to what visual processing needs to accomplish for the organism.

To test it, the authors train a three-dimensional ResNet to predict an agent's self-motion parameters from visual inputs in a simulated environment. They then compare the network's responses with a large collection of single-neuron recordings from non-human primate dorsal visual areas. The trained network accounts well for the recorded neurons' selectivity.

Networks trained for action recognition through supervised or self-supervised learning do not explain the dorsal responses in the reported comparison, despite exposure to naturalistic videos containing moving objects. This makes the training objective central to the interpretation: motion-containing inputs alone did not produce the same explanatory result. The findings show that an ecologically relevant self-motion objective can account for properties of the primate dorsal stream.
summary.tldr: A network trained to estimate self-motion explains primate dorsal-stream neuron selectivity better than the action-recognition networks examined.

title: Your head is there to move you around: Goal-driven models of the primate dorsal pathway

abstract: Remote sensing datasets pose a number of interesting challenges to machine learning researchers and practitioners, from domain shift (spatially, semantically and temporally) to highly imbalanced labels. In addition, the outputs of models trained on remote sensing datasets can contribute to positive societal impacts, for example in food security and climate change. However, there are many barriers that limit the accessibility of satellite data to the machine learning community, including a lack of large labeled datasets as well as an understanding of the range of satellite products available, how these products should be processed, and how to manage multi-dimensional geospatial data. To lower these barriers and facilitate the use of satellite datasets by the machine learning community, we present CropHarvest---a satellite dataset of more than 90,000 geographically-diverse samples with agricultural labels. The data and accompanying python package are available at https://github.com/nasaharvest/cropharvest.

To lower these barriers and facilitate the use of satellite datasets by the machine learning community, we present CropHarvest---a satellite dataset of more than 90,000 geographically-diverse samples with agricultural labels. paragraphs: Satellite data can support agricultural machine learning, but using it requires more than choosing a model. Researchers need labeled examples, familiarity with satellite products, appropriate processing, and ways to handle multidimensional geographic information. CropHarvest is introduced to reduce these barriers and make satellite-based research more accessible to the machine learning community.

The dataset contains more than 90,000 geographically diverse samples with agricultural labels. It is accompanied by a Python package, providing both a collection of labeled data and software intended to facilitate its use. The paper's contribution centers on making this kind of research resource available across a broad set of locations.

The motivating challenges include changes in data across geography, meaning, and time, together with highly uneven label frequencies. These issues make agricultural remote sensing a useful setting for studying how models handle varied data. The authors also point to potential societal applications in food security and climate change, positioning CropHarvest as enabling infrastructure for research toward those goals.
summary.tldr: CropHarvest provides over 90,000 geographically diverse agricultural samples and a Python package to lower barriers to satellite-based machine learning.

title: CropHarvest: A global dataset for crop-type classification

abstract: Unmeasured confounding poses a significant threat to the validity of causal inference. Despite that various ad hoc methods are developed to remove confounding effects, they are subject to certain fairly strong assumptions. In this work, we consider the estimation of conditional causal effects in the presence of unmeasured confounding using observational data and historical controls. Under an interpretable transportability condition, we prove the partial identifiability of conditional average treatment effect on the treated group (CATT). For tree-based models, a new notion, \emph{confounding entropy}, is proposed to measure the discrepancy introduced by unobserved confounders between the conditional outcome distribution of the treated and control groups. The confounding entropy generalizes conventional confounding bias, and can be estimated effectively using historical controls. We develop a new method, debiased causal tree, whose splitting rule is to minimize the empirical risk regularized by the confounding entropy. Notably, our method integrates current observational data (for empirical risk) and their historical controls (for confounding entropy) harmoniously. We highlight that, debiased causal tree can not only estimate CATT well in the presence of unmeasured confounding, but also is a robust estimator of conditional average treatment effect (CATE) against the imbalance of the treated and control populations when all confounders are observed. An extension of combining multiple debiased causal trees to further reduce biases by gradient boosting is considered. The computational feasibility and statistical power of our method are evidenced by simulations and a study of a credit card balance dataset.

This paper supplements current observations with historical controls and proves partial identifiability of conditional average treatment effects on the treated under an interpretable transportability condition.

The result depends on the transportability condition and available historical controls; it does not establish unrestricted causal identification from observational data despite arbitrary hidden confounding.
summary.tldr: Historical controls help regularize causal trees against unmeasured confounding under a transportability assumption.

title: Debiased Causal Tree: Heterogeneous Treatment Effects Estimation with Unmeasured Confounding

abstract: Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) represent a gold standard when developing policy guidelines. However, RCTs are often narrow, and lack data on broader populations of interest. Causal effects in these populations are often estimated using observational datasets, which may suffer from unobserved confounding and selection bias. Given a set of observational estimates (e.g., from multiple studies), we propose a meta-algorithm that attempts to reject observational estimates that are biased. We do so using validation effects, causal effects that can be inferred from both RCT and observational data. After rejecting estimators that do not pass this test, we generate conservative confidence intervals on the extrapolated causal effects for subgroups not observed in the RCT. Under the assumption that at least one observational estimator is asymptotically normal and consistent for both the validation and extrapolated effects, we provide guarantees on the coverage probability of the intervals output by our algorithm. To facilitate hypothesis testing in settings where causal effect transportation across datasets is necessary, we give conditions under which a doubly-robust estimator of group average treatment effects is asymptotically normal, even when flexible machine learning methods are used for estimation of nuisance parameters. We illustrate the properties of our approach on semi-synthetic experiments based on the IHDP dataset, and show that it compares favorably to standard meta-analysis techniques.

paragraphs: Randomized trials offer strong evidence about treatment effects, but often cover only a narrow population. Observational studies can reach additional groups, although hidden confounding and selection bias may distort their estimates. This paper proposes checking observational estimators against trial evidence before using them to estimate effects for groups absent from the trial.

The method uses validation effects that can be estimated from both randomized and observational data. It attempts to reject observational estimators that fail this comparison, then builds conservative confidence intervals for extrapolated effects using the surviving estimators. Passing validation is therefore part of a screening procedure, rather than a declaration that an observational estimate must be unbiased.

The authors also give conditions supporting asymptotic normality of a doubly robust group-effect estimator when nuisance quantities are learned with flexible machine learning. Semi-synthetic experiments based on IHDP illustrate the approach and show favorable comparisons with standard meta-analysis.
summary.tldr: The method screens observational causal estimators against randomized-trial evidence before constructing conservative intervals for populations outside the trial.

title: Falsification before Extrapolation in Causal Effect Estimation

abstract: Despite significant progress on multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) in recent years, coordination in complex domains remains a challenge. Work in MARL often focuses on solving tasks where agents interact with all other agents and entities in the environment; however, we observe that real-world tasks are often composed of several isolated instances of local agent interactions (subtasks), and each agent can meaningfully focus on one subtask to the exclusion of all else in the environment. In these composite tasks, successful policies can often be decomposed into two levels of decision-making: agents are allocated to specific subtasks and each agent acts productively towards their assigned subtask alone. This decomposed decision making provides a strong structural inductive bias, significantly reduces agent observation spaces, and encourages subtask-specific policies to be reused and composed during training, as opposed to treating each new composition of subtasks as unique. We introduce ALMA, a general learning method for taking advantage of these structured tasks. ALMA simultaneously learns a high-level subtask allocation policy and low-level agent policies. We demonstrate that ALMA learns sophisticated coordination behavior in a number of challenging environments, outperforming strong baselines. ALMA's modularity also enables it to better generalize to new environment configurations. Finally, we find that while ALMA can integrate separately trained allocation and action policies, the best performance is obtained only by training all components jointly. Our code is available at https://github.com/shariqiqbal2810/ALMA

paragraphs: Coordinating many agents becomes difficult when every agent must consider everything happening in an environment. ALMA addresses tasks that have a useful structure: they consist of local subtasks, and an agent can meaningfully concentrate on one assigned subtask. For these composite tasks, coordination can be separated into deciding who works where and deciding how each agent should act.

ALMA learns both levels together. A high-level policy allocates agents to subtasks, while low-level policies guide their actions within those assignments. This structure reduces what individual agents need to observe and encourages reuse of subtask policies across different combinations of work. A new combination can therefore benefit from behaviors learned for its constituent subtasks.

Across challenging environments, the authors report sophisticated coordination, stronger performance than strong baselines, and better generalization to new configurations. They also examine combining allocation and action policies trained separately. Although ALMA supports that combination, joint training produces the best reported performance, indicating that allocation decisions and local behaviors benefit from adapting to one another.
summary.tldr: ALMA jointly learns subtask assignments and local agent behaviors to improve coordination and generalization in composite multi-agent tasks.

title: ALMA: Hierarchical Learning for Composite Multi-Agent Tasks

abstract: Polyphone disambiguation aims to capture accurate pronunciation knowledge from natural text sequences for reliable Text-to-speech (TTS) systems. However, previous approaches require substantial annotated training data and additional efforts from language experts, making it difficult to extend high-quality neural TTS systems to out-of-domain daily conversations and countless languages worldwide. This paper tackles the polyphone disambiguation problem from a concise and novel perspective: we propose Dict-TTS, a semantic-aware generative text-to-speech model with an online website dictionary (the existing prior information in the natural language). Specifically, we design a semantics-to-pronunciation attention (S2PA) module to match the semantic patterns between the input text sequence and the prior semantics in the dictionary and obtain the corresponding pronunciations; The S2PA module can be easily trained with the end-to-end TTS model without any annotated phoneme labels. Experimental results in three languages show that our model outperforms several strong baseline models in terms of pronunciation accuracy and improves the prosody modeling of TTS systems. Further extensive analyses demonstrate that each design in Dict-TTS is effective. The code is available at https://github.com/Zain-Jiang/Dict-TTS.

paragraphs: Text-to-speech systems must choose the correct pronunciation when a written form has multiple possible readings. That choice depends on meaning and context. Previous approaches require substantial annotated data and language expertise, making it difficult to extend pronunciation handling to unfamiliar conversations and additional languages.

Dict-TTS brings existing dictionary knowledge into a generative speech model. Its semantics-to-pronunciation attention module compares the meaning patterns in an input text sequence with semantic information in an online dictionary, then obtains the corresponding pronunciations. The module trains together with the end-to-end speech system without requiring annotated phoneme labels.

Experiments in three languages show better pronunciation accuracy than several strong baseline models, along with improved modeling of prosody. Further analyses support the effectiveness of the model’s individual design choices. The central contribution is a way to connect contextual meaning with dictionary pronunciation knowledge inside the speech-generation process. The reported results support that design across the three evaluated languages, including benefits for how the generated speech is delivered.
summary.tldr: Dict-TTS uses dictionary semantics to learn context-appropriate pronunciation without annotated phoneme labels.

title: Dict-TTS: Learning to Pronounce with Prior Dictionary Knowledge for Text-to-Speech

abstract: Electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) is a powerful method for investigating the structures of protein molecules, with important implications for understanding the molecular processes of life and drug development. In this technique, many noisy, two-dimensional projection images of protein molecules in unknown poses are combined into one or more three-dimensional reconstructions. The presence of multiple structural states in the data represents a major bottleneck in existing processing pipelines, often requiring expert user supervision. Variational auto-encoders (VAEs) have recently been proposed as an attractive means for learning the data manifold of data sets with a large number of different states. These methods are based on a coordinate-based approach, similar to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), to make volumetric reconstructions from 2D image data in Fourier-space. Although NeRF is a powerful method for real-space reconstruction, many of the benefits of the method do not transfer to Fourier-space, e.g. inductive bias for spatial locality. We present an approach where the VAE reconstruction is expressed on a volumetric grid, and demonstrate how this model can be trained efficiently through a novel backpropagation method that exploits the sparsity of the projection operation in Fourier-space. We achieve improved results on a simulated data set and at least equivalent results on an experimental data set when compared to the coordinate-based approach, while also substantially lowering computational cost. Our approach is computationally more efficient, especially in inference, enabling interactive analysis of the latent space by the user.

Data containing multiple structural states make reconstruction particularly challenging. Variational autoencoders can help represent this variation, but coordinate-based reconstructions in Fourier space do not inherit all the advantages that similar representations offer in ordinary spatial reconstruction.

This paper instead expresses the VAE reconstruction on a volumetric grid. It makes that representation efficient to train through a backpropagation method that exploits the sparsity of the Fourier-space projection operation. The change connects the reconstruction representation and its training procedure: a grid becomes practical because gradient computation takes advantage of the structure of the projection.

Compared with the coordinate-based approach, the method improves results on a simulated dataset and achieves at least equivalent results on an experimental dataset, while substantially reducing computational cost. The efficiency gain is especially strong during inference. That enables users to interactively analyze the latent space, making exploration of the learned structural variation more practical.
summary.tldr: Grid-based VAE reconstruction with sparse Fourier backpropagation reduces cryo-EM computation while matching or improving the reported reconstruction results.

title: Sparse Fourier Backpropagation in Cryo-EM Reconstruction

abstract: In this paper, we revisit the smooth and strongly-convex-strongly-concave minimax optimization problem. Zhang et al. (2021) and Ibrahim et al. (2020) established the lower bound $\Omega\left(\sqrt{\kappa_x\kappa_y} \log \frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)$ on the number of gradient evaluations required to find an ϵ-accurate solution, where κx and κy are condition numbers for the strong convexity and strong concavity assumptions. However, the existing state-of-the-art methods do not match this lower bound: algorithms of Lin et al. (2020) and Wang and Li (2020) have gradient evaluation complexity $\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{\kappa_x\kappa_y} \log^3 \frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)$ and $\mathcal{O}\left( \sqrt{\kappa_x\kappa_y}\log^3 (\kappa_x\kappa_y)\log\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)$, respectively. We fix this fundamental issue by providing the first algorithm with $\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{\kappa_x\kappa_y} \log \frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)$ gradient evaluation complexity. We design our algorithm in three steps: (i) we reformulate the original problem as a minimization problem via the pointwise conjugate function; (ii) we apply a specific variant of the proximal point algorithm to the reformulated problem; (iii) we compute the proximal operator inexactly using the optimal algorithm for operator norm reduction in monotone inclusions.

paragraphs: The paper considers minimax optimization where one set of variables minimizes an objective and another maximizes it. The objective is smooth, strongly convex in the minimizing variables, and strongly concave in the maximizing variables. For this problem class, a known lower bound specifies how many gradient evaluations may be required to reach a desired accuracy.

Earlier algorithms exceeded that lower bound by extra logarithmic factors. The proposed method removes this gap, requiring O(sqrt(kappa_x kappa_y) log(1/epsilon)) gradient evaluations. The two condition numbers describe the conditioning associated with strong convexity and strong concavity, while epsilon specifies the target accuracy.

The construction has three parts: reformulate the minimax problem as minimization using a pointwise conjugate, apply a particular proximal point method, and approximately compute its proximal steps with an optimal monotone-inclusion procedure. Matching the lower bound establishes optimal gradient-evaluation complexity for the stated problem class, giving a precise sense in which the algorithm is optimal.
summary.tldr: A reformulation and carefully computed proximal steps achieve the known optimal gradient-evaluation complexity for smooth strongly convex–strongly concave minimax problems.

title: The First Optimal Algorithm for Smooth and Strongly-Convex-Strongly-Concave Minimax Optimization

abstract: This paper studies multi-agent reinforcement learning in Markov games, with the goal of learning Nash equilibria or coarse correlated equilibria (CCE) sample-optimally. All prior results suffer from at least one of the two obstacles: the curse of multiple agents and the barrier of long horizon, regardless of the sampling protocol in use. We take a step towards settling this problem, assuming access to a flexible sampling mechanism: the generative model. Focusing on non-stationary finite-horizon Markov games, we develop a fast learning algorithm called Q-FTRL and an adaptive sampling scheme that leverage the optimism principle in online adversarial learning (particularly the Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL) method). Our algorithm learns an $\varepsilon$-approximate CCE in a general-sum Markov game using $$ \widetilde{O}\bigg( \frac{H^4 S \sum_{i=1}^m A_i}{\varepsilon^2} \bigg) $$ samples, where $m$ is the number of players, $S$ indicates the number of states, $H$ is the horizon, and $A_i$ denotes the number of actions for the $i$-th player. This is minimax-optimal (up to log factor) when $m$ is fixed. When applied to two-player zero-sum Markov games, our algorithm provably finds an $\varepsilon$-approximate Nash equilibrium with a minimal number of samples. Along the way, we derive a refined regret bound for FTRL that makes explicit the role of variance-type quantities, which might be of independent interest.

paragraphs: This paper asks how many samples are needed to learn equilibrium behavior in multi-agent Markov games. It focuses on finite-horizon games whose dynamics can vary across time and assumes access to a generative model, a flexible sampling mechanism. That sampling assumption is part of the setting in which its guarantees apply.

The authors introduce Q-FTRL and an adaptive sampling strategy, combining optimistic learning with Follow-the-Regularized-Leader. For general-sum games, the algorithm learns an approximately coarse correlated equilibrium with sample complexity proportional, up to logarithmic factors, to H⁴ times the number of states times the sum of players’ action counts, divided by the squared target error. The dependence uses the sum of action counts rather than their product.

For a fixed number of players, the bound is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors. In two-player zero-sum games, the method also has a sample-optimal guarantee for an approximate Nash equilibrium. The analysis additionally refines FTRL’s regret bound to expose the contribution of variance-related quantities.
summary.tldr: With generative-model sampling, Q-FTRL achieves equilibrium-learning sample bounds that are minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors for fixed player counts.

title: Minimax-Optimal Multi-Agent RL in Markov Games With a Generative Model

abstract: One-shot Federated Learning (FL) has recently emerged as a promising approach, which allows the central server to learn a model in a single communication round. Despite the low communication cost, existing one-shot FL methods are mostly impractical or face inherent limitations, \eg a public dataset is required, clients' models are homogeneous, and additional data/model information need to be uploaded. To overcome these issues, we propose a novel two-stage \textbf{D}ata-fre\textbf{E} o\textbf{N}e-\textbf{S}hot federated l\textbf{E}arning (DENSE) framework, which trains the global model by a data generation stage and a model distillation stage. DENSE is a practical one-shot FL method that can be applied in reality due to the following advantages:(1) DENSE requires no additional information compared with other methods (except the model parameters) to be transferred between clients and the server;(2) DENSE does not require any auxiliary dataset for training;(3) DENSE considers model heterogeneity in FL, \ie different clients can have different model architectures.Experiments on a variety of real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method.For example, DENSE outperforms the best baseline method Fed-ADI by 5.08\% on CIFAR10 dataset.

paragraphs: One-shot federated learning aims to build a global model using a single communication round between clients and a central server. That saves communication, but existing methods can require public data, matching client architectures, or additional uploaded information. DENSE addresses these practical constraints while preserving the single-round setting.

The framework has two stages: data generation followed by model distillation. Generated data supports the process of transferring information from client models into the global model. Clients transfer model parameters without additional data or model information, and training requires no auxiliary dataset. The framework also accommodates clients whose models have different architectures.

These properties matter because they reduce the coordination and shared-resource requirements of combining separately trained models. Experiments on several real-world datasets favor DENSE over the compared methods. As a concrete example, the authors report a 5.08% improvement over Fed-ADI on CIFAR10. The results support the proposed generation-and-distillation pipeline as a practical approach to the constraints studied in one-shot federated learning.
summary.tldr: DENSE combines heterogeneous client models in one communication round using data generation and distillation without an auxiliary dataset.

title: DENSE: Data-Free One-Shot Federated Learning

abstract: Learning latent vector representations via embedding models has been shown promising in machine learning. However, most of the embedding models are still limited to a single type of observation data. We propose a Gaussian copula embedding model to learn latent vector representations of items in a heterogeneous data setting. The proposed model can effectively incorporate different types of observed data and, at the same time, yield robust embeddings. We demonstrate the proposed model can effectively learn in many different scenarios, outperforming competing models in modeling quality and task performance.

paragraphs: Embedding models represent items as latent vectors that can support modeling and prediction tasks. The paper addresses a restriction of many such models: they are designed around a single type of observed data. When information about an item comes in several forms, that restriction limits what the representation-learning method can incorporate.

The authors propose a Gaussian copula embedding model for this heterogeneous setting. Its central purpose is to learn item representations while incorporating different types of observations within the same model. The abstract reports that the resulting embeddings are robust, making the ability to combine observations part of a broader claim about representation quality.

The evaluation covers multiple scenarios and reports improvements over competing models in both modeling quality and task performance. These two findings concern different uses of the learned representations: describing the observed data and supporting a task built on those representations. Together, they support the proposed model as an effective approach to heterogeneous embedding problems in the settings studied.
summary.tldr: Gaussian copula embeddings combine heterogeneous observations into robust item representations and outperform competing models in the reported evaluations.

title: Gaussian Copula Embeddings

abstract: The error-backpropagation (backprop) algorithm remains the most common solution to the credit assignment problem in artificial neural networks. In neuroscience, it is unclear whether the brain could adopt a similar strategy to correctly modify its synapses. Recent models have attempted to bridge this gap while being consistent with a range of experimental observations. However, these models are either unable to effectively backpropagate error signals across multiple layers or require a multi-phase learning process, neither of which are reminiscent of learning in the brain. Here, we introduce a new model, Bursting Cortico-Cortical Networks (BurstCCN), which solves these issues by integrating known properties of cortical networks namely bursting activity, short-term plasticity (STP) and dendrite-targeting interneurons. These error signals are encoded at distal dendrites and induce burst-dependent plasticity as a result of excitatory-inhibitory top-down inputs. First, we demonstrate that our model can effectively backpropagate errors through multiple layers using a single-phase learning process. Next, we show both empirically and analytically that learning in our model approximates backprop-derived gradients. Finally, we demonstrate that our model is capable of learning complex image classification tasks (MNIST and CIFAR-10). Overall, our results suggest that cortical features across sub-cellular, cellular, microcircuit and systems levels jointly underlie single-phase efficient deep learning in the brain.

title: Single-phase deep learning in cortico-cortical networks

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a class of popular methods for expensive black-box optimization, and has been widely applied to many scenarios. However, BO suffers from the curse of dimensionality, and scaling it to high-dimensional problems is still a challenge. In this paper, we propose a variable selection method MCTS-VS based on Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS), to iteratively select and optimize a subset of variables. That is, MCTS-VS constructs a low-dimensional subspace via MCTS and optimizes in the subspace with any BO algorithm. We give a theoretical analysis of the general variable selection method to reveal how it can work. Experiments on high-dimensional synthetic functions and real-world problems (e.g., MuJoCo locomotion tasks) show that MCTS-VS equipped with a proper BO optimizer can achieve state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization is useful when evaluating a candidate solution is expensive and the objective behaves like a black box. Its difficulty grows when a solution has many adjustable variables. This paper tackles that high-dimensional search problem by repeatedly choosing a smaller set of variables to optimize.

MCTS-VS uses Monte Carlo tree search to construct a low-dimensional subspace through variable selection. A Bayesian optimizer then searches within that subspace, and the process iteratively selects and optimizes subsets. The framework can work with any Bayesian optimization algorithm, separating the choice of variables from the optimizer used to explore them.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis of general variable selection to explain how this strategy can work. Experiments include high-dimensional synthetic objectives and real-world problems such as MuJoCo locomotion tasks. They show that MCTS-VS can reach state-of-the-art performance when paired with a suitable Bayesian optimizer. The qualification matters: compatibility with many optimizers does not imply that every pairing achieves the same performance.
summary.tldr: MCTS-VS uses tree search to select smaller variable subsets, enabling effective high-dimensional Bayesian optimization with a suitable optimizer.

title: Monte Carlo Tree Search based Variable Selection for High Dimensional Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Kronecker regression is a highly-structured least squares problem $\min_{\mathbf{x}} \lVert \mathbf{K}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \rVert_{2}^2$, where the design matrix $\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{A}^{(1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathbf{A}^{(N)}$ is a Kronecker product of factor matrices. This regression problem arises in each step of the widely-used alternating least squares (ALS) algorithm for computing the Tucker decomposition of a tensor. We present the first subquadratic-time algorithm for solving Kronecker regression to a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation that avoids the exponential term $O(\varepsilon^{-N})$ in the running time. Our techniques combine leverage score sampling and iterative methods. By extending our approach to block-design matrices where one block is a Kronecker product, we also achieve subquadratic-time algorithms for (1) Kronecker ridge regression and (2) updating the factor matrix of a Tucker decomposition in ALS, which is not a pure Kronecker regression problem, thereby improving the running time of all steps of Tucker ALS. We demonstrate the speed and accuracy of this Kronecker regression algorithm on synthetic data and real-world image tensors.

paragraphs: Kronecker regression is a least-squares problem whose design matrix is built as a Kronecker product of smaller factor matrices. This structure appears repeatedly when alternating least squares computes a Tucker tensor decomposition. Faster regression routines can therefore reduce the cost of recurring steps in an important method for representing multidimensional data.

The authors present the first subquadratic-time algorithm for a multiplicative 1 + ε approximation that avoids a running-time term proportional to ε raised to minus the number of factors. The approach combines leverage-score sampling with iterative methods. Removing that particular exponential dependence addresses a computational obstacle as the number of factor matrices increases.

summary.tldr: A sampling-and-iteration algorithm accelerates approximate Kronecker regression and all Tucker ALS steps while avoiding an exponential accuracy-dependent runtime term.

title: Subquadratic Kronecker Regression with Applications to Tensor Decomposition

abstract: Unlabeled data examples awaiting annotations contain open-set noise inevitably. A few active learning studies have attempted to deal with this open-set noise for sample selection by filtering out the noisy examples. However, because focusing on the purity of examples in a query set leads to overlooking the informativeness of the examples, the best balancing of purity and informativeness remains an important question. In this paper, to solve this purity-informativeness dilemma in open-set active learning, we propose a novel Meta-Query-Net (MQ-Net) that adaptively finds the best balancing between the two factors. Specifically, by leveraging the multi-round property of active learning, we train MQ-Net using a query set without an additional validation set. Furthermore, a clear dominance relationship between unlabeled examples is effectively captured by MQ-Net through a novel skyline regularization. Extensive experiments on multiple open-set active learning scenarios demonstrate that the proposed MQ-Net achieves 20.14% improvement in terms of accuracy, compared with the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Active learning selects unlabeled examples to send for annotation. When the pool contains open-set noise, selection must account for both whether an example belongs to the relevant set and how informative it would be. Filtering aggressively for purity can overlook useful examples, creating a tension between clean selections and valuable learning opportunities.

Meta-Query-Net learns to balance purity and informativeness adaptively. It uses the repeated rounds of active learning to train from a query set, avoiding the need for an additional validation set. A skyline regularization term also helps it capture clear dominance relationships between unlabeled examples, incorporating those relationships into the selection process.

Experiments across multiple open-set active learning scenarios report a 20.14% accuracy improvement over state-of-the-art methods. The result supports learning the balance between the two selection criteria rather than focusing exclusively on filtering noise. The approach matters because annotation choices determine which information becomes available in later rounds, and the proposed method uses that multi-round structure to improve how those choices are made.
summary.tldr: Meta-Query-Net adaptively balances sample purity and informativeness in open-set active learning, reporting a 20.14% accuracy improvement over compared methods.

title: Meta-Query-Net: Resolving Purity-Informativeness Dilemma in Open-set Active Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of minimizing the number of matrix-vector queries needed for accurate trace estimation in the dynamic setting where our underlying matrix is changing slowly, such as during an optimization process. Specifically, for any $m$ matrices $\mathbf{A}_1,...,\mathbf{A}_m$ with consecutive differences bounded in Schatten-$1$ norm by $\alpha$, we provide a novel binary tree summation procedure that simultaneously estimates all $m$ traces up to $\epsilon$ error with $\delta$ failure probability with an optimal query complexity of $\widetilde{O}(m \alpha\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}/\epsilon + m\log(1/\delta))$, improving the dependence on both $\alpha$ and $\delta$ from Dharangutte and Musco (NeurIPS, 2021). Our procedure works without additional norm bounds on $\mathbf{A}_i$ and can be generalized to a bound for the $p$-th Schatten norm for $p \in [1,2]$, giving a complexity of $\widetilde{O}(m \alpha(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}/\epsilon)^p +m \log(1/\delta))$. By using novel reductions to communication complexity and information-theoretic analyses of Gaussian matrices, we provide matching lower bounds for static and dynamic trace estimation in all relevant parameters, including the failure probability. Our lower bounds (1) give the first tight bounds for Hutchinson's estimator in the matrix-vector product model with Frobenius norm error {\it even in the static setting}, and (2) are the first unconditional lower bounds for dynamic trace estimation, resolving open questions of prior work.

summary.tldr: A binary-tree procedure estimates traces of slowly changing matrices with near-matching optimal query bounds, supported by static and dynamic lower bounds.

title: Optimal Query Complexities for Dynamic Trace Estimation

abstract: Pre-trained language models (LMs) are shown to easily generate toxic language. In this work, we systematically explore domain-adaptive training to reduce the toxicity of language models. We conduct this study on three dimensions: training corpus, model size, and parameter efficiency. For the training corpus, we demonstrate that using self-generated datasets consistently outperforms the existing baselines across various model sizes on both automatic and human evaluations, even when it uses a 3 1 smaller training corpus. We then comprehensively study detoxifying LMs with parameter sizes ranging from 126M up to 530B (3× larger than GPT3), a scale that has never been studied before. We find that i) large LMs have similar toxicity levels as smaller ones given the same pre-training corpus, and ii) large LMs require more endeavor to unlearn the toxic content seen at pretraining. We also explore parameter-efficient training methods for detoxification. We demonstrate that adding and training adapter-only layers in LMs not only saves a lot of parameters but also achieves a better trade-off between toxicity and perplexity than whole model adaptation for large-scale models. Our code will be available at: https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM/.

paragraphs: This study investigates additional training aimed at reducing toxic language from pretrained language models. It examines three choices together: the adaptation corpus, the size of the model, and which parameters are updated. The models studied range from 126 million to 530 billion parameters, allowing the authors to examine detoxification across substantially different scales.

Using datasets generated by the models themselves consistently outperforms the existing baselines across model sizes in both automatic and human evaluations, including with a smaller training corpus. Together, the findings show that corpus construction and adaptation strategy matter alongside scale, and that larger models are not automatically easier to detoxify.
summary.tldr: Self-generated adaptation data and adapter-only training improve detoxification, while larger models require more effort to unlearn toxic content.

title: Exploring the Limits of Domain-Adaptive Training for Detoxifying Large-Scale Language Models

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) refers to the decentralized and privacy-preserving machine learning framework in which multiple clients collaborate (with the help of a central server) to train a global model without sharing their data. However, most existing FL methods only focus on maximizing the model's performance on the source clients' data (e.g., mobile users) without considering its generalization ability to unknown target data (e.g., a new user). In this paper, we incorporate the problem of Domain Generalization (DG) into Federated Learning to tackle the aforementioned issue. However, virtually all existing DG methods require a centralized setting where data is shared across the domains, which violates the principles of decentralized FL and hence not applicable. To this end, we propose a simple yet novel representation learning framework, namely FedSR, which enables domain generalization while still respecting the decentralized and privacy-preserving natures of this FL setting. Motivated by classical machine learning algorithms, we aim to learn a simple representation of the data for better generalization. In particular, we enforce an L2-norm regularizer on the representation and a conditional mutual information (between the representation and the data given the label) regularizer to encourage the model to only learn essential information (while ignoring spurious correlations such as the background). Furthermore, we provide theoretical connections between the above two objectives and representation alignment in domain generalization. Extensive experimental results suggest that our method significantly outperforms relevant baselines in this particular problem.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients train a shared model without pooling their data. Good performance on participating clients, however, does not necessarily mean the model will work well for a new client. FedSR addresses this domain-generalization problem while preserving the decentralized setting, where methods requiring shared data across domains cannot be applied directly.

The approach encourages the model to learn a simple representation containing information essential for prediction. It combines an L2 penalty on the representation with a conditional mutual-information penalty between the representation and the input, given the label.
