The authors connect these two objectives theoretically to representation alignment, a central idea in domain generalization. Their experiments suggest substantial improvements over relevant baselines for generalizing federated models to unknown target data. The significance is that generalization is addressed through the learned representation while respecting the data-sharing restrictions that define this federated setting.
summary.tldr: FedSR encourages simple, label-relevant representations to improve federated models’ generalization to unseen clients without sharing client data.

title: FedSR: A Simple and Effective Domain Generalization Method for Federated Learning

abstract: Generative models of observations under interventions have been a vibrant topic of interest across machine learning and the sciences in recent years. For example, in drug discovery, there is a need to model the effects of diverse interventions on cells in order to characterize unknown biological mechanisms of action. We propose the Sparse Additive Mechanism Shift Variational Autoencoder, SAMS-VAE, to combine compositionality, disentanglement, and interpretability for perturbation models. SAMS-VAE models the latent state of a perturbed sample as the sum of a local latent variable capturing sample-specific variation and sparse global variables of latent intervention effects. Crucially, SAMS-VAE sparsifies these global latent variables for individual perturbations to identify disentangled, perturbation-specific latent subspaces that are flexibly composable. We evaluate SAMS-VAE both quantitatively and qualitatively on a range of tasks using two popular single cell sequencing datasets.In order to measure perturbation-specific model-properties, we also introduce a framework for evaluation of perturbation models based on average treatment effects with links to posterior predictive checks. SAMS-VAE outperforms comparable models in terms of generalization across in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks, including a combinatorial reasoning task under resource paucity, and yields interpretable latent structures which correlate strongly to known biological mechanisms. Our results suggest SAMS-VAE is an interesting addition to the modeling toolkit for machine learning-driven scientific discovery.

paragraphs: SAMS-VAE models how interventions change cellular observations while seeking representations that are interpretable and composable. This is useful for studying perturbations whose biological mechanisms may be unknown. The model separates variation specific to an individual sample from shared effects associated with an intervention.

It represents a perturbed sample’s latent state as the sum of a local variable and global intervention-effect variables. Sparsity restricts each perturbation’s global effects to a subset of the latent representation. This is intended to identify distinct perturbation-specific subspaces that can be combined flexibly, linking the model’s internal organization to reasoning about multiple interventions.

The authors evaluate SAMS-VAE on two single-cell sequencing datasets and introduce an evaluation framework using average treatment effects with connections to posterior predictive checks. Its interpretable latent structures also correlate strongly with known biological mechanisms. These results support its use as a scientific modeling tool without equating those correlations with newly established mechanisms.
summary.tldr: SAMS-VAE separates sample variation from sparse intervention effects, improving evaluated cellular-perturbation predictions while learning interpretable, composable latent structures.

title: Modelling Cellular Perturbations with the Sparse Additive Mechanism Shift Variational Autoencoder

abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) has been a fundamental challenge in machine learning for decades. The primary family of SSL algorithms, known as pseudo-labeling, involves assigning pseudo-labels to confident unlabeled instances and incorporating them into the training set. Therefore, the selection criteria of confident instances are crucial to the success of SSL. Recently, there has been growing interest in the development of SSL methods that use dynamic or adaptive thresholds. Yet, these methods typically apply the same threshold to all samples, or use class-dependent thresholds for instances belonging to a certain class, while neglecting instance-level information. In this paper, we propose the study of instance-dependent thresholds, which has the highest degree of freedom compared with existing methods. Specifically, we devise a novel instance-dependent threshold function for all unlabeled instances by utilizing their instance-level ambiguity and the instance-dependent error rates of pseudo-labels, so instances that are more likely to have incorrect pseudo-labels will have higher thresholds. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our instance-dependent threshold function provides a bounded probabilistic guarantee for the correctness of the pseudo-labels it assigns.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled examples alongside labeled data. A common approach assigns predicted labels to unlabeled examples and trains on those predictions when confidence is high enough. Because an incorrect predicted label can enter the training set, the rule deciding which examples to accept is central to the method.

InstanT makes that acceptance threshold depend on each individual example. Existing adaptive approaches commonly share a threshold across all examples or across members of a class. The proposed function instead uses an example's ambiguity and its instance-dependent pseudo-label error rate. Examples more likely to receive an incorrect label must clear a higher confidence threshold.

The authors also establish a bounded probabilistic guarantee for the correctness of labels assigned through their threshold function. This provides a mathematical basis for connecting acceptance decisions to individual uncertainty. The contribution is a finer-grained way to select training examples: confidence requirements can vary within a class, reflecting differences between examples that a shared threshold would overlook.
summary.tldr: InstanT sets individual pseudo-label confidence thresholds using example ambiguity and error rates, with a bounded probabilistic correctness guarantee.

title: InstanT: Semi-supervised Learning with Instance-dependent Thresholds

abstract: Engineering design problems frequently require solving systems ofpartial differential equations with boundary conditions specified onobject geometries in the form of a triangular mesh. These boundarygeometries are provided by a designer and are problem dependent.The efficiency of the design process greatly benefits from fast turnaroundtimes when repeatedly solving PDEs on various geometries. However,most current work that uses machine learning to speed up the solutionprocess relies heavily on a fixed parameterization of the geometry, whichcannot be changed after training. This severely limits the possibility ofreusing a trained model across a variety of design problems.In this work, we propose a novel neural operator architecture which acceptsboundary geometry, in the form of triangular meshes, as input and produces anapproximate solution to a given PDE as output. Once trained, the model can beused to rapidly estimate the PDE solution over a new geometry, without the need forretraining or representation of the geometry to a pre-specified parameterization.

paragraphs: Engineering design often requires solving partial differential equations repeatedly as an object’s shape changes. Boundary conditions are specified on geometries that designers commonly supply as triangular meshes. Fast approximate solutions can shorten this repeated process, but many learned solvers depend on a fixed geometry parameterization established during training.

The paper proposes a neural operator that takes the boundary mesh itself as input and outputs an approximate solution to a given partial differential equation. This changes how geometry enters the model: the input can describe the object directly through its mesh, without first fitting it into a prescribed set of geometric parameters.

Once trained, the architecture can rapidly estimate solutions on new geometries without retraining or converting those geometries to a fixed parameterization. That capability matters for reusing a learned solver across design problems whose shapes may not fit the same restricted description. The stated contribution is flexibility in representing boundary geometry while retaining the rapid approximate prediction offered by a trained model.

title: Nonparametric Boundary Geometry in Physics Informed Deep Learning

abstract: Point cloud data collected in real-world applications are often incomplete. This is because they are observed from partial viewpoints, which capture only a specific perspective or angle, or due to occlusion and low resolution. Existing completion approaches rely on datasets of specific predefined objects to guide the completion of incomplete, and possibly noisy, point clouds. However, these approaches perform poorly with Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) objects, which are either absent from the dataset or poorly represented. In recent years, the field of text-guided image generation has made significant progress, leading to major breakthroughs in text guided shape generation. We describe an approach called SDS-Complete that uses a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model and leverages the text semantic of a given incomplete point cloud of an object, to obtain a complete surface representation. SDS-Complete can complete a variety of objects at test time optimization without the need for an expensive collection of 3D information. We evaluate SDS-Complete on incomplete scanned objects, captured by real-world depth sensors and LiDAR scanners, and demonstrate that is effective in handling objects which are typically absent from common datasets.

paragraphs: Real-world point clouds often show only part of an object because of limited viewpoints, occlusion, or low resolution. Completion methods trained on predefined object collections can struggle when the scanned object is absent from those collections or poorly represented. This paper explores a different source of guidance for filling in the missing surface.

SDS-Complete uses a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model together with textual semantic information about the incomplete object. It optimizes a complete surface representation at test time. The approach draws on an existing image-generation model without requiring an expensive collection of three-dimensional information for the completion task.

The authors evaluate the method on incomplete scans acquired using real-world depth sensors and LiDAR. They demonstrate effectiveness on objects typically missing from common datasets. The result supports transferring semantic knowledge from text-guided image generation into surface completion. Test-time optimization is central to this approach: completion is obtained by optimizing for the supplied object, rather than relying only on a predefined collection of familiar three-dimensional shapes.
summary.tldr: SDS-Complete uses text semantics and a pretrained image diffusion model to complete partial point clouds, including objects poorly covered by common datasets.

title: Point Cloud Completion with Pretrained Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

abstract: Adversarial contrastive learning (ACL) is a technique that enhances standard contrastive learning (SCL) by incorporating adversarial data to learn a robust representation that can withstand adversarial attacks and common corruptions without requiring costly annotations. To improve transferability, the existing work introduced the standard invariant regularization (SIR) to impose style-independence property to SCL, which can exempt the impact of nuisance style factors in the standard representation. However, it is unclear how the style-independence property benefits ACL-learned robust representations. In this paper, we leverage the technique of causal reasoning to interpret the ACL and propose adversarial invariant regularization (AIR) to enforce independence from style factors. We regulate the ACL using both SIR and AIR to output the robust representation. Theoretically, we show that AIR implicitly encourages the representational distance between different views of natural data and their adversarial variants to be independent of style factors. Empirically, our experimental results show that invariant regularization significantly improves the performance of state-of-the-art ACL methods in terms of both standard generalization and robustness on downstream tasks. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to apply causal reasoning to interpret ACL and develop AIR for enhancing ACL-learned robust representations. Our source code is at https://github.com/GodXuxilie/Enhancing_ACL_via_AIR.

paragraphs: Adversarial contrastive learning uses adversarial data to learn representations that resist attacks and common corruptions without expensive annotations. A related technique, standard invariant regularization, encourages ordinary contrastive representations to ignore nuisance style factors. This paper investigates how independence from style can also help representations learned through adversarial contrastive training.

The authors use causal reasoning to interpret the learning process and introduce adversarial invariant regularization, or AIR. Their method combines AIR with standard invariant regularization. The theoretical result concerns distances in representation space: AIR implicitly encourages the distances between views of natural examples and their adversarial variants to be independent of style factors.

This matters because style-related variation can affect the relationships that contrastive learning uses to organize representations. The proposed regularization targets that dependence while retaining adversarial training. In experiments, adding invariant regularization significantly improves leading adversarial contrastive methods on both ordinary generalization and robustness in downstream tasks. The theoretical claim is an encouragement toward style-independent distances, while the reported performance gains are empirical.
summary.tldr: Adversarial invariant regularization encourages style-independent representation distances and empirically improves downstream generalization and robustness.

title: Enhancing Adversarial Contrastive Learning via Adversarial Invariant Regularization

abstract: Tensor decomposition is an important tool for multiway data analysis. In practice, the data is often sparse yet associated with rich temporal information. Existing methods, however, often under-use the time information and ignore the structural knowledge within the sparsely observed tensor entries. To overcome these limitations and to better capture the underlying temporal structure, we propose Dynamic EMbedIngs fOr dynamic Tensor dEcomposition (DEMOTE). We develop a neural diffusion-reaction process to estimate dynamic embeddings for the entities in each tensor mode. Specifically, based on the observed tensor entries, we build a multi-partite graph to encode the correlation between the entities. We construct a graph diffusion process to co-evolve the embedding trajectories of the correlated entities and use a neural network to construct a reaction process for each individual entity. In this way, our model can capture both the commonalities and personalities during the evolution of the embeddings for different entities. We then use a neural network to model the entry value as a nonlinear function of the embedding trajectories. For model estimation, we combine ODE solvers to develop a stochastic mini-batch learning algorithm. We propose a stratified sampling method to balance the cost of processing each mini-batch so as to improve the overall efficiency. We show the advantage of our approach in both simulation studies and real-world applications. The code is available at https://github.com/wzhut/Dynamic-Tensor-Decomposition-via-Neural-Diffusion-Reaction-Processes.

paragraphs: Tensor decomposition analyzes data organized along several dimensions, but sparse observations can still contain valuable timing and relationship information. The paper proposes DEMOTE to use both sources of structure. Instead of assigning each entity an unchanging representation, it learns embedding trajectories that evolve over time.

DEMOTE builds a multipartite graph from observed tensor entries to encode correlations between entities. A graph diffusion process couples the trajectories of related entities, while a neural reaction process models each entity's individual evolution. This division lets the model represent shared patterns and entity-specific behavior together. Another neural network predicts tensor-entry values as nonlinear functions of those evolving representations.

For learning, the authors combine ordinary differential equation solvers with stochastic minibatch optimization. They also introduce stratified sampling to balance the processing cost of minibatches and improve overall efficiency. Simulation studies and real-world applications show advantages for the approach. The contribution connects temporal modeling with the structure already present in sparse observations, rather than treating those two sources of information separately.
summary.tldr: DEMOTE models time-varying tensor data with coupled graph diffusion and entity-specific neural reactions.

title: Dynamic Tensor Decomposition via Neural Diffusion-Reaction Processes

abstract: Multi-agent collaborative perception has recently received widespread attention as an emerging application in driving scenarios. Despite the advancements in previous efforts, challenges remain due to various noises in the perception procedure, including communication redundancy, transmission delay, and collaboration heterogeneity. To tackle these issues, we propose \textit{How2comm}, a collaborative perception framework that seeks a trade-off between perception performance and communication bandwidth. Our novelties lie in three aspects. First, we devise a mutual information-aware communication mechanism to maximally sustain the informative features shared by collaborators. The spatial-channel filtering is adopted to perform effective feature sparsification for efficient communication. Second, we present a flow-guided delay compensation strategy to predict future characteristics from collaborators and eliminate feature misalignment due to temporal asynchrony. Ultimately, a pragmatic collaboration transformer is introduced to integrate holistic spatial semantics and temporal context clues among agents. Our framework is thoroughly evaluated on several LiDAR-based collaborative detection datasets in real-world and simulated scenarios. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of How2comm and the effectiveness of all its vital components. The code will be released at https://github.com/ydk122024/How2comm.

paragraphs: How2comm addresses collaborative perception in driving, where multiple agents share information to improve what they can detect. Sharing creates its own difficulties: messages can contain redundant features, arrive late, and come from heterogeneous collaborators. The framework seeks a useful trade-off between perception quality and communication bandwidth.

Its communication mechanism uses mutual information to preserve informative shared features, with filtering across spatial locations and channels to make those features sparse. A flow-guided compensation strategy predicts collaborators' future features to address misalignment caused by asynchronous information. A collaboration transformer then combines spatial semantics and temporal context across agents.

These components address connected parts of the collaboration process: deciding what to send, compensating for when it arrives, and integrating it with other observations. Evaluations on several LiDAR-based collaborative detection datasets include real-world and simulated scenarios. The reported experiments show superior performance and support the effectiveness of the framework's major components, providing empirical evidence for treating communication and perception together.
summary.tldr: How2comm combines selective feature sharing, delay compensation, and joint spatial-temporal processing for collaborative perception.

title: How2comm: Communication-Efficient and Collaboration-Pragmatic Multi-Agent Perception

abstract: Backdoor attacks are serious security threats to machine learning models where an adversary can inject poisoned samples into the training set, causing a backdoored model which predicts poisoned samples with particular triggers to particular target classes, while behaving normally on benign samples. In this paper, we explore the task of purifying a backdoored model using a small clean dataset. By establishing the connection between backdoor risk and adversarial risk, we derive a novel upper bound for backdoor risk, which mainly captures the risk on the shared adversarial examples (SAEs) between the backdoored model and the purified model. This upper bound further suggests a novel bi-level optimization problem for mitigating backdoor using adversarial training techniques. To solve it, we propose Shared Adversarial Unlearning (SAU). Specifically, SAU first generates SAEs, and then, unlearns the generated SAEs such that they are either correctly classified by the purified model and/or differently classified by the two models, such that the backdoor effect in the backdoored model will be mitigated in the purified model. Experiments on various benchmark datasets and network architectures show that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance for backdoor defense. The code is available at https://github.com/SCLBD/BackdoorBench (PyTorch) and https://github.com/shawkui/MindTrojan (MindSpore).

paragraphs: A backdoored model can behave normally on benign inputs while sending inputs containing an attacker’s trigger to a chosen class. This paper studies how to purify such a model using a small clean dataset. Its starting point is a theoretical connection between backdoor risk and adversarial risk, intended to identify which adversarial failures are most relevant to purification.

The authors derive an upper bound on backdoor risk that mainly captures risk on adversarial examples shared by the original backdoored model and the purified model. This leads to a bi-level optimization problem and the Shared Adversarial Unlearning method. SAU generates these shared examples, then updates the purified model so that it classifies them correctly, disagrees with the original model, or both.

The purpose of this update is to weaken the shared adversarial behavior associated with the backdoor effect. Experiments across benchmark datasets and network architectures report state-of-the-art backdoor-defense performance. The result links a risk-bound argument to a practical purification procedure, using shared vulnerabilities between the two models to guide which behaviors should be unlearned.
summary.tldr: SAU mitigates backdoors by generating and unlearning adversarial examples shared between a compromised model and its purified version.

title: Shared Adversarial Unlearning: Backdoor Mitigation by Unlearning Shared Adversarial Examples

abstract: Neural rendering is fuelling a unification of learning, 3D geometry and video understanding that has been waiting for more than two decades. Progress, however, is still hampered by a lack of suitable datasets and benchmarks. To address this gap, we introduce EPIC Fields, an augmentation of EPIC-KITCHENS with 3D camera information. Like other datasets for neural rendering, EPIC Fields removes the complex and expensive step of reconstructing cameras using photogrammetry, and allows researchers to focus on modelling problems. We illustrate the challenge of photogrammetry in egocentric videos of dynamic actions and propose innovations to address them. Compared to other neural rendering datasets, EPIC Fields is better tailored to video understanding because it is paired with labelled action segments and the recent VISOR segment annotations. To further motivate the community, we also evaluate two benchmark tasks in neural rendering and segmenting dynamic objects, with strong baselines that showcase what is not possible today. We also highlight the advantage of geometry in semi-supervised video object segmentations on the VISOR annotations. EPIC Fields reconstructs 96\% of videos in EPIC-KITCHENS, registering 19M frames in 99 hours recorded in 45 kitchens, and is available from: http://epic-kitchens.github.io/epic-fields

paragraphs: EPIC Fields adds 3D camera information to EPIC-KITCHENS so researchers can study geometry and video understanding together. Recovering cameras from video is a difficult and expensive preparatory step, especially in first-person recordings containing dynamic actions. The authors introduce innovations for this reconstruction problem and provide the resulting camera information as part of the dataset.

The resource combines geometry with existing action labels and VISOR segmentation annotations. This pairing makes it useful for questions that involve both how a scene is arranged and what happens within it. The reconstruction covers 96% of EPIC-KITCHENS videos, registering 19 million frames across 99 hours of recordings from 45 kitchens.

The paper also evaluates benchmark tasks in neural rendering and dynamic-object segmentation. Strong baselines expose remaining challenges, giving researchers concrete problems to work on with the new resource. Separately, the authors demonstrate an advantage from geometry in semi-supervised video-object segmentation using VISOR annotations. The contribution therefore includes both reusable reconstruction data and evidence of its relevance to video analysis.
summary.tldr: EPIC Fields enriches EPIC-KITCHENS with reconstructed 3D camera information and benchmarks connecting neural rendering with video understanding.

title: EPIC Fields: Marrying 3D Geometry and Video Understanding

abstract: Real-time novel-view image synthesis on mobile devices is prohibitive due to the limited computational power and storage. Using volumetric rendering methods, such as NeRF and its derivatives, on mobile devices is not suitable due to the high computational cost of volumetric rendering. On the other hand, recent advances in neural light field representations have shown promising real-time view synthesis results on mobile devices. Neural light field methods learn a direct mapping from a ray representation to the pixel color. The current choice of ray representation is either stratified ray sampling or Plücker coordinates, overlooking the classic light slab (two-plane) representation, the preferred representation to interpolate between light field views. In this work, we find that using the light slab representation is an efficient representation for learning a neural light field. More importantly, it is a lower-dimensional ray representation enabling us to learn the 4D ray space using feature grids which are significantly faster to train and render. Although mostly designed for frontal views, we show that the light-slab representation can be further extended to non-frontal scenes using a divide-and-conquer strategy. Our method provides better rendering quality than prior light field methods and a significantly better trade-off between rendering quality and speed than prior light field methods.

The contribution ties a classical representation to an efficient learned rendering approach suited to mobile constraints.
summary.tldr: LightSpeed combines a two-plane ray representation with feature grids to improve neural-light-field rendering quality and speed.

title: LightSpeed: Light and Fast Neural Light Fields on Mobile Devices

abstract: This paper investigates an under-explored but important problem: given a collection of pre-trained neural networks, predicting their performance on each multi-modal task without fine-tuning them, such as image recognition, referring, captioning, visual question answering, and text question answering.A brute-force approach is to finetune all models on all target datasets, bringing high computational costs. Although recent-advanced approaches employed lightweight metrics to measure models’ transferability, they often depend heavily on the prior knowledge of a single task, making them inapplicable in a multi-modal multi-task scenario. To tackle this issue, we propose an efficient multi-task model selector (EMMS), which employs large-scale foundation models to transform diverse label formats such as categories, texts, and bounding boxes of different downstream tasks into a unified noisy label embedding. EMMS can estimate a model’s transferability through a simple weighted linear regression, which can be efficiently solved by an alternating minimization algorithm with a convergence guarantee. Extensive experiments on 5 downstream tasks with 24 datasets show that EMMS is fast, effective, and generic enough to assess the transferability of pre-trained models, making it the first model selection method in the multi-task scenario. For instance, compared with the state- of-the-art method LogME enhanced by our label embeddings, EMMS achieves 9.0%, 26.3%, 20.1%, 54.8%, 12.2% performance gain on image recognition, referring, captioning, visual question answering, and text question answering, while bringing 5.13×, 6.29×, 3.59×, 6.19×, and 5.66× speedup in wall-clock time, respectively. The code is available at https://github.com/OpenGVLab/Multitask-Model-Selector.

paragraphs: Choosing among pretrained models can be expensive if every candidate must be fine-tuned on every target dataset. This paper asks whether their suitability can instead be estimated across varied multimodal tasks, including recognition, captioning, referring, and question answering. Existing lightweight transferability measures often depend on task-specific knowledge, making that broader comparison difficult.

EMMS uses foundation models to convert different label formats, including categories, text, and bounding boxes, into a common noisy embedding representation. It then estimates a candidate model’s transferability with weighted linear regression. An alternating minimization algorithm solves this regression efficiently, with a convergence guarantee. The shared representation lets one selection framework work across otherwise incompatible label formats.

Experiments cover five downstream tasks and 24 datasets. Against LogME augmented with the same label embeddings, EMMS reports performance gains ranging from 9.0% to 54.8% across the tasks, alongside wall-clock speedups from 3.59 to 6.29 times. summary.tldr: EMMS uses foundation-model label embeddings and weighted regression to efficiently estimate pretrained models’ transferability across multimodal tasks.

title: Foundation Model is Efficient Multimodal Multitask Model Selector

abstract: A popular perspective in Reinforcement learning (RL) casts the problem as probabilistic inference on a graphical model of the Markov decision process (MDP). The core object of study is the probability of each state-action pair being visited under the optimal policy. Previous approaches to approximate this quantity can be arbitrarily poor, leading to algorithms that do not implement genuine statistical inference and consequently do not perform well in challenging problems. In this work, we undertake a rigorous Bayesian treatment of the posterior probability of state-action optimality and clarify how it flows through the MDP. We first reveal that this quantity can indeed be used to generate a policy that explores efficiently, as measured by regret. Unfortunately, computing it is intractable, so we derive a new variational Bayesian approximation yielding a tractable convex optimization problem and establish that the resulting policy also explores efficiently. We call our approach VAPOR and show that it has strong connections to Thompson sampling, K-learning, and maximum entropy exploration. We conclude with some experiments demonstrating the performance advantage of a deep RL version of VAPOR.

paragraphs: One view of reinforcement learning treats decision-making as probabilistic inference over a model of the environment. A central quantity is the probability that an optimal policy visits a particular state-action pair. This paper argues that earlier approximations to this quantity can be arbitrarily poor and develops a rigorous Bayesian treatment of state-action optimality.

The authors explain how the posterior probability propagates through the Markov decision process and show that it can generate an exploration policy with efficient regret behavior. Exact computation is intractable, so they introduce a variational Bayesian approximation. This approximation leads to a tractable convex optimization problem while retaining an efficient-exploration result for the resulting policy.

The approach, VAPOR, has strong connections to Thompson sampling, K-learning, and maximum-entropy exploration. Experiments with a deep reinforcement-learning version demonstrate a performance advantage. The contribution links a carefully defined Bayesian target to a practical approximation, providing theoretical support for exploration as well as empirical evidence for a neural implementation.
summary.tldr: VAPOR derives a tractable Bayesian approximation to state-action optimality with efficient-exploration guarantees and encouraging deep-RL results.

title: Probabilistic Inference in Reinforcement Learning Done Right

abstract: We study private and robust multi-armed bandits (MABs), where the agent receives Huber's contaminated heavy-tailed rewards and meanwhile needs to ensure differential privacy. We consider both the finite $k$-th raw moment and the finite $k$-th central moment settings for heavy-tailed rewards distributions with $k\ge 2$. We first present its minimax lower bound, characterizing the information-theoretic limit of regret with respect to privacy budget, contamination level, and heavy-tailedness. Then, we propose a meta-algorithm that builds on a private and robust mean estimation sub-routine \texttt{PRM} that essentially relies on reward truncation and the Laplace mechanism. For the above two different heavy-tailed settings, we give corresponding schemes of \texttt{PRM}, which enable us to achieve nearly-optimal regrets. Moreover, our two proposed truncation-based or histogram-based \texttt{PRM} schemes achieve the optimal trade-off between estimation accuracy, privacy and robustness. Finally, we support our theoretical results and show the effectiveness of our algorithms with experimental studies.
originalAbstract: We study private and robust multi-armed bandits (MABs), where the agent receives Huber's contaminated heavy-tailed rewards and meanwhile needs to ensure differential privacy. We consider both the finite $k$-th raw moment and the finite $k$-th central moment settings for heavy-tailed rewards distributions with $k\ge 2$. We first present its minimax lower bound, characterizing the information-theoretic limit of regret with respect to privacy budget, contamination level, and heavy-tailedness. Then, we propose a meta-algorithm that builds on a private and robust mean estimation sub-routine \texttt{PRM} that essentially relies on reward truncation and the Laplace mechanism. For the above two different heavy-tailed settings, we give corresponding schemes of \texttt{PRM}, which enable us to achieve nearly-optimal regrets. Moreover, our two proposed truncation-based or histogram-based \texttt{PRM} schemes achieve the optimal trade-off between estimation accuracy, privacy and robustness. Finally, we support our theoretical results and show the effectiveness of our algorithms with experimental studies.

paragraphs: A bandit learner repeatedly chooses among options while learning their rewards. This paper studies a difficult combination: rewards can be heavy-tailed, some observations follow Huber's contamination model, and the learner must preserve differential privacy. The analysis covers distributions with a finite kth raw moment or a finite kth central moment, for k at least two.

The authors first establish a minimax lower bound on regret, describing unavoidable losses as privacy requirements, contamination, and heavy tails vary. They then build a general algorithm around private, robust mean estimation. Its estimation routines use reward truncation and the Laplace mechanism, with separate constructions for the two moment settings.

The resulting bandit algorithms achieve nearly optimal regret. The proposed truncation-based and histogram-based mean estimators also attain optimal trade-offs among accuracy, privacy, and robustness. Experimental studies support the theoretical findings. The contribution links the fundamental difficulty of private, contaminated decision-making to concrete estimation procedures that approach those limits under the stated moment assumptions.
summary.tldr: Private, robust reward estimators enable nearly optimal bandit regret under contamination and heavy-tailed rewards.

title: On Private and Robust Bandits

abstract: Contrastive learning is quickly becoming an essential tool in neuroscience for extracting robust and meaningful representations of neural activity. Despite numerous applications to neuronal population data, there has been little exploration of how these methods can be adapted to key primary data analysis tasks such as spike sorting or cell-type classification. In this work, we propose a novel contrastive learning framework, CEED (Contrastive Embeddings for Extracellular Data), for high-density extracellular recordings. We demonstrate that through careful design of the network architecture and data augmentations, it is possible to generically extract representations that far outperform current specialized approaches. We validate our method across multiple high-density extracellular recordings. All code used to run CEED can be found at https://github.com/ankitvishnu23/CEED.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning has become useful for extracting meaningful representations of neural activity, but its application to primary extracellular-data analysis has been less explored. The paper focuses on this earlier stage of analysis, including tasks such as spike sorting and cell-type classification, using high-density recordings of activity outside cells.

The authors introduce Contrastive Embeddings for Extracellular Data, or CEED. Their approach emphasizes careful choices of network architecture and data augmentations to learn useful representations. These design decisions adapt the contrastive-learning framework to the characteristics of extracellular recordings, with the aim of extracting broadly useful features for analysis.

Validation across multiple high-density recordings shows that the learned representations substantially outperform the specialized approaches used in the comparisons. The result supports the possibility of learning general representations that serve these primary analysis tasks effectively. The paper's contribution is both the CEED framework and empirical evidence that adapting contrastive learning to this data type can offer advantages over the evaluated task-specific methods.
summary.tldr: CEED adapts contrastive learning to high-density extracellular recordings and learns representations that substantially outperform compared specialized approaches.

title: Towards robust and generalizable representations of extracellular data using contrastive learning

abstract: The kinematics of human movements and locomotion are closely linked to the activation and contractions of muscles. To investigate this, we present a multimodal dataset with benchmarks collected using a novel pair of Intelligent Knee Sleeves (Texavie MarsWear Knee Sleeves) for human pose estimation. Our system utilizes synchronized datasets that comprise time-series data from the Knee Sleeves and the corresponding ground truth labels from visualized motion capture camera system. We employ these to generate 3D human models solely based on the wearable data of individuals performing different activities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this camera-free system and machine learning algorithms in the assessment of various movements and exercises, including extension to unseen exercises and individuals. The results show an average error of 7.21 degrees across all eight lower body joints when compared to the ground truth, indicating the effectiveness and reliability of the Knee Sleeve system for the prediction of different lower body joints beyond knees. The results enable human pose estimation in a seamless manner without being limited by visual occlusion or the field of view of cameras. Our results show the potential of multimodal wearable sensing in a variety of applications from home fitness to sports, healthcare, and physical rehabilitation focusing on pose and movement estimation.

The system connects wearable signals to human motion by collecting sleeve time-series data alongside synchronised motion-capture measurements. Those camera measurements provide reference labels for learning and evaluating the relationship between the wearable data and body pose.

The trained system generates three-dimensional human models using wearable data alone. Cameras therefore supply ground truth during data collection, while movement estimation itself can operate without them. The study covers different activities and reports extension to exercises and individuals not previously seen. It also examines joints beyond the knees, showing that the sensing arrangement supports a broader lower-body estimate.

The reported average error is 7.21 degrees across eight lower-body joints relative to the reference measurements. This supports the system's effectiveness in the evaluated movement settings. Because estimation relies on wearables, it avoids restrictions from camera occlusion and field of view. The authors identify potential uses in fitness, sport, healthcare, and rehabilitation.
summary.tldr: Smart textile knee sleeves estimate 3D lower-body motion without cameras at prediction time, reporting a 7.21-degree average error across eight joints.

title: Intelligent Knee Sleeves: A Real-time Multimodal Dataset for 3D Lower Body Motion Estimation Using Smart Textile

abstract: Forming accurate memory of sequential stimuli is a fundamental function of biological agents. However, the computational mechanism underlying sequential memory in the brain remains unclear. Inspired by neuroscience theories and recent successes in applying predictive coding (PC) to \emph{static} memory tasks, in this work we propose a novel PC-based model for \emph{sequential} memory, called \emph{temporal predictive coding} (tPC). We show that our tPC models can memorize and retrieve sequential inputs accurately with a biologically plausible neural implementation. Importantly, our analytical study reveals that tPC can be viewed as a classical Asymmetric Hopfield Network (AHN) with an implicit statistical whitening process, which leads to more stable performance in sequential memory tasks of structured inputs. Moreover, we find that tPC exhibits properties consistent with behavioral observations and theories in neuroscience, thereby strengthening its biological relevance. Our work establishes a possible computational mechanism underlying sequential memory in the brain that can also be theoretically interpreted using existing memory model frameworks.

paragraphs: Remembering a sequence requires preserving relationships across successive inputs. This paper proposes temporal predictive coding, or tPC, as a computational model of that ability. It extends predictive-coding ideas previously applied to static memory and presents a biologically plausible neural implementation that can accurately memorize and retrieve sequential inputs.

The analysis connects tPC to a classical Asymmetric Hopfield Network with an implicit statistical whitening process. Whitening adjusts the statistical structure of the inputs, and this implicit operation leads to more stable sequential-memory performance for structured inputs. The connection explains the proposed model through an existing memory framework while identifying a feature that changes its behavior.

The authors also find that tPC exhibits properties consistent with behavioral observations and neuroscience theories. These results strengthen its biological relevance alongside the analytical account of memory performance. The paper presents tPC as a possible computational mechanism for sequential memory in the brain, with support from accurate retrieval, theoretical interpretation, and alignment with observed behavior.
summary.tldr: Temporal predictive coding models sequential memory through a biologically plausible mechanism linked to Hopfield networks with implicit statistical whitening.

title: Sequential Memory with Temporal Predictive Coding

abstract: We propose a novel algorithm for data augmentation in nonlinear over-parametrized regression. Our data augmentation algorithm borrows from the literature on causality. Contrary to the current state-of-the-art solutions that rely on modifications of Mixup algorithm, we extend the recently proposed distributionally robust Anchor regression (AR) method for data augmentation. Our Anchor Data Augmentation (ADA) uses several replicas of the modified samples in AR to provide more training examples, leading to more robust regression predictions. We apply ADA to linear and nonlinear regression problems using neural networks. ADA is competitive with state-of-the-art C-Mixup solutions.

Our Anchor Data Augmentation (ADA) uses several replicas of the modified samples in AR to provide more training examples, leading to more robust regression predictions. We apply ADA to linear and nonlinear regression problems using neural networks. ADA is competitive with state-of-the-art C-Mixup solutions.

paragraphs: Anchor Data Augmentation addresses regression, where a model predicts numerical values, with particular attention to nonlinear models that have many parameters. The paper asks how to create additional training examples that support more robust predictions. Its starting point is Anchor regression, a distributionally robust method connected to the causality literature.

The proposed algorithm turns the sample modifications used in Anchor regression into a data augmentation procedure. It uses several replicas of modified samples to expand the training set. This gives the robustness-oriented construction a second role: it becomes a way to supply additional examples for training regression models, including neural networks.

The authors apply the method to both linear and nonlinear regression problems and report performance competitive with leading C-Mixup approaches. That comparison supports Anchor Data Augmentation as another viable approach to regression augmentation, without establishing that it always performs better. Its central contribution is the connection between a distributionally robust regression method and the practical task of generating more training data.
summary.tldr: Anchor Data Augmentation adapts a distributionally robust regression method to generate training examples and achieves performance competitive with C-Mixup.

title: Anchor Data Augmentation

abstract: The interest in leveraging physics-based inductive bias in deep learning has resulted in recent development of _hybrid deep generative models (hybrid-DGMs)_ that integrates known physics-based mathematical expressions in neural generative models. To identify these hybrid-DGMs requires inferring parameters of the physics-based component along with their neural component. The identifiability of these hybrid-DGMs, however, has not yet been theoretically probed or established. How does the existing theory of the un-identifiability of general DGMs apply to hybrid-DGMs? What may be an effective approach to consutrct a hybrid-DGM with theoretically-proven identifiability? This paper provides the first theoretical probe into the identifiability of hybrid-DGMs, and present meta-learning as a novel solution to construct identifiable hybrid-DGMs. On synthetic and real-data benchmarks, we provide strong empirical evidence for the un-identifiability of existing hybrid-DGMs using unconditional priors, and strong identifiability results of the presented meta-formulations of hybrid-DGMs.

paragraphs: Hybrid deep generative models combine known physics-based expressions with learned neural components. Fitting such a model involves inferring both sets of parameters. The paper asks whether those components are identifiable: whether the available observations distinguish the underlying model components sufficiently to recover them, rather than supporting ambiguous explanations.

Incorporating physics does not by itself settle that question. The authors investigate how existing non-identifiability theory for general deep generative models applies to hybrid models, providing a theoretical examination of the hybrid setting. They present meta-learning as a way to construct hybrid formulations with theoretically established identifiability.

Experiments on synthetic and real-data benchmarks provide strong evidence of non-identifiability in existing hybrid models that use unconditional priors. The proposed meta-learning formulations show strong identifiability results on those benchmarks. The contribution matters because the physics parameters are part of what these models seek to infer: the work examines whether the combined model can distinguish its explanations, and offers a construction intended to make that inference better founded.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes ambiguity in physics–neural generative models and introduces meta-learning formulations with theoretically established identifiability.

title: On the Identifiability of Hybrid Deep Generative Models: Meta-Learning as a Solution

abstract: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a prominent machine learning paradigm in edge computing environments, enabling edge devices to collaboratively optimize a global model without sharing their private data. However, existing FL frameworks suffer from efficacy deterioration due to the system heterogeneity inherent in edge computing, especially in the presence of domain shifts across local data. In this paper, we propose a heterogeneous FL framework DapperFL, to enhance model performance across multiple domains. In DapperFL, we introduce a dedicated Model Fusion Pruning (MFP) module to produce personalized compact local models for clients to address the system heterogeneity challenges. The MFP module prunes local models with fused knowledge obtained from both local and remaining domains, ensuring robustness to domain shifts. Additionally, we design a Domain Adaptive Regularization (DAR) module to further improve the overall performance of DapperFL. The DAR module employs regularization generated by the pruned model, aiming to learn robust representations across domains. Furthermore, we introduce a specific aggregation algorithm for aggregating heterogeneous local models with tailored architectures and weights. We implement DapperFL on a real-world FL platform with heterogeneous clients. Experimental results on benchmark datasets with multiple domains demonstrate that DapperFL outperforms several state-of-the-art FL frameworks by up to 2.28%, while significantly achieving model volume reductions ranging from 20% to 80%. Our code is available at: https://github.com/jyzgh/DapperFL.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets devices train a shared model while keeping their data local. Edge devices nevertheless differ in their resources, and their data can come from different domains. These differences make it difficult for one training framework to serve all clients effectively. DapperFL addresses device heterogeneity and differences between local data domains together.

Its Model Fusion Pruning module produces compact models tailored to individual clients. Before pruning, it combines knowledge from the client's own domain and other domains, helping the resulting model handle domain shifts. A Domain Adaptive Regularization module then uses guidance generated by the pruned model to encourage representations that work across domains.

The framework also includes an aggregation procedure for combining local models with different architectures and weights. The authors implement it on a real federated learning platform with heterogeneous clients. Across multidomain benchmark datasets, they report improvements of up to 2.28% over several leading frameworks and model size reductions of 20% to 80%, supporting the usefulness of jointly adapting model size and domain knowledge.
summary.tldr: DapperFL combines domain-aware pruning, regularization, and aggregation to train smaller personalized models across heterogeneous devices.

title: DapperFL: Domain Adaptive Federated Learning with Model Fusion Pruning for Edge Devices

abstract: We introduce Lifelong ICL, a problem setting that challenges long-context language models (LMs) to learn a sequence of language tasks through in-context learning (ICL). We further introduce Task Haystack, an evaluation suite dedicated to assessing and diagnosing how long-context LMs utilizes contexts in Lifelong ICL. When given a task instruction and test inputs, long-context LMs are expectedto leverage the relevant demonstrations in the Lifelong ICL prompt, avoid distraction and interference from other tasks, and achieve test accuracies that are not significantly worse than those of the Single-task ICL baseline.Task Haystack draws inspiration from the widely-adopted “needle-in-a-haystack” (NIAH) evaluation, but presents distinct new challenges. It requires models (1) to utilize the contexts at a deeper level, rather than resorting to simple copying and pasting; (2) to navigate through long streams of evolving topics and tasks, proxying the complexities and dynamism of contexts in real-world scenarios. Additionally, Task Haystack inherits the controllability of NIAH, providing model developers with tools and visualizations to identify model vulnerabilities effectively.We benchmark 14 long-context LMs using Task Haystack, finding that frontier models like GPT-4o still struggle with the setting, failing on 15% of cases on average. Most open-weight models further lack behind by a large margin, with failure rates reaching up to 61%. In our controlled analysis, we identify factors such as distraction and recency bias as contributors to these failure cases. Further, performance declines when task instructions are paraphrased at test time or when ICL demonstrations are repeated excessively, raising concerns about the robustness, instruction understanding, and true context utilization of long-context LMs. We release our code and data to encourage future research that investigates and addresses these limitations.

paragraphs: A long context window is useful only if a model can apply the relevant information amid competing material. Lifelong ICL tests this by presenting a sequence of language tasks through demonstrations. At evaluation time, the model must use the examples relevant to the requested task without suffering substantial interference from the others.

Task Haystack evaluates this ability against a single-task in-context-learning baseline. Inspired by needle-in-a-haystack tests, it requires deeper use of demonstrations and navigation through changing tasks. Its controlled setup and diagnostic visualizations help identify where a long-context model's performance breaks down.

Across 14 models, GPT-4o fails on an average of 15% of cases, while failure rates for open-weight models reach 61%. Controlled analyses implicate distraction and recency bias. Performance also declines when instructions are paraphrased or demonstrations are repeated excessively. These findings expose weaknesses in instruction understanding and context use, showing why retrieving information from a long prompt is only part of the challenge.
summary.tldr: Task Haystack reveals that long-context models struggle to apply relevant demonstrations reliably across sequences of tasks.

title: Stress-Testing Long-Context Language Models with Lifelong ICL and Task Haystack

abstract: Deep Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) relies on neural networks with numerous parameters in multi-agent scenarios, often incurring substantial computational overhead. Consequently, there is an urgent need to expedite training and enable model compression in MARL. This paper proposes the utilization of dynamic sparse training (DST), a technique proven effective in deep supervised learning tasks, to alleviate the computational burdens in MARL training. However, a direct adoption of DST fails to yield satisfactory MARL agents, leading to breakdowns in value learning within deep sparse value-based MARL models. Motivated by this challenge, we introduce an innovative Multi-Agent Sparse Training (MAST) framework aimed at simultaneously enhancing the reliability of learning targets and the rationality of sample distribution to improve value learning in sparse models. Specifically, MAST incorporates the Soft Mellowmax Operator with a hybrid TD-($\lambda$) schema to establish dependable learning targets. Additionally, it employs a dual replay buffer mechanism to enhance the distribution of training samples. Building upon these aspects, MAST utilizes gradient-based topology evolution to exclusively train multiple MARL agents using sparse networks. Our comprehensive experimental investigation across various value-based MARL algorithms on multiple benchmarks demonstrates, for the first time, significant reductions in redundancy of up to $20\times$ in Floating Point Operations (FLOPs) for both training and inference, with less than 3% performance degradation.

paragraphs: Large neural networks make multi-agent reinforcement learning computationally expensive. Dynamic sparse training offers a way to reduce that burden, but directly transferring it from supervised learning can disrupt value learning. This paper introduces MAST to make sparse networks more effective within value-based multi-agent methods.

MAST addresses both learning targets and the distribution of training examples. It combines the Soft Mellowmax Operator with a hybrid TD-lambda scheme to produce more dependable targets, and uses two replay buffers to improve the sample distribution. Gradient-based topology evolution then changes the sparse network structure during training, allowing agents to be trained using sparse networks throughout.

Across multiple value-based algorithms and benchmarks, the authors report up to a twentyfold reduction in floating-point operations for training and inference, with less than 3% performance degradation. The results indicate that sparsity can yield substantial computational savings when the learning process is adapted to support it. The method’s contribution is therefore both network compression and changes that help preserve reliable value learning under sparse computation.
summary.tldr: MAST stabilizes sparse multi-agent value learning, reporting up to twentyfold FLOP reductions with less than 3% performance degradation.

title: Value-Based Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Dynamic Sparse Training

abstract: In this work we analyze various scaling limits of the training dynamics of transformer models in the feature learning regime. We identify the set of parameterizations which admit well defined infinite width and depth limits that allow the attention layers to update throughout training, a relevant notion of feature learning in these models. We then use tools from dynamical mean field theory (DMFT) to analyze various infinite limits (infinite heads, infinite key/query dimension, and infinite depth) which have different statistical descriptions depending on which infinite limit is taken and how attention layers are scaled. We provide numerical evidence of convergence to the limits and show they maintain the correct scale of updates for both SGD and Adam.
originalAbstract: In this work we analyze various scaling limits of the training dynamics of transformer models in the feature learning regime. We identify the set of parameterizations which admit well defined infinite width and depth limits that allow the attention layers to update throughout training, a relevant notion of feature learning in these models. We then use tools from dynamical mean field theory (DMFT) to analyze various infinite limits (infinite heads, infinite key/query dimension, and infinite depth) which have different statistical descriptions depending on which infinite limit is taken and how attention layers are scaled. We provide numerical evidence of convergence to the limits and show they maintain the correct scale of updates for both SGD and Adam.

paragraphs: Studying increasingly large transformers can reveal how their training behavior depends on model scale. This paper focuses on limits that preserve feature learning: attention layers must remain able to change during training. The central question is which parameterizations produce a mathematically well-defined large-model limit while retaining that ability.

The authors identify suitable parameterizations and analyze several ways to make a transformer infinite. These include increasing the number of attention heads, increasing key and query dimensionality, and increasing depth. Using dynamical mean field theory, they show that the resulting statistical descriptions depend on both the chosen limit and the scaling of attention layers.

Numerical results provide evidence that finite models converge toward the analyzed limits. The limits also maintain appropriately scaled updates for both SGD and Adam. The work therefore supplies a framework for understanding transformer training at large scale while preserving changing attention features, and explains why different routes to larger models need not share one statistical description.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes large-transformer limits that preserve attention learning and shows how different scaling choices change training dynamics.

title: Infinite Limits of Multi-head Transformer Dynamics

abstract: We study the problem of PAC learning $\gamma$-margin halfspaces with Massart noise. We propose a simple proper learning algorithm, the Perspectron, that has sample complexity $\widetilde{O}((\epsilon\gamma)^{-2})$ and achieves classification error at most $\eta+\epsilon$ where $\eta$ is the Massart noise rate. Prior works (DGT19, CKMY20) came with worse sample complexity guarantees (in both $\epsilon$ and $\gamma$) or could only handle random classification noise (DDKWZ23,KITBMV23)--- a much milder noise assumption. We also show that our results extend to the more challenging setting of learning generalized linear models with a known link function under Massart noise, achieving a similar sample complexity to the halfspace case. This significantly improves upon the prior state-of-the-art in this setting due to CKMY20, who introduced this model.

Prior works (DGT19, CKMY20) came with worse sample complexity guarantees (in both $\epsilon$ and $\gamma$) or could only handle random classification noise (DDKWZ23,KITBMV23)--- a much milder noise assumption. We also show that our results extend to the more challenging setting of learning generalized linear models with a known link function under Massart noise, achieving a similar sample complexity to the halfspace case. paragraphs: This paper studies learning linear decision boundaries when the data have a margin and labels are corrupted by Massart noise. The margin parameter γ measures the separation assumed in the learning problem. Massart noise is a more demanding setting than random classification noise, so guarantees that work only for random corruption do not cover the full problem considered here.

The authors introduce Perspectron, a simple proper learning algorithm, meaning that its learned classifier remains a halfspace. It achieves classification error at most η + ε, where η is the Massart noise rate and ε is the additional allowed error. Its sample complexity is approximately 1/(εγ)², with logarithmic factors suppressed by the stated bound.

This improves earlier guarantees in their dependence on accuracy and margin, while accommodating the stronger noise model. The paper also extends the results to generalized linear models under Massart noise, provided the link function is known, with similar sample complexity. The contribution concerns efficient learning under those explicit margin and noise conditions, together with a stronger result for the stated generalized model.
summary.tldr: Perspectron improves sample guarantees for learning margin-separated halfspaces under Massart noise and extends to generalized linear models with known links.

title: Learning Noisy Halfspaces with a Margin: Massart is No Harder than Random

abstract: Molecular learning is pivotal in many real-world applications, such as drug discovery. Supervised learning requires heavy human annotation, which is particularly challenging for molecular data, e.g., the commonly used density functional theory (DFT) is highly computationally expensive. Active learning (AL) automatically queries labels for most informative samples, thereby remarkably alleviating the annotation hurdle. In this paper, we present a principled AL paradigm for molecular learning, where we treat molecules as 3D molecular graphs. Specifically, we propose a new diversity sampling method to eliminate mutual redundancy built on distributions of 3D geometries. We first propose a set of new 3D graph isometries for 3D graph isomorphism analysis. Our method is provably at least as expressive as the Geometric Weisfeiler-Lehman (GWL) test. The moments of the distributions of the associated geometries are then extracted for efficient diversity computing. To ensure our AL paradigm selects samples with maximal uncertainties, we carefully design a Bayesian geometric graph neural network to compute uncertainties specifically for 3D molecular graphs. We pose active sampling as a quadratic programming (QP) problem using the proposed components. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our AL paradigm, as well as the proposed diversity and uncertainty methods.

abstract: Despite the widespread use of statistical prior models in various fields, such models for neural network gradients have long been overlooked. The inherent challenge stems from their high-dimensional structures and complex interdependencies, which complicate effective modeling. In this work, we demonstrate the potential of large language models (LLMs) to act as gradient priors in a zero-shot setting. We examine the property by considering lossless gradient compression -- a critical application in distributed learning -- that depends heavily on precise probability modeling. To achieve this, we introduce LM-GC, a novel method that integrates LLMs with arithmetic coding. Our technique converts plain gradients into text-like formats, enhancing token efficiency by up to 38 times compared to their plain representations. We ensure that this data conversion maintains a close alignment with the structure of plain gradients and the symbols commonly recognized by LLMs. Our experiments indicate that LM-GC surpasses existing state-of-the-art lossless compression methods, improving compression rates by 10% up to 17.2% across various datasets and architectures. Additionally, our approach shows promising compatibility with lossy compression techniques such as quantization and sparsification. These findings highlight the significant potential of LLMs as a model for effectively handling gradients. Code is available at https://github.com/hui-po-wang/LM-GC.

paragraphs: Gradients have complex relationships across many dimensions, making their probability distributions difficult to model. Accurate probability estimates are valuable for lossless compression, where the original values must be recoverable exactly. This paper investigates whether a large language model can supply such estimates for gradients in a zero-shot setting, with distributed learning as a motivating application.

The proposed LM-GC method combines a language model with arithmetic coding. It converts gradients into a text-like representation designed to preserve their structure while using symbols familiar to the language model. This conversion improves token efficiency by up to 38 times compared with plain representations, allowing the model to process gradient information more compactly.

Across the tested datasets and architectures, LM-GC improves compression rates by 10% to 17.2% over existing leading lossless methods. The authors also report promising compatibility with quantization and sparsification, which are themselves lossy techniques. Together, these findings suggest that language models can capture useful statistical regularities in numerical training data, extending their potential role beyond conventional text processing.
summary.tldr: LM-GC uses language-model probability estimates and arithmetic coding to improve lossless gradient compression without task-specific training.

title: Language Models as Zero-shot Lossless Gradient Compressors: Towards General Neural Parameter Prior Models

abstract: Vision transformer model (ViT) is widely used and performs well in vision tasks due to its ability to capture long-range dependencies. However, the time complexity and memory consumption increase quadratically with the number of input patches which limits the usage of ViT in real-world applications. Previous methods have employed linear attention to mitigate the complexity of the original self-attention mechanism at the expense of effectiveness. In this paper, we propose QT-ViT models that improve the previous linear self-attention using quadratic Taylor expansion. Specifically, we substitute the softmax-based attention with second-order Taylor expansion, and then accelerate the quadratic expansion by reducing the time complexity with a fast approximation algorithm. The proposed method capitalizes on the property of quadratic expansion to achieve superior performance while employing linear approximation for fast inference. Compared to previous studies of linear attention, our approach does not necessitate knowledge distillation or high-order attention residuals to facilitate the training process. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed QT-ViTs, showcasing the state-of-the-art results. Particularly, the proposed QT-ViTs consistently surpass the previous SOTA EfficientViTs under different model sizes, and achieve a new Pareto-front in terms of accuracy and speed.

QT-ViT aims to improve the balance between computational efficiency and predictive performance through a different approximation of attention.

The method replaces softmax-based attention with a second-order Taylor expansion. It then uses a fast approximation algorithm to reduce the computational cost of evaluating that quadratic expression. The design seeks to retain the useful properties of the richer expansion while enabling fast inference through a linear approximation.

The reported improvement is therefore about achievable tradeoffs: the proposed attention design supports a better combination of accuracy and speed in the evaluated models.
summary.tldr: QT-ViT combines a quadratic Taylor approximation of attention with fast computation to improve the measured accuracy-speed tradeoff.

title: QT-ViT: Improving Linear Attention in ViT with Quadratic Taylor Expansion

abstract: We study the problem of multi-agent reinforcement learning (multi-agent RL) with differential privacy (DP) constraints. This is well-motivated by various real-world applications involving sensitive data, where it is critical to protect users' private information. We first extend the definitions of Joint DP (JDP) and Local DP (LDP) to two-player zero-sum episodic Markov Games, where both definitions ensure trajectory-wise privacy protection. Then we design a provably efficient algorithm based on optimistic Nash value iteration and privatization of Bernstein-type bonuses. The algorithm is able to satisfy JDP and LDP requirements when instantiated with appropriate privacy mechanisms. Furthermore, for both notions of DP, our regret bound generalizes the best known result under the single-agent RL case, while our regret could also reduce to the best known result for multi-agent RL without privacy constraints. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first results towards understanding trajectory-wise privacy protection in multi-agent RL.

paragraphs: The paper studies how multiple reinforcement-learning agents can learn while protecting sensitive interaction data. Its setting is a two-player, zero-sum game played over episodes, where one player's gains oppose the other's. The privacy target is an entire trajectory of interaction, making the sequence of observations and actions the unit of protection.

The authors extend joint differential privacy and local differential privacy to this setting. They then construct a provably efficient algorithm using optimistic Nash value iteration and privatized Bernstein-type bonuses. These bonuses are part of the learning procedure's treatment of uncertainty. With appropriate privacy mechanisms, the algorithm can satisfy either of the two privacy definitions.

The analysis gives regret guarantees for both privacy notions, linking privacy protection to the cost of learning effective decisions. The bounds generalize the best known single-agent results and can also reduce to the best known multi-agent result without privacy constraints. The authors present this as, to their knowledge, the first theoretical progress on trajectory-level privacy in multi-agent reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: The paper develops trajectory-level privacy definitions and a provably efficient private learning algorithm for two-player zero-sum episodic games.

title: Differentially Private Reinforcement Learning with Self-Play

abstract: World models can foresee the outcomes of different actions, which is of paramount importance for autonomous driving. Nevertheless, existing driving world models still have limitations in generalization to unseen environments, prediction fidelity of critical details, and action controllability for flexible application. In this paper, we present Vista, a generalizable driving world model with high fidelity and versatile controllability. Based on a systematic diagnosis of existing methods, we introduce several key ingredients to address these limitations. To accurately predict real-world dynamics at high resolution, we propose two novel losses to promote the learning of moving instances and structural information. We also devise an effective latent replacement approach to inject historical frames as priors for coherent long-horizon rollouts. For action controllability, we incorporate a versatile set of controls from high-level intentions (command, goal point) to low-level maneuvers (trajectory, angle, and speed) through an efficient learning strategy. After large-scale training, the capabilities of Vista can seamlessly generalize to different scenarios. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets show that Vista outperforms the most advanced general-purpose video generator in over 70% of comparisons and surpasses the best-performing driving world model by 55% in FID and 27% in FVD. Moreover, for the first time, we utilize the capacity of Vista itself to establish a generalizable reward for real-world action evaluation without accessing the ground truth actions.

paragraphs: Driving world models predict how scenes may evolve under different actions. title: Vista: A Generalizable Driving World Model with High Fidelity and Versatile Controllability

abstract: A common source of anxiety for the computational neuroscience student is the question “will my recurrent neural network (RNN) model finally learn that task?”. Unlike in machine learning where any architectural modification of an RNN (e.g. GRU or LSTM) is acceptable if it speeds up training, the RNN models trained as _models of brain dynamics_ are subject to plausibility constraints that fundamentally exclude the usual machine learning hacks. The “vanilla” RNNs commonly used in computational neuroscience find themselves plagued by ill-conditioned loss surfaces that complicate training and significantly hinder our capacity to investigate the brain dynamics underlying complex tasks. Moreover, some tasks may require very long time horizons which backpropagation cannot handle given typical GPU memory limits. Here, we develop SOFO, a second-order optimizer that efficiently navigates loss surfaces whilst _not_ requiring backpropagation. By relying instead on easily parallelized batched forward-mode differentiation, SOFO enjoys constant memory cost in time. Morever, unlike most second-order optimizers which involve inherently sequential operations, SOFO's effective use of GPU parallelism yields a per-iteration wallclock time essentially on par with first-order gradient-based optimizers. We show vastly superior performance compared to Adam on a number of RNN tasks, including a difficult double-reaching motor task and the learning of an adaptive Kalman filter algorithm trained over a long horizon.

These models face plausibility constraints that can rule out architectural changes commonly used to simplify machine learning training. Their loss surfaces can also be difficult to optimize, while long task horizons make backpropagation demanding in GPU memory.
