summary.tldr: SOFO trains neuroscience RNNs using parallel forward-mode second-order optimization with memory cost constant in the time horizon.

title: Second-order forward-mode optimization of recurrent neural networks for neuroscience

abstract: There has been exciting progress in generating images from natural language or layout conditions. However, these methods struggle to faithfully reproduce complex scenes due to the insufficient modeling of multiple objects and their relationships. To address this issue, we leverage the scene graph, a powerful structured representation, for complex image generation. Different from the previous works that directly use scene graphs for generation, we employ the generative capabilities of variational autoencoders and diffusion models in a generalizable manner, compositing diverse disentangled visual clues from scene graphs. Specifically, we first propose a Semantics-Layout Variational AutoEncoder (SL-VAE) to jointly derive (layouts, semantics) from the input scene graph, which allows a more diverse and reasonable generation in a one-to-many mapping. We then develop a Compositional Masked Attention (CMA) integrated with a diffusion model, incorporating (layouts, semantics) with fine-grained attributes as generation guidance. To further achieve graph manipulation while keeping the visual content consistent, we introduce a Multi-Layered Sampler (MLS) for an "isolated" image editing effect. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms recent competitors based on text, layout, or scene graph, in terms of generation rationality and controllability.

paragraphs: Complex image generation requires coordinating multiple objects, their attributes, and their relationships. This paper uses scene graphs to make that structure explicit, then separates the graph's visual guidance into components that can be recombined. The aim is to generate coherent scenes while providing control over their content.

A Semantics-Layout Variational AutoEncoder jointly derives semantic information and spatial layouts from the graph. Its one-to-many mapping allows a single graph to support diverse plausible visual arrangements. A diffusion model then uses Compositional Masked Attention to incorporate those layouts, semantics, and fine-grained attributes as generation guidance.

Experiments report improvements over recent text-, layout-, and scene-graph-based competitors in generation rationality and controllability. The contribution links structured scene descriptions to both diverse generation and targeted modification: objects and relationships guide the image without forcing every graph to correspond to only one visual realization.
summary.tldr: The method turns scene graphs into separate semantic and layout cues for controllable diffusion generation and localized, visually consistent editing.

title: Scene Graph Disentanglement and Composition for Generalizable Complex Image Generation

abstract: Conditional validity and length efficiency are two crucial aspects of conformal prediction (CP). Conditional validity ensures accurate uncertainty quantification for data subpopulations, while proper length efficiency ensures that the prediction sets remain informative. Despite significant efforts to address each of these issues individually, a principled framework that reconciles these two objectives has been missing in the CP literature. In this paper, we develop Conformal Prediction with Length-Optimization (CPL) - a novel and practical framework that constructs prediction sets with (near-) optimal length while ensuring conditional validity under various classes of covariate shifts, including the key cases of marginal and group-conditional coverage. In the infinite sample regime, we provide strong duality results which indicate that CPL achieves conditional validity and length optimality. In the finite sample regime, we show that CPL constructs conditionally valid prediction sets. Our extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate the superior prediction set size performance of CPL compared to state-of-the-art methods across diverse real-world and synthetic datasets in classification, regression, and large language model-based multiple choice question answering. An Implementation of our algorithm can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/shayankiyani98/CP.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction produces sets of possible answers to express uncertainty. Two properties matter together: the sets should provide appropriate coverage for the relevant populations, and they should be small enough to remain informative. The paper develops Conformal Prediction with Length-Optimization, or CPL, to address these objectives within one framework.

CPL constructs prediction sets with optimal or near-optimal length while ensuring conditional validity under various classes of covariate shifts. The framework includes marginal coverage and group-conditional coverage as key cases. Its theoretical results distinguish sample regimes: with infinitely many samples, strong duality establishes conditional validity and length optimality; with finite samples, the authors establish conditional validity.

Experiments compare CPL with state-of-the-art methods on real and synthetic data, covering classification, regression, and language-model-based multiple-choice answering. The authors report better prediction-set sizes across these evaluations. The contribution is a principled connection between coverage requirements and set-size optimization, with theoretical guarantees stated separately for infinite and finite data and empirical evidence about the resulting efficiency.
summary.tldr: CPL jointly addresses prediction-set size and coverage, with conditional-validity guarantees and length-optimality results in the infinite-sample regime.

title: Length Optimization in Conformal Prediction

abstract: Empowering 3D Gaussian Splatting with generalization ability is appealing. However, existing generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting methods are largely confined to narrow-range interpolation between stereo images due to their heavy backbones, thus lacking the ability to accurately localize 3D Gaussian and support free-view synthesis across wide view range. In this paper, we present a novel framework FreeSplat that is capable of reconstructing geometrically consistent 3D scenes from long sequence input towards free-view synthesis.Specifically, we firstly introduce Low-cost Cross-View Aggregation achieved by constructing adaptive cost volumes among nearby views and aggregating features using a multi-scale structure. Subsequently, we present the Pixel-wise Triplet Fusion to eliminate redundancy of 3D Gaussians in overlapping view regions and to aggregate features observed across multiple views. Additionally, we propose a simple but effective free-view training strategy that ensures robust view synthesis across broader view range regardless of the number of views. Our empirical results demonstrate state-of-the-art novel view synthesis peformances in both novel view rendered color maps quality and depth maps accuracy across different numbers of input views. We also show that FreeSplat performs inference more efficiently and can effectively reduce redundant Gaussians, offering the possibility of feed-forward large scene reconstruction without depth priors. Our code will be made open-source upon paper acceptance.

paragraphs: FreeSplat aims to reconstruct indoor scenes from long image sequences so that they can be viewed from a broad range of positions. Existing generalizable Gaussian splatting methods are described as largely limited to interpolation within narrow ranges between stereo images. The paper connects this limitation to heavy feature-processing backbones and difficulty accurately placing the scene's 3D Gaussians.

Its first component gathers information across nearby views using adaptive cost volumes and a multiscale feature structure. Pixel-wise Triplet Fusion then combines observations from multiple views while removing redundant Gaussians where views overlap. A separate training strategy prepares the model for wider viewpoint changes across different numbers of input images. These components address both scene consistency and the cost of combining many observations.

Experiments report state-of-the-art rendered color quality and depth accuracy across varying input-view counts. FreeSplat also performs inference more efficiently and reduces redundant Gaussians. The findings support broader-view reconstruction from sequences, while the authors frame feed-forward reconstruction of large scenes without depth priors as a possibility opened by the approach.
summary.tldr: FreeSplat combines information across long image sequences and removes redundant Gaussians to improve efficient, geometrically consistent synthesis over wider viewpoints.

title: FreeSplat: Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting Towards Free View Synthesis of Indoor Scenes

abstract: Pretrained diffusion models (DMs) have recently been popularly used in solving inverse problems (IPs). The existing methods mostly interleave iterative steps in the reverse diffusion process and iterative steps to bring the iterates closer to satisfying the measurement constraint. However, such interleaving methods struggle to produce final results that look like natural objects of interest (i.e., manifold feasibility) and fit the measurement (i.e., measurement feasibility), especially for nonlinear IPs. Moreover, their capabilities to deal with noisy IPs with unknown types and levels of measurement noise are unknown. In this paper, we advocate viewing the reverse process in DMs as a function and propose a novel plug-in method for solving IPs using pretrained DMs, dubbed DMPlug. DMPlug addresses the issues of manifold feasibility and measurement feasibility in a principled manner, and also shows great potential for being robust to unknown types and levels of noise. Through extensive experiments across various IP tasks, including two linear and three nonlinear IPs, we demonstrate that DMPlug consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, often by large margins especially for nonlinear IPs.

This gives the reconstruction procedure a different organization from methods that interleave the two kinds of iterative steps.

The authors evaluate DMPlug on two linear and three nonlinear inverse problems. They report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, often by large margins on nonlinear tasks. They also describe promising robustness to measurement noise whose type and level are unknown. That robustness is presented as demonstrated potential, rather than a universal guarantee covering every possible noise process.
summary.tldr: DMPlug treats reverse diffusion as a function to improve measurement-consistent reconstruction, with strong reported results especially on nonlinear inverse problems.

title: DMPlug: A Plug-in Method for Solving Inverse Problems with Diffusion Models

abstract: This paper introduces the confounded pure exploration transductive linear bandit (CPET-LB) problem. As a motivating example, often online services cannot directly assign users to specific control or treatment experiences either for business or practical reasons. In these settings, naively comparing treatment and control groups that may result from self-selection can lead to biased estimates of underlying treatment effects. Instead, online services can employ a properly randomized encouragement that incentivizes users toward a specific treatment. Our methodology provides online services with an adaptive experimental design approach for learning the best-performing treatment for such encouragement designs. We consider a more general underlying model captured by a linear structural equation and formulate pure exploration linear bandits in this setting. Though pure exploration has been extensively studied in standard adaptive experimental design settings, we believe this is the first work considering a setting where noise is confounded. Elimination-style algorithms using experimental design methods in combination with a novel finite-time confidence interval on an instrumental variable style estimator are presented with sample complexity upper bounds nearly matching a minimax lower bound. Finally, experiments are conducted that demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.

If users choose their own experiences, comparing the resulting groups can confuse treatment effects with preexisting differences between users. This paper studies how a service can instead randomize encouragements that influence treatment choice, then adapt its experiment to identify the best treatment.

The authors formulate this setting as a confounded pure exploration transductive linear bandit problem, using a linear structural equation model. Their algorithms combine experimental design with elimination: evidence gathered during the experiment is used to rule out treatment candidates. A new finite-time confidence interval for an instrumental-variable-style estimator supplies the uncertainty estimates needed for this process despite confounded noise.

The analysis gives sample-complexity upper bounds that nearly match a minimax lower bound, and experiments demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution is a way to allocate randomized encouragements adaptively when direct treatment assignment is unavailable, while accounting for the bias that would undermine a naive comparison of self-selected groups.
summary.tldr: The paper develops adaptive encouragement experiments for identifying the best treatment when direct assignment is unavailable and self-selection creates confounding.

title: Adaptive Experimentation When You Can't Experiment

abstract: We address data-driven learning of the infinitesimal generator of stochastic diffusion processes, essential for understanding numerical simulations of natural and physical systems. The unbounded nature of the generator poses significant challenges, rendering conventional analysis techniques for Hilbert-Schmidt operators ineffective. To overcome this, we introduce a novel framework based on the energy functional for these stochastic processes. Our approach integrates physical priors through an energy-based risk metric in both full and partial knowledge settings. We evaluate the statistical performance of a reduced-rank estimator in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) in the partial knowledge setting. Notably, our approach provides learning bounds independent of the state space dimension and ensures non-spurious spectral estimation. Additionally, we elucidate how the distortion between the intrinsic energy-induced metric of the stochastic diffusion and the RKHS metric used for generator estimation impacts the spectral learning bounds.

The generator describes the process’s instantaneous evolution and is relevant to understanding simulations of natural and physical systems. Its unbounded nature creates a technical obstacle: conventional analysis for Hilbert–Schmidt operators cannot directly handle the learning problem.

The authors introduce a framework based on the process’s energy functional. An energy-based measure of estimation risk incorporates physical prior information in settings with either full or partial knowledge. For the partial-knowledge setting, they analyze a reduced-rank estimator in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, giving a statistical account of its performance.

The resulting learning bounds do not depend on the dimension of the state space, and the framework ensures non-spurious spectral estimation. The analysis also explains how a mismatch between the process’s energy-induced geometry and the kernel space’s geometry affects spectral learning bounds. This connects estimation quality to the compatibility of the mathematical representation with the process being learned.
summary.tldr: An energy-based framework learns stochastic diffusion generators with dimension-independent bounds and non-spurious spectral estimation.

title: Learning the Infinitesimal Generator of Stochastic Diffusion Processes

abstract: Effectively designing molecular geometries is essential to advancing pharmaceutical innovations, a domain, which has experienced great attention through the success of generative models and, in particular, diffusion models. However, current molecular diffusion models are tailored towards a specific downstream task and lack adaptability. We introduce UniGuide, a framework for controlled geometric guidance of unconditional diffusion models that allows flexible conditioning during inference without the requirement of extra training or networks. We show how applications such as structure-based, fragment-based, and ligand-based drug design are formulated in the UniGuide framework and demonstrate on-par or superior performance compared to specialised models. Offering a more versatile approach, UniGuide has the potential to streamline the development of molecular generative models, allowing them to be readily used in diverse application scenarios.

UniGuide introduces a framework for controlling molecular geometry that makes an unconditional diffusion model usable with different forms of conditioning.

The guidance is applied during inference and requires neither additional training nor extra networks. This places the conditioning mechanism at the point where molecules are generated, allowing the same framework to express multiple geometric design tasks. The authors show how structure-based, fragment-based, and ligand-based drug design can all be formulated within UniGuide.

The reported evaluations find performance on par with or better than specialized models. That result supports the practical value of a common guidance framework across the examined applications. The broader promise is to streamline molecular generative model development by making trained models easier to reuse under different requirements, while the abstract presents that wider development benefit as a potential outcome.
summary.tldr: UniGuide adds flexible geometric conditioning to unconditional molecular diffusion models during inference, without extra training or networks.

title: Unified Guidance for Geometry-Conditioned Molecular Generation

abstract: The heterogeneity issue in federated learning (FL) has attracted increasing attention, which is attempted to be addressed by most existing methods. Currently, due to systems and objectives heterogeneity, enabling clients to hold models of different architectures and tasks of different demands has become an important direction in FL. Most existing FL methods are based on the homogeneity assumption, namely, different clients have the same architectural models with the same tasks, which are unable to handle complex and multivariate data and tasks. To flexibly address these heterogeneity limitations, we propose a novel federated multi-task learning framework with the help of tensor trace norm, FedSAK. Specifically, it treats each client as a task and splits the local model into a feature extractor and a prediction head. Clients can flexibly choose shared structures based on heterogeneous situations and upload them to the server, which learns correlations among client models by mining model low-rank structures through tensor trace norm.Furthermore, we derive convergence and generalization bounds under non-convex settings. Evaluated on 6 real-world datasets compared to 13 advanced FL models, FedSAK demonstrates superior performance.

paragraphs: Federated learning becomes harder when participating clients need different model architectures or perform different tasks. Methods that assume everyone uses the same model for the same objective cannot directly accommodate this diversity. FedSAK addresses this problem by organizing federated learning as a collection of related client-specific tasks.

Each client separates its local model into a feature extractor and a prediction head. Clients can select which structures to share according to their particular heterogeneity and upload those structures to the server. The server uses a tensor trace norm to discover low-rank structure among the models. This provides a way to learn relationships across clients while allowing flexibility in what they contribute.

The authors derive convergence and generalization bounds in non-convex settings, giving theoretical support alongside practical evaluation. Across six real-world datasets, FedSAK is reported to outperform thirteen advanced federated learning methods. The stated results support flexible coupling as a useful approach when collaboration must accommodate differences in both model design and task requirements.
summary.tldr: FedSAK uses low-rank relationships among selectively shared model structures to support federated learning across heterogeneous architectures and tasks.

title: A Swiss Army Knife for Heterogeneous Federated Learning: Flexible Coupling via Trace Norm

abstract: Time series segmentation is a fundamental task in analyzing temporal data across various domains, from human activity recognition to energy monitoring. While numerous state-of-the-art methods have been developed to tackle this problem, the evaluation of their performance remains critically limited. Existing measures predominantly focus on change point accuracy or rely on point-based metrics such as Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), which fail to capture the quality of the detected segments, ignore the nature of errors, and offer limited interpretability. In this paper, we address these shortcomings by introducing two novel evaluation measures: WARI (Weighted Adjusted Rand Index), a temporal extension of ARI that accounts for the position of segmentation errors, and SMS (State Matching Score), a fine-grained metric that identifies and scores four distinct and fundamental types of segmentation errors while allowing error-specific weighting. We empirically validate WARI and SMS on synthetic and real-world benchmarks, showing that they not only provide a more accurate assessment of segmentation quality but also uncover insights, such as error provenance and type, that are inaccessible with traditional measures.

paragraphs: Time-series segmentation divides temporal data into meaningful segments, but evaluating the resulting segments requires more than checking individual change points. The paper argues that existing measures can obscure where errors occur and what kinds of errors were made. A single score may therefore give limited insight into the quality of the detected temporal structure.

The authors introduce two evaluation measures. Weighted Adjusted Rand Index, or WARI, extends ARI to account for the temporal positions of segmentation errors. State Matching Score, or SMS, distinguishes and scores four fundamental error types. SMS also permits different weights for different error types, allowing the evaluation to reflect their relative importance.

Tests on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show that the measures provide a more informative assessment of segmentation quality and reveal error type and provenance that traditional measures miss. The contribution is an improved way to assess segmentation outputs and understand their failures. It makes evaluation more useful for diagnosing what a method gets wrong, alongside comparing overall performance.
summary.tldr: WARI and SMS evaluate time-series segmentation using error location and error type, making quality assessments more interpretable.

title: Toward Interpretable Evaluation Measures for Time Series Segmentation

abstract: Reconstruction and joint-embedding have emerged as two leading paradigms in Self‑Supervised Learning (SSL). Reconstruction methods focus on recovering the original sample from a different view in input space. On the other hand, joint-embedding methods align the representations of different views in latent space. Both approaches offer compelling advantages, yet practitioners lack clear guidelines for choosing between them. In this work, we unveil the core mechanisms that distinguish each paradigm. By leveraging closed-form solutions for both approaches, we precisely characterize how the view generation process, e.g. data augmentation, impacts the learned representations. We then demonstrate that, unlike supervised learning, both SSL paradigms require a minimal alignment between augmentations and irrelevant features to achieve asymptotic optimality with increasing sample size. Our findings indicate that in scenarios where these irrelevant features have a large magnitude, joint-embedding methods are preferable because they impose a strictly weaker alignment condition compared to reconstruction-based methods. These results not only clarify the trade-offs between the two paradigms but also substantiate the empirical success of joint-embedding approaches on real-world challenging datasets.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning can learn by reconstructing an original sample from another view or by aligning different views in a learned representation space. Both approaches are widely used, but choosing between them requires understanding what each preserves. This paper derives closed-form solutions to study how the process that generates views, including data augmentation, shapes the representations learned.

The analysis finds that both approaches need a minimum alignment between augmentations and irrelevant features to become asymptotically optimal as the sample size increases. In the studied setting, having more data alone therefore does not remove the importance of how views are constructed. The authors contrast this requirement with supervised learning.

When irrelevant features have large magnitude, joint-embedding methods require strictly weaker alignment than reconstruction methods. This establishes a conditional reason to prefer prediction in latent space: it can achieve optimality under a less demanding relationship between augmentations and irrelevant features. The result clarifies a trade-off between the paradigms and offers theoretical support for joint embedding’s empirical success on challenging datasets.
summary.tldr: The analysis shows that joint embedding needs weaker augmentation alignment than reconstruction when irrelevant features have large magnitude.

title: Joint‑Embedding vs Reconstruction: Provable Benefits of Latent Space Prediction for Self‑Supervised Learning

abstract: While vision-language-action models (VLAs) have shown promising robotic behaviors across a diverse set of manipulation tasks, they achieve limited success rates when deployed on novel tasks out of the box. To allow these policies to safely interact with their environments, we need a failure detector that gives a timely alert such that the robot can stop, backtrack, or ask for help. However, existing failure detectors are trained and tested only on one or a few specific tasks, while generalist VLAs require the detector to generalize and detect failures also in unseen tasks and novel environments. In this paper, we introduce the multitask failure detection problem and propose SAFE, a failure detector for generalist robot policies such as VLAs. We analyze the VLA feature space and find that VLAs have sufficient high-level knowledge about task success and failure, which is generic across different tasks. Based on this insight, we design SAFE to learn from VLA internal features and predict a single scalar indicating the likelihood of task failure. SAFE is trained on both successful and failed rollouts and is evaluated on unseen tasks. SAFE is compatible with different policy architectures. We test it on OpenVLA, $\pi_0$, and $\pi_0$-FAST in both simulated and real-world environments extensively. We compare SAFE with diverse baselines and show that SAFE achieves state-of-the-art failure detection performance and the best trade-off between accuracy and detection time using conformal prediction. More qualitative results and code can be found at the project webpage: https://vla-safe.github.io/

summary.tldr: SAFE reads robot policies’ internal features to detect likely failures on unseen tasks and balance accuracy with timely alerts.

title: SAFE: Multitask Failure Detection for Vision-Language-Action Models

abstract: This paper investigates the structure of linear operators introduced in Hernandez et al. [2023] that decode specific relational facts in transformer language models. We extend their single-relation findings to a collection of relations and systematically chart their organization. We show that such collections of relation decoders can be highly compressed by simple order-3 tensor networks without significant loss in decoding accuracy. To explain this surprising redundancy, we develop a cross-evaluation protocol, in which we apply each linear decoder operator to the subjects of every other relation. Our results reveal that these linear maps do not encode distinct relations, but extract recurring, coarse-grained semantic properties (e.g., country of capital city and country of food are both in the country-of-X property). This property-centric structure clarifies both the operators' compressibility and highlights why they generalize only to new relations that are semantically close. Our findings thus interpret linear relational decoding in transformer language models as primarily property-based, rather than relation-specific.

paragraphs: Linear operators can extract relational facts from representations inside Transformer language models. This paper studies how a collection of these operators is organized, extending earlier work on individual relations. The authors find that simple order-three tensor networks can compress the collection substantially without a significant loss in decoding accuracy, suggesting considerable shared structure.

To investigate that redundancy, they apply each relation decoder to the subjects belonging to every other relation. This cross-evaluation reveals that the operators extract recurring, broad semantic properties. For example, decoders associated with a capital city's country and a food's country share the more general property of identifying a country associated with something.

That property-based organization explains both compressibility and the observed limits of generalization: the operators transfer only to new relations that are semantically close. The findings refine what these linear decoders reveal about language-model representations. Their success at recovering facts appears to depend primarily on shared coarse semantic properties, rather than each operator uniquely encoding its named relation.
summary.tldr: Linear relation decoders share broad semantic properties, explaining their compressibility and transfer mainly to semantically similar relations.

title: The Structure of Relation Decoding Linear Operators in Large Language Models

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated the ability to tackle increasingly complex tasks through advanced reasoning, long-form content generation, and tool use. Solving these tasks often involves long inference-time computations. In human problem solving, a common strategy to expedite work is collaboration: by dividing the problem into sub-tasks, exploring different strategies concurrently, etc. Recent research has shown that LLMs can also operate in parallel by implementing explicit cooperation frameworks, such as voting mechanisms or the explicit creation of independent sub-tasks that can be executed in parallel. However, each of these frameworks may not be suitable for all types of tasks, which can hinder their applicability. In this work, we propose a different design approach: we run LLM "workers" in parallel , allowing them to synchronize via a concurrently-updated attention cache and prompt these workers to decide how best to collaborate. Our approach allows the instances to come up with their own collaboration strategy for the problem at hand, all the while "seeing" each other's partial progress in the concurrent cache. We implement this approach via Hogwild! Inference: a parallel LLM inference engine where multiple instances of the same LLM run in parallel with the same attention cache, with "instant" access to each other's generated tokens. Hogwild! inference takes advantage of Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) to avoid recomputation while improving parallel hardware utilization. We find that modern reasoning-capable LLMs can perform inference with shared Key-Value cache out of the box, without additional fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Hogwild! Inference explores how multiple copies of a language model can collaborate during generation. Existing parallel approaches often prescribe a coordination pattern, such as voting or splitting work into independent tasks. The paper instead lets workers choose how to cooperate while observing one another's partial progress.

The engine runs multiple instances of the same model with a shared, concurrently updated attention cache. Prompts ask the workers to decide how to collaborate on the current problem, making the collaboration strategy part of their reasoning process.

The authors find that modern reasoning-capable models can operate with this shared key-value cache without additional fine-tuning. summary.tldr: Hogwild! Inference lets parallel language-model workers collaborate through a shared attention cache without additional fine-tuning.

title: Hogwild! Inference: Parallel LLM Generation via Concurrent Attention

abstract: 360 video captures the complete surrounding scenes with the ultra-large field of view of 360x180. This makes 360 scene understanding tasks, *e.g.*, segmentation and tracking, crucial for appications, such as autonomous driving, robotics. With the recent emergence of foundation models, the community is, however, impeded by the lack of large-scale, labelled real-world datasets. This is caused by the inherent spherical properties, *e.g.*, severe distortion in polar regions, and content discontinuities, rendering the annotation costly yet complex. This paper introduces **Leader360V**, the **first** large-scale (10K+), labeled real-world 360 video datasets for instance segmentation and tracking. Our datasets enjoy high scene diversity, ranging from indoor and urban settings to natural and dynamic outdoor scenes. To automate annotation, we design an automatic labeling pipeline, which subtly coordinates pre-trained 2D segmentors and large language models (LLMs) to facilitate the labeling. The pipeline operates in three novel stages. Specifically, in the **Initial Annotation Phase**, we introduce a Semantic- and Distortion-aware Refinement (**SDR**) module, which combines object mask proposals from multiple 2D segmentors with LLM-verified semantic labels. These are then converted into mask prompts to guide SAM2 in generating distortion-aware masks for subsequent frames. In the **Auto-Refine Annotation Phase**, missing or incomplete regions are corrected either by applying the SDR again or resolving the discontinuities near the horizontal borders. The **Manual Revision Phase** finally incorporates LLMs and human annotators to further refine and validate the annotations. Extensive user studies and evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of our labeling pipeline. Meanwhile, experiments confirm that Leader360V significantly enhances model performance for 360 video segmentation and tracking, paving the way for more scalable 360 scene understanding. We release our dataset and code at {https://leader360v.github.io/Leader360V\_HomePage/} for better understanding.

User studies and evaluations support the effectiveness of this labeling process, while experiments show that training with Leader360V significantly improves 360-video segmentation and tracking performance. The dataset and pipeline jointly address the problem: expanding labeled coverage while explicitly handling geometric complications that make ordinary annotation methods difficult to apply.
summary.tldr: Leader360V provides large-scale labeled 360 video and a distortion-aware annotation pipeline that improves segmentation and tracking in the reported experiments.

title: Leader360V: A Large-scale, Real-world 360 Video Dataset for Multi-task Learning in Diverse Environment

abstract: Equivariant neural networks provide a principled framework for incorporating symmetry into learning architectures and have been extensively analyzed through the lens of their *separation power*, that is, the ability to distinguish inputs modulo symmetry. This notion plays a central role in settings such as graph learning, where it is often formalized via the Weisfeilern–Leman hierarchy. In contrast, the *universality* of equivariant models—their capacity to approximate target functions—remains comparatively underexplored. In this work, we investigate the approximation power of equivariant neural networks beyond separation constraints. We show that separation power does not fully capture expressivity: models with identical separation power may differ in their approximation ability. To demonstrate this, we characterize the universality classes of shallow invariant networks, providing a general framework for understanding which functions these architectures can approximate. Since equivariant models reduce to invariant ones under projection, this analysis yields sufficient conditions under which shallow equivariant networks fail to be universal. Conversely, we identify settings where shallow models do achieve separation-constrained universality. These positive results, however, depend critically on structural properties of the symmetry group, such as the existence of adequate normal subgroups, which may not hold in important cases like permutation symmetry.

paragraphs: Symmetry-aware networks are often judged by separation power: whether they can distinguish inputs that are not equivalent under the relevant symmetry. This paper shows that this criterion does not fully describe what such networks can express. Two models can distinguish the same inputs yet differ in which target functions they can approximate.

The authors characterize approximation classes for shallow invariant networks, whose outputs remain unchanged under symmetry transformations. Because equivariant models can be projected into invariant ones, this analysis also provides sufficient conditions for shallow equivariant networks to fail universality. The practical conceptual lesson is that input distinguishability and function approximation are separate questions, and both matter when assessing a symmetry-aware architecture.
summary.tldr: Equivariant networks with identical input-separation power can have different approximation abilities, depending in part on the structure of their symmetry groups.

title: On Universality Classes of Equivariant Networks

abstract: Compiler auto-tuning optimizes pass sequences to improve performance metrics such as Intermediate Representation (IR) instruction count. Although recent advances leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating compiler tuning, two significant challenges still remain: the absence of high-quality reasoning datasets for agents training, and limited effective interactions with the compilation environment. In this work, we introduce Compiler-R1, the first reinforcement learning (RL)-driven framework specifically augmenting LLM capabilities for compiler auto-tuning. Compiler-R1 features a curated, high-quality reasoning dataset and a novel two-stage end-to-end RL training pipeline, enabling efficient environment exploration and learning through an outcome-based reward. Extensive experiments across seven datasets demonstrate Compiler-R1 achieving an average 8.46\% IR instruction count reduction compared to opt -Oz, showcasing the strong potential of RL-trained LLMs for compiler optimization. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/Panhaolin2001/Compiler-R1.

The paper identifies two obstacles for existing language-model approaches: insufficient reasoning data for training and limited effective interaction with the compilation environment.

The proposed framework addresses both obstacles through a curated reasoning dataset and a two-stage reinforcement learning pipeline. Training uses an outcome-based reward, so the agent learns from the results of its compiler interactions. The approach connects reasoning preparation with exploration of the environment in which pass sequences are actually evaluated.

Across seven datasets, Compiler-R1 achieves an average 8.46% reduction in intermediate-representation instruction count relative to opt -Oz. This supports the usefulness of reinforcement learning for the particular optimization measure studied. The reported result concerns instruction count; its significance is that an agent trained through compiler outcomes can improve pass selection against the stated reference configuration.
summary.tldr: Compiler-R1 uses reasoning data and reinforcement learning to tune compiler passes, reducing IR instruction count by 8.46% on average versus opt -Oz.

title: Compiler-R1: Towards Agentic Compiler Auto-tuning with Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study matching markets with ties, where workers on one side of the market may have tied preferences over jobs, determined by their matching utilities. Unlike classical two-sided markets with strict preferences, no single stable matching exists that is utility-maximizing for all workers. To address this challenge, we introduce the \emph{Optimal Stable Share} (OSS)-ratio, which measures the ratio of a worker's maximum achievable utility in any stable matching to their utility in a given matching. We prove that distributions over only stable matchings can incur linear utility losses, i.e., an $\Omega (N)$ OSS-ratio, where $N$ is the number of workers. To overcome this, we design an algorithm that efficiently computes a distribution over (possibly non-stable) matchings, achieving an asymptotically tight $O (\log N)$ OSS-ratio. When exact utilities are unknown, our second algorithm guarantees workers a logarithmic approximation of their optimal utility under bounded instability. Finally, we extend our offline approximation results to a bandit learning setting where utilities are only observed for matched pairs. In this setting, we consider worker-optimal stable regret, design an adaptive algorithm that smoothly interpolates between markets with strict preferences and those with statistical ties, and establish a lower bound revealing the fundamental trade-off between strict and tied preference regimes.

paragraphs: When workers can value multiple jobs equally, stable matching no longer offers a single outcome that maximizes every worker's utility. The paper introduces the Optimal Stable Share ratio to measure this conflict. It compares a worker's best utility across stable matchings with the utility that worker receives in a particular matching.

The authors prove that randomizing only over stable matchings can still produce utility losses growing linearly with the number of workers. Allowing possibly unstable matchings changes the achievable guarantee: their efficient algorithm computes a distribution with an asymptotically tight logarithmic ratio. A second algorithm handles unknown exact utilities, providing a logarithmic utility approximation while keeping instability bounded.

The paper then extends the analysis to bandit learning, where utilities are observed only for pairs that are actually matched. An adaptive algorithm bridges strict preferences and statistical ties using worker-optimal stable regret. A lower bound exposes a fundamental trade-off between those regimes. Together, the results quantify how utility protection, stability, and incomplete information interact when preferences contain ties.
summary.tldr: Allowing controlled departures from stable matching enables much stronger worker-utility guarantees in markets with tied preferences.

title: Stable Matching with Ties: Approximation Ratios and Learning

abstract: Most multimodal models treat every negative pair alike, ignoring the ambiguous negatives that differ from the positive by only a small detail. We propose Boundary-A ware Curriculum with Local Attention(BACL), a lightweight add-on that turns these borderline cases into a curriculum signal. A Boundary-aware Negative Sampler gradually raises difficulty, while a Contrastive Local Attention loss highlights where the mismatch occurs. The two modules are fully differentiable and work with any off-the-shelf dual encoder. Theory predicts a fast $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/n)$ error rate; practice shows up to +32 \% R@1 over CLIP and new SOTA on four large-scale benchmarks, all without extra labels.

paragraphs: Multimodal alignment requires models to distinguish matching pairs from mismatched ones. Some mismatches are obvious, while others differ from a correct match by only a small detail. This paper argues that treating all negative pairs alike overlooks useful information in these ambiguous cases, and introduces Boundary-aware Curriculum with Local Attention, or BACL.

The authors describe both components as fully differentiable and compatible with off-the-shelf dual encoders.

The theoretical analysis predicts an error rate of approximately 1/n, up to logarithmic factors. Empirically, the authors report improvements of up to 32% in recall at rank one over CLIP and state-of-the-art results on four large benchmarks, without additional labels. These results support using subtle mismatches as structured learning signals rather than giving every negative pair the same treatment.
summary.tldr: BACL improves multimodal alignment by gradually introducing harder mismatches and directing attention to the details that make them incorrect.

title: Aligning by Misaligning: Boundary-aware Curriculum Learning for Multimodal Alignment

abstract: Recent studies reveal that vision-language models (VLMs) become more susceptible to harmful requests and jailbreak attacks after integrating the vision modality, exhibiting greater vulnerability than their text-only LLM backbones. To uncover the root cause of this phenomenon, we conduct an in-depth analysis and identify a key issue: multimodal inputs introduce an modality-induced activation shift toward a “safer” direction compared to their text-only counterparts, leading VLMs to systematically overestimate the safety of harmful inputs. We refer to this issue as safety perception distortion. To mitigate such distortion, we propose Activation Shift Disentanglement and Calibration (ShiftDC), a training-free method that decomposes and calibrates the modality-induced activation shift to reduce its impact on safety. By isolating and removing the safety-relevant component, ShiftDC restores the inherent safety alignment of the LLM backbone while preserving the vision-language capabilities of VLMs. Experiments demonstrate that ShiftDC significantly enhances safety alignment without impairing model utility.

paragraphs: Adding vision can make a language model more vulnerable to harmful requests than its text-only backbone. This paper traces the problem to a modality-induced activation shift that makes multimodal inputs appear safer, causing systematic overestimation of their acceptability.

Activation Shift Disentanglement and Calibration, or ShiftDC, decomposes that shift and removes its safety-relevant component without additional training. The goal is to recover the backbone’s existing safety alignment while retaining useful visual-language processing.

Experiments show stronger safety alignment without reduced utility in the evaluated tasks. The contribution is a targeted explanation and correction of a representation-level failure, rather than treating all multimodal capability as the source of the problem. It suggests that safety behavior learned in one modality may need explicit calibration when another modality changes the internal representation presented to the same decision machinery.
summary.tldr: ShiftDC calibrates visual-modality activation shifts that can weaken a language model’s safety judgments.

title: Understanding and Rectifying Safety Perception Distortion in VLMs

abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving (E2E-AD) has emerged as a promising paradigm that unifies perception, prediction, and planning into a holistic, data-driven framework. However, achieving robustness to varying camera viewpoints, a common real-world challenge due to diverse vehicle configurations, remains an open problem. In this work, we propose VR-Drive, a novel E2E-AD framework that addresses viewpoint generalization by jointly learning 3D scene reconstruction as an auxiliary task to enable planning-aware view synthesis. Unlike prior scene-specific synthesis approaches, VR-Drive adopts a feed-forward inference strategy that supports online training-time augmentation from sparse views without additional annotations. To further improve viewpoint consistency, we introduce a viewpoint-mixed memory bank that facilitates temporal interaction across multiple viewpoints and a viewpoint-consistent distillation strategy that transfers knowledge from original to synthesized views. Trained in a fully end-to-end manner, VR-Drive effectively mitigates synthesis-induced noise and improves planning under viewpoint shifts. In addition, we release a new benchmark dataset to evaluate E2E-AD performance under novel camera viewpoints, enabling comprehensive analysis. Our results demonstrate that VR-Drive is a scalable and robust solution for the real-world deployment of end-to-end autonomous driving systems.

VR-Drive addresses it by jointly learning three-dimensional scene reconstruction as an auxiliary task, using that reconstruction to synthesize views in a way connected to planning.

Its practical significance lies in making viewpoint variation part of the learning process and providing a dedicated way to measure performance under that variation.
summary.tldr: VR-Drive combines planning-aware view synthesis, cross-view memory, and distillation to improve end-to-end driving under camera viewpoint shifts.

title: VR-Drive: Viewpoint-Robust End-to-End Driving with Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting

abstract: Novel view synthesis is an important problem with many applications, including AR/VR, gaming, and robotic simulations. With the recent rapid development of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods, it is becoming difficult to keep track of the current state of the art (SoTA) due to methods using different evaluation protocols, codebases being difficult to install and use, and methods not generalizing well to novel 3D scenes. In our experiments, we show that even tiny differences in the evaluation protocols of various methods can artificially boost the performance of these methods. This raises questions about the validity of quantitative comparisons performed in the literature. To address these questions, we propose NerfBaselines, an evaluation framework which provides consistent benchmarking tools, ensures reproducibility, and simplifies the installation and use of various methods. We validate our implementation experimentally by reproducing the numbers reported in the original papers. For improved accessibility, we release a web platform that compares commonly used methods on standard benchmarks. We strongly believe NerfBaselines is a valuable contribution to the community as it ensures that quantitative results are comparable and thus truly measure progress in the field of novel view synthesis.

summary.tldr: NerfBaselines standardizes novel-view synthesis evaluation after showing that small protocol differences can artificially inflate performance.

title: NerfBaselines: Consistent and Reproducible Evaluation of Novel View Synthesis Methods

abstract: As sequential learning algorithms are increasingly applied to real life, ensuring data privacy while maintaining their utilities emerges as a timely question. In this context, regret minimisation in stochastic bandits under $\epsilon$-global Differential Privacy (DP) has been widely studied. The present literature poses a significant gap between the best-known regret lower and upper bound in this setting, though they ``match in order''. Thus, we revisit the regret lower and upper bounds of $\epsilon$-global DP bandits and improve both. First, we prove a tighter regret lower bound involving a novel information-theoretic quantity characterising the hardness of $\epsilon$-global DP in stochastic bandits. This quantity smoothly interpolates between Kullback–Leibler divergence and Total Variation distance, depending on the privacy budget $\epsilon$. Then, we choose two asymptotically optimal bandit algorithms, i.e., KL-UCB and IMED, and propose their DP versions using a unified blueprint, i.e., (a) running in arm-dependent phases, and (b) adding Laplace noise to achieve privacy. For Bernoulli bandits, we analyse the regrets of these algorithms and show that their regrets asymptotically match our lower bound up to a constant arbitrary close to 1. At the core of our algorithms lies a new concentration inequality for sums of Bernoulli variables under Laplace mechanism, which is a new DP version of the Chernoff bound. Finally, our numerical experiments validate that DP-KLUCB and DP-IMED achieve lower regret than the existing $\epsilon$-global DP bandit algorithms.

Differential privacy adds a requirement to protect the data informing its decisions. This paper revisits how much regret, or lost reward relative to optimal choices, is unavoidable under epsilon-global differential privacy, closing a gap left by bounds that previously agreed only in order.

The authors strengthen the lower bound using a new information-theoretic quantity that varies with the privacy budget. The analysis introduces a private counterpart of the Chernoff bound for Bernoulli sums under the Laplace mechanism. Numerical experiments report lower regret than existing epsilon-global private bandit algorithms. The strongest matching result is specifically asymptotic and established for Bernoulli rewards.
summary.tldr: Private versions of KL-UCB and IMED nearly attain a sharper asymptotic regret lower bound for Bernoulli bandits.

title: Optimal Regret of Bandits under Differential Privacy

abstract: We introduce *Error Broadcast and Decorrelation* (EBD), a novel learning framework for neural networks that addresses credit assignment by directly broadcasting output errors to individual layers, circumventing weight transport of backpropagation. EBD is rigorously grounded in the stochastic orthogonality property of Minimum Mean Square Error estimators. This fundamental principle states that the error of an optimal estimator is orthogonal to functions of the input. Guided by this insight, EBD defines layerwise loss functions that directly penalize correlations between layer activations and output errors, thereby establishing a principled foundation for error broadcasting. This theoretically sound mechanism naturally leads to the experimentally observed three-factor learning rule and integrates with biologically plausible frameworks to enhance performance and plausibility. Numerical experiments demonstrate EBD’s competitive or better performance against other error-broadcast methods on benchmark datasets. Our findings establish EBD as an efficient, biologically plausible, and principled alternative for neural network training.

This fundamental principle states that the error of an optimal estimator is orthogonal to functions of the input. Guided by this insight, EBD defines layerwise loss functions that directly penalize correlations between layer activations and output errors, thereby establishing a principled foundation for error broadcasting. paragraphs: Error Broadcast and Decorrelation, or EBD, addresses how a neural network assigns responsibility for output errors to its internal layers. It sends output errors directly to individual layers, avoiding the weight transport associated with backpropagation. The paper provides a mathematical basis for deciding how each layer should respond to this shared error signal.

That basis comes from a property of minimum mean square error estimation: an optimal estimator’s error is orthogonal to functions of its input. EBD uses this idea to define local losses that penalize correlations between layer activations and output errors. Each layer therefore receives an objective tied to the relationship between its activity and the network’s remaining mistakes.

The resulting mechanism leads to a three-factor learning rule and can be integrated with biologically plausible learning frameworks. Numerical experiments find performance competitive with or better than other error-broadcast methods on benchmark datasets. The work supports EBD as a principled alternative training framework, while its connection to natural learning is presented in terms of biological plausibility.
summary.tldr: EBD trains layers using broadcast output errors and decorrelation objectives grounded in a property of optimal mean-square-error estimation.

title: Error Broadcast and Decorrelation as a Potential Artificial and Natural Learning Mechanism

abstract: Spatio-temporal prediction plays a crucial role in intelligent transportation, weather forecasting, and urban planning. While integrating multi-modal data has shown potential for enhancing prediction accuracy, key challenges persist: (i) inadequate fusion of multi-modal information, (ii) confounding factors that obscure causal relations, and (iii) high computational complexity of prediction models. To address these challenges, we propose E$^2$-CSTP, an Effective and Efficient Causal multi-modal Spatio-Temporal Prediction framework. E$^2$-CSTP leverages cross-modal attention and gating mechanisms to effectively integrate multi-modal data. Building on this, we design a dual-branch causal inference approach: the primary branch focuses on spatio-temporal prediction, while the auxiliary branch mitigates bias by modeling additional modalities and applying causal interventions to uncover true causal dependencies. To improve model efficiency, we integrate GCN with the Mamba architecture for accelerated spatio-temporal encoding. Extensive experiments on 4 real-world datasets show that E$^2$-CSTP significantly outperforms 9 state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 9.66% improvements in accuracy as well as 17.37%-56.11% reductions in computational overhead.

paragraphs: Predicting changes across locations and time can benefit from combining several kinds of data. However, simply adding information does not ensure that a model uses it effectively: different inputs can be poorly combined, and confounding factors can hide the relationships that matter. E²-CSTP addresses these problems alongside the computational cost of prediction.

The framework uses cross-modal attention and gates to combine information from different modalities. It then separates prediction and bias mitigation into two branches. The primary branch makes the spatio-temporal forecast, while an auxiliary branch models additional modalities and applies causal interventions. For efficiency, the model combines graph convolutional networks with Mamba to encode spatial and temporal information. Across four real-world datasets, the authors report better results than nine comparison methods, with accuracy improvements reaching 9.66% and computational overhead reductions ranging from 17.37% to 56.11%. These findings support the framework’s joint emphasis on information fusion, causal modeling, and efficient computation.
summary.tldr: E²-CSTP combines multimodal fusion, causal interventions, and efficient spatial-temporal encoding to improve prediction accuracy while reducing computation.

title: Causal Spatio-Temporal Prediction: An Effective and Efficient Multi-Modal Approach

abstract: Modeling and reconstructing multidimensional physical dynamics from sparse and off-grid observations presents a fundamental challenge in scientific research. Recently, diffusion-based generative modeling shows promising potential for physical simulation. However, current approaches typically operate on on-grid data with preset spatiotemporal resolution, but struggle with the sparsely observed and continuous nature of real-world physical dynamics. To fill the gaps, we present SDIFT, Sequential DIffusion in Functional Tucker space, a novel framework that generates full-field evolution of physical dynamics from irregular sparse observations. SDIFT leverages the functional Tucker model as the latent space representer with proven universal approximation property, and represents sparse observations as latent functions and Tucker core sequences. We then construct a sequential diffusion model with temporally augmented UNet in the functional Tucker space, denoising noise drawn from a Gaussian process to generate the sequence of core tensors. We then construct a sequential diffusion model with temporally augmented UNet in the functional Tucker space, denoising noise drawn from a Gaussian process to generate the sequence of core tensors. paragraphs: Physical measurements often sample only a small number of irregular locations and times. Reconstructing an entire evolving field from those observations is difficult for generative methods built around fixed spatial and temporal grids. SDIFT addresses this mismatch by representing dynamics in a space designed to accommodate continuous positions and sparse observations.

Its representation uses a functional Tucker model, combining latent functions with sequences of compact core tensors. The paper establishes a universal approximation property for this representation. A sequential diffusion model then generates core-tensor sequences by denoising Gaussian-process noise, using a UNet augmented to model temporal structure. This places the generative process inside the functional representation rather than directly on a preset observation grid.

A message-passing posterior sampling mechanism lets observations at a limited number of times guide generation of the full sequence. The authors evaluate SDIFT on supernova explosions, ocean sound-speed fields, and an organic liquid system. They report substantial improvements in reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency over state-of-the-art approaches across these three physical settings.
summary.tldr: SDIFT reconstructs evolving physical fields from sparse, irregular observations using sequential diffusion in a continuous functional representation.

title: Generating Full-field Evolution of Physical Dynamics from Irregular Sparse Observations

abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a powerful representation for real-time, high-performance rendering, enabling a wide range of applications. However, representing 3D scenes with numerous explicit Gaussian primitives imposes significant storage and memory overhead. Recent studies have shown that high-quality rendering can be achieved with a substantially reduced number of Gaussians when represented with high-precision attributes. Nevertheless, existing 3DGS compression methods still rely on a relatively large number of Gaussians, focusing primarily on attribute compression. This is because a smaller set of Gaussians becomes increasingly sensitive to lossy attribute compression, leading to severe quality degradation. Since the number of Gaussians is directly tied to computational costs, it is essential to reduce the number of Gaussians effectively rather than only optimizing storage. In this paper, we propose Optimized Minimal Gaussians representation (OMG), which significantly reduces storage while using a minimal number of primitives. First, we determine the distinct Gaussian from the near ones, minimizing redundancy without sacrificing quality. Second, we propose a compact and precise attribute representation that efficiently captures both continuity and irregularity among primitives. Additionally, we propose a sub-vector quantization technique for improved irregularity representation, maintaining fast training with a negligible codebook size. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OMG reduces storage requirements by nearly 50% compared to the previous state-of-the-art and enables 600+ FPS rendering while maintaining high rendering quality. Our source code is available at https://maincold2.github.io/omg/.

Reducing the primitive count can also reduce computation. However, a small set becomes more sensitive to errors from compressing its attributes, making compactness and rendering quality difficult to preserve together.

Optimized Minimal Gaussians, or OMG, addresses both the number of primitives and their attribute representation. It identifies distinct Gaussians among nearby ones to reduce redundancy without sacrificing quality. It then uses a compact, precise representation designed to capture both continuity and irregularity across primitives. A sub-vector quantization technique further represents irregularity with a negligible codebook size while maintaining fast training.

The experiments report nearly 50% lower storage requirements than the previous state of the art, together with rendering above 600 frames per second and high visual quality. These findings support jointly optimizing primitive count and attribute precision: reducing storage alone does not address the computational costs associated with retaining a large number of Gaussians.
summary.tldr: OMG combines fewer Gaussian primitives with precise compact attributes, reporting nearly 50% less storage and rendering above 600 FPS.

title: Optimized Minimal 3D Gaussian Splatting

abstract: Motivated by real-life supply chain management, we study a repeated newsvendor problem in which the learner is a mediator that facilitates trades between suppliers and retailers in a sequence of supplier/retailer interactions. At each time step, a new supplier and retailer join the mediator's platform with a private production cost and utility function, respectively, and the platform proposes a unitary trading price. The supplier accepts the proposed price if it meets or exceeds their unitary production cost and communicates their decision to the platform; simultaneously, the retailer decides the quantity to purchase at the proposed trading price based on their private utility function and sends their decision to the platform. If the supplier accepts the trading price, the transaction proceeds, and the retailer purchases their chosen quantity of units, paying the product of this quantity and the trading price to the supplier. The mediator's objective is to maximize social welfare. We design an online mediator's pricing strategy that features sharp regret rates under some natural assumptions, and we investigate the necessity of these assumptions, proving that relaxing any of them leads to unlearnability.

paragraphs: This paper studies a trading platform that repeatedly sets a unit price for a new supplier and retailer. The supplier has a private production cost, and the retailer has a private utility function. The platform must learn how to price trades from the decisions these participants communicate, while aiming to maximize social welfare.

At each interaction, the supplier accepts or rejects the proposed price, while the retailer independently chooses a purchase quantity at that price. Trade occurs only if the supplier accepts. The retailer then buys its chosen quantity and pays the supplier the quantity multiplied by the unit price. This makes pricing depend on both willingness to supply and quantity demanded.

The authors design an online pricing strategy with sharp regret rates under specified natural assumptions. They also examine those assumptions and prove that relaxing any of them makes the problem unlearnable in their setting. The contribution therefore includes both a successful learning strategy and a characterization of conditions necessary for the stated learnability result.
summary.tldr: The paper derives sharp regret guarantees for repeated mediated pricing under assumptions whose relaxation makes the studied problem unlearnable.

title: Online Learning in the Repeated Mediated Newsvendor Problem

abstract: This position paper argues for two claims regarding AI testing and evaluation. First, to remain informative about deployment behaviour, evaluations need account for the possibility that AI systems understand their circumstances and reason strategically. Second, game-theoretic analysis can inform evaluation design by formalising and scrutinising the reasoning in evaluation-based safety cases. Drawing on examples from existing AI systems, a review of relevant research, and formal strategic analysis of a stylised evaluation scenario, we present evidence for these claims and motivate several research directions.

First, to remain informative about deployment behaviour, evaluations need account for the possibility that AI systems understand their circumstances and reason strategically. Second, game-theoretic analysis can inform evaluation design by formalising and scrutinising the reasoning in evaluation-based safety cases. Drawing on examples from existing AI systems, a review of relevant research, and formal strategic analysis of a stylised evaluation scenario, we present evidence for these claims and motivate several research directions.

paragraphs: This position paper examines what AI evaluations can tell us about behavior after deployment. Its central concern is that an AI system might understand the circumstances in which it is being tested and reason strategically about them. If that possibility matters, interpreting test results requires considering how the testing situation influences the behavior being observed.

The authors make two connected arguments. First, evaluations must account for possible strategic reasoning if they are to remain informative about deployment. Second, game theory can help formalize the reasoning used to turn evaluation results into safety claims. This offers a way to scrutinize the connection between observed test behavior and the conclusions drawn from it.

The paper supports these arguments through examples involving existing AI systems, a review of relevant research, and formal analysis of a simplified evaluation scenario. It also motivates further research directions. The claim is about accommodating a possible source of misleading evidence, rather than establishing that every AI system reasons strategically or that every evaluation is uninformative.
summary.tldr: This position paper argues that AI evaluations should account for possible strategic behavior and use game theory to examine evaluation-based safety claims.

title: AI Testing Should Account for Sophisticated Strategic Behaviour

abstract: Data attribution methods quantify the influence of training data on model outputs and are becoming increasingly relevant for a wide range of LLM research and applications, including dataset curation, model interpretability, data valuation. However, there remain critical gaps in systematic LLM-centric evaluation of data attribution methods. To this end, we introduce DATE-LM (Data Attribution Evaluation in Language Models), a unified benchmark for evaluating data attribution methods through real-world LLM applications. DATE-LM measures attribution quality through three key tasks — training data selection, toxicity/bias filtering, and factual attribution. Our benchmark is designed for ease of use, enabling researchers to configure and run large-scale evaluations across diverse tasks and LLM architectures. Furthermore, we use DATE-LM to conduct a large-scale evaluation of existing data attribution methods. Our findings show that no single method dominates across all tasks, data attribution methods have trade-offs with simpler baselines, and method performance is sensitive to task-specific evaluation design. Finally, we release a public leaderboard for quick comparison of methods and to facilitate community engagement. We hope DATE-LM serves as a foundation for future data attribution research in LLMs.

paragraphs: Data attribution methods estimate how training examples influence a language model's outputs. Such estimates can guide data selection, help interpret model behavior, and inform assessments of data value. DATE-LM addresses the difficulty of evaluating these methods systematically by testing attribution through practical language-model applications within a shared benchmark.

The benchmark covers training data selection, toxicity and bias filtering, and factual attribution. These tasks ask different things of an attribution method, connecting its scores to distinct uses. DATE-LM is designed to support configurable, large-scale evaluations across tasks and model architectures, and includes a public leaderboard for comparing methods.

The authors' evaluation finds no method that performs best across every task. Attribution methods also involve trade-offs relative to simpler baselines, and their apparent quality changes with task-specific evaluation choices. The implication is that an attribution ranking needs to be interpreted in relation to its intended application. DATE-LM makes those comparisons more systematic while showing why one overall winner would obscure meaningful differences.
summary.tldr: DATE-LM evaluates data attribution through three practical language-model tasks and finds that method quality depends strongly on the task and evaluation design.

title: DATE-LM: Benchmarking Data Attribution Evaluation for Large Language Models

abstract: For robotic manipulation, existing robotics datasets and simulation benchmarks predominantly cater to robot-arm platforms. However, for humanoid robots equipped with dual arms and dexterous hands, simulation tasks and high-quality demonstrations are notably lacking. Bimanual dexterous manipulation is inherently more complex, as it requires coordinated arm movements and hand operations, making autonomous data collection challenging. This paper presents HumanoidGen, an automated task creation and demonstration collection framework that leverages atomic dexterous operations and LLM reasoning to generate relational constraints. Specifically, we provide spatial annotations for both assets and dexterous hands based on the atomic operations, and perform an LLM planner to generate a chain of actionable spatial constraints for arm movements based on object affordances and scenes. To further improve planning ability, we employ a variant of Monte Carlo tree search to enhance LLM reasoning for long-horizon tasks and insufficient annotation. In experiments, we create a novel benchmark with augmented scenarios to evaluate the quality of the collected data. The results show that the performance of the 2D and 3D diffusion policies can scale with the generated dataset. Project page is https://openhumanoidgen.github.io.

paragraphs: Humanoid robots with two arms and dexterous hands need demonstrations that coordinate arm motion with detailed hand operations. Existing datasets and simulation benchmarks primarily serve robot-arm platforms, leaving fewer suitable tasks and demonstrations for this more complex setting. HumanoidGen addresses the gap through automated task creation and demonstration collection.

The framework combines atomic dexterous operations with language-model reasoning. It spatially annotates objects and hands around these operations, then uses a language-model planner to produce a sequence of actionable spatial constraints for arm movement. Planning takes account of the scene and the actions objects afford. A variant of Monte Carlo tree search strengthens reasoning for longer tasks and cases with insufficient annotation.

The authors create a benchmark with augmented scenarios to assess the generated data. Their experiments show that the performance of both 2D and 3D diffusion policies can scale with the generated dataset. This supports the framework’s value as a source of training demonstrations, connecting structured task planning to the data needed for coordinated humanoid manipulation.
summary.tldr: HumanoidGen combines atomic hand operations, spatial constraints, and language-model planning to generate two-handed humanoid manipulation demonstrations.

title: HumanoidGen: Data Generation for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation via LLM Reasoning

abstract: We model sensory streams as observations from high-dimensional stochastic dynamical systems and conceptualize sensory neurons as self-supervised learners of compact representations of such dynamics. From prior experience, neurons learn {\it coherent sets}—regions of stimulus state space whose trajectories evolve cohesively over finite times—and assign membership indices to new stimuli. Coherent sets are identified via spectral clustering of the {\it stochastic Koopman operator (SKO)}, where the sign pattern of a subdominant singular function partitions the state space into minimally coupled regions. For multivariate Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes, this singular function reduces to a linear projection onto the dominant singular vector of the whitened state-transition matrix. Encoding this singular vector as a receptive field enables neurons to compute membership indices via the projection sign in a biologically plausible manner. Each neuron detects either a {\it predictive} coherent set (stimuli with common futures) or a {\it retrospective} coherent set (stimuli with common pasts), suggesting a functional dichotomy among neurons. Since neurons lack access to explicit dynamical equations, the requisite singular vectors must be estimated directly from data, for example, via past–future canonical correlation analysis on lag-vector representations—an approach that naturally extends to nonlinear dynamics. This framework provides a novel account of neuronal temporal filtering, the ubiquity of rectification in neural responses, and known functional dichotomies. Coherent-set clustering thus emerges as a fundamental computation underlying sensory processing and transferable to bio-inspired artificial systems.
