paragraphs: This paper models sensory input as observations of a high-dimensional stochastic system and proposes that neurons learn groups of stimuli with related temporal behavior. These coherent sets contain states whose trajectories remain cohesive over a finite period. A neuron then assigns new stimuli a membership index based on the temporal structure learned from experience.

The mathematical construction identifies these sets through spectral clustering of the stochastic Koopman operator. For multivariate Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes, the relevant singular function becomes a linear projection onto a particular direction in a whitened transition matrix. Representing that direction as a receptive field lets a neuron determine membership from the projection’s sign, providing a biologically plausible implementation.

The framework distinguishes neurons detecting common futures from those detecting common pasts. Since neurons do not have access to the underlying equations, the required directions can be estimated from observations using past–future canonical correlation analysis, with an extension to nonlinear dynamics. The authors propose this as an account of temporal filtering, response rectification, and neuronal functional divisions, with potential applications to bio-inspired artificial systems.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes that sensory neurons identify stimulus groups with shared pasts or futures by learning coherent sets in sensory dynamics.

title: Neurons as Detectors of Coherent Sets in Sensory Dynamics

abstract: Ring attractors, mathematical models inspired by neural circuit dynamics, provide a biologically plausible mechanism to improve learning speed and accuracy in Reinforcement Learning (RL). Serving as specialized brain-inspired structures that encode spatial information and uncertainty, ring attractors explicitly encode the action space, facilitate the organization of neural activity, and enable the distribution of spatial representations across the neural network in the context of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). These structures also provide temporal filtering that stabilizes action selection during exploration, for example, by preserving the continuity between rotation angles in robotic control or adjacency between tactical moves in game-like environments. The application of ring attractors in the action selection process involves mapping actions to specific locations on the ring and decoding the selected action based on neural activity. We investigate the application of ring attractors by both building an exogenous model and integrating them as part of DRL agents. Our approach significantly improves state-of-the-art performance on the Atari 100k benchmark, achieving a 53\% increase in performance over selected baselines.

This paper uses ring attractors, models inspired by neural circuit dynamics, to represent those relationships in reinforcement learning. The structures encode spatial information and uncertainty while organizing the neural activity used to select actions.

Actions are assigned positions on a ring, and the selected action is decoded from activity in that representation. The attractor dynamics also provide temporal filtering, helping stabilize choices during exploration. The researchers investigate both an external ring-attractor model and versions integrated into deep reinforcement learning agents, examining how this structure can participate in action selection.

On the Atari 100k benchmark, the approach reports a 53% performance increase over selected baselines and an improvement in state-of-the-art performance. The result supports the usefulness of explicitly structuring the action representation in the evaluated setting. Its significance lies in connecting spatial organization and temporal stability to learning performance, with the numerical improvement referring specifically to the baseline comparisons reported.
summary.tldr: Ring attractors organize and stabilize reinforcement-learning action selection, yielding a reported 53% performance increase over selected Atari 100k baselines.

title: Spatial-Aware Decision-Making with Ring Attractors in Reinforcement Learning Systems

abstract: In this paper we consider deterministic policy gradient algorithms for reinforcement learning with continuous actions. The deterministic policy gradient has a particularly appealing form: it is the expected gradient of the action-value function. This simple form means that the deterministic policy gradient can be estimated much more efficiently than the usual stochastic policy gradient. To ensure adequate exploration, we introduce an off-policy actor-critic algorithm that learns a deterministic target policy from an exploratory behaviour policy. Deterministic policy gradient algorithms outperformed their stochastic counterparts in several benchmark problems, particularly in high-dimensional action spaces.

This simple form means that the deterministic policy gradient can be estimated much more efficiently than the usual stochastic policy gradient. To ensure adequate exploration, we introduce an off-policy actor-critic algorithm that learns a deterministic target policy from an exploratory behaviour policy. paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with continuous actions requires a way to improve decisions across a continuous range of possibilities. This paper studies policy gradients for deterministic policies, which select a particular action for a given state. The key result is a simple gradient form expressed through the expected gradient of the action-value function.

That form allows the deterministic policy gradient to be estimated much more efficiently than the usual stochastic policy gradient. Exploration still needs explicit attention, because the policy being learned is deterministic. The authors introduce an off-policy actor-critic algorithm that learns this target policy from an exploratory behavior policy. The behavior policy supplies experience while the target policy is improved.

On several benchmark problems, deterministic policy gradient algorithms outperform their stochastic counterparts, with particularly strong results in high-dimensional action spaces. These findings support the practical significance of the efficient gradient form for continuous control. The paper's approach combines a deterministic decision rule with exploratory data collection, linking the mathematical result to an implementable learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: An efficiently estimable deterministic policy gradient supports off-policy actor-critic learning and performs especially well on benchmarks with high-dimensional actions.

title: Deterministic Policy Gradient Algorithms

abstract: We introduce a new embarrassingly parallel parameter learning algorithm for Markov random fields which is efficient for a large class of practical models. Our algorithm parallelizes naturally over cliques and, for graphs of bounded degree, its complexity is linear in the number of cliques. Unlike its competitors, our algorithm is fully parallel and for log-linear models it is also data efficient, requiring only the local sufficient statistics of the data to estimate parameters.

Unlike its competitors, our algorithm is fully parallel and for log-linear models it is also data efficient, requiring only the local sufficient statistics of the data to estimate parameters.

paragraphs: Learning the parameters of a Markov random field requires estimating relationships represented by its graph. This paper introduces an algorithm that distributes this work over the graph's cliques, the groups of mutually connected variables. It is designed to be efficient for a large class of practical models.

The algorithm is embarrassingly parallel: its learning tasks naturally separate by clique and can be carried out in parallel. For graphs of bounded degree, the authors establish complexity that grows linearly with the number of cliques. That condition is part of the scaling result, linking the computational claim to the graph's connectivity.

For log-linear models, the method also needs only local sufficient statistics to estimate parameters. These statistics summarize the relevant local information in the observations, reducing the data each estimation task needs. The contribution combines computational separation with a local data requirement. Together, these properties explain why the approach is suited to parallel parameter learning in the model classes described.
summary.tldr: Clique-wise parallel learning gives linear complexity for bounded-degree Markov random fields and uses only local sufficient statistics for log-linear models.

title: Linear and Parallel Learning of Markov Random Fields

abstract: We present an algorithm for finding landmarks along a manifold. These landmarks provide a small set of locations spaced out along the manifold such that they capture the low-dimensional non-linear structure of the data embedded in the high-dimensional space. The approach does not select points directly from the dataset, but instead we optimize each landmark by moving along the continuous manifold space (as approximated by the data) according to the gradient of an objective function. We borrow ideas from active learning with Gaussian processes to define the objective, which has the property that a new landmark is "repelled" by those currently selected, allowing for exploration of the manifold. We derive a stochastic algorithm for learning with large datasets and show results on several datasets, including the Million Song Dataset and articles from the New York Times.

paragraphs: High-dimensional data can contain a lower-dimensional nonlinear structure, described here as a manifold. The paper seeks a small collection of landmarks spread across that structure. Such landmarks are intended to capture its shape through a limited set of locations, making their placement central to the quality of the representation.

The method optimizes landmark positions in the continuous manifold space approximated from the data. It therefore permits locations beyond the observed data points. Each landmark moves according to the gradient of an objective inspired by active learning with Gaussian processes. The objective makes previously chosen landmarks repel a new one, encouraging it to explore other parts of the manifold.

The authors also derive a stochastic algorithm for large datasets. They demonstrate the approach on several collections, including the Million Song Dataset and New York Times articles. The key contribution is a continuous, objective-driven method for placing representative locations, with a selection mechanism that encourages coverage and an algorithm designed to handle substantial data volumes.
summary.tldr: Gaussian-process-inspired optimization places landmarks continuously along a data manifold, using repulsion to encourage broad coverage.

title: Landmarking Manifolds with Gaussian Processes

abstract: We provide non-asymptotic bounds for the well-known temporal difference learning algorithm TD(0) with linear function approximators. These include high-probability bounds as well as bounds in expectation. Our analysis suggests that a step-size inversely proportional to the number of iterations cannot guarantee optimal rate of convergence unless we assume (partial) knowledge of the stationary distribution for the Markov chain underlying the policy considered. We also provide bounds for the iterate averaged TD(0) variant, which gets rid of the step-size dependency while exhibiting the optimal rate of convergence. Furthermore, we propose a variant of TD(0) with linear approximators that incorporates a centering sequence, and establish that it exhibits an exponential rate of convergence in expectation. We demonstrate the usefulness of our bounds on two synthetic experimental settings.

These include high-probability bounds as well as bounds in expectation. Our analysis suggests that a step-size inversely proportional to the number of iterations cannot guarantee optimal rate of convergence unless we assume (partial) knowledge of the stationary distribution for the Markov chain underlying the policy considered. We also provide bounds for the iterate averaged TD(0) variant, which gets rid of the step-size dependency while exhibiting the optimal rate of convergence. Furthermore, we propose a variant of TD(0) with linear approximators that incorporates a centering sequence, and establish that it exhibits an exponential rate of convergence in expectation. We demonstrate the usefulness of our bounds on two synthetic experimental settings.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes TD(0) with linear function approximation, providing error guarantees after a finite number of updates. It gives both bounds on expected error and bounds that hold with high probability. This makes the analysis informative about learning progress before the limiting regime where convergence is usually considered.

The results expose a difficulty with step sizes proportional to the inverse iteration count. The analysis suggests this schedule cannot guarantee the optimal convergence rate without at least partial knowledge of the policy’s underlying Markov chain stationary distribution. The authors also analyze an iterate-averaged version of TD(0), which removes that step-size dependency while achieving the optimal rate.

A further contribution is a TD(0) variant incorporating a centering sequence. The authors establish exponential convergence in expectation for this variant, a different type of guarantee from a high-probability statement. Two synthetic experimental settings demonstrate the usefulness of the bounds. Together, the results connect finite-time analysis with concrete algorithmic changes intended to improve the convergence behavior of value estimation.
summary.tldr: Finite-time TD(0) analysis motivates iterate averaging and a centered variant with exponential convergence in expectation.

title: On TD(0) with function approximation: Concentration bounds and a centered variant with exponential convergence

abstract: Zero-shot learning consists in learning how to recognize new concepts by just having a description of them. Many sophisticated approaches have been proposed to address the challenges this problem comprises. In this paper we describe a zero-shot learning approach that can be implemented in just one line of code, yet it is able to outperform state of the art approaches on standard datasets. The approach is based on a more general framework which models the relationships between features, attributes, and classes as a two linear layers network, where the weights of the top layer are not learned but are given by the environment. We further provide a learning bound on the generalization error of this kind of approaches, by casting them as domain adaptation methods. In experiments carried out on three standard real datasets, we found that our approach is able to perform significantly better than the state of art on all of them, obtaining a ratio of improvement up to 17%.

paragraphs: Zero-shot learning asks a model to recognize a concept from its description, without requiring training examples of that concept. This paper proposes a particularly simple approach to that problem. Its central contribution is that a compact learning rule can perform strongly despite the complexity usually associated with connecting observed features to descriptions of unfamiliar classes.

The method belongs to a broader framework connecting features, attributes, and classes through two linear layers. The upper layer receives its weights from the environment instead of learning them from the training data. This supplied information provides the link to class descriptions. The authors also analyze generalization by treating the framework as a domain adaptation problem and deriving a learning bound.

Experiments on three standard real datasets report significantly better performance than the state of the art on all three, with an improvement ratio reaching 17%. The result supports the value of this simple construction in the tested settings. The theoretical contribution complements those experiments by examining how this family of methods can generalize.
summary.tldr: A simple two-layer linear framework recognizes unseen classes from descriptions and outperforms prior approaches on three datasets.

title: An embarrassingly simple approach to zero-shot learning

abstract: We introduce a new model for representation learning and classification of video sequences. Our model is based on a convolutional neural network coupled with a novel temporal pooling layer. The temporal pooling layer relies on an inner-optimization problem to efficiently encode temporal semantics over arbitrarily long video clips into a fixed-length vector representation. Importantly, the representation and classification parameters of our model can be estimated jointly in an end-to-end manner by formulating learning as a bilevel optimization problem. Furthermore, the model can make use of any existing convolutional neural network architecture (e.g., AlexNet or VGG) without modification or introduction of additional parameters. We demonstrate our approach on action and activity recognition tasks.

Importantly, the representation and classification parameters of our model can be estimated jointly in an end-to-end manner by formulating learning as a bilevel optimization problem. Furthermore, the model can make use of any existing convolutional neural network architecture (e.g., AlexNet or VGG) without modification or introduction of additional parameters. We demonstrate our approach on action and activity recognition tasks.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a video classification model that combines a convolutional neural network with a temporal pooling layer. The layer converts information from a video sequence into a vector of fixed length while encoding temporal semantics. This addresses the need to represent clips of different lengths in a form that a common classifier can use.

The temporal representation is produced through an inner optimization problem. Training the overall model is then formulated as bilevel optimization: the representation-producing optimization sits inside the larger learning problem. This arrangement allows the representation and classification parameters to be learned jointly, so temporal summarization participates directly in end-to-end training.

The approach supports arbitrarily long clips and can use existing convolutional architectures, including AlexNet or VGG, without modifying them or introducing additional parameters. The authors demonstrate it on action and activity recognition tasks. Its significance lies in making an optimization-based temporal summary compatible with joint learning, while retaining existing convolutional architectures as the foundation for the video model.
summary.tldr: An optimization-based temporal pooling layer lets video representations and classifiers learn jointly from variable-length clips.

title: Learning End-to-end Video Classification with Rank-Pooling

abstract: The problem of learning a sparse model is conceptually interpreted as the process of identifying active features/samples and then optimizing the model over them. Recently introduced safe screening allows us to identify a part of non-active features/samples. So far, safe screening has been individually studied either for feature screening or for sample screening. In this paper, we introduce a new approach for safely screening features and samples simultaneously by alternatively iterating feature and sample screening steps. A significant advantage of considering them simultaneously rather than individually is that they have a synergy effect in the sense that the results of the previous safe feature screening can be exploited for improving the next safe sample screening performances, and vice-versa. We first theoretically investigate the synergy effect, and then illustrate the practical advantage through intensive numerical experiments for problems with large numbers of features and samples.

paragraphs: Learning a sparse model can be viewed as identifying which features and samples are active, then optimizing over them. Safe screening helps by identifying some inactive features or samples that can be excluded. This paper brings feature screening and sample screening together, extending a line of work that had studied the two separately.

The proposed procedure alternates between screening features and screening samples. Its central insight is that the steps can reinforce each other: the outcome of feature screening can improve the next sample-screening step, and sample screening can improve subsequent feature screening. Information gained on one side of the problem therefore supports further reductions on the other.

The authors theoretically investigate this synergy and then demonstrate its practical advantages through extensive numerical experiments involving many features and samples. The contribution is a coordinated screening process whose two parts exchange useful information. It offers a way to reduce the remaining optimization problem while retaining the safe-screening basis for identifying inactive elements.
summary.tldr: Alternating safe feature and sample screening lets each step strengthen the other and reduce sparse-learning problems more effectively.

title: Simultaneous Safe Screening of Features and Samples in Doubly Sparse Modeling

abstract: We show how to efficiently project a vector onto the top principal components of a matrix, *without explicitly computing these components*. Specifically, we introduce an iterative algorithm that provably computes the projection using few calls to any black-box routine for ridge regression. By avoiding explicit principal component analysis (PCA), our algorithm is the first with no runtime dependence on the number of top principal components. We show that it can be used to give a fast iterative method for the popular principal component regression problem, giving the first major runtime improvement over the naive method of combining PCA with regression. To achieve our results, we first observe that ridge regression can be used to obtain a "smooth projection" onto the top principal components. We then sharpen this approximation to true projection using a low-degree polynomial approximation to the matrix step function. Step function approximation is a topic of long-term interest in scientific computing. We extend prior theory by constructing polynomials with simple iterative structure and rigorously analyzing their behavior under limited precision.

paragraphs: The paper separates projecting a vector onto a matrix's leading principal components from explicitly computing those components. It introduces an iterative projection algorithm that uses a small number of calls to a black-box ridge-regression routine. The resulting runtime has no dependence on the number of leading components, a property the authors identify as a first.

The key observation is that ridge regression supplies a smooth version of the desired projection. The algorithm sharpens this approximation using a low-degree polynomial approximation to a matrix step function. This supplies a computational route from an accessible regression operation to the projection operation the user actually needs.

The method also yields a fast iterative algorithm for principal component regression, improving on the direct approach of performing PCA and then regression. To support this construction, the paper develops step-function approximation polynomials with a simple iterative structure and analyzes their behavior under limited precision. The contribution therefore links a practical reduction to ridge regression with mathematical control of its approximation procedure.
summary.tldr: An iterative ridge-regression-based algorithm computes principal-component projections without explicitly finding the components and accelerates principal component regression.

title: Principal Component Projection Without Principal Component Analysis

abstract: Coordinate descent (CD) is a scalable and simple algorithm for solving many optimization problems in machine learning. Despite this fact, CD can also be very computationally wasteful. Due to sparsity in sparse regression problems, for example, the majority of CD updates often result in no progress toward the solution. To address this inefficiency, we propose a modified CD algorithm named “StingyCD.” By skipping over many updates that are guaranteed to not decrease the objective value, StingyCD significantly reduces convergence times. Since StingyCD only skips updates with this guarantee, however, StingyCD does not fully exploit the problem’s sparsity. For this reason, we also propose StingyCD+, an algorithm that achieves further speed-ups by skipping updates more aggressively. Since StingyCD and StingyCD+ rely on simple modifications to CD, it is also straightforward to use these algorithms with other approaches to scaling optimization. In empirical comparisons, StingyCD and StingyCD+ improve convergence times considerably for several L1-regularized optimization problems.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent is attractive because it solves optimization problems through simple coordinate updates. In sparse regression, however, many of those updates may accomplish nothing. This paper focuses on that wasted computation: an algorithm can spend substantial time revisiting coordinates without moving its objective closer to the desired solution.

The proposed StingyCD algorithm skips updates when they are guaranteed not to decrease the objective value. This lets it avoid certified unproductive work while retaining the basic coordinate descent structure. The guarantee also limits how aggressively it can exploit sparsity. The authors therefore introduce StingyCD+, which skips updates more aggressively and achieves additional speedups.

Because both methods make relatively simple changes to coordinate descent, the authors describe them as straightforward to combine with other approaches for scaling optimization. Empirical comparisons on several L1-regularized problems show considerable reductions in convergence time. The main lesson is that identifying work that will not improve the objective can accelerate an otherwise simple optimizer; the more aggressive variant extends that strategy beyond StingyCD's guaranteed-skipping rule.
summary.tldr: StingyCD speeds coordinate descent by skipping provably unproductive updates, while StingyCD+ skips more aggressively for further gains.

title: StingyCD: Safely Avoiding Wasteful Updates in Coordinate Descent

abstract: The Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) has achieved great success in generating realistic (real-valued) synthetic data. However, convergence issues and difficulties dealing with discrete data hinder the applicability of GAN to text. We propose a framework for generating realistic text via adversarial training. We employ a long short-term memory network as generator, and a convolutional network as discriminator. Instead of using the standard objective of GAN, we propose matching the high-dimensional latent feature distributions of real and synthetic sentences, via a kernelized discrepancy metric. This eases adversarial training by alleviating the mode-collapsing problem. Our experiments show superior performance in quantitative evaluation, and demonstrate that our model can generate realistic-looking sentences.
originalAbstract: The Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) has achieved great success in generating realistic (real-valued) synthetic data. However, convergence issues and difficulties dealing with discrete data hinder the applicability of GAN to text. We propose a framework for generating realistic text via adversarial training. We employ a long short-term memory network as generator, and a convolutional network as discriminator. Instead of using the standard objective of GAN, we propose matching the high-dimensional latent feature distributions of real and synthetic sentences, via a kernelized discrepancy metric. This eases adversarial training by alleviating the mode-collapsing problem. Our experiments show superior performance in quantitative evaluation, and demonstrate that our model can generate realistic-looking sentences.

paragraphs: Generating text through adversarial training presents difficulties beyond those encountered with continuous data. Sentences contain discrete choices, and adversarial optimization can struggle to converge. This paper develops a text-generation framework that changes the training objective, aiming to make the interaction between the generator and discriminator more effective.

The generator is a long short-term memory network, while a convolutional network serves as the discriminator. Rather than using the standard adversarial objective, the method compares distributions of learned features from real and generated sentences. A kernel-based discrepancy measures their difference in a high-dimensional feature space, giving training a distribution-matching target.

The authors report that this approach alleviates mode collapse, the problem of a generator producing too narrow a range of outputs, and thereby eases adversarial training. Their experiments show superior quantitative performance and realistic-looking generated sentences. The contribution connects sentence generation with feature-distribution matching: training attends to the distribution of sentence representations, with reported benefits for both optimization and output quality.
summary.tldr: Matching real and generated sentence feature distributions makes adversarial text training easier and improves the reported generation results.

title: Adversarial Feature Matching for Text Generation

abstract: The famous Policy Iteration algorithm alternates between policy improvement and policy evaluation. Implementations of this algorithm with several variants of the latter evaluation stage, e.g, n-step and trace-based returns, have been analyzed in previous works. However, the case of multiple-step lookahead policy improvement, despite the recent increase in empirical evidence of its strength, has to our knowledge not been carefully analyzed yet. In this work, we introduce the first such analysis. Namely, we formulate variants of multiple-step policy improvement, derive new algorithms using these definitions and prove their convergence. Moreover, we show that recent prominent Reinforcement Learning algorithms are, in fact, instances of our framework. We thus shed light on their empirical success and give a recipe for deriving new algorithms for future study.

Implementations of this algorithm with several variants of the latter evaluation stage, e.g, n-step and trace-based returns, have been analyzed in previous works. However, the case of multiple-step lookahead policy improvement, despite the recent increase in empirical evidence of its strength, has to our knowledge not been carefully analyzed yet. In this work, we introduce the first such analysis. Namely, we formulate variants of multiple-step policy improvement, derive new algorithms using these definitions and prove their convergence. Moreover, we show that recent prominent Reinforcement Learning algorithms are, in fact, instances of our framework. We thus shed light on their empirical success and give a recipe for deriving new algorithms for future study.

paragraphs: Policy iteration alternates between improving a policy and evaluating how well it performs. Earlier analyses had explored several ways to extend the evaluation stage, including returns that span multiple steps. The improvement stage raises a separate question: what happens when choosing a better policy involves looking several steps ahead?

This paper develops an analysis of that multiple-step improvement process. The authors define variants of lookahead policy improvement, turn those definitions into algorithms, and prove convergence. This gives the improvement stage its own theoretical treatment, rather than treating all uses of multiple steps as changes to policy evaluation.

The framework also encompasses recent prominent reinforcement learning algorithms as particular instances. That connection helps explain their reported empirical success through a shared mathematical structure. The contribution therefore serves two purposes: it analyzes existing approaches and supplies a way to derive additional algorithms. The abstract presents those future algorithms as candidates for study, rather than claiming that every possible extension will perform better.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes multiple-step policy improvement, proves convergence for derived algorithms, and connects existing methods through a common framework.

title: Beyond the One-Step Greedy Approach in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We propose new positive definite kernels for permutations. First we introduce a weighted version of the Kendall kernel, which allows to weight unequally the contributions of different item pairs in the permutations depending on their ranks. Like the Kendall kernel, we show that the weighted version is invariant to relabeling of items and can be computed efficiently in O(n ln(n)) operations, where n is the number of items in the permutation. Second, we propose a supervised approach to learn the weights by jointly optimizing them with the function estimated by a kernel machine. Third, while the Kendall kernel considers pairwise comparison between items, we extend it by considering higher-order comparisons among tuples of items and show that the supervised approach of learning the weights can be systematically generalized to higher-order permutation kernels.
originalAbstract: We propose new positive definite kernels for permutations. First we introduce a weighted version of the Kendall kernel, which allows to weight unequally the contributions of different item pairs in the permutations depending on their ranks. Like the Kendall kernel, we show that the weighted version is invariant to relabeling of items and can be computed efficiently in O(n ln(n)) operations, where n is the number of items in the permutation. Second, we propose a supervised approach to learn the weights by jointly optimizing them with the function estimated by a kernel machine. Third, while the Kendall kernel considers pairwise comparison between items, we extend it by considering higher-order comparisons among tuples of items and show that the supervised approach of learning the weights can be systematically generalized to higher-order permutation kernels.

paragraphs: Learning from permutations requires a way to compare ordered arrangements of items. This paper develops new positive-definite kernels for that purpose, beginning with a weighted version of the Kendall kernel. The weighting allows different pairs of items to contribute unequally according to their ranks, making the comparison sensitive to where items appear.

The weighted kernel retains two useful properties of the Kendall kernel. Relabeling the items does not change it, and it can be computed in O(n log n) operations for a permutation containing n items. The authors also introduce supervised weight learning, optimizing the weights jointly with the function estimated by a kernel machine.

The paper then expands the comparison beyond pairs to higher-order tuples of items. The supervised weight-learning approach extends systematically to these higher-order permutation kernels. Together, the contributions provide ways to vary both the importance of ranking relationships and the number of items considered in each relationship, while keeping those choices connected to the supervised learning task.
summary.tldr: New permutation kernels learn rank-dependent comparison weights and extend Kendall-style comparisons from item pairs to larger tuples.

title: The Weighted Kendall and High-order Kernels for Permutations

abstract: We propose a contextual-bandit approach for demand side management by offering price incentives. More precisely, a target mean consumption is set at each round and the mean consumption is modeled as a complex function of the distribution of prices sent and of some contextual variables such as the temperature, weather, and so on. The performance of our strategies is measured in quadratic losses through a regret criterion. We offer $T^{2/3}$ upper bounds on this regret (up to poly-logarithmic terms)—and even faster rates under stronger assumptions—for strategies inspired by standard strategies for contextual bandits (like LinUCB, see Li et al., 2010). Simulations on a real data set gathered by UK Power Networks, in which price incentives were offered, show that our strategies are effective and may indeed manage demand response by suitably picking the price levels.

More precisely, a target mean consumption is set at each round and the mean consumption is modeled as a complex function of the distribution of prices sent and of some contextual variables such as the temperature, weather, and so on. The performance of our strategies is measured in quadratic losses through a regret criterion. We offer $T^{2/3}$ upper bounds on this regret (up to poly-logarithmic terms)—and even faster rates under stronger assumptions—for strategies inspired by standard strategies for contextual bandits (like LinUCB, see Li et al., 2010). Simulations on a real data set gathered by UK Power Networks, in which price incentives were offered, show that our strategies are effective and may indeed manage demand response by suitably picking the price levels.

paragraphs: This paper uses contextual bandits to select price incentives that guide electricity demand toward a target. At each round, a desired mean consumption is specified. Actual mean consumption is modeled as a complex function of the distribution of offered prices and contextual information, including temperature and weather, so effective price selection must account for changing conditions.

The proposed strategies adapt ideas from established contextual-bandit methods such as LinUCB. Performance is measured through quadratic losses, which penalize deviations from the target, and analyzed using regret. The authors establish regret upper bounds growing as T to the two-thirds power, apart from polylogarithmic factors, and obtain faster rates when stronger assumptions hold.

Simulations use a real UK Power Networks dataset involving price incentives. The results indicate that the strategies can choose useful price levels and may support demand-response management. The evidence therefore combines theoretical tracking guarantees with data-based simulation results; the stated practical finding is promising demand control through price selection, rather than a demonstrated guarantee of exact target attainment.
summary.tldr: Contextual-bandit strategies choose electricity-price incentives to track consumption targets, with regret bounds and encouraging simulations on real demand-response data.

title: Target Tracking for Contextual Bandits: Application to Demand Side Management

abstract: We formally study the problem of classification under adversarial perturbations from a learner’s perspective as well as a third-party who aims at certifying the robustness of a given black-box classifier. We analyze a PAC-type framework of semi-supervised learning and identify possibility and impossibility results for proper learning of VC-classes in this setting. We further introduce a new setting of black-box certification under limited query budget, and analyze this for various classes of predictors and perturbation. We also consider the viewpoint of a black-box adversary that aims at finding adversarial examples, showing that the existence of an adversary with polynomial query complexity can imply the existence of a sample efficient robust learner.
originalAbstract: We formally study the problem of classification under adversarial perturbations from a learner’s perspective as well as a third-party who aims at certifying the robustness of a given black-box classifier. We analyze a PAC-type framework of semi-supervised learning and identify possibility and impossibility results for proper learning of VC-classes in this setting. We further introduce a new setting of black-box certification under limited query budget, and analyze this for various classes of predictors and perturbation. We also consider the viewpoint of a black-box adversary that aims at finding adversarial examples, showing that the existence of an adversary with polynomial query complexity can imply the existence of a sample efficient robust learner.

paragraphs: Robust classification raises several related questions: whether a learner can acquire a robust predictor, whether an outside party can certify an existing predictor, and whether an attacker can find inputs that break it. This paper studies all three perspectives, including situations where the classifier is accessible only through queries.

For learning, the authors analyze a semi-supervised framework with PAC-style guarantees. They identify both possibility and impossibility results for proper learning of VC classes, where the returned predictor must belong to the specified hypothesis class. For certification, they introduce a setting with a limited query budget and investigate different predictor classes and kinds of perturbation.

The paper also establishes a conditional connection between attacking and learning. The existence of a black-box adversary using polynomially many queries can imply the existence of a robust learner that uses samples efficiently. This links the ability to discover adversarial examples with the feasibility of robust learning, while making the implication depend on the stated adversary condition.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes when robust learning and black-box certification are possible, and connects efficient adversarial attacks to sample-efficient robust learning.

title: Black-box Certification and Learning under Adversarial Perturbations

abstract: A general framework for online learning with partial information is one where feedback graphs specify which losses can be observed by the learner. We study a challenging scenario where feedback graphs vary stochastically with time and, more importantly, where graphs and losses are dependent. This scenario appears in several real-world applications that we describe where the outcome of actions are correlated. We devise a new algorithm for this setting that exploits the stochastic properties of the graphs and that benefits from favorable regret guarantees. We present a detailed theoretical analysis of this algorithm, and also report the result of a series of experiments on real-world datasets, which show that our algorithm outperforms standard baselines for online learning with feedback graphs.

We study a challenging scenario where feedback graphs vary stochastically with time and, more importantly, where graphs and losses are dependent. This scenario appears in several real-world applications that we describe where the outcome of actions are correlated. We devise a new algorithm for this setting that exploits the stochastic properties of the graphs and that benefits from favorable regret guarantees. We present a detailed theoretical analysis of this algorithm, and also report the result of a series of experiments on real-world datasets, which show that our algorithm outperforms standard baselines for online learning with feedback graphs.

paragraphs: In online learning with partial information, a learner does not necessarily observe every action's loss. A feedback graph describes which losses become visible. This paper studies a setting where those graphs change randomly over time and, crucially, are statistically dependent on the losses themselves.

That dependence makes the feedback mechanism part of the learning problem: which information is observed is connected to the outcomes being learned about. The authors motivate the setting through applications with correlated action outcomes. They design an algorithm that uses the stochastic properties of the feedback graphs, rather than treating the pattern of observations as unrelated to the losses.

The paper provides a detailed theoretical analysis and favorable regret guarantees, which assess accumulated performance relative to a comparison benchmark. Experiments on real-world datasets also report improvements over standard algorithms for learning with feedback graphs. The contribution is to handle a more interconnected observation process while retaining theoretical control, with empirical evidence supporting the approach in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A new online learning algorithm exploits randomly changing feedback graphs even when the graphs and observed losses are dependent.

title: Online Learning with Dependent Stochastic Feedback Graphs

abstract: Multi-kernel learning (MKL) exhibits reliable performance in nonlinear function approximation tasks. Instead of using one kernel, it learns the optimal kernel from a pre-selected dictionary of kernels. The selection of the dictionary has crucial impact on both the performance and complexity of MKL. Specifically, inclusion of a large number of irrelevant kernels may impair the accuracy, and increase the complexity of MKL algorithms. To enhance the accuracy, and alleviate the computational burden, the present paper develops a novel scheme which actively chooses relevant kernels. The proposed framework models the pruned kernel combination as feedback collected from a graph, that is refined ’on the fly.’ Leveraging the random feature approximation, we propose an online scalable multi-kernel learning approach with graph feedback, and prove that the proposed algorithm enjoys sublinear regret. Numerical tests on real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the novel approach.

Specifically, inclusion of a large number of irrelevant kernels may impair the accuracy, and increase the complexity of MKL algorithms. To enhance the accuracy, and alleviate the computational burden, the present paper develops a novel scheme which actively chooses relevant kernels. The proposed framework models the pruned kernel combination as feedback collected from a graph, that is refined ’on the fly.’ Leveraging the random feature approximation, we propose an online scalable multi-kernel learning approach with graph feedback, and prove that the proposed algorithm enjoys sublinear regret. paragraphs: Multi-kernel learning chooses a useful kernel from a predefined dictionary for nonlinear function approximation. The dictionary creates a practical tradeoff: including many irrelevant kernels can both hurt accuracy and increase computational cost. This paper develops an online method that actively selects relevant kernels rather than treating the original collection as equally useful throughout learning.

The framework represents feedback from the pruned kernel combination through a graph that is refined as learning proceeds. This graph-based feedback supports the evolving selection process. The authors also use random-feature approximation to make the resulting multi-kernel learning approach scalable. Kernel selection, feedback structure, and approximation therefore form parts of the same online procedure.

The paper proves that the proposed algorithm has sublinear regret, meaning its cumulative regret grows more slowly than the number of rounds. Numerical tests on real datasets demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution addresses the dictionary's influence on both accuracy and complexity through active selection, while providing a theoretical online-learning guarantee for the resulting method.
summary.tldr: An online multi-kernel learner actively selects kernels using evolving graph feedback and achieves sublinear regret.

title: Online Multi-Kernel Learning with Graph-Structured Feedback

abstract: We address the problem of training models with black-box and hard-to-optimize metrics by expressing the metric as a monotonic function of a small number of easy-to-optimize surrogates. We pose the training problem as an optimization over a relaxed surrogate space, which we solve by estimating local gradients for the metric and performing inexact convex projections. We analyze gradient estimates based on finite differences and local linear interpolations, and show convergence of our approach under smoothness assumptions with respect to the surrogates. Experimental results on classification and ranking problems verify the proposal performs on par with methods that know the mathematical formulation, and adds notable value when the form of the metric is unknown.
originalAbstract: We address the problem of training models with black-box and hard-to-optimize metrics by expressing the metric as a monotonic function of a small number of easy-to-optimize surrogates. We pose the training problem as an optimization over a relaxed surrogate space, which we solve by estimating local gradients for the metric and performing inexact convex projections. We analyze gradient estimates based on finite differences and local linear interpolations, and show convergence of our approach under smoothness assumptions with respect to the surrogates. Experimental results on classification and ranking problems verify the proposal performs on par with methods that know the mathematical formulation, and adds notable value when the form of the metric is unknown.

paragraphs: A model’s evaluation metric may be difficult to optimize directly, especially when its mathematical formula is unavailable. This paper tackles that problem by expressing the metric as a monotonic function of a small collection of easier-to-optimize surrogate quantities. Those surrogates provide a manageable space in which to guide training.

The method formulates optimization over a relaxed surrogate space, estimates local gradients of the desired metric, and performs inexact convex projections. The authors analyze two ways to estimate the gradients: finite differences and local linear interpolation. Both use local information about how the metric changes rather than requiring its full mathematical expression.

The convergence analysis assumes smoothness with respect to the surrogates, so the guarantee depends on structure in the relationship between those quantities and the metric. Experiments on classification and ranking show performance comparable to methods given the metric’s formula, with notable value when the formula is unknown. The contribution is an adaptive route from accessible surrogate objectives to a harder or opaque evaluation target.
summary.tldr: The method optimizes difficult or unknown metrics through a small surrogate space, with convergence under stated smoothness assumptions.

title: Optimizing Black-box Metrics with Adaptive Surrogates

abstract: State-of-the-art neural machine translation models generate a translation from left to right and every step is conditioned on the previously generated tokens. The sequential nature of this generation process causes fundamental latency in inference since we cannot generate multiple tokens in each sentence in parallel. We propose an attention-masking based model, called Disentangled Context (DisCo) transformer, that simultaneously generates all tokens given different contexts. The DisCo transformer is trained to predict every output token given an arbitrary subset of the other reference tokens. We also develop the parallel easy-first inference algorithm, which iteratively refines every token in parallel and reduces the number of required iterations. Our extensive experiments on 7 translation directions with varying data sizes demonstrate that our model achieves competitive, if not better, performance compared to the state of the art in non-autoregressive machine translation while significantly reducing decoding time on average.

The paper also introduces parallel easy-first inference, which repeatedly refines all tokens in parallel and reduces the number of iterations needed.

Experiments cover seven translation directions with different amounts of training data. The model achieves competitive, and sometimes better, performance relative to the non-autoregressive state of the art while substantially reducing average decoding time. The contribution joins a training design for flexible context with an inference procedure for parallel refinement, addressing translation quality and sequential generation costs together.
summary.tldr: DisCo combines flexible masked context with parallel token refinement to accelerate translation while retaining competitive reported quality.

title: Non-autoregressive Machine Translation with Disentangled Context Transformer

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to leverage the knowledge learned from a labeled source dataset to solve similar tasks in a new unlabeled domain. Prior UDA methods typically require to access the source data when learning to adapt the model, making them risky and inefficient for decentralized private data. This work tackles a practical setting where only a trained source model is available and investigates how we can effectively utilize such a model without source data to solve UDA problems. We propose a simple yet generic representation learning framework, named \emph{Source HypOthesis Transfer} (SHOT). SHOT freezes the classifier module (hypothesis) of the source model and learns the target-specific feature extraction module by exploiting both information maximization and self-supervised pseudo-labeling to implicitly align representations from the target domains to the source hypothesis. To verify its versatility, we evaluate SHOT in a variety of adaptation cases including closed-set, partial-set, and open-set domain adaptation. Experiments indicate that SHOT yields state-of-the-art results among multiple domain adaptation benchmarks.

The proposed SHOT framework keeps the source model’s classifier fixed and adapts its feature extractor to the target domain. It combines information maximization with self-supervised pseudo-labeling to make target representations align with the existing classifier. The fixed classifier acts as the reference for adaptation, while changes to the feature extractor let unfamiliar target inputs become useful to that reference.

The authors evaluate SHOT across closed-set, partial-set, and open-set adaptation, covering several relationships between source and target class sets. They report state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks. The findings support the usefulness of transferring a trained model without retaining source-data access during adaptation, while the benchmark evidence establishes performance in the evaluated settings rather than a universal adaptation guarantee.
summary.tldr: SHOT adapts a source model to unlabeled target data by freezing its classifier and learning target features without accessing the source dataset.

title: Do We Really Need to Access the Source Data? Source Hypothesis Transfer for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

abstract: We develop a framework for the average-case analysis of random quadratic problems and derive algorithms that are optimal under this analysis. This yields a new class of methods that achieve acceleration given a model of the Hessian’s eigenvalue distribution. We develop explicit algorithms for the uniform, Marchenko-Pastur, and exponential distributions. These methods have a simple momentum-like update, in which each update only makes use on the current gradient and previous two iterates. Furthermore, the momentum and step-size parameters can be estimated without knowledge of the Hessian’s smallest singular value, in contrast with classical accelerated methods like Nesterov acceleration and Polyak momentum. Through empirical benchmarks on quadratic and logistic regression problems, we identify regimes in which the the proposed methods improve over classical (worst-case) accelerated methods.

The contribution connects assumptions about the overall curvature distribution to practical, momentum-like optimization rules.
summary.tldr: Modeling the Hessian’s eigenvalue distribution yields simple optimization methods with average-case acceleration and empirical advantages in some regimes.

title: Acceleration through spectral density estimation

abstract: In this paper we tackle the problem of routing multiple agents in a coordinated manner. This is a complex problem that has a wide range of applications in fleet management to achieve a common goal, such as mapping from a swarm of robots and ride sharing. Traditional methods are typically not designed for realistic environments which contain sparsely connected graphs and unknown traffic, and are often too slow in runtime to be practical. In contrast, we propose a graph neural network based model that is able to perform multi-agent routing based on learned value iteration in a sparsely connected graph with dynamically changing traffic conditions. Moreover, our learned communication module enables the agents to coordinate online and adapt to changes more effectively. We created a simulated environment to mimic realistic mapping performed by autonomous vehicles with unknown minimum edge coverage and traffic conditions; our approach significantly outperforms traditional solvers both in terms of total cost and runtime. We also show that our model trained with only two agents on graphs with a maximum of 25 nodes can easily generalize to situations with more agents and/or nodes.

paragraphs: Routing several agents toward a shared goal requires both route planning and coordination. Sparse road connections and changing, initially unknown traffic complicate the task. The paper develops a learned routing system for these conditions, motivated by applications such as vehicle mapping and ride sharing.

The model uses a graph neural network to perform learned value iteration over a sparsely connected graph. A learned communication module lets agents coordinate while operating and adjust to changes. Route decisions can therefore reflect both the graph and information exchanged among the agents as conditions evolve.

The authors create a simulated autonomous-vehicle mapping environment with unknown minimum edge-coverage requirements and traffic conditions. In this environment, their approach significantly improves total cost and runtime over traditional solvers. They also report that a model trained with two agents on graphs of at most 25 nodes generalizes to settings with more agents or nodes. This demonstrates transfer beyond the training scale in the evaluated routing situations.
summary.tldr: A graph-based routing network combines learned planning and communication to coordinate agents under changing traffic and generalize beyond its training scale.

title: Multi-Agent Routing Value Iteration Network

abstract: Exploration is critical for good results in deep reinforcement learning and has attracted much attention. However, existing multi-agent deep reinforcement learning algorithms still use mostly noise-based techniques. Very recently, exploration methods that consider cooperation among multiple agents have been developed. However, existing methods suffer from a common challenge: agents struggle to identify states that are worth exploring, and hardly coordinate exploration efforts toward those states. To address this shortcoming, in this paper, we propose cooperative multi-agent exploration (CMAE): agents share a common goal while exploring. The goal is selected from multiple projected state spaces by a normalized entropy-based technique. Then, agents are trained to reach the goal in a coordinated manner. We demonstrate that CMAE consistently outperforms baselines on various tasks, including a sparse-reward version of multiple-particle environment (MPE) and the Starcraft multi-agent challenge (SMAC).

The paper targets these two difficulties: deciding where exploration should go and getting agents to pursue that destination together.

Cooperative multi-agent exploration, or CMAE, gives the agents a shared exploration goal. It selects that goal using a normalized entropy-based technique applied to multiple projected state spaces. These projections supply different views of the state for goal selection. Once a goal is chosen, the agents are trained to reach it cooperatively, connecting the selection rule to coordinated behavior.

The authors report consistent improvements over baselines across the evaluated tasks, including a sparse-reward multiple-particle environment and the StarCraft multi-agent challenge. These results support shared goal selection as a useful organizing mechanism for exploration. The contribution combines a way to identify exploration targets with a way to align the agents’ efforts toward those targets.
summary.tldr: CMAE improves multi-agent exploration by selecting a shared goal and training agents to reach it cooperatively.

title: Cooperative Exploration for Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has become effective in tackling discrete cooperative game scenarios. However, MARL has yet to penetrate settings beyond those modelled by team and zero-sum games, confining it to a small subset of multi-agent systems. In this paper, we introduce a new generation of MARL learners that can handle \textit{nonzero-sum} payoff structures and continuous settings. In particular, we study the MARL problem in a class of games known as stochastic potential games (SPGs) with continuous state-action spaces. Unlike cooperative games, in which all agents share a common reward, SPGs are capable of modelling real-world scenarios where agents seek to fulfil their individual goals. We prove theoretically our learning method, $\ourmethod$, enables independent agents to learn Nash equilibrium strategies in \textit{polynomial time}. We demonstrate our framework tackles previously unsolvable tasks such as \textit{Coordination Navigation} and \textit{large selfish routing games} and that it outperforms the state of the art MARL baselines such as MADDPG and COMIX in such scenarios.

It focuses on stochastic potential games, a structured class of nonzero-sum games that accommodates these different agent objectives.

The authors introduce a learning method and prove that independent agents can learn Nash-equilibrium strategies in polynomial time for the studied setting. It also outperforms the named multi-agent baselines MADDPG and COMIX in those scenarios. These findings support extending multi-agent reinforcement learning to individual incentives and continuous environments when the game has the potential structure analyzed in the paper.
summary.tldr: A learning method achieves polynomial-time Nash-equilibrium learning in continuous stochastic potential games and improves results on studied tasks.

title: Learning in Nonzero-Sum Stochastic Games with Potentials

abstract: We prove fast mixing and characterize the stationary distribution of the Langevin Algorithm for inverting random weighted DNN generators. This result extends the work of Hand and Voroninski from efficient inversion to efficient posterior sampling. In practice, to allow for increased expressivity, we propose to do posterior sampling in the latent space of a pre-trained generative model. To achieve that, we train a score-based model in the latent space of a StyleGAN-2 and we use it to solve inverse problems. Our framework, Score-Guided Intermediate Layer Optimization (SGILO), extends prior work by replacing the sparsity regularization with a generative prior in the intermediate layer. Experimentally, we obtain significant improvements over the previous state-of-the-art, especially in the low measurement regime.

paragraphs: Inverse problems seek an underlying signal from measurements. This paper moves beyond finding a single inversion toward efficiently sampling possible solutions from a posterior distribution. Its theoretical contribution proves fast mixing for Langevin sampling when inverting randomly weighted neural-network generators and characterizes the sampler's stationary distribution.

For a more expressive practical model, the authors perform posterior sampling in the latent space of a pretrained generator. The theoretical and practical components address related but distinct settings: the mixing result concerns randomly weighted generators, while the implemented framework uses a pretrained model. Together, they motivate sampling guided by intermediate representations as a useful approach to reconstruction from limited observations.
summary.tldr: SGILO guides posterior sampling with a learned intermediate-layer prior and improves inverse-problem results, especially with few measurements.

title: Score-Guided Intermediate Level Optimization: Fast Langevin Mixing for Inverse Problems

abstract: Learning meaningful representations of data that can address challenges such as batch effect correction and counterfactual inference is a central problem in many domains including computational biology. Adopting a Conditional VAE framework, we show that marginal independence between the representation and a condition variable plays a key role in both of these challenges. We propose the Contrastive Mixture of Posteriors (CoMP) method that uses a novel misalignment penalty defined in terms of mixtures of the variational posteriors to enforce this independence in latent space. We show that CoMP has attractive theoretical properties compared to previous approaches, and we prove counterfactual identifiability of CoMP under additional assumptions. We demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on a set of challenging tasks including aligning human tumour samples with cancer cell-lines, predicting transcriptome-level perturbation responses, and batch correction on single-cell RNA sequencing data. We also find parallels to fair representation learning and demonstrate that CoMP is competitive on a common task in the field.

paragraphs: Combining biological datasets and predicting responses under changed conditions both require representations that separate meaningful variation from condition-related effects. Using a conditional variational autoencoder, this paper identifies marginal independence between the learned representation and a condition variable as an important ingredient for batch correction and counterfactual inference.

The proposed Contrastive Mixture of Posteriors method, or CoMP, encourages that independence through a misalignment penalty built from mixtures of variational posterior distributions. Together, these results show how one representation-learning principle can support several distinct applications.
summary.tldr: CoMP encourages condition-independent latent representations for data integration and counterfactual prediction, with conditional identifiability guarantees and strong empirical results.

title: Contrastive Mixture of Posteriors for Counterfactual Inference, Data Integration and Fairness

abstract: Most deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms distill experience into parametric behavior policies or value functions via gradient updates. While effective, this approach has several disadvantages: (1) it is computationally expensive, (2) it can take many updates to integrate experiences into the parametric model, (3) experiences that are not fully integrated do not appropriately influence the agent’s behavior, and (4) behavior is limited by the capacity of the model. In this paper we explore an alternative paradigm in which we train a network to map a dataset of past experiences to optimal behavior. Specifically, we augment an RL agent with a retrieval process (parameterized as a neural network) that has direct access to a dataset of experiences. This dataset can come from the agent’s past experiences, expert demonstrations, or any other relevant source. The retrieval process is trained to retrieve information from the dataset that may be useful in the current context, to help the agent achieve its goal faster and more efficiently. The proposed method facilitates learning agents that at test time can condition their behavior on the entire dataset and not only the current state, or current trajectory. We integrate our method into two different RL agents: an offline DQN agent and an online R2D2 agent. In offline multi-task problems, we show that the retrieval-augmented DQN agent avoids task interference and learns faster than the baseline DQN agent. On Atari, we show that retrieval-augmented R2D2 learns significantly faster than the baseline R2D2 agent and achieves higher scores. We run extensive ablations to measure the contributions of the components of our proposed method.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Curriculum reinforcement learning (CRL) allows solving complex tasks by generating a tailored sequence of learning tasks, starting from easy ones and subsequently increasing their difficulty. Although the potential of curricula in RL has been clearly shown in a variety of works, it is less clear how to generate them for a given learning environment, resulting in a variety of methods aiming to automate this task. In this work, we focus on the idea of framing curricula as interpolations between task distributions, which has previously been shown to be a viable approach to CRL. Identifying key issues of existing methods, we frame the generation of a curriculum as a constrained optimal transport problem between task distributions. Benchmarks show that this way of curriculum generation can improve upon existing CRL methods, yielding high performance in a variety of tasks with different characteristics.

paragraphs: Curriculum reinforcement learning trains an agent through a sequence of tasks that starts easier and becomes more demanding. Such sequences can help solve complex tasks, but deciding how to generate a useful curriculum remains a separate challenge. This paper studies how to automate that choice for a learning environment.

The authors build on the idea of expressing a curriculum as an interpolation between distributions over tasks. In this view, curriculum generation changes which tasks the learner is likely to encounter as training progresses. After identifying issues with existing approaches, they formulate this movement between task distributions as a constrained optimal transport problem. This gives the construction of the curriculum an explicit optimization formulation.

Benchmark results show that the resulting curricula can improve on existing curriculum reinforcement learning methods across tasks with different characteristics. The finding supports constrained transport as a useful way to organize learning experiences. The reported benefit is empirical: the approach achieves high performance in the evaluated settings, rather than establishing that every environment benefits from the same curriculum construction.
summary.tldr: Formulating curriculum generation as constrained transport between task distributions improves reinforcement learning performance in varied benchmarks.

title: Curriculum Reinforcement Learning via Constrained Optimal Transport

abstract: In recent years, algebraic topology and its modern development, the theory of persistent homology, has shown great potential in graph representation learning. In this paper, based on the mathematics of algebraic topology, we propose a novel solution for inductive relation prediction, an important learning task for knowledge graph completion. To predict the relation between two entities, one can use the existence of rules, namely a sequence of relations. Previous works view rules as paths and primarily focus on the searching of paths between entities. The space of rules is huge, and one has to sacrifice either efficiency or accuracy. In this paper, we consider rules as cycles and show that the space of cycles has a unique structure based on the mathematics of algebraic topology. By exploring the linear structure of the cycle space, we can improve the searching efficiency of rules. We propose to collect cycle bases that span the space of cycles. We build a novel GNN framework on the collected cycles to learn the representations of cycles, and to predict the existence/non-existence of a relation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks.

paragraphs: Predicting missing relations in a knowledge graph can depend on rules expressed as sequences of existing relations. Searching for such rules is difficult because there are many possible sequences. This paper addresses inductive relation prediction by changing how those rules are represented and searched, drawing on the mathematics of algebraic topology.

Previous approaches primarily treat rules as paths between entities. The authors instead view them as cycles and exploit the linear structure of the cycle space. They collect cycle bases that span this space, providing a structured way to represent its possibilities. The purpose is to improve rule-search efficiency without facing the same direct tradeoff between searching extensively and maintaining accuracy.

A graph neural network then learns representations of the collected cycles and uses them to predict whether a relation exists. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks. The distinctive contribution is the connection between a mathematical organization of graph cycles and a learned predictor: the cycle structure guides what information is collected before the neural network learns from it.
summary.tldr: Representing relational rules through cycle bases lets a graph neural network search structured rule information more efficiently and achieve strong benchmark results.

title: Cycle Representation Learning for Inductive Relation Prediction

abstract: A misspecified reward can degrade sample efficiency and induce undesired behaviors in reinforcement learning (RL) problems. We propose symbolic reward machines for incorporating high-level task knowledge when specifying the reward signals. Symbolic reward machines augment existing reward machine formalism by allowing transitions to carry predicates and symbolic reward outputs. This formalism lends itself well to inverse reinforcement learning, whereby the key challenge is determining appropriate assignments to the symbolic values from a few expert demonstrations. We propose a hierarchical Bayesian approach for inferring the most likely assignments such that the concretized reward machine can discriminate expert demonstrated trajectories from other trajectories with high accuracy. Experimental results show that learned reward machines can significantly improve training efficiency for complex RL tasks and generalize well across different task environment configurations.

Symbolic reward machines augment existing reward machine formalism by allowing transitions to carry predicates and symbolic reward outputs. This formalism lends itself well to inverse reinforcement learning, whereby the key challenge is determining appropriate assignments to the symbolic values from a few expert demonstrations. We propose a hierarchical Bayesian approach for inferring the most likely assignments such that the concretized reward machine can discriminate expert demonstrated trajectories from other trajectories with high accuracy. Experimental results show that learned reward machines can significantly improve training efficiency for complex RL tasks and generalize well across different task environment configurations.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can learn inefficiently or develop unwanted behavior when its reward does not properly express the intended task. This paper proposes symbolic reward machines as a way to combine high-level task knowledge with reward learning. They extend reward machines by allowing their transitions to contain predicates and symbolic reward outputs.

The symbolic values leave parts of the reward specification to be inferred from demonstrations. The central problem is assigning those values using only a few examples of expert behavior. The authors develop a hierarchical Bayesian approach that seeks likely assignments under which the completed reward machine distinguishes expert trajectories from other trajectories with high accuracy.

This approach gives task structure and demonstrations complementary roles: the structure expresses high-level knowledge, while demonstrations help determine its concrete reward values. Experiments show that the learned machines can substantially improve training efficiency on complex reinforcement learning tasks and generalize across different environment configurations. These results support learning rewards within a structured representation rather than specifying every reward value manually.
summary.tldr: Symbolic reward machines combine task knowledge with Bayesian inference from a few expert demonstrations to learn rewards that improve reinforcement learning efficiency.

title: A Hierarchical Bayesian Approach to Inverse Reinforcement Learning with Symbolic Reward Machines

abstract: Paging is a prototypical problem in the area of online algorithms. It has also played a central role in the development of learning-augmented algorithms. Previous work on learning-augmented paging has investigated predictions on (i) when the current page will be requested again (reoccurrence predictions), (ii) the current state of the cache in an optimal algorithm (state predictions), (iii) all requests until the current page gets requested again, and (iv) the relative order in which pages are requested. We study learning-augmented paging from the new perspective of requiring the least possible amount of predicted information. More specifically, the predictions obtained alongside each page request are limited to one bit only. We develop algorithms satisfy all three desirable properties of learning-augmented algorithms – that is, they are consistent, robust and smooth – despite being limited to a one-bit prediction per request. We also present lower bounds establishing that our algorithms are essentially best possible.
