paragraphs: Paging algorithms decide which requested items to keep in a cache as requests arrive. Learning-augmented approaches help those decisions with predictions about the future. Earlier work considered information such as a page's next request time, future request order, or the contents of an optimal cache. This paper asks how little predicted information can still be useful.

The authors restrict the prediction accompanying each request to a single bit. Despite that severe information limit, they construct algorithms with all three standard desirable properties: consistency, robustness, and smoothness. In plain terms, the algorithms benefit from accurate predictions, retain protection when predictions are poor, and degrade gradually as prediction quality worsens.

The paper also proves lower bounds showing that its algorithms are essentially best possible. Those bounds complement the constructions by limiting how much better another algorithm could do in the studied setting. The contribution demonstrates that helpful prediction interfaces can be extremely compact: strong paging guarantees do not always require detailed forecasts of future requests or complete descriptions of an optimal cache.
summary.tldr: One prediction bit per page request is enough for paging algorithms with consistency, robustness, smoothness, and essentially optimal guarantees.

title: Paging with Succinct Predictions

abstract: The generalization performance of machine learning methods depends heavily on the quality of data representation. However, existing researches rarely consider representation learning from the perspective of generalization error. In this paper, we prove that generalization error of representation learning function can be estimated effectively by solving two convex optimization problems. Based on it, we propose a general representation learning framework. And then, we apply the proposed framework to two most commonly used nonlinear mapping methods, i.e., kernel based method and deep neural network (DNN), and thus design a kernel selection method and a DNN boosting framework, correspondingly. Finally, extensive experiments verify the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

A representation changes how a model sees its inputs, so its quality can strongly affect generalization. The authors make generalization error a direct basis for designing representation learning methods, connecting the choice of representation to performance beyond the training examples.

Their central theoretical result shows that the generalization error of a representation learning function can be effectively estimated by solving two convex optimization problems. This turns an otherwise difficult assessment into a pair of structured optimization tasks. The authors use that result to build a general framework for learning representations with attention to their generalization performance.

They then instantiate the framework for two common forms of nonlinear representation: kernel methods and deep neural networks. These applications produce a kernel selection method and a boosting framework for deep networks. Experiments support the effectiveness of the resulting methods. The contribution therefore connects a theoretical way to estimate generalization error with concrete procedures for choosing or improving representations.
summary.tldr: The paper builds a representation learning framework around generalization-error estimation using two convex optimization problems.

title: A General Representation Learning Framework with Generalization Performance Guarantees

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm to learn from relational data mostly through applying the message passing mechanism. However, this approach may exhibit suboptimal performance when applied to graphs possessing various structural issues. In this work, we focus on understanding and alleviating the effect of graph structural noise on GNN performance. To evaluate the graph structural noise in real data, we propose edge signal-to-noise ratio (ESNR), a novel metric evaluating overall edge noise level with respect to data features or labels based on random matrix theory. We have found striking concordance between the proposed ESNR metric and the GNN performance in various simulated and real data. To reduce the effect of the noise, we propose GPS (Graph Propensity Score) graph rewiring, which estimates the edge likelihood for rewiring data graphs based on self-supervised link prediction. We provide a theoretical guarantee for GPS graph rewiring and demonstrate its efficacy by comprehensive benchmarks.

This paper addresses both measuring such noise and reducing its effect. Its starting point is that edge quality should be assessed relative to the data’s features or labels, rather than considering graph structure alone.

The authors propose edge signal-to-noise ratio, or ESNR, using random matrix theory to evaluate the overall level of edge noise. They find strong agreement between this metric and GNN performance on simulated and real data. This provides evidence that the measure captures a structural property relevant to learning, though the reported agreement is an empirical finding.

To improve the graph, the paper introduces Graph Propensity Score rewiring. GPS estimates edge likelihoods through self-supervised link prediction and uses those estimates to rewire the data graph. The authors provide a theoretical guarantee and benchmark evidence for the method. The combined contribution supplies a diagnostic measure and a learning-based approach to changing noisy connections.
summary.tldr: The paper measures graph edge noise with ESNR and reduces its effects through self-supervised, likelihood-based GPS rewiring.

title: Towards Understanding and Reducing Graph Structural Noise for GNNs

abstract: Training a neural network requires choosing a suitable learning rate, which involves a trade-off between speed and effectiveness of convergence. While there has been considerable theoretical and empirical analysis of how large the learning rate can be, most prior work focuses only on late-stage training. In this work, we introduce the maximal initial learning rate $\eta^{\ast}$ - the largest learning rate at which a randomly initialized neural network can successfully begin training and achieve (at least) a given threshold accuracy. Using a simple approach to estimate $\eta^{\ast}$, we observe that in constant-width fully-connected ReLU networks, $\eta^{\ast}$ behaves differently from the maximum learning rate later in training. Specifically, we find that $\eta^{\ast}$ is well predicted as a power of depth $\times$ width, provided that (i) the width of the network is sufficiently large compared to the depth, and (ii) the input layer is trained at a relatively small learning rate. We further analyze the relationship between $\eta^{\ast}$ and the sharpness $\lambda_{1}$ of the network at initialization, indicating they are closely though not inversely related. We formally prove bounds for $\lambda_{1}$ in terms of depth $\times$ width that align with our empirical results.

It proves sharpness bounds in terms of depth times width that agree with the empirical observations. These results clarify how network dimensions relate to early training behavior while preserving the distinction between empirical learning-rate scaling and formally established sharpness bounds.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes the largest successful starting learning rate in deep ReLU networks and connects its conditional scaling to initialization sharpness.

title: Maximal Initial Learning Rates in Deep ReLU Networks

abstract: Generative flow networks (GFlowNets) are amortized variational inference algorithms that are trained to sample from unnormalized target distributions over compositional objects. A key limitation of GFlowNets until this time has been that they are restricted to discrete spaces. We present a theory for generalized GFlowNets, which encompasses both existing discrete GFlowNets and ones with continuous or hybrid state spaces, and perform experiments with two goals in mind. First, we illustrate critical points of the theory and the importance of various assumptions. Second, we empirically demonstrate how observations about discrete GFlowNets transfer to the continuous case and show strong results compared to non-GFlowNet baselines on several previously studied tasks. This work greatly widens the perspectives for the application of GFlowNets in probabilistic inference and various modeling settings.

paragraphs: Generative flow networks learn to sample compositional objects according to a target distribution whose normalization need not be known. The paper addresses a restriction of the existing framework: its focus on discrete spaces. That restriction limits the kinds of variables and modeling problems the framework can directly describe.

The authors develop a generalized theory that includes discrete, continuous, and hybrid state spaces. A hybrid space can contain both discrete and continuous elements. Bringing these cases into one theory makes the extension more than a separate continuous variant: the existing discrete formulation is included within the broader framework.

They illustrate important parts of the theory and why its assumptions matter, and they test whether observations from discrete GFlowNets carry over to continuous settings. The authors report such empirical transfer and strong results against non-GFlowNet baselines on several previously studied tasks. The contribution therefore combines a broader mathematical foundation with evidence that the extension can be useful for probabilistic inference and modeling.
summary.tldr: A generalized GFlowNet theory covers discrete, continuous, and hybrid spaces, with experiments supporting its continuous-space applications.

title: A theory of continuous generative flow networks

abstract: We study the problem of histogram estimation under user-level differential privacy, where the goal is to preserve the privacy of all entries of any single user. We consider the heterogeneous scenario where the quantity of data can be different for each user. In this scenario, the amount of noise injected into the histogram to obtain differential privacy is proportional to the maximum user contribution, which can be amplified by few outliers. One approach to circumvent this would be to bound (or limit) the contribution of each user to the histogram. However, if users are limited to small contributions, a significant amount of data will be discarded. In this work, we propose algorithms to choose the best user contribution bound for histogram estimation under both bounded and unbounded domain settings. When the size of the domain is bounded, we propose a user contribution bounding strategy that almost achieves a two-approximation with respect to the best contribution bound in hindsight. For unbounded domain histogram estimation, we propose an algorithm that is logarithmic-approximation with respect to the best contribution bound in hindsight. This result holds without any distribution assumptions on the data. Experiments on both real and synthetic datasets verify our theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms. We also show that clipping bias introduced by bounding user contribution may be reduced under mild distribution assumptions, which can be of independent interest.

Because the required noise grows with the largest contribution, a few unusually prolific users can substantially reduce accuracy. Capping contributions controls that noise, but setting the cap too low discards useful data.

This paper develops algorithms for selecting the contribution cap in two settings. For a bounded domain, the proposed strategy nearly achieves a two-approximation relative to the best cap chosen with hindsight. For an unbounded domain, it provides a logarithmic approximation relative to that hindsight choice, without assuming a particular data distribution.

These guarantees address the practical trade-off between privacy noise and information lost through clipping. Experiments on real and synthetic data support the theoretical findings and the algorithms’ effectiveness. The authors also show that clipping bias may be reduced under mild distribution assumptions; that additional result has assumptions distinct from the distribution-free unbounded-domain approximation guarantee.
summary.tldr: The paper develops principled contribution caps that balance discarded data against privacy noise when estimating user-private histograms.

title: Algorithms for bounding contribution for histogram estimation under user-level privacy

abstract: Recent studies have revealed the intriguing few-shot learning ability of pretrained language models (PLMs): They can quickly adapt to a new task when fine-tuned on a small amount of labeled data formulated as prompts, without requiring abundant task-specific annotations. Despite their promising performance, most existing few-shot approaches that only learn from the small training set still underperform fully supervised training by nontrivial margins. In this work, we study few-shot learning with PLMs from a different perspective: We first tune an autoregressive PLM on the few-shot samples and then use it as a generator to synthesize a large amount of novel training samples which augment the original training set. To encourage the generator to produce label-discriminative samples, we train it via weighted maximum likelihood where the weight of each token is automatically adjusted based on a discriminative meta-learning objective. A classification PLM can then be fine-tuned on both the few-shot and the synthetic samples with regularization for better generalization and stability. Our approach FewGen achieves an overall better result across seven classification tasks of the GLUE benchmark than existing few-shot learning methods, improving no-augmentation methods by 5+ average points, and outperforming augmentation methods by 3+ average points.

paragraphs: Few-shot language-model training starts with very few labeled examples, leaving a substantial performance gap relative to fully supervised learning. FewGen addresses the shortage by first tuning an autoregressive language model on the available examples, then using it to generate a larger synthetic training set.

The generator is trained to produce samples that help distinguish labels. Its maximum-likelihood objective assigns adjustable weights to individual tokens, with a discriminative meta-learning objective determining those weights automatically. A classification language model then trains on both original and generated examples, using regularization to improve generalization and stability.

Across seven GLUE classification tasks, FewGen achieves better overall results than existing few-shot methods. The reported average improvement exceeds five points over methods without augmentation and three points over augmentation methods. These findings support tuning the generator specifically for the classification value of its samples. The approach uses the small labeled set to shape additional training data, then transfers that expanded supervision to the classifier.
summary.tldr: FewGen tunes a language model to generate label-discriminative training examples, improving few-shot classification across seven GLUE tasks.

title: Tuning Language Models as Training Data Generators for Augmentation-Enhanced Few-Shot Learning

abstract: Wider adoption of neural networks in many critical domains such as finance and healthcare is being hindered by the need to explain their predictions and to impose additional constraints on them. Monotonicity constraint is one of the most requested properties in real-world scenarios and is the focus of this paper. One of the oldest ways to construct a monotonic fully connected neural network is to constrain signs on its weights. Unfortunately, this construction does not work with popular non-saturated activation functions as it can only approximate convex functions. We show this shortcoming can be fixed by constructing two additional activation functions from a typical unsaturated monotonic activation function and employing each of them on the part of neurons. Our experiments show this approach of building monotonic neural networks has better accuracy when compared to other state-of-the-art methods, while being the simplest one in the sense of having the least number of parameters, and not requiring any modifications to the learning procedure or post-learning steps. Finally, we prove it can approximate any continuous monotone function on a compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

paragraphs: A monotonic prediction must move in a specified direction when a relevant input increases. Such constraints are useful when a model must respect known relationships, particularly in areas such as finance and healthcare. A traditional neural-network construction enforces monotonicity by restricting weight signs, but with popular unsaturated activations this approach can only approximate convex functions.

The paper expands that construction by deriving two additional activation functions from a typical unsaturated monotonic activation. Different subsets of neurons use these related activations. This preserves the desired monotonic behavior while overcoming the restriction to convex shapes, making the model capable of expressing a broader range of constrained relationships.

The authors prove that the resulting network can approximate any continuous monotone function on a compact subset of a finite-dimensional real space. Their experiments report better accuracy than the compared state-of-the-art methods with fewer parameters. The construction also requires neither changes to the learning procedure nor additional steps after learning, making the expressiveness result relevant to a comparatively simple training workflow.
summary.tldr: A simple activation-function construction makes sign-constrained monotonic networks more expressive without changing their training procedure.

title: Constrained Monotonic Neural Networks

abstract: This manuscript considers the problem of learning a random Gaussian network function using a fully connected network with frozen intermediate layers and trainable readout layer. This problem can be seen as a natural generalization of the widely studied random features model to deeper architectures. First, we prove Gaussian universality of the test error in a ridge regression setting where the learner and target networks share the same intermediate layers, and provide a sharp asymptotic formula for it. Establishing this result requires proving a deterministic equivalent for traces of the deep random features sample covariance matrices which can be of independent interest. Second, we conjecture the asymptotic Gaussian universality of the test error in the more general setting of arbitrary convex losses and generic learner/target architectures. We provide extensive numerical evidence for this conjecture, which requires the derivation of closed-form expressions for the layer-wise post-activation population covariances. In light of our results, we investigate the interplay between architecture design and implicit regularization.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes learning with deep networks whose intermediate layers remain frozen while only the output layer is trained. The target is itself a random Gaussian network function. This extends the random features setting to deeper architectures and allows the authors to examine how architecture influences prediction error without training every layer.

For ridge regression, when the learner and target share their intermediate layers, the authors prove Gaussian universality of test error and derive a sharp asymptotic formula. Establishing this result involves a deterministic equivalent for traces of deep random feature covariance matrices: a predictable mathematical expression for quantities that otherwise depend on random matrices.

In this broader setting, Gaussian universality remains a conjecture supported by extensive numerical evidence, rather than a proved result. Closed-form layerwise covariance expressions support this analysis. Together, the results provide a way to investigate how network architecture interacts with implicit regularization and generalization.
summary.tldr: The paper proves test-error universality for a specific deep random features setting and provides numerical evidence for a broader conjecture.

title: Deterministic equivalent and error universality of deep random features learning

abstract: We demonstrate a substantial gap between the privacy guarantees of the Adaptive Batch Linear Queries (ABLQ) mechanism under different types of batch sampling: (i) Shuffling, and (ii) Poisson subsampling; the typical analysis of Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) follows by interpreting it as a post-processing of ABLQ. While shuffling-based DP-SGD is more commonly used in practical implementations, it has not been amenable to easy privacy analysis, either analytically or even numerically. On the other hand, Poisson subsampling-based DP-SGD is challenging to scalably implement, but has a well-understood privacy analysis, with multiple open-source numerically tight privacy accountants available. This has led to a common practice of using shuffling-based DP-SGD in practice, but using the privacy analysis for the corresponding Poisson subsampling version. Our result shows that there can be a substantial gap between the privacy analysis when using the two types of batch sampling, and thus advises caution in reporting privacy parameters for DP-SGD.

paragraphs: Privacy guarantees for differentially private stochastic gradient descent depend on how training batches are sampled. Practical implementations commonly use shuffling, whereas well-developed privacy analyses often assume Poisson subsampling. The paper examines the consequences of using an analysis for one sampling procedure to describe an implementation using the other.

The authors study Adaptive Batch Linear Queries, a mechanism through which the usual DP-SGD privacy analysis can be understood by post-processing. They demonstrate that its privacy guarantees can differ substantially between shuffling and Poisson subsampling. This directly challenges the practice of treating the two sampling schemes as interchangeable when reporting privacy parameters.

The mismatch arises from a practical tension: shuffling has been difficult to analyze even numerically, while Poisson sampling has strong accounting tools but is challenging to implement scalably. The result establishes that a substantial gap can occur, rather than claiming that every shuffled implementation suffers the same discrepancy. Its implication is that reported privacy guarantees require careful attention to the batch-sampling procedure actually used.
summary.tldr: Privacy analyses for Poisson-sampled DP-SGD can differ substantially from those for shuffled batches, challenging a common implementation-accounting mismatch.

title: How Private are DP-SGD Implementations?

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have a risk of remembering sensitive data from their training datasets, inadvertently leading to substantial information leakage through privacy attacks like membership inference attacks. DP-SGD is a simple but effective defense method, incorporating Gaussian noise into gradient updates to safeguard sensitive information. With the prevalence of large neural networks, DP-signSGD, a variant of DP-SGD, has emerged, aiming to curtail memory usage while maintaining security. However, it is noteworthy that most DP-signSGD algorithms default to Gaussian noise, suitable only for DP-SGD, without scant discussion of its appropriateness for signSGD. Our study delves into an intriguing question: "Can we find a more efficient substitute for Gaussian noise to secure privacy in DP-signSGD?" We propose an answer with a Logistic mechanism, which conforms to signSGD principles and is interestingly evolved from an exponential mechanism. In this paper, we provide both theoretical and experimental evidence showing that our method surpasses DP-signSGD.

paragraphs: Neural networks can retain sensitive information from training data, creating exposure to attacks such as membership inference. Differentially private SGD addresses this through noisy gradient updates. Its sign-based variant, DP-signSGD, seeks to reduce memory demands while preserving privacy, but many implementations carry over Gaussian noise from the original gradient-update setting.

The central design decision is to match the privacy mechanism to the discrete update procedure, treating the choice of noise distribution as part of the optimizer's design.

The authors provide theoretical and experimental evidence that their method surpasses DP-signSGD. The stated contribution is therefore both a mechanism tailored to sign-based updates and evidence supporting that substitution. The work highlights that a privacy mechanism used with one optimization procedure deserves renewed analysis when the update representation changes, especially when the motivation for that change includes the memory requirements of large neural networks.
summary.tldr: A Logistic privacy mechanism tailored to signSGD offers a theoretically and experimentally supported alternative to Gaussian-noise DP-signSGD.

title: Rethinking DP-SGD in Discrete Domain: Exploring Logistic Distribution in the Realm of signSGD

abstract: Novel reinforcement learning algorithms, or improvements on existing ones, are commonly justified by evaluating their performance on benchmark environments and are compared to an ever-changing set of standard algorithms. However, despite numerous calls for improvements, experimental practices continue to produce misleading or unsupported claims. One reason for the ongoing substandard practices is that conducting rigorous benchmarking experiments requires substantial computational time. This work investigates the sources of increased computation costs in rigorous experiment designs. We show that conducting rigorous performance benchmarks will likely have computational costs that are often prohibitive. As a result, we argue for using an additional experimentation paradigm to overcome the limitations of benchmarking.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning research often evaluates a new algorithm by comparing its performance with standard algorithms on benchmark environments. This position paper questions how much that practice can reliably establish under realistic computational constraints. Its concern is that experiments continue to support misleading or insufficiently justified claims despite repeated calls for better evaluation.

The authors investigate why rigorous experimental designs require more computation. Their argument connects the quality of the evidence to the resources needed to obtain it: making benchmark comparisons reliable can demand substantial computational time. They conclude that the costs of rigorous performance benchmarking are likely to be prohibitive in many cases.

The paper therefore advocates an additional experimentation paradigm to complement benchmarking. It presents a methodological argument about how research evidence is produced, rather than a new reinforcement-learning algorithm. Its implication is that improving scientific practice requires considering whether the desired experiment is computationally feasible, alongside whether it is rigorous. Benchmark results remain part of the research process, but the authors argue that additional forms of experimentation are needed to address their limitations.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that rigorous reinforcement-learning benchmarking is often prohibitively costly and should be complemented by another experimentation paradigm.

title: Position: Benchmarking is Limited in Reinforcement Learning Research

abstract: Real-time inference is a challenge of real-world reinforcement learning due to temporal differences in time-varying environments: the system collects data from the past, updates the decision model in the present, and deploys it in the future. We tackle a common belief that continually updating the decision is optimal to minimize the temporal gap. We propose forecasting an online reinforcement learning framework and show that strategically pausing decision updates yields better overall performance by effectively managing aleatoric uncertainty. Theoretically, we compute an optimal ratio between policy update and hold duration, and show that a non-zero policy hold duration provides a sharper upper bound on the dynamic regret. Our experimental evaluations on three different environments also reveal that a non-zero policy hold duration yields higher rewards compared to continuous decision updates.

paragraphs: In a changing environment, reinforcement learning faces a timing mismatch: observations describe the past, training happens in the present, and the updated policy acts in the future. This paper questions whether continuously updating the policy is always the best response to that mismatch. It studies when deliberately holding a policy fixed can improve overall performance.

The authors propose a forecasting framework for online reinforcement learning that strategically alternates policy updates with periods of holding the policy unchanged. The approach manages aleatoric uncertainty, meaning randomness inherent in observations or outcomes. Their theoretical analysis computes an optimal ratio between update time and hold time and gives a sharper upper bound on dynamic regret with a nonzero hold duration.

Experiments in three environments also produce higher rewards when the policy is held for a nonzero duration than when decisions are continuously updated. These results give both theoretical and empirical support for scheduling pauses in policy learning. The finding is about managing adaptation timing in the studied changing environments, rather than assuming that more frequent updates necessarily help.
summary.tldr: Strategic pauses in policy updates improve theoretical regret bounds and experimental rewards in the studied non-stationary reinforcement learning settings.

title: Pausing Policy Learning in Non-stationary Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We propose SPHINX-X, an extensive Multi-modality Large Language Model (MLLM) series developed upon SPHINX. To improve the architecture and training efficiency, we modify the SPHINX framework by removing redundant visual encoders, bypassing fully-padded sub-images with skip tokens, and simplifying multi-stage training into a one-stage all-in-one paradigm. To fully unleash the potential of MLLMs, we assemble a comprehensive multi-domain and multi-modal dataset covering publicly available resources in language, vision, and vision-language tasks. We further enrich this collection with our curated OCR intensive and Set-of-Mark datasets, extending the diversity and generality. By training over different base LLMs including TinyLlama-1.1B, InternLM2-7B, LLaMA2-13B, and Mixtral-8$\times$7B, we obtain a spectrum of MLLMs that vary in parameter size and multilingual capabilities. Comprehensive benchmarking reveals a strong correlation between the multi-modal performance with the data and parameter scales. Code and models are released at https://github.com/Alpha-VLLM/LLaMA2-Accessory.

paragraphs: SPHINX-X is a family of multimodal language models built by revising the SPHINX architecture and expanding its training data. The paper combines improvements to training efficiency with a study of models at different parameter scales. This creates a common framework for investigating how data and model size relate to multimodal performance.

The architecture removes redundant visual encoders, uses skip tokens for fully padded sub-images, and replaces multistage training with one combined stage. The authors assemble public language, vision, and vision-language resources, adding curated OCR-intensive and Set-of-Mark datasets. These changes address both the processing pipeline and the breadth of information available during training.

Training on TinyLlama-1.1B, InternLM2-7B, LLaMA2-13B, and Mixtral-8×7B produces models with different sizes and multilingual capabilities. Extensive benchmarking finds a strong correlation between multimodal performance and the scales of data and parameters. The finding describes an observed relationship across the evaluated family, while the broader contribution is a streamlined framework and expanded data collection for developing models across that range.
summary.tldr: SPHINX-X streamlines multimodal training and expands data, finding strong performance correlations with data and parameter scale.

title: SPHINX-X: Scaling Data and Parameters for a Family of Multi-modal Large Language Models

abstract: Robotic behavior synthesis, the problem of understanding multimodal inputs and generating precise physical control for robots, is an important part of Embodied AI. Despite successes in applying multimodal large language models for high-level understanding, it remains challenging to translate these conceptual understandings into detailed robotic actions while achieving generalization across various scenarios. In this paper, we propose a tree-structured multimodal code generation framework for generalized robotic behavior synthesis, termed RoboCodeX. RoboCodeX decomposes high-level human instructions into multiple object-centric manipulation units consisting of physical preferences such as affordance and safety constraints, and applies code generation to introduce generalization ability across various robotics platforms. To further enhance the capability to map conceptual and perceptual understanding into control commands, a specialized multimodal reasoning dataset is collected for pre-training and an iterative self-updating methodology is introduced for supervised fine-tuning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RoboCodeX achieves state-of-the-art performance in both simulators and real robots on four different kinds of manipulation tasks and one embodied navigation task.

paragraphs: Understanding a human instruction and turning it into precise robot actions are different challenges. RoboCodeX addresses the connection between them: it uses multimodal information and generated code to synthesize robotic behavior, aiming to generalize across scenarios and robotic platforms.

The framework organizes code generation as a tree and breaks high-level instructions into object-centered manipulation units. These units incorporate physical considerations, including affordances and safety constraints, so the decomposition includes information about how objects can be manipulated. A specialized multimodal reasoning dataset supports pretraining, while an iterative self-updating method supports supervised fine-tuning. Both are intended to strengthen the mapping from conceptual and perceptual understanding to control commands.

Experiments cover four kinds of manipulation tasks and one embodied navigation task, using simulators and real robots. The authors report state-of-the-art performance across these evaluations. The findings support structured decomposition and code generation as a way to connect multimodal understanding with executable robotic behavior in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: RoboCodeX decomposes multimodal instructions into object-centered units and generates code for robotic manipulation and navigation.

title: RoboCodeX: Multimodal Code Generation for Robotic Behavior Synthesis

abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) / machine learning (ML) gain widespread adoption, practitioners are increasingly seeking means to quantify and control the risk these systems incur. This challenge is especially salient when such systems have autonomy to collect their own data, such as in black-box optimization and active learning, where their actions induce sequential feedback-loop shifts in the data distribution. Conformal prediction is a promising approach to uncertainty and risk quantification, but prior variants’ validity guarantees have assumed some form of “quasi-exchangeability” on the data distribution, thereby excluding many types of sequential shifts. In this paper we prove that conformal prediction can theoretically be extended to any joint data distribution, not just exchangeable or quasi-exchangeable ones. Although the most general case is exceedingly impractical to compute, for concrete practical applications we outline a procedure for deriving specific conformal algorithms for any data distribution, and we use this procedure to derive tractable algorithms for a series of AI/ML-agent-induced covariate shifts. We evaluate the proposed algorithms empirically on synthetic black-box optimization and active learning tasks.

paragraphs: When a learning system chooses what data to collect, its decisions can change the distribution of future observations. Black-box optimization and active learning create exactly this kind of feedback. Such sequential changes can fall outside the exchangeability-like assumptions used by previous conformal prediction guarantees.

The paper proves that conformal prediction can theoretically accommodate any joint data distribution. This expands the scope of possible validity guarantees beyond exchangeable and quasi-exchangeable settings. However, computing the construction in its most general form is exceedingly impractical. The existence result therefore establishes what is theoretically possible without claiming a universally convenient implementation.

To make the theory useful, the authors outline a procedure for deriving conformal algorithms for specific distributions. They apply it to several forms of agent-induced covariate shift and obtain tractable algorithms. Evaluations use synthetic black-box optimization and active learning tasks. The practical contribution is a route from a specified pattern of sequential distribution change to an appropriate conformal procedure.
summary.tldr: Conformal validity extends theoretically to any joint distribution, with tractable constructions for selected agent-induced shifts.

title: Conformal Validity Guarantees Exist for Any Data Distribution (and How to Find Them)

abstract: Value-based reinforcement learning is the current State-Of-The-Art due to high sampling efficiency. However, our study shows it suffers from low exploitation in early training period and bias sensitiveness. To address these issues, we propose to augment the decision-making process with hypothesis, a weak form of environment description. Our approach relies on prompting the learning agent with accurate hypotheses, and designing a ready-to-adapt policy through incremental learning. We propose the ALH algorithm, showing detailed analyses on a typical learning scheme and a diverse set of Mujoco benchmarks. Our algorithm produces a significant improvement over value-based learning algorithms and other strong baselines. Our code is available at Github URL.

paragraphs: The paper examines a weakness in value-based reinforcement learning despite its strong sample efficiency. The authors find that these methods can make limited use of available knowledge early in training and can be sensitive to bias. Their focus is on improving how the agent chooses actions during learning, particularly when its learned values are still developing.

The proposed approach adds hypotheses to the decision process. A hypothesis is a limited description of the environment that gives the agent additional guidance. The method relies on these hypotheses being accurate and combines them with incremental learning to build a policy that is ready to adapt. ALH is the algorithm developed around this combination of descriptive guidance and policy adaptation.

The authors analyze a representative learning scheme and evaluate ALH on a varied collection of MuJoCo benchmarks. They report significant improvements over value-based methods and other strong baselines. These findings support using accurate environmental hypotheses to improve decisions, with the accuracy of that guidance remaining an explicit requirement of the approach.
summary.tldr: ALH combines accurate environmental hypotheses with incremental policy learning to improve reinforcement-learning decisions and reported benchmark performance.

title: Augmenting Decision with Hypothesis in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: While modern best practices advocate for scalable architectures that support long-range interactions, object-centric models are yet to fully embrace these architectures. In particular, existing object-centric models for handling sequential inputs, due to their reliance on RNN-based implementation, show poor stability and capacity and are slow to train on long sequences. We introduce Parallelizable Spatiotemporal Binder or PSB, the first temporally-parallelizable slot learning architecture for sequential inputs. Unlike conventional RNN-based approaches, PSB produces object-centric representations, known as slots, for all time-steps in parallel. This is achieved by refining the initial slots across all time-steps through a fixed number of layers equipped with causal attention. By capitalizing on the parallelism induced by our architecture, the proposed model exhibits a significant boost in efficiency. In experiments, we test PSB extensively as an encoder within an auto-encoding framework paired with a wide variety of decoder options. Compared to the state-of-the-art, our architecture demonstrates stable training on longer sequences, achieves parallelization that results in a 60% increase in training speed, and yields performance that is on par with or better on unsupervised 2D and 3D object-centric scene decomposition and understanding.

paragraphs: Object-centric video models represent scenes using slots, with each slot providing a representation organized around an object. Existing approaches often process sequences through recurrent networks, which can make long sequences slow to train on and create difficulties with stability and capacity. This paper introduces an architecture that parallelizes slot learning across time.

The Parallelizable Spatiotemporal Binder, or PSB, refines initial slots for all time steps through a fixed number of layers equipped with causal attention. Producing the slots in parallel creates an opportunity for more efficient training while retaining a mechanism for interactions across the sequence.

The authors evaluate PSB as an encoder in an autoencoding framework with a variety of decoders. Compared with state-of-the-art approaches, the experiments show stable training on longer sequences and a reported 60% increase in training speed. Performance on unsupervised 2D and 3D scene decomposition and understanding is comparable or better. These results connect the architectural change to both computational benefits and the quality of the learned object-centric representations.
summary.tldr: PSB learns video object slots across time in parallel, reporting 60% faster training and comparable or better scene-understanding performance.

title: Parallelized Spatiotemporal Slot Binding for Videos

abstract: Regression trees are a human-comprehensible machine-learning model that can represent complex relationships. They are typically trained using greedy heuristics because computing optimal regression trees is NP-hard. Contrary to this standard practice, we consider optimal methods and improve the scalability of optimal methods by developing three new dynamic programming approaches. First, we improve the performance of a piecewise constant regression tree method using a special algorithm for trees of depth two. Second, we provide the first optimal dynamic programming method for piecewise multiple linear regression. Third, we develop the first optimal method for piecewise simple linear regression, for which we also provide a special algorithm for trees of depth two. The experimental results show that our methods improve scalability by one or more orders of magnitude over the state-of-the-art optimal methods while performing similarly or better in out-of-sample performance.

paragraphs: Regression trees describe complex relationships through understandable branching decisions. Finding an optimal tree is NP-hard, so training usually relies on greedy choices. This paper works on optimal methods directly, developing dynamic programming approaches that make exact optimization more scalable for trees whose regions contain either constant or linear predictions.

There are three main contributions. A specialized algorithm for depth-two trees improves a piecewise constant regression tree method. A second approach provides the first optimal dynamic programming method for piecewise multiple linear regression. A third supplies the first optimal method for piecewise simple linear regression, also with a specialized depth-two algorithm. These approaches expand the kinds of predictive models that can be fitted optimally within tree regions.

Experiments show scalability improvements of at least one order of magnitude over state-of-the-art optimal methods, alongside similar or better out-of-sample performance. The results make optimal regression tree construction more practical in the tested settings. They also show that the computational gains need not come at the expense of predictive performance on unseen data.
summary.tldr: New dynamic programming methods make optimal constant and linear regression trees substantially more scalable while preserving or improving tested predictive performance.

title: Piecewise Constant and Linear Regression Trees: An Optimal Dynamic Programming Approach

abstract: We take the first step in studying general sequential decision-making under two adaptivity constraints: rare policy switch and batch learning. First, we provide a general class called the Eluder Condition class, which includes a wide range of reinforcement learning classes. Then, for the rare policy switch constraint, we provide a generic algorithm to achieve a $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\log K) $ switching cost with a $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{K})$ regret on the EC class. For the batch learning constraint, we provide an algorithm that provides a $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{K}+K/B)$ regret with the number of batches $B.$ This paper is the first work considering rare policy switch and batch learning under general function classes, which covers nearly all the models studied in the previous works such as tabular MDP (Bai et al. 2019, Zhang et al. 2020), linear MDP (Wang et al. 2021, Gao et al. 2021), low eluder dimension MDP (Kong et al., 2021; Velegkas et al., 2022), generalized linear function approximation (Qiao et al. 2023), and also some new classes such as the low $D_\Delta$-type Bellman eluder dimension problem, linear mixture MDP, kernelized nonlinear regulator and undercomplete partially observed Markov decision process (POMDP).

paragraphs: A sequential decision maker may be unable to revise its behavior whenever new information arrives. This paper studies two forms of that restriction: changing policies only rarely, and learning from observations in batches. Its goal is to understand how much performance can be retained when opportunities to adapt are limited.

The authors introduce the Eluder Condition class, a shared framework covering many reinforcement learning models. Within this class, their rare-switching algorithm achieves regret of order square root of K while requiring switching cost of order log K, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Regret measures accumulated performance loss relative to a comparison policy.

For batch learning, the stated regret scales as square root of K plus K divided by B, again suppressing logarithmic factors, where B is the number of batches. This expresses how fewer learning opportunities can increase the bound. The contribution is a unified analysis spanning previously studied models and additional classes, including some partially observed problems, rather than a separate treatment for each model.
summary.tldr: A unified framework gives regret guarantees for reinforcement learning with rare policy changes or batched updates.

title: A General Framework for Sequential Decision-Making under Adaptivity Constraints

abstract: The popularity of multiagent reinforcement learning (MARL) is growing rapidly with the demand for real-world tasks that require swarm intelligence. However, a noticeable drawback of MARL is its low sample efficiency, which leads to a huge amount of interactions with the environment. Surprisingly, few MARL works focus on this practical problem especially in the parallel environment setting, which greatly hampers the application of MARL into the real world. In response to this gap, in this paper, we propose Multiagent Reinforcement Learning with Reset Replay (MARR) to greatly improve the sample efficiency of MARL by enabling MARL training at a high replay ratio in the parallel environment setting for the first time. To achieve this, first, a reset strategy is introduced for maintaining the network plasticity to ensure that MARL continually learns with a high replay ratio. Second, MARR incorporates a data augmentation technique to boost the sample efficiency further. Extensive experiments in SMAC and MPE show that MARR significantly improves the performance of various MARL approaches with much fewer environment interactions.

paragraphs: Multiagent reinforcement learning can require many interactions with an environment before agents learn effective behavior. This paper focuses on improving that sample efficiency when training uses parallel environments. Its proposed method, Multiagent Reinforcement Learning with Reset Replay, or MARR, aims to obtain more learning from the experience already collected.

MARR supports training at a high replay ratio, meaning collected experience is reused extensively for learning. To sustain that process, it introduces a reset strategy that maintains network plasticity, or the ability to keep learning. It also adds data augmentation to further improve the usefulness of the available training data.

Experiments in SMAC and MPE show that MARR improves the performance of several multiagent reinforcement learning approaches while requiring substantially fewer environment interactions. The results support the combination of repeated data use, maintained learning capacity, and augmentation in the parallel-environment setting. The contribution is an approach to making existing multiagent methods learn more efficiently from their interaction data.
summary.tldr: MARR combines network resets and data augmentation to enable extensive replay and reduce multiagent learning’s need for environment interactions.

title: Sample-Efficient Multiagent Reinforcement Learning with Reset Replay

abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL)—the problem of learning reward functions from demonstrations of an expert policy—plays a critical role in developing intelligent systems. While widely used in applications, theoretical understandings of IRL present unique challenges and remain less developed compared with standard RL. For example, it remains open how to do IRL efficiently in standard offline settings with pre-collected data, where states are obtained from a behavior policy (which could be the expert policy itself), and actions are sampled from the expert policy. This paper provides the first line of results for efficient IRL in vanilla offline and online settings using polynomial samples and runtime. Our algorithms and analyses seamlessly adapt the pessimism principle commonly used in offline RL, and achieve IRL guarantees in stronger metrics than considered in existing work. We provide lower bounds showing that our sample complexities are nearly optimal. As an application, we also show that the learned rewards can transfer to another target MDP with suitable guarantees when the target MDP satisfies certain similarity assumptions with the original (source) MDP.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning infers reward functions from an expert's demonstrations. This paper studies whether that inference can be performed efficiently, especially when learning must use previously collected data. In the offline setting considered, a behavior policy supplies the states and the expert policy supplies the actions; the behavior policy may itself be the expert.

The authors develop algorithms for both offline and online settings with polynomial sample requirements and runtime. Their analysis adapts the pessimism principle used in offline reinforcement learning, taking a conservative approach to uncertainty. They establish guarantees under stronger evaluation metrics than earlier work and derive lower bounds showing that their sample requirements are nearly optimal.

The paper also examines whether inferred rewards remain useful in another Markov decision process. It provides transfer guarantees when the target environment satisfies specified similarity assumptions relative to the source environment. Thus, the contribution addresses both efficient reward inference and conditional reuse of those rewards, with the transfer claim explicitly depending on similarity between the two environments.
summary.tldr: The paper gives efficient offline and online inverse-reinforcement-learning algorithms with nearly optimal sample complexity and reward-transfer guarantees under similarity assumptions.

title: Is Inverse Reinforcement Learning Harder than Standard Reinforcement Learning? A Theoretical Perspective

abstract: Classification is a cornerstone of machine learning research. Most of the existing classifiers assume that the concepts corresponding to classes can be precisely defined. This notion diverges from the widely accepted understanding in cognitive science, which posits that real-world concepts are often inherently ambiguous. To bridge this big gap, we propose a Human Cognition-Inspired Hierarchical Fuzzy Learning Machine (HC-HFLM), which leverages a novel hierarchical alignment loss to integrate rich class knowledge from human knowledge system into learning process. We further theoretically prove that minimizing this loss can align the hierarchical structure derived from data with those contained in class knowledge, resulting in clear semantics and high interpretability. Systematic experiments verify that the proposed method can achieve significant gains in interpretability and generalization performance.
originalAbstract: Classification is a cornerstone of machine learning research. Most of the existing classifiers assume that the concepts corresponding to classes can be precisely defined. This notion diverges from the widely accepted understanding in cognitive science, which posits that real-world concepts are often inherently ambiguous. To bridge this big gap, we propose a Human Cognition-Inspired Hierarchical Fuzzy Learning Machine (HC-HFLM), which leverages a novel hierarchical alignment loss to integrate rich class knowledge from human knowledge system into learning process. We further theoretically prove that minimizing this loss can align the hierarchical structure derived from data with those contained in class knowledge, resulting in clear semantics and high interpretability. Systematic experiments verify that the proposed method can achieve significant gains in interpretability and generalization performance.

paragraphs: Many classifiers treat the concepts represented by their classes as precisely defined. This paper takes inspiration from the cognitive-science view that real-world concepts are often ambiguous. Its Human Cognition-Inspired Hierarchical Fuzzy Learning Machine aims to incorporate human class knowledge into learning while accommodating that ambiguity.

The central mechanism is a hierarchical alignment loss. It brings the hierarchical structure learned from data into correspondence with the structure represented in class knowledge. The authors theoretically prove that minimizing this loss can produce such alignment. This gives the learned hierarchy an explicit semantic connection to the supplied knowledge, supporting interpretation of what the model has learned.

Systematic experiments report significant improvements in both interpretability and generalization. The approach therefore links its training objective, theoretical result, and empirical findings around one idea: relationships among concepts should help organize the classifier’s learned structure. Its significance lies in using class knowledge within the learning process itself, so that predictive learning and semantic organization can support one another.
summary.tldr: HC-HFLM uses a hierarchical alignment loss to connect learned class structure with human knowledge, improving interpretability and generalization in experiments.

title: Human Cognition-Inspired Hierarchical Fuzzy Learning Machine

abstract: Continual Generalized Category Discovery (C-GCD) faces a critical challenge: incrementally learning new classes from unlabeled data streams while preserving knowledge of old classes. Existing methods struggle with catastrophic forgetting, especially when unlabeled data mixes known and novel categories. We address this by analyzing C-GCD’s forgetting dynamics through a Bayesian lens, revealing that covariance misalignment between old and new classes drives performance degradation. Building on this insight, we propose Variational Bayes C-GCD (VB-CGCD), a novel framework that integrates variational inference with covariance-aware nearest-class-mean classification. VB-CGCD adaptively aligns class distributions while suppressing pseudo-label noise via stochastic variational updates. Experiments show VB-CGCD surpasses prior art by +15.21% with the overall accuracy in the final session on standard benchmarks. We also introduce a new challenging benchmark with only 10% labeled data and extended online phases—VB-CGCD achieves a 67.86% final accuracy, significantly higher than state-of-the-art (38.55%), demonstrating its robust applicability across diverse scenarios. Code is available at: https://github.com/daihao42/VB-CGCD

paragraphs: Continual generalized category discovery asks a model to learn new categories from an unlabeled stream while retaining previously learned categories. The challenge intensifies when the stream mixes familiar and unfamiliar classes. This paper analyzes forgetting from a Bayesian perspective and identifies covariance misalignment between old and new classes as a driver of declining performance.

The proposed VB-CGCD framework combines variational inference with a nearest-class-mean classifier that accounts for covariance. Rather than relying only on class centers, the method incorporates how class distributions vary. It adaptively aligns those distributions and uses stochastic variational updates to suppress noise from pseudo-labels, the labels assigned by the model itself.

On standard benchmarks, the authors report a +15.21% improvement over prior art in final-session overall accuracy. They also introduce a harder benchmark with only 10% labeled data and longer online phases. There, VB-CGCD reaches 67.86% final accuracy compared with 38.55% for the stated state of the art. These results support distribution alignment as a useful approach to learning new categories while reducing forgetting.
summary.tldr: VB-CGCD uses Bayesian distribution alignment to reduce forgetting and pseudo-label noise during continual discovery of new categories.

title: Continual Generalized Category Discovery: Learning and Forgetting from a Bayesian Perspective

abstract: List learning is an important topic in both theoretical and empirical machine learning research, playing a key role in the recent breakthrough result of (Brukhim et al., 2022) on the characterization of multiclass PAC learnability, as well as addressing label ambiguity in computer vision classification tasks, among others. In this paper, we study the problem of list transductive online learning. In this framework, the learner outputs a list of multiple labels for each instance rather than just one, as in traditional multiclass classification. In the realizable setting, we demonstrate a trichotomy of possible rates of the minimax number of mistakes. In particular, if the learner plays for $\text{T} \in \mathbb{N}$ rounds, its minimax number of mistakes can only be of the orders $\Theta(\text{T})$, $\Theta(\log \text{T})$, or $\Theta(1)$. This resolves an open question raised by (Hanneke et al., 2024). On the other hand, in the agnostic setting, we characterize the learnability by constructively proving the $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{\text{T}})$ upper bound on the minimax expected regret. Along the way, we also answer another open question asked by (Moran et al., 2023). To establish these results, we introduce two new combinatorial complexity dimensions, called the Level-constrained $(\mathrm{L+1})$-Littlestone dimension and Level-constrained $(\mathrm{L+1})$-Branching dimension, if the list size is $\mathrm{L} \in \mathbb{N}$. Eventually, we conclude our work by raising an open question regarding eliminating the factor list size, which seems to be a crucial step, as it has consistently appeared in previous works on this subject.

paragraphs: This paper studies an online learning setting in which each prediction is a list of possible labels. Allowing several labels changes the learning problem: the learner must manage ambiguity while making predictions over successive rounds. The authors ask how the best achievable worst-case mistake count can grow as the number of rounds increases.

In the realizable setting, where the labels are compatible with the learning class, they prove that only three growth rates are possible. Mistakes grow linearly with the number of rounds, logarithmically, or remain bounded by a constant. This trichotomy rules out intermediate growth rates within the studied framework and resolves an open question.

For the agnostic setting, the authors characterize learnability through a constructive expected-regret upper bound that scales with the square root of the number of rounds, up to logarithmic factors. Two new combinatorial dimensions underpin the analysis. The paper also leaves open whether a factor depending on list size can be removed, identifying a specific remaining issue in the theory.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that realizable list transductive online learning has only three possible mistake-growth rates and characterizes agnostic learnability.

title: A Trichotomy for List Transductive Online Learning

abstract: Endowing deep models with the ability to generalize in dynamic scenarios is of vital significance for real-world deployment, given the continuous and complex changes in data distribution. Recently, evolving domain generalization (EDG) has emerged to address distribution shifts over time, aiming to capture evolving patterns for improved model generalization. However, existing EDG methods may suffer from spurious correlations by modeling only the dependence between data and targets across domains, creating a shortcut between task-irrelevant factors and the target, which hinders generalization. To this end, we design a time-aware structural causal model (SCM) that incorporates dynamic causal factors and the causal mechanism drifts, and propose Static-DYNamic Causal Representation Learning (SYNC), an approach that effectively learns time-aware causal representations. Specifically, it integrates specially designed information-theoretic objectives into a sequential VAE framework which captures evolving patterns, and produces the desired representations by preserving intra-class compactness of causal factors both across and within domains. Moreover, we theoretically show that our method can yield the optimal causal predictor for each time domain. Results on both synthetic and real-world datasets exhibit that SYNC can achieve superior temporal generalization performance.

paragraphs: Models deployed over time encounter changing data distributions. Methods for evolving domain generalization try to learn these changes, but may pick up shortcuts linking task-irrelevant factors to prediction targets. This paper proposes SYNC, which uses a causal account of temporal change to learn representations intended to generalize as domains evolve.

The authors design a time-aware structural causal model that includes both changing causal factors and shifts in causal mechanisms. SYNC implements this perspective through a sequential variational autoencoder with specially designed information-theoretic objectives. It also preserves compact representations of causal factors belonging to the same class, both within a domain and across domains.

The theoretical analysis shows that the method can yield an optimal causal predictor for each time domain. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report superior temporal generalization. Together, these findings support modeling how causal information evolves, alongside keeping same-class causal representations coherent, as a way to reduce the influence of misleading temporal correlations on prediction.
summary.tldr: SYNC learns time-aware causal representations to improve generalization as data distributions and causal mechanisms evolve.

title: Learning Time-Aware Causal Representation for Model Generalization in Evolving Domains

abstract: Deep learning models with a large number of parameters, often referred to as over-parameterized models, have achieved exceptional performance across various tasks. Despite concerns about overfitting, these models frequently generalize well to unseen data, thanks to effective regularization techniques, with data augmentation being among the most widely used. While data augmentation has shown great success in classification tasks using label-preserving transformations, its application in regression problems has received less attention. Recently, a novel manifold learning approach for generating synthetic data was proposed, utilizing a first-order approximation of the data manifold. Building on this foundation, we present a theoretical framework and practical tools for approximating and sampling general data manifolds. Furthermore, we introduce the Curvature-Enhanced Manifold Sampling (CEMS) method for regression tasks. CEMS leverages a second-order representation of the data manifold to enable efficient sampling and reconstruction of new data points. Extensive evaluations across multiple datasets and comparisons with state-of-the-art methods demonstrate that CEMS delivers superior performance in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios, while introducing only minimal computational overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/azencot-group/CEMS.

paragraphs: Data augmentation creates additional training examples to help models generalize. In classification, transformations can often preserve a class label, but augmentation for regression has received less attention. This paper develops a geometric approach to generating examples for tasks with numerical outputs, building on earlier work that approximates the structure of data locally.

The proposed Curvature-Enhanced Manifold Sampling method uses a second-order representation of the data manifold. A first-order approximation describes local directions; a second-order representation also captures curvature. The authors develop both a theoretical framework and practical tools for approximating and sampling general manifolds, then use this representation to sample and reconstruct new data points efficiently.

Across multiple datasets, the reported evaluations show better performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods, both within the training distribution and outside it. The added computational overhead is reported to be minimal. The contribution is therefore a way to make regression augmentation account for local bending in the data’s geometry, with empirical evidence that this richer approximation improves predictive performance.
summary.tldr: CEMS uses a second-order geometric representation to generate regression training data, improving reported performance with minimal computational overhead.

title: Curvature Enhanced Data Augmentation for Regression

abstract: Current multimodal learning strategies primarily optimize in the original token space. Such a framework is easy to incorporate with the backbone of pretrained language model, but might result in modality collapse. To alleviate such issues, we leverage the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) on the multimodal tasks, which converts the input embedding into the output embedding space by a predictor and then conducts the cross-modal alignment on the latent space. We implement this predictor by a Multi-Gate Mixture of Experts (MMoE) and name the framework as M3-JEPA, accordingly. The gating function disentangles the modality-specific and shared information and derives information-theoretic optimality. The framework is implemented with both contrastive and regularization loss, and solved by alternative gradient descent (AGD) between different multimodal tasks. By thoroughly designed experiments, we show that M3-JEPA can obtain state-of-the-art performance on different modalities and tasks, generalize to unseen datasets and domains, and is computationally efficient in both training and inference. Our observation suggests that M3-JEPA might become a new basis to self-supervised learning in the open world.

paragraphs: Multimodal systems must connect information across different kinds of input while retaining what makes each modality distinctive. The paper argues that learning primarily in the original token space can lead to modality collapse. M3-JEPA instead aligns modalities in a learned representation space, using a predictor to map input embeddings into the space of output embeddings.

The predictor is a multi-gate mixture of experts. Its gating mechanism separates information shared across modalities from information specific to each one, with an accompanying information-theoretic optimality result. Training combines contrastive and regularization losses and alternates gradient descent between different multimodal tasks. Together, these choices organize how the system shares information without treating every modality as interchangeable.

The reported experiments show state-of-the-art performance across different modalities and tasks, generalization to unseen datasets and domains, and computational efficiency during training and inference. These findings support latent-space prediction as a useful approach to multimodal alignment. The authors also suggest that the framework could provide a basis for open-world self-supervised learning, presenting that broader role as a possibility.
summary.tldr: M3-JEPA aligns modalities through latent-space prediction and gated experts that separate shared information from modality-specific information.

title: M3-JEPA: Multimodal Alignment via Multi-gate MoE based on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture

abstract: The multi-domain fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) confronts a notorious trade-off among abilities across domains. Existing studies attribute this trade-off to the conflicts between samples rooted in inherent semantics. Recent approaches attempt to mitigate these conflicts through the empirical investigation or heuristic strategies. However, without a fundamental understanding of interactions between samples, they yield only marginal improvements, while incurring substantial trial-and-error costs. To address this challenge, we move beyond empirical studies by modeling interactions between samples as their influence on each other’s loss, estimated using gradients. Intriguingly, we find that these interactions evolve throughout training rather than being purely determined by inherent semantics. Building on this insight, we propose EVolving Interaction-guided Curriculum (EVIC), which iteratively selects samples that positively influence the overall dataset for training. By dynamically adapting the training curriculum to prioritize samples that contribute the most to the model training, EVIC effectively mitigates conflicts and improves the sample efficiency. Extensive experiments on a mixed dataset covering coding, math, and general tasks with several model architectures show that EVIC significantly outperforms all baselines across diverse capabilities.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a language model across several domains can improve one ability while weakening another. This paper examines those conflicts through interactions between individual training samples. It models an interaction as the influence one sample has on another sample’s loss, using gradients to estimate that influence during training.

The key finding is that these interactions change as training proceeds. Whether two samples help or hinder each other is therefore not determined solely by their semantic content. The proposed Evolving Interaction-guided Curriculum, or EVIC, uses this observation to repeatedly select samples that have a positive influence on the dataset overall, adapting the training curriculum to the model’s evolving state.

Experiments combine coding, mathematics, and general tasks across several model architectures. The authors report that EVIC significantly outperforms all evaluated baselines across diverse capabilities while improving sample efficiency and reducing conflicts. The result supports choosing training examples according to their current contribution to learning, rather than treating helpfulness as a permanent property of the examples.
summary.tldr: EVIC improves multi-domain fine-tuning by repeatedly selecting samples according to their changing influence on overall learning.

title: Boosting Multi-Domain Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models through Evolving Interactions between Samples

abstract: Spectral graph convolution, an important tool of data filtering on graphs, relies on two essential decisions: selecting spectral bases for signal transformation and parameterizing the kernel for frequency analysis. While recent techniques mainly focus on standard Fourier transform and vector-valued spectral functions, they fall short in flexibility to model signal distributions over large spatial ranges, and capacity of spectral function. In this paper, we present a novel wavelet-based graph convolution network, namely WaveGC, which integrates multi-resolution spectral bases and a matrix-valued filter kernel. Theoretically, we establish that WaveGC can effectively capture and decouple short-range and long-range information, providing superior filtering flexibility, surpassing existing graph wavelet neural networks. To instantiate WaveGC, we introduce a novel technique for learning general graph wavelets by separately combining odd and even terms of Chebyshev polynomials. This approach strictly satisfies wavelet admissibility criteria. Our numerical experiments showcase the consistent improvements in both short-range and long-range tasks. This underscores the effectiveness of the proposed model in handling different scenarios.

paragraphs: WaveGC addresses how neural networks filter information on graphs at different spatial scales. Spectral graph convolution depends on both a representation for transforming graph signals and a filter that acts on that representation. The paper argues that commonly used Fourier representations and vector-valued filters restrict flexibility when signals contain information spread across large regions.

The proposed network combines wavelet representations at multiple resolutions with a matrix-valued filter. This gives the model a richer way to handle information at different scales. The theoretical analysis establishes that WaveGC can capture and separate short-range and long-range information, supporting more flexible filtering than existing graph wavelet neural networks.

To construct the wavelets, the authors combine odd and even Chebyshev polynomial terms separately. This construction satisfies the mathematical admissibility requirements for wavelets. Numerical experiments report consistent improvements on tasks involving both nearby and distant graph information. Together, the theory and experiments support the value of designing the signal representation and filtering mechanism jointly.
summary.tldr: WaveGC combines multiresolution graph wavelets with matrix-valued filters to better separate and use short-range and long-range information.

title: A General Graph Spectral Wavelet Convolution via Chebyshev Order Decomposition

abstract: To address the challenge of scarce computational resources in genomic modeling, we introduce GERM, a genomic foundation model optimized for accessibility and adaptability. GERM improves upon models like DNABERT-2 by eliminating outliers that hinder low-rank adaptation and post-training quantization, enhancing both efficiency and robustness. We replace the vanilla attention layer with an outlier-free mechanism inspired by associative memory models. By removing outliers during both pre-training and fine-tuning, this approach accelerates adaptation, reduces computational costs, and enhances quantization robustness within acceptable loss margins. Additionally, we propose GERM-T, a strategy that employs small-step continual learning within the outlier-free framework, leveraging original checkpoints to avoid retraining from scratch. Empirically, GERM improves fine-tuning performance by 37.98% and quantization by 64.34% over the baseline model. It also reduces average kurtosis by 92.14% and maximum infinity norm by 82.77%. Compared to leading methods, GERM consistently delivers superior performance, offering a practical solution for genomic modeling in resource-constrained settings.

Its approach is to remove those outliers through the model's attention mechanism, improving the practicality of genomic modeling when computational resources are scarce.

They apply outlier removal during pretraining and fine-tuning, reporting faster adaptation, lower computational costs, and more robust quantization within acceptable loss margins.
