summary.tldr: GERM uses outlier-free attention to improve genomic model adaptation and quantization, with a checkpoint-based strategy that avoids retraining from scratch.

title: Fast and Low-Cost Genomic Foundation Models via Outlier Removal

abstract: Remote sensing pansharpening aims to reconstruct spatial-spectral properties during the fusion of panchromatic (PAN) images and lowresolution multi-spectral (LR-MS) images, finally generating the high-resolution multi-spectral (HRMS) images. In the mainstream modeling strategies, i.e., CNN and Transformer, the input images are treated as the equal-sized grid of pixels in the Euclidean space. They have limitations in facing remote sensing images with irregular ground objects. Graph is the more flexible structure, however, there are two major challenges when modeling spatial-spectral properties with graph: 1) constructing the customized graph structure for spatial-spectral relationship priors; 2) learning the unified spatial-spectral representation through the graph. To address these challenges, we propose the spatial-spectral heterogeneous graph learning network, named HetSSNet. Specifically, HetSSNet initially constructs the heterogeneous graph structure for pansharpening, which explicitly describes pansharpening-specific relationships. Subsequently, the basic relationship pattern generation module is designed to extract the multiple relationship patterns from the heterogeneous graph. Finally, relationship pattern aggregation module is exploited to collaboratively learn unified spatial-spectral representation across different relationships among nodes with adaptive importance learning from local and global perspectives. Extensive experiments demonstrate the significant superiority and generalization of HetSSNet.

paragraphs: Pansharpening combines a panchromatic image with a lower-resolution multispectral image to produce a high-resolution multispectral result. The task must reconstruct both spatial and spectral properties. The paper argues that treating images as uniform pixel grids limits common convolutional and Transformer models when they encounter irregular ground objects in remote-sensing imagery.

HetSSNet represents the fusion problem with a heterogeneous graph that explicitly describes relationships specific to pansharpening. Its first challenge is choosing a graph structure that captures relevant spatial and spectral relationships. A relationship-pattern generation module then extracts multiple patterns from that graph, providing several ways to represent how the image information is connected.

A relationship-pattern aggregation module combines these patterns into a unified spatial-spectral representation. It learns their importance adaptively from both local and global perspectives, allowing different relationships to contribute differently. The authors report substantial superiority and generalization in extensive experiments. The stated contribution is a complete graph-based fusion pipeline, covering relationship construction, extraction, and aggregation for the same reconstruction task.
summary.tldr: HetSSNet uses a heterogeneous graph and adaptive relationship aggregation to fuse spatial and spectral information for remote-sensing pansharpening.

title: HetSSNet: Spatial-Spectral Heterogeneous Graph Learning Network for Panchromatic and Multispectral Images Fusion

abstract: Decoding functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) signals into text has been a key challenge in the neuroscience community, with the potential to advance brain-computer interfaces and uncover deeper insights into brain mechanisms. However, existing approaches often struggle with suboptimal predictive performance, limited task variety, and poor generalization across subjects. In response to this, we propose MindLLM, a model designed for subject-agnostic and versatile fMRI-to-text decoding. MindLLM consists of an fMRI encoder and an off-the-shelf LLM. The fMRI encoder employs a neuroscience-informed attention mechanism, which is capable of accommodating subjects with varying input shapes and thus achieves high-performance subject-agnostic decoding. Moreover, we introduce Brain Instruction Tuning (BIT), a novel approach that enhances the model’s ability to capture diverse semantic representations from fMRI signals, facilitating more versatile decoding. We evaluate MindLLM on comprehensive fMRI-to-text benchmarks. Results demonstrate that our model outperforms the baselines, improving downstream tasks by $12.0%$, unseen subject generalization by $24.5%$, and novel task adaptation by $25.0%$. Furthermore, the attention patterns in MindLLM provide interpretable insights into its decision-making process.
originalAbstract: Decoding functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) signals into text has been a key challenge in the neuroscience community, with the potential to advance brain-computer interfaces and uncover deeper insights into brain mechanisms. However, existing approaches often struggle with suboptimal predictive performance, limited task variety, and poor generalization across subjects. In response to this, we propose MindLLM, a model designed for subject-agnostic and versatile fMRI-to-text decoding. MindLLM consists of an fMRI encoder and an off-the-shelf LLM. The fMRI encoder employs a neuroscience-informed attention mechanism, which is capable of accommodating subjects with varying input shapes and thus achieves high-performance subject-agnostic decoding. Moreover, we introduce Brain Instruction Tuning (BIT), a novel approach that enhances the model’s ability to capture diverse semantic representations from fMRI signals, facilitating more versatile decoding. We evaluate MindLLM on comprehensive fMRI-to-text benchmarks. Results demonstrate that our model outperforms the baselines, improving downstream tasks by $12.0%$, unseen subject generalization by $24.5%$, and novel task adaptation by $25.0%$. Furthermore, the attention patterns in MindLLM provide interpretable insights into its decision-making process.

The model combines a dedicated fMRI encoder with an off-the-shelf large language model.

The encoder uses a neuroscience-informed attention mechanism that can accommodate different input shapes across participants. This supports a shared decoding approach across subjects. The authors also introduce Brain Instruction Tuning, which helps the model extract diverse semantic representations from brain signals. Together, these components address variation in both the incoming measurements and the kinds of meaning the model needs to express.

They also find that the attention patterns provide interpretable insights into model decisions. title: MindLLM: A Subject-Agnostic and Versatile Model for fMRI-to-text Decoding

abstract: Rectified-flow-based diffusion transformers like FLUX and OpenSora have demonstrated outstanding performance in the field of image and video generation. Despite their robust generative capabilities, these models often struggle with inversion inaccuracies, which could further limit their effectiveness in downstream tasks such as image and video editing. To address this issue, we propose RF-Solver, a novel training-free sampler that effectively enhances inversion precision by mitigating the errors in the ODE-solving process of rectified flow. Specifically, we derive the exact formulation of the rectified flow ODE and apply the high-order Taylor expansion to estimate its nonlinear components, significantly enhancing the precision of ODE solutions at each timestep. Building upon RF-Solver, we further propose RF-Edit, a general feature-sharing-based framework for image and video editing. By incorporating self-attention features from the inversion process into the editing process, RF-Edit effectively preserves the structural information of the source image or video while achieving high-quality editing results. Our approach is compatible with any pre-trained rectified-flow-based models for image and video tasks, requiring no additional training or optimization. Extensive experiments across generation, inversion, and editing tasks in both image and video modalities demonstrate the superiority and versatility of our method. The source code is available at https://github.com/wangjiangshan0725/RF-Solver-Edit.

paragraphs: Rectified-flow models can generate strong images and videos, but errors when inverting existing content can reduce their usefulness for editing. This paper targets the numerical errors involved in solving the underlying ordinary differential equation. Its RF-Solver is a training-free sampler designed to make inversion more precise.

The authors derive an exact formulation of the rectified-flow equation and use a high-order Taylor expansion to approximate its nonlinear components. This improves the precision of the numerical solution at each time step. Building on the solver, RF-Edit transfers self-attention features from inversion into editing, helping preserve the source image’s or video’s structure while making the requested changes.

The approach is presented as compatible with pretrained rectified-flow models for both image and video tasks, without additional training or optimization. Experiments across generation, inversion, and editing report superior performance and versatility. The two contributions address connected problems: more accurate numerical inversion provides a stronger basis for editing, and feature sharing helps carry structural information from the original content into the edited result.
summary.tldr: RF-Solver improves rectified-flow inversion without training, while RF-Edit reuses inversion features to preserve structure during image and video editing.

title: Taming Rectified Flow for Inversion and Editing

abstract: In embodied AI, a persistent challenge is enabling agents to robustly adapt to novel domains without requiring extensive data collection or retraining. To address this, we present a world model implanting framework (WorMI) that combines the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) with independently learned, domain-specific world models through test-time composition. By allowing seamless implantation and removal of the world models, the embodied agent’s policy achieves and maintains cross-domain adaptability. In the WorMI framework, we employ a prototype-based world model retrieval approach, utilizing efficient trajectory-based abstract representation matching, to incorporate relevant models into test-time composition. We also develop a world-wise compound attention method that not only integrates the knowledge from the retrieved world models but also aligns their intermediate representations with the reasoning model’s representation within the agent’s policy. This framework design effectively fuses domain-specific knowledge from multiple world models, ensuring robust adaptation to unseen domains. We evaluate our WorMI on the VirtualHome and ALFWorld benchmarks, demonstrating superior zero-shot and few-shot performance compared to several LLM-based approaches across a range of unseen domains. These results highlight the framework’s potential for scalable, real-world deployment in embodied agent scenarios where adaptability and data efficiency are essential.

paragraphs: Embodied agents must adapt when the environments they act in change, ideally without extensive new data collection or retraining. WorMI addresses this through test-time composition: it connects a language model's reasoning capabilities with independently learned world models that contain knowledge specific to different domains. Those world models can be inserted and removed as needed.

The framework retrieves relevant models by matching abstract trajectory representations against prototypes. It then uses a compound attention mechanism to combine information from the retrieved world models and align their intermediate representations with the reasoning model's representations. This alignment lets separately learned sources of environmental knowledge contribute within the agent's policy.

Evaluations on VirtualHome and ALFWorld show stronger zero-shot and few-shot performance than several language-model-based approaches across unseen domains. The results support retrieving and composing world models as a route to adaptation in those benchmarks. The authors present scalable real-world deployment as a potential application, building on the demonstrated ability to combine domain knowledge at test time.
summary.tldr: WorMI retrieves and integrates domain-specific world models at test time to improve embodied agents' adaptation to unseen environments.

title: World Model Implanting for Test-time Adaptation of Embodied Agents

abstract: Bilevel optimization is widely applied in many machine learning tasks such as hyper-parameter learning and meta learning. Recently, many algorithms have been proposed to solve these bilevel optimization problems, which rely on the smoothness condition of objective functions of the bilevel optimization. In fact, some machine learning tasks such as learning language model do not satisfy the smoothness condition of objective functions. More recently, some methods have begun to study generalized smooth bilevel optimization. However, these proposed methods for generalized smooth bilevel optimization only focus on the (strongly) convex lower objective function. Meanwhile, these methods only consider the generalized-smooth upper-level objective, but still require the standard smooth lower-level objective in the bilevel optimization. To fill this gap, in the paper, thus we study the generalized-smooth bilevel optimization with the nonconvex lower-level objective function, where both upper-level and lower-level objectives are generalized-smooth. We propose an efficient single-loop Hessian/Jacobian-free penalty normalized gradient (i.e., PNGBiO) method. Moreover, we prove that our PNGBiO obtains a fast convergence rate of $O(\frac{1}{T^{1/4}})$ for finding a stationary solution, where $T$ denotes the iteration number. Meanwhile, we also propose a stochastic version of our PNGBiO (i.e., S-PNGBiO) method to solve stochastic bilevel problems, and prove that our S-PNGBiO has a fast convergence rate of $O(\frac{1}{T^{1/6}})$. Some experimental results on hyper-parameter learning and meta learning demonstrate efficiency of our proposed methods.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization links two optimization problems: an upper-level choice depends on the outcome of a lower-level problem. This structure appears in hyperparameter learning and meta learning. Many existing algorithms require standard smoothness conditions that some machine learning objectives do not satisfy. Previous work allowing generalized smoothness still imposed stronger restrictions on the lower-level objective.

This paper studies a setting where both objectives are generalized-smooth and the lower-level objective can be nonconvex. The proposed PNGBiO algorithm combines a penalty formulation with normalized gradient updates in a single loop. It is Hessian/Jacobian-free, avoiding explicit use of those derivative structures. The authors also introduce S-PNGBiO for stochastic bilevel problems.

The analysis proves a convergence rate of O(1/T^(1/4)) for PNGBiO and O(1/T^(1/6)) for its stochastic version, where T is the iteration count. These guarantees concern finding a stationary solution, rather than establishing a global optimum. Experiments on hyperparameter learning and meta learning demonstrate efficiency, complementing the broader objective conditions covered by the theory.
summary.tldr: PNGBiO provides convergence guarantees for bilevel optimization with generalized-smooth objectives and a nonconvex lower-level problem.

title: Generalized Smooth Bilevel Optimization with Nonconvex Lower-Level

abstract: Scaling LLM-based embodied agents from text-only environments to complex multimodal settings remains a major challenge. Recent work identifies a perception–reasoning–decision gap in standalone Vision–Language Models (VLMs), which often overlook task-critical information. In this paper, we introduce PRISM, a framework that tightly couples perception (VLM) and decision (LLM) through a dynamic question–answer (DQA) pipeline. Instead of passively accepting the VLM’s description, the LLM critiques it, probes the VLM with goal-oriented questions, and synthesizes a compact image description. This closed-loop interaction yields a sharp, task-driven understanding of the scene. We evaluate PRISM on the ALFWorld and Room-to-Room (R2R) benchmarks. We show that: (1) PRISM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art image-based models, (2) our Interactive goal-oriented perception pipeline yields systematic and substantial gains, and (3) PRISM is fully automatic, eliminating the need for handcrafted questions or answers.

paragraphs: An embodied agent needs a description of its surroundings that includes the details relevant to its next decision. A standalone vision-language model can overlook those details, leaving a gap between seeing a scene and acting effectively within it. PRISM addresses this gap by tightly connecting visual perception with language-model reasoning.

Its dynamic question-and-answer pipeline lets the decision-making language model critique the visual model’s description and ask follow-up questions directed at the current goal. The answers are synthesized into a compact image description. This closed loop makes perception responsive to the task, with reasoning helping determine which visual information needs further attention.

On ALFWorld and Room-to-Room, the authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art image-based models and systematic, substantial gains from interactive, goal-oriented perception. The pipeline is fully automatic and does not require handcrafted questions or answers. These results support the value of interleaving perception and reasoning during sequential decisions, so the agent’s representation of the scene reflects what it needs to accomplish.
summary.tldr: PRISM lets a decision-making LLM question a visual model about task-relevant details, improving embodied-agent performance in two benchmarks.

title: PRISM: Perception Reasoning Interleaved for Sequential Decision Making.

abstract: Scientific embodied agents could automate laboratory workflows, but laboratory success is trajectory-level: an agent must remain safe throughout execution, not merely reach a final goal. In benchtop settings a small pose, force, or tilt error can cause irreversible spillage or equipment damage, yet most robot benchmarks evaluate reversible, high-tolerance manipulation and imitation-trained policies receive no recovery signal for execution drift. We introduce SafeLab, a generative simulation benchmark that couples a verified generative engine, an automated expert for teleoperation-free demonstrations, and a safety-aware RL interface, with 63 calibrated laboratory assets, 64 tasks across 9 manipulation categories, and 6,400 expert trajectories. Across state-of-the-art policies, it reveals unsafe-but-successful trajectories—large gaps between task success and Safe Success Rate—most acutely in liquid handling, force-limited actuation, and bimanual glassware rearrangement. Bounded residual RL then learns execution-level corrections that raise the simulated Safe Success Rate by up to 43.0 percentage points without retraining the base policy. Finally, 50 open-loop physical replays show 86% agreement between simulated and observed safety outcomes, supporting SafeLab as a scalable platform for screening and training safer laboratory agents.

paragraphs: A laboratory robot can complete its assigned task while taking unsafe actions along the way. SafeLab evaluates this distinction by treating safety as a property of the entire execution. The benchmark combines a verified generative simulation engine, an automated demonstration expert, and an interface for safety-aware reinforcement learning. This agreement supports using SafeLab to screen and train laboratory agents, while preserving the distinction between simulated improvement and physical validation.
summary.tldr: SafeLab measures safety throughout laboratory robot tasks and shows that learned execution corrections can improve safe success.

title: SafeLab: An Interactive High-Fidelity Benchmark for Embodied Safety in Scientific Robotics

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a dominant paradigm for enhancing LLMs’ reasoning capabilities. However, RL algorithms with PPO-Clip are inherently limited by exploration collapse. Subsequent works remain primarily heuristic and fail to identify the essential cause of PPO-Clip’s failure. This work reveals the fundamental flaw of PPO-Clip: it implicitly measures policy discrepancy using Euclidean metric, which is theoretically inconsistent with the intrinsic geometry on the policy Riemannian manifold. This geometric mismatch results in overly conservative updates in low-probability regions while aggressive in high-probability regions, ultimately collapsing exploration. To correct this geometric flaw, we propose Riemannian Isometric Policy Optimization (RIPO), which guarantees isometric policy updates on the Riemannian manifold, effectively balancing exploration and exploitation. We further show that RIPO achieves a favorable bias-variance trade-off, which stabilizes optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RIPO significantly surpasses existing LLM RL algorithms across seven competition-level benchmarks (up to 60% improvement over GRPO on AIME24).

paragraphs: This paper studies why reinforcement learning for language-model reasoning can lose its ability to explore. It attributes exploration collapse in PPO-Clip to a mismatch between how the algorithm measures policy changes and the geometry of the space of policies. According to the analysis, treating that space with a Euclidean metric distorts the size of updates.

The distortion produces updates that are overly cautious in low-probability regions and overly aggressive in high-probability regions. The proposed Riemannian Isometric Policy Optimization, or RIPO, instead guarantees isometric updates with respect to the policy manifold’s geometry. This gives the exploration–exploitation balance a geometric foundation. The paper also establishes a favorable bias–variance trade-off that helps stabilize optimization.

Experiments report significant improvements over existing language-model reinforcement-learning algorithms across seven competition-level benchmarks. The largest highlighted result is an improvement of up to 60% over GRPO on AIME24. Together, the theory and experiments support the paper’s central argument: the geometry used to control policy changes can materially affect both continued exploration and reasoning performance.
summary.tldr: RIPO uses the geometry of policy space to address exploration collapse, with reported reasoning gains across seven competition-level benchmarks.

title: Beyond Euclidean Clipping: Overcoming Exploration Collapse in LLM RL via Riemannian Isometric Policy Optimization

abstract: Mixture models, such as Gaussian mixture models (GMMs), are widely used in machine learning to represent complex data distributions. A key challenge, especially in high-dimensional settings, is to determine the mixture order and estimate the mixture parameters. We study the problem of approximating a target measure, available only through finitely many of its moments, by a mixture of distributions from a parametric family (e.g., Gaussian, exponential, Poisson), with approximation quality measured by the 2-Wasserstein ($\operatorname{W_2}$) or the total variation ($\operatorname{TV}$) distance. Unlike many existing approaches, the parameter set is not assumed to be finite; it is modeled as a compact basic semi-algebraic set. We introduce a hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations with asymptotic convergence to the desired optimal value. In addition, when a certain rank condition is satisfied, the convergence is even finite and recovery of an optimal mixing measure is obtained. We also present an application to clustering, where our framework serves either as a stand-alone method or as a preprocessing step that yields both the number of clusters and strong initial parameter estimates, thereby accelerating convergence of standard (local) clustering algorithms

paragraphs: Mixture modeling requires deciding both how many components to use and what their parameters should be. This paper studies approximation of a target distribution known only through finitely many moments. Candidate components come from a parametric family, such as Gaussian, exponential, or Poisson distributions, and approximation quality is measured using Wasserstein or total variation distance.

The parameter space need not be a finite list. Instead, it is assumed to be a compact basic semi-algebraic set, giving the optimization problem a specific mathematical structure. The authors construct a hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations whose optimal values converge asymptotically to the desired optimum.

A stronger conclusion holds when a stated rank condition is satisfied: convergence becomes finite, and an optimal mixing measure can be recovered. The paper also applies the framework to clustering, either directly or as preprocessing that supplies the cluster count and strong initial parameter estimates. Those estimates accelerate standard local clustering algorithms. The distinction between general asymptotic convergence and conditional finite recovery is central to the guarantees.
summary.tldr: Semidefinite relaxations approximate optimal mixture distributions from moments, with finite recovery when a rank condition holds.

title: Mixtures Closest To A Given Measure: A Semidefinite Programming Approach

abstract: Recursive retraining of generative models poses a critical representation challenge: when synthetic outputs are curated based on a fixed reward signal, the model tends to collapse onto a narrow set of outputs that over-optimize that objective, causing diversity to vanish and failing to represent the full range of preferences. Prior work has suggested that such collapse is unavoidable without adding real data into the mix. In this paper, we revisit that conclusion from an alignment perspective and show that collapse can be mitigated through curation based on multiple reward functions. We formalize the dynamics of recursive training under heterogeneous preferences and prove that, under certain conditions, the model converges to a stable distribution that allocates probability mass across competing high-reward regions. The limiting distribution preserves diversity and provably satisfies a weighted Nash bargaining solution, offering a formal interpretation of value aggregation in synthetic retraining loops.

paragraphs: When a generative model repeatedly trains on its own curated outputs, the curation rule helps determine what survives into later generations. Selecting outputs with one fixed reward can push the model toward a narrow set of favored answers. Diversity then disappears as the retraining process repeatedly reinforces the same objective.

This paper studies whether using multiple reward functions can change that outcome. It formalizes recursive training when preferences are heterogeneous, so different reward functions favor different regions of the output space. Under certain conditions, the authors prove convergence to a stable distribution that continues to assign probability to competing high-reward regions.

The limiting distribution also satisfies a weighted Nash bargaining solution, giving the balance among preferences a formal interpretation. The result supports a conditional alternative to the claim that synthetic retraining must collapse unless real data are added. Within the analyzed setting, the way outputs are curated can preserve diversity and aggregate multiple values. It does not establish that any collection of rewards will automatically prevent collapse.
summary.tldr: Under certain conditions, curating synthetic outputs with multiple reward functions yields stable, diverse retraining dynamics with a weighted Nash bargaining interpretation.

title: Curated Synthetic Data Doesn’t Have to Collapse: A Theoretical Study of Generative Retraining with Pluralistic Preferences

abstract: Understanding climate dynamics requires going beyond correlations in observational data to uncover their underlying causal process. Latent drivers, such as atmospheric processes, play a critical role in temporal dynamics, while direct causal influences also exist among geographically proximate observed variables. Traditional Causal Representation Learning (CRL) typically focuses on latent factors but overlooks such observable-to-observable causal relations, limiting its applicability to climate analysis. In this paper, we introduce a unified framework that jointly uncovers (i) causal relations among observed variables and (ii) latent driving forces together with their interactions. We establish conditions under which both the hidden dynamic processes and the causal structure among observed variables are simultaneously identifiable from time-series data. Remarkably, our guarantees hold even in the nonparametric setting, leveraging contextual information to recover latent variables and observable relations. Building on these insights, we propose CaDRe (Causal Discovery and Representation learning), a time-series generative model with structural constraints that integrates CRL and causal discovery. Experiments on synthetic datasets validate our theoretical results. On real-world climate datasets, CaDRe not only delivers competitive forecasting accuracy but also recovers visualized causal graphs aligned with domain expertise, thereby offering interpretable insights into climate systems.

This paper develops a unified framework for recovering observed-variable causal links together with latent drivers and their interactions.

The theoretical contribution identifies conditions under which both parts can be recovered simultaneously from time-series data. These guarantees extend to a nonparametric setting and use contextual information to recover hidden variables and observable relationships. summary.tldr: CaDRe jointly models hidden climate drivers and causal links among observed variables, with conditional identifiability guarantees and interpretable empirical results.

title: Learning General Causal Structures with Hidden Dynamic Process for Climate Analysis

abstract: Oncologists are increasingly relying on multiple modalities to model the complexity of diseases. Within this landscape, transcriptomic and epigenetic data have proven to be particularly instrumental and play an increasingly vital role in clinical applications. However, their integration into multimodal models remains a challenge, especially considering their high dimensionality. In this work, we present a novel bimodal model that jointly learns representations of bulk RNA-seq and DNA methylation leveraging self-supervision from masked language modeling. We implement an architecture that reduces the memory footprint usually attributed to purely transformer-based models when dealing with long sequences. We demonstrate that the obtained bimodal embeddings can be used to fine-tune cancer-type classification and survival models that achieve state-of-the-art performance compared to unimodal models. Furthermore, we introduce a robust learning framework that maintains downstream task performance despite missing modalities, enhancing the model’s applicability in real-world clinical settings.

In this work, we present a novel bimodal model that jointly learns representations of bulk RNA-seq and DNA methylation leveraging self-supervision from masked language modeling. We implement an architecture that reduces the memory footprint usually attributed to purely transformer-based models when dealing with long sequences. We demonstrate that the obtained bimodal embeddings can be used to fine-tune cancer-type classification and survival models that achieve state-of-the-art performance compared to unimodal models. Furthermore, we introduce a robust learning framework that maintains downstream task performance despite missing modalities, enhancing the model’s applicability in real-world clinical settings.

paragraphs: Bulk RNA sequencing and DNA methylation provide two kinds of biological information relevant to cancer modeling. Combining them is challenging because both contain many measurements. The paper develops a joint representation model so that downstream predictions can use information from both modalities within a shared learning framework.

Training uses masked language modeling as a self-supervised objective: the model learns from partially hidden inputs rather than relying solely on downstream outcome labels. Its architecture reduces the memory demands associated with purely transformer-based approaches to long sequences. This addresses a practical obstacle to learning from high-dimensional biological inputs.

The resulting joint embeddings support finetuned cancer-type classification and survival models. The authors report state-of-the-art performance in comparisons with unimodal models. They also introduce a learning framework that maintains downstream performance when modalities are missing. This matters for the intended clinical setting, where the usefulness of combining measurements depends partly on whether the model remains effective when a complete set is unavailable.
summary.tldr: A memory-conscious masked modeling approach combines RNA-seq and DNA methylation for cancer prediction while supporting missing modalities.

title: Bimodal masked language modeling for bulk RNA-seq and DNA methylation representation learning

abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient specialization of foundation models, but the proliferation of task-specific adapters fragments capabilities across many adapters, complicating reuse and deployment. We study the problem of merging $T$ LoRAs into a single rank-$r$ LoRA, thereby preserving the benefits of low-rank structure. Existing Merge-then-Compress pipelines treat the rank constraint as an afterthought: they merge adapters in the full parameter space, then compress the merged result to rank $r$ via truncated SVD. However, full-parameter merging may destroy the low-rank structure, making it difficult for subsequent compression to recover an effective rank-$r$ LoRA. We propose Compress-then-Merge (CtM), a reversed pipeline that enforces the rank-$r$ bottleneck before merging: CtM computes shared $r$-dimensional subspaces using only the LoRA weights to capture cross-adapter common structure, projects each adapter into the shared subspaces to obtain $r\times r$ coordinates, and then applies standard merging rules in this reduced space. CtM guarantees a rank-$r$ LoRA by construction, avoiding post-hoc truncation, and enables efficient computation in the core space spanned by concatenated LoRA factors. Experiments across multiple models and tasks show that CtM consistently outperforms existing single-LoRA-output baselines while narrowing the performance gap to full-parameter merging methods.

paragraphs: LoRA adapters specialize a foundation model through compact parameter updates, but maintaining many task-specific adapters complicates deployment and reuse. This paper asks how to combine multiple adapters into one while retaining a chosen low rank. Existing approaches first merge full parameter updates and then compress the result, potentially losing structure that the final compact adapter needs.

Compress-then-Merge reverses that order. It uses the adapter weights to identify shared subspaces of the desired dimension, then projects each adapter into those subspaces. Standard merging rules operate on the resulting small coordinate matrices. The output satisfies the rank constraint by construction, so there is no subsequent truncation step that might discard parts of an already merged update.

The method also supports efficient computation within a space built from the concatenated LoRA factors. Across the reported models and tasks, it consistently outperforms other methods that produce a single LoRA and narrows the performance gap to full-parameter merging. The findings support treating the compact representation as part of the merging problem from the beginning.
summary.tldr: Compress-then-Merge combines LoRA adapters inside shared low-dimensional subspaces, preserving the rank constraint and improving reported single-adapter performance.

title: Compress then Merge: From Multiple LoRAs into One Low-Rank Adapter

abstract: Graph Prompt Learning (GPL) has recently emerged as a promising paradigm for downstream adaptation of pre-trained graph models, mitigating the misalignment between pre-training objectives and downstream tasks. Recently, the focus of GPL has shifted from in-domain to cross-domain scenarios, which is closer to the real world applications, where the pre-training source and downstream target often differ substantially in data distribution. However, why GPLs remain effective under such domain shifts is still unexplored. Empirically, we observe that representative GPL methods are competitive with two simple baselines in cross-domain settings: full fine-tuning (FT) and linear probing (LP), motivating us to explore a deeper understanding of the prompting mechanism. We provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that jointly leveraging these two complementary branches yields a smaller estimation error than using either branch alone, formally proving that cross-domain GPL benefits from the integration between pre-trained knowledge and task-specific adaptation. Based on this insight, we propose GP2F, a dual-branch GPL method that explicitly instantiates the two extremes: (1) a frozen branch that retains pre-trained knowledge, and (2) an adapted branch with lightweight adapters for task-specific adaptation. We then perform adaptive fusion under topology constraints via a contrastive loss and a topology-consistent loss. Extensive experiments on cross-domain few-shot node and graph classification demonstrate that our method outperforms existing methods.

summary.tldr: GP2F adaptively combines frozen pretrained graph knowledge with lightweight task adaptation to improve cross-domain few-shot classification.

title: GP2F: Cross-Domain Graph Prompting with Adaptive Fusion of Pre-trained Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Structured pruning reduces LLM inference cost by removing low-importance architectural components. This can be viewed as learning a multiplicative gate for each component under an $\ell_0$ sparsity constraint. Due to the discreteness of the $\ell_0$ norm, prior work typically adopts stochastic hard-concrete relaxations to enable differentiable optimization; however, this stochasticity can introduce a train–test mismatch when sampled masks are discretized for deployment and restricting masks to a bounded, near-binary range. To address this, we propose Deterministic Differentiable Pruning (DDP), a mask-only optimization method that eliminates stochasticity by directly optimizing a deterministic soft surrogate of the discrete $\ell_0$ objective. Compared with prior approaches, DDP offers greater expressiveness, reduced train–test mismatch, and faster convergence. We apply our method to several dense and MoE models, including Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, achieving a performance loss as small as 1% on downstream tasks while outperforming previous methods at 20% sparsity. We further demonstrate end-to-end inference speedups in realistic deployment settings with vLLM.

paragraphs: Structured pruning lowers language-model inference cost by removing architectural components judged less important. One way to select components is to learn gates that control their contribution while constraining how many remain active. Because counting active components creates a discrete optimization problem, earlier methods often introduce randomly sampled, approximately binary gates to make training differentiable.

Deterministic Differentiable Pruning replaces that sampling process with a deterministic, smooth approximation to the sparsity objective. It optimizes the masks alone. This addresses the mismatch between random masks used during training and the fixed choices needed at deployment, while offering more expressive masks than bounded, near-binary alternatives. The authors report faster convergence as well as reduced training-to-deployment mismatch.

The method is evaluated on dense and mixture-of-experts models, including Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B. At 20% sparsity it outperforms earlier methods, with downstream performance loss as small as 1% in the reported evaluations. Tests using vLLM also show end-to-end inference speedups, connecting the pruning results to practical deployment benefits.
summary.tldr: DDP learns deterministic pruning masks that reduce model cost while limiting performance loss and delivering measured inference speedups.

title: Deterministic Differentiable Structured Pruning for Large Language Models

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training is a dominant approach for improving the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), yet growing evidence suggests that its gains arise primarily from distribution sharpening rather than the acquisition of new capabilities. Recent work has shown that sampling from the power distribution of LLMs using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) can recover performance comparable to RL post-training without relying on external rewards; however, the high computational cost of MCMC makes such approaches impractical for widespread adoption. In this work, we propose a theoretically grounded alternative that eliminates the need for iterative MCMC. We derive a novel formulation showing that the global power distribution can be approximated by a token-level scaled low-temperature one, where the scaling factor captures future trajectory quality. Leveraging this insight, we introduce a training-free and verifier-free algorithm that sharpens the base model’s generative distribution autoregressively. Empirically, we evaluate our method on math, QA, and code tasks, and show that our method matches or surpasses one-shot GRPO without relying on any external rewards, while reducing inference latency by over $10\times$ compared to MCMC-based sampling.

paragraphs: This paper explores whether better reasoning can be obtained by changing how a language model samples answers, without further training. Its motivation is evidence suggesting that much of reinforcement-learning post-training’s benefit comes from sharpening an existing output distribution. Earlier power-distribution sampling approaches recover comparable performance, but their iterative MCMC procedures are expensive.

The authors derive an approximation to the global power distribution using token-level, scaled low-temperature sampling. The scaling factor captures the quality of future trajectories, connecting each local token choice to the quality of possible continuations. This produces an autoregressive algorithm that sharpens the base model’s distribution without requiring training, a verifier, or external rewards.

Evaluations on mathematics, question answering, and code show that the method matches or exceeds one-shot GRPO while reducing inference latency by more than tenfold relative to MCMC-based sampling. The results support a cheaper sampling route to reasoning improvements in those evaluations. The theoretical contribution explains how a sequence-level sampling objective can be approximated through token-level decisions.
summary.tldr: A training-free token-level approximation to power sampling matches or exceeds one-shot GRPO in evaluations with over tenfold lower latency than MCMC sampling.

title: Scalable Power Sampling: Unlocking Efficient, Training-Free Reasoning for LLMs via Distribution Sharpening

abstract: Recent advanced diffusion methods typically derive strong generative priors by scaling diffusion transformers. However, scaling fails to generalize when adapted for real-time compression scenarios that demand lightweight models. In this paper, we explore the design of real-time and lightweight diffusion codecs by addressing two pivotal questions. First, does diffusion pre-training benefit lightweight diffusion codecs? Through systematic analysis, we find that generation-oriented pre-training is less effective at small model scales whereas compression-oriented pre-training yields consistently better performance. Second, are transformers essential? We find that while global attention is crucial for standard generation, lightweight convolutions suffice for compression-oriented diffusion when paired with distillation. Guided by these findings, we establish a one-step lightweight convolution diffusion codec that achieves real-time 60 FPS encoding and 42 FPS decoding at 1080p. Further enhanced by distillation and adversarial learning, the proposed codec reduces bitrate by 85% at a comparable FID to MS-ILLM, bridging the gap between generative compression and practical real-time deployment. Codes are released at https://github.com/microsoft/GenCodec/tree/main/CoD_Lite.

paragraphs: CoD-Lite studies how to build a diffusion image codec small and fast enough for real-time compression. The paper questions whether design choices that work for large image generators also work under these tighter constraints. It focuses on two choices: what the model should learn during pretraining, and whether its architecture needs transformers.

The analysis finds that generation-oriented pretraining is less effective at small model scales, whereas compression-oriented pretraining performs consistently better. It also finds that lightweight convolutions can suffice for compression-oriented diffusion when combined with distillation. These findings motivate a convolutional codec that performs its diffusion computation in one step, with further improvements from distillation and adversarial learning.

The resulting codec achieves reported speeds of 60 frames per second for encoding and 42 for decoding at 1080p. It also uses 85% less bitrate than MS-ILLM at comparable FID. That comparison concerns the stated FID measure, rather than establishing equivalence on every aspect of reconstruction quality. The contribution is a compression-specific design supported by both analysis and real-time performance results.
summary.tldr: CoD-Lite combines compression-oriented pretraining, convolutions, and distillation to deliver a lightweight one-step diffusion codec with real-time 1080p performance.

title: CoD-Lite: Real-Time Diffusion-Based Generative Image Compression

abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL) policies are vulnerable to action hijacking even when only a few timesteps are compromised. Recent adversarial attacks and adversarial training methods have been explored, but under an explicit attack budget, existing attacks often fail to accurately expose critical coordination weaknesses and incur substantial training cost. We propose Budgeted Hierarchical Efficient Attack (BHEA), a budgeted hierarchical adversarial attack that separates decisions on when and which agents to hijack from action replacement, enabling more precise vulnerability discovery under limited attack opportunities. We further show that training cooperative policies against BHEA substantially improves robustness to limited-step action hijacking while reducing training overhead. Experiments on the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) demonstrate stronger attacks under the same attack budget and improved robustness. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/BHEA-068D.

paragraphs: Cooperative reinforcement-learning agents can lose coordination when an adversary replaces their actions at only a few moments. Under a strict attack budget, the challenge is identifying which interventions expose the most consequential weaknesses. The paper argues that existing attacks can miss those weaknesses while also making adversarial training expensive.

Budgeted Hierarchical Efficient Attack, or BHEA, separates the attack into distinct decisions. One part decides when to intervene and which agents to hijack; another chooses the replacement actions. This hierarchy gives the attack a structured way to allocate scarce intervention opportunities while searching for failures in the team’s coordinated behavior.

Experiments on the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge show stronger attacks under the same budget. Training cooperative policies against BHEA also substantially improves robustness to limited-step action hijacking and reduces training overhead. The approach therefore serves two connected purposes: revealing coordination weaknesses more effectively and supplying adversarial experience that helps policies withstand this form of disruption. The stated robustness improvements concern the budgeted action-hijacking setting studied in the paper.
summary.tldr: BHEA makes limited-budget attacks on cooperative agents more effective and improves robustness when used for adversarial training.

title: Budget-Efficient Attacks and Robustness Training for Cooperative MARL

abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is the dominant parameter-efficient fine-tuning method due to its favorable compute-performance trade-off, yet it suffers from catastrophic forgetting. We study forgetting through a tractable mean-field self-attention toy model, where tokens evolve as an interacting particle system and LoRA acts as a low-rank perturbation. Using tools from partial differential equations and dynamical systems, we characterize regimes suggesting a phase transition between forgetting and non-forgetting behavior. We show that one phase transition appears with respect to the norm of the perturbation, and the other with respect to the depth of the Transformers. We further bound the time-to-deviation in terms of the perturbation size and spectral quantities, and corroborate the predicted trends with experiments and exploratory analyses on real models under LoRA fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Low-Rank Adaptation reduces the cost of fine-tuning, but adapted models can still lose previously learned capabilities. This paper studies that forgetting through a simplified mean-field model of self-attention. In the model, tokens behave as interacting particles, and the LoRA update enters as a low-rank perturbation of their dynamics.

One transition depends on the size of the perturbation, measured by its norm, and another depends on Transformer depth. The analysis therefore links forgetting to both the strength of adaptation and the extent of attention processing.

The authors also bound the time until the perturbed dynamics deviate, using perturbation size and spectral quantities. Experiments and exploratory analyses of real models under LoRA fine-tuning corroborate the predicted trends. The theoretical results concern a tractable toy model, while the real-model evidence connects its qualitative predictions to practical adaptation behavior.
summary.tldr: A mean-field attention model links LoRA forgetting transitions to update magnitude and Transformer depth, with experiments supporting the predicted trends.

title: Understanding Catastrophic Forgetting In LoRA via Mean-Field Attention Dynamics

abstract: Proximal constraints are fundamental to the stability of the Large Language Model reinforcement learning. While the canonical clipping mechanism in PPO serves as an efficient surrogate for trust regions, we identify a critical bottleneck: fixed bounds strictly constrain the upward update margin of low-probability actions, disproportionately suppressing high-advantage tail strategies and inducing rapid entropy collapse. To address this, we introduce Band-constrained Policy Optimization (BandPO). BandPO replaces canonical clipping with Band, a unified theoretical operator that projects trust regions defined by $f$-divergences into dynamic, probability-aware clipping intervals. Theoretical analysis confirms that Band effectively resolves this exploration bottleneck. We formulate this mapping as a convex optimization problem, guaranteeing a globally optimal numerical solution while deriving closed-form solutions for specific divergences. Extensive experiments across diverse models and datasets demonstrate that BandPO consistently outperforms canonical clipping and Clip-Higher, while robustly mitigating entropy collapse. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/OpenMOSS/BandPO.

paragraphs: Language-model reinforcement learning needs to control how much a policy changes during an update. PPO uses fixed clipping bounds as an efficient approximation to a trust region. This paper identifies a drawback: for actions that already have low probability, those bounds severely restrict upward movement, even when the actions have high estimated advantage.

BandPO replaces fixed clipping with probability-aware intervals. Its Band operator translates trust regions defined through f-divergences into bounds tailored to action probabilities. This connects the intended restriction on policy change to the clipping mechanism used during optimization. The mapping is formulated as a convex optimization problem, supporting a globally optimal numerical solution, with closed-form solutions available for particular divergences.

The theoretical analysis establishes that Band addresses the identified exploration bottleneck. Experiments across different models and datasets report consistent improvements over canonical clipping and Clip-Higher, together with reduced entropy collapse. Entropy collapse means the policy's choices rapidly become less diverse. The findings suggest that adapting update bounds to action probability can preserve exploration while retaining proximal constraints on learning.
summary.tldr: BandPO derives probability-aware clipping bounds from trust regions to improve LLM reinforcement learning and mitigate entropy collapse.

title: BandPO: Bridging Trust Regions and Ratio Clipping via Probability-Aware Bounds for LLM Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) aim to estimate whether a specific data point was used in the training of a given model. Existing state-of-the-art attacks typically rely on training multiple reference models to approximate the conditional score distribution for individual data points, which leads to significant computational overhead and limits their practical applicability. In this work, we propose a novel approach – Bayesian Membership Inference Attack (BMIA), which performs conditional attack through Bayesian sampling. Specifically, we apply Laplace approximation to a single reference model to obtain a posterior over model parameters, enabling direct estimation of the conditional score distribution. Theoretically, we demonstrate that Bayesian sampling reduces intra-model variance, thereby improving attack power. This insight naturally motivates the multi-reference variant that further enhances performance when additional reference models are available. Extensive experiments across image, text, and tabular datasets indicate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both effectiveness and efficiency.

paragraphs: A membership inference attack estimates whether a particular data point appeared in a model’s training set. Strong existing attacks often train many reference models to characterize the score distribution associated with each point. That repeated training makes the attack computationally costly. Bayesian Membership Inference Attack, or BMIA, seeks to obtain this information more efficiently.

BMIA applies a Laplace approximation to one reference model, constructing an approximate posterior distribution over its parameters. Sampling from that distribution enables direct estimation of the conditional score distribution used by the attack. The paper’s theoretical analysis shows that Bayesian sampling reduces intra-model variance, connecting this statistical effect to stronger attack performance.

The same reasoning motivates a version that uses several reference models when they are available, further improving performance. Experiments across image, text, and tabular data report state-of-the-art effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution links a computational shortcut to a statistical explanation: parameter sampling can provide useful attack information without relying solely on separately training a large collection of reference models.
summary.tldr: BMIA uses Bayesian parameter sampling to estimate membership-attack score distributions more efficiently and improve attack effectiveness.

title: How does Bayesian Sampling help Membership Inference Attacks?

abstract: Current audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) are predominantly restricted to 2D perception, relying on RGB video and monaural audio. This design choice introduces a fundamental dimensionality mismatch that precludes reliable source localization and spatial reasoning in complex 3D environments. We address this limitation by presenting JAEGER, a framework that extends AV-LLMs to 3D space, to enable joint spatial grounding and reasoning through the integration of RGB-D observations and multi-channel first-order ambisonics. A core contribution of our work is the neural intensity vector (Neural IV), a learned spatial audio representation that encodes robust directional cues to enhance direction-of-arrival estimation, even in adverse acoustic scenarios with overlapping sources. To facilitate large-scale training and systematic evaluation, we propose SpatialSceneQA, a benchmark of 61k instruction-tuning samples curated from simulated physical environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach consistently surpasses 2D-centric baselines across diverse spatial perception and reasoning tasks, underscoring the necessity of explicit 3D modelling for advancing AI in physical environments. Our source code, pre-trained model checkpoints, and datasets are available at https://github.com/liuzhan22/JAEGER.

paragraphs: Audio-visual language models commonly receive color video and monaural sound, inputs that leave important spatial information unrepresented. JAEGER addresses the resulting difficulty in locating sound sources and reasoning about three-dimensional scenes. It combines RGB-D observations, which include depth, with multichannel first-order ambisonic audio to support joint spatial grounding and reasoning.

The framework introduces a learned audio representation called the Neural Intensity Vector. It encodes directional cues to improve estimates of where sounds originate, including challenging acoustic conditions with overlapping sources. This gives the model an explicit spatial representation of audio alongside its visual information, addressing the dimensional mismatch highlighted by the authors.

The paper also introduces SpatialSceneQA, containing 61,000 instruction-tuning samples from simulated physical environments for training and evaluation. Experiments report consistent improvements over two-dimensional baselines across spatial perception and reasoning tasks. The results support explicit three-dimensional modeling in these simulated settings, connecting richer sensory inputs with stronger understanding of where events occur in a scene.
summary.tldr: JAEGER combines depth-aware vision and directional audio to improve three-dimensional spatial understanding in simulated environments.

title: JAEGER: Joint 3D Audio-Visual Grounding and Reasoning in Simulated Physical Environments

abstract: Existing fair multi-view clustering methods typically suffer from a severe trade-off between clustering utility and fairness, while incurring prohibitive quadratic complexity on large-scale datasets. To address these challenges, we propose Causal Disentangled Anchor Learning (CDAL), a novel framework that achieves scalable fairness via structural disentanglement. Guided by a structural causal model perspective, CDAL utilizes a dual-anchor mechanism to structurally separate latent representations into orthogonal semantic and sensitive subspaces. We further ensure statistical independence through a linearized Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) constraint, which is optimized via an efficient alternating scheme. Theoretically, we prove the identifiability of the disentangled factors and guarantee the algorithm’s global convergence and linear time complexity $\mathcal{O}(n)$. Extensive experiments on large-scale benchmarks demonstrate that CDAL outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a superior utility-fairness trade-off. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Tracesource/CDAL.

paragraphs: CDAL addresses two obstacles in fair clustering from multiple views of the same data: preserving useful cluster structure while limiting sensitive information, and avoiding computational costs that grow quadratically with dataset size. Its approach makes the separation of semantic and sensitive information part of the representation’s structure.

It also applies a linearized Hilbert–Schmidt Independence Criterion constraint to enforce statistical independence. Experiments on large datasets report a better utility–fairness trade-off than existing leading methods. The findings combine a theoretical account of the learned separation with empirical evidence that fairness and useful clustering can be balanced more effectively at scale.
summary.tldr: CDAL separates semantic and sensitive information to improve the fairness–utility trade-off in clustering with linear-time scaling.

title: Causal Disentangled Anchor Learning for Scalable Fair Multi-view Clustering

abstract: We study infinite-horizon discounted Markov decision processes (DMDPs) under a generative model. Motivated by the Algorithms with Advice framework (Mitzenmacher and Vassilvitskii, 2022), we propose a novel framework to investigate how black-box predictions of the transition matrix can enhance sample efficiency in solving DMDPs and improve sample complexity bounds. We focus on DMDPs with $N$ state–action pairs and discount factor $\gamma$. We first provide an impossibility result showing that, in the presence of predictions with unknown accuracy, no sampling policy can compute an $\epsilon$-optimal policy with a sample complexity better than $\tilde{O}((1-\gamma)^{-3} N \epsilon^{-2})$, which matches the state-of-the-art minimax sample complexity bound without prediction. In complement, we design an algorithm based on minimax optimization techniques that leverages predictions of the transition matrix without requiring knowledge of the prediction error. Our algorithm achieves a sample complexity bound that depends on the prediction error and is uniformly better than $\tilde{O}((1-\gamma)^{-4} N \epsilon^{-2})$, the previous best result derived from convex optimization methods. In some cases, our bound even improves upon the state-of-the-art $\tilde{O}((1-\gamma)^{-3} N \epsilon^{-2})$, despite not having access to the prediction quality.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether predictions about state transitions can reduce the samples needed to solve an infinite-horizon discounted Markov decision process. The setting provides a generative model for obtaining samples, plus black-box predictions of the transition matrix. The challenge is that the algorithm does not know how accurate those predictions are.

The authors first establish a worst-case barrier. With unknown prediction accuracy, no sampling policy can universally improve on the established minimax sample-complexity scaling for finding an approximately optimal policy without predictions. This prevents interpreting predictive advice as an automatic reduction in the information that must be collected.

They then develop a minimax-optimization algorithm whose sample bound adapts to prediction error without requiring that error as an input. Its bound uniformly improves on the previous convex-optimization-based result and, in some cases, improves on the standard minimax benchmark. These conclusions are compatible: predictions cannot guarantee a better worst case across all settings, yet can produce stronger guarantees in favorable cases. The contribution combines that opportunity with an explicit account of its worst-case limit.
summary.tldr: Transition predictions can improve discounted-MDP sample efficiency in favorable cases without known prediction accuracy, despite a worst-case impossibility bound.

title: Efficiently Solving Discounted MDPs via Predictions with Unknown Prediction Errors

abstract: We develop a theory of generalization and scaling for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Transformers that cleanly separates active per-input capacity from routing combinatorics. By conditioning on fixed routing patterns and union-bounding across them, we derive a sup-norm covering-number bound whose metric entropy scales with the active parameter budget and incurs a MoE-specific routing overhead. Combined with a standard ERM analysis for squared loss, this yields a generalization bound under a $d$-dimensional manifold data model and $C^\beta$ targets, showing that approximation and estimation trade off as in dense networks once active parameters are accounted for appropriately. We further prove a constructive approximation theorem for MoE architectures, showing that, under the approximation construction, error can decrease either by scaling active capacity or by increasing the number of experts, depending on the dominant bottleneck. From these results we derive neural scaling laws for model size, data size, and compute-optimal tradeoffs. Overall, our results provide a transparent statistical reference point for reasoning about MoE scaling, clarifying which behaviors are certified by worst-case theory and which must arise from data-dependent routing structure or optimization dynamics.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts Transformers distribute computation among experts, making their statistical capacity depend on both the parameters active for an input and the possible routing decisions. This paper develops theory that separates those contributions. The distinction helps explain how a model’s total size relates to the computation and capacity actually used for each example.

The analysis first fixes routing patterns and then combines bounds across those patterns. The resulting measure of model complexity scales with active parameters and includes an additional routing cost. Under a manifold model of the data and smooth target functions, an analysis of squared-loss training yields a generalization bound with an approximation–estimation trade-off resembling that of dense networks.

A constructive approximation theorem shows that error can decrease by increasing active capacity or adding experts, depending on the dominant bottleneck in the construction. The authors derive scaling laws for model size, data, and compute-optimal choices. These results provide a worst-case statistical reference for separating theoretically certified behavior from effects attributable to routing structure or optimization.
summary.tldr: The paper derives MoE generalization and scaling results by separating active parameter capacity from the additional complexity of routing.

title: Generalization and Scaling Laws for Mixture-of-ExpertsTransformers

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) excels at finding general-purpose latent representations from complex data, yet lacks a unifying theoretical framework that explains the diverse existing methods and guides the design of new ones. We cast SSL as latent distribution matching (LDM): learning representations that maximize their log-probability under an assumed latent model (alignment), while maximizing latent entropy to prevent collapse (uniformity). This view unifies independent component analysis with contrastive, non-contrastive, and predictive SSL methods, including stop gradient approaches. Leveraging LDM, we derive a nonlinear, sampling-free Bayesian filtering model with a Kalman-based predictor for high-dimensional timeseries. We further prove that predictive LDM yields identifiable latent representations under mild assumptions, even with nonlinear predictors. Overall, LDM clarifies the assumptions behind established SSL methods and provides principled guidance for developing new approaches.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning produces useful representations without relying on conventional task labels, but its many methods lack a single explanatory framework. This paper casts them as latent distribution matching. Representations are trained to have high probability under an assumed latent model while also maintaining high entropy, which prevents collapse to uninformative representations.

These two aims correspond to alignment and uniformity. The framework connects independent component analysis with contrastive, non-contrastive, and predictive methods, including approaches using stop gradients. By expressing them through a common objective, it makes their underlying assumptions more explicit and provides a basis for designing methods from a specified latent model.

The authors use the framework to derive a nonlinear Bayesian filtering model for high-dimensional time series, with a Kalman-based predictor and no sampling requirement. They also prove that predictive latent distribution matching yields identifiable representations under mild assumptions, even with nonlinear predictors. The contribution therefore combines a unifying interpretation with a concrete model derivation and a conditional theoretical guarantee about recovering latent representations.
summary.tldr: Latent distribution matching unifies self-supervised objectives and yields a sampling-free filtering model plus conditional identifiability guarantees.

title: Understanding Self-Supervised Learning via Latent Distribution Matching

abstract: Complex problems, whether in math, logic, or planning, are solved by humans through a sequence of steps where the result of one step informs the next. In this work, we adopt the perspective that the reasoning power of Transformers is fundamentally limited by a fixed maximum number of steps along any latent path of computation. To address this, we introduce Turbo Connection (TurboConn), a novel architecture that overcomes the fixed-depth constraint by routing multiple residual connections from the higher-layer hidden states of each token $t$ to the lower layers of token $t+1$. Fine-tuning pre-trained LLMs with our method not only yields accuracy gains of 0.9% to over 10% on benchmarks like GSM8K, Parity, and multi-step arithmetic, but also demonstrates that the density of these backward connections is critical; our dense interaction significantly outperforms "sparse" alternatives that only pass a single hidden state or vector. Notably, TurboConn can be integrated into pre-trained LLMs to overcome task-specific plateaus: while a fine-tuned Qwen-3-1.7B achieves only 53.78% on Parity, adding our architectural modification enables the model to reach 100% accuracy, all without the necessity to retrain the full model from scratch or sophisticated curriculum learning. Our results provide strong empirical evidence that the depth of the computational path is a key factor in reasoning ability, also offering a new mechanism to enhance LLMs without significantly affecting generation latency.

paragraphs: This paper views transformer reasoning through the length of its internal computational paths. A fixed stack of layers limits how many processing steps occur along a path. Turbo Connection extends those paths across consecutive tokens by routing multiple residual connections from higher layers of one token into lower layers of the next.

The mechanism lets later token computation reuse several high-level states from the preceding token. Experiments show that connection density matters: passing multiple states through dense interactions substantially outperforms sparse alternatives that transfer only one state or vector. The modification can be added to pretrained models and fine-tuned, so its use does not require training an entire model from scratch.

Reported accuracy gains range from 0.9% to over 10% on tasks including GSM8K, parity, and multistep arithmetic. In the reported parity comparison, a fine-tuned Qwen-3-1.7B improves from 53.78% to 100% after the architectural modification. The authors also report no significant generation-latency impact. These findings provide empirical support for computational-path depth as an important contributor to reasoning performance, including overcoming task-specific performance plateaus.
summary.tldr: TurboConn feeds higher-layer states into the next token’s lower layers, extending computational paths and improving reasoning after fine-tuning.

title: Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers

abstract: Quantization has significantly improved the compute and memory efficiency of Large Language Model (LLM) training. However, existing approaches still rely on accumulating their updates in high-precision: concretely, gradient updates must be applied to a high-precision weight buffer, known as $\textit{master weights}$. This buffer introduces substantial memory overhead, particularly for Sparse Mixture of Experts (SMoE) models, where model parameters and optimizer states dominate memory usage. To address this, we introduce the Error-Compensating Optimizer (ECO), which eliminates master weights by applying updates directly to quantized parameters. ECO quantizes weights after each step and carefully injects the resulting quantization error into the optimizer momentum, forming an error-feedback loop with no additional memory. We prove that, under standard assumptions and a decaying learning rate, ECO converges to a constant-radius neighborhood of the optimum, while naive master-weight removal can incur an error that is inversely proportional to the learning rate. We show empirical results for pretraining small Transformers (30–800M), a Gemma-3 1B model, and a 2.1B parameter Sparse MoE model with FP8 quantization, and fine-tuning DeepSeek-MoE-16B in INT4 precision. Throughout, ECO matches baselines with master weights up to near-lossless accuracy, significantly shifting the static memory vs validation loss Pareto frontier.

paragraphs: Low-precision training often keeps a separate high-precision copy of the weights so that small gradient updates can accumulate accurately. These master weights consume substantial memory, particularly in sparse mixture-of-experts models. ECO removes this buffer and applies updates directly to the quantized parameters.

After each update, ECO quantizes the weights and feeds the resulting error into the optimizer’s momentum. This uses existing optimizer memory to carry an error-correction signal into later steps. Across these settings, ECO nearly preserves the accuracy of master-weight baselines while improving the trade-off between static memory and validation loss. The result makes error compensation central to removing the buffer: reduced storage comes with a mechanism for retaining information otherwise lost through quantization.
summary.tldr: ECO removes full-precision master weights by feeding quantization errors into optimizer momentum, reducing memory with nearly preserved empirical accuracy.

title: ECO: Quantized Training without Full-Precision Master Weights

abstract: As increasingly capable agents are deployed, a central safety challenge is how to retain meaningful human control without modifying the underlying system. We study a minimal control interface in which an agent chooses whether to act autonomously (play) or defer (ask), while a human simultaneously chooses whether to be permissive (trust) or engage in oversight (oversee), and model this interaction as a two-player Markov Game. When this game forms a Markov Potential Game, we prove an alignment guarantee: any increase in the agent’s utility from acting more autonomously cannot decrease the human’s value. This establishes a form of intrinsic alignment where the agent’s incentive to seek autonomy is structurally coupled to the human’s welfare. Practically, the framework induces a transparent control layer encouraging the agent to defer when risky and act when safe. While we use gridworld simulations to illustrate the emergence of this collaboration, our primary validation involves an agentic tool-use task where two 30B-parameter language models are fine-tuned via independent policy gradient. We demonstrate that even as the agents learn to coordinate on the fly, this framework effectively reduces safety violations in realistic, open-ended environments.

paragraphs: This paper studies a small control interface for balancing an agent's autonomy with human oversight. The agent chooses whether to act or ask, while the human simultaneously chooses whether to trust or oversee. Modeling those choices as a two-player Markov game makes their interaction over time part of the learning problem.

The key theoretical guarantee is conditional: when the interaction forms a Markov Potential Game, an increase in the agent's utility from greater autonomy cannot reduce the human's value. The empirical results support the control mechanism, while the formal alignment guarantee remains tied to the stated potential-game condition.
summary.tldr: A cooperative act-or-defer game reduces safety violations and conditionally links an agent's gains from autonomy to human welfare.

title: The Oversight Game: Learning to Cooperatively Balance an AI Agent’s Safety and Autonomy

abstract: Simulation-Based Inference (SBI) is critical for scientific discovery, with generative models offering a promising path toward efficient inference. However, existing methods struggle with effective multimodal modeling. They often rely on brute-force fusion strategies that ignore the structural disparities between parameters and observations, thus limiting estimation fidelity. In this work, we introduce FUSE (Feynman-Kac steered mUlti-modal flow matching for efficient Simulation-based posterior Estimation). Unlike prior work, FUSE employs a dual-track architecture that preserves the distinct features of multimodal inputs while facilitating dynamic interaction. Additionally, we propose an FK-steered sampling strategy that leverages intermediate observation likelihoods to guide the generative trajectories, effectively improving the sample quality during inference. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on standard SBI benchmarks, producing posteriors that closely match ground-truth MCMC. Furthermore, in a real-world exoplanet orbital estimation task, FUSE successfully resolves complex parameter degeneracies that challenge existing methods, highlighting its potential to accelerate complex scientific discoveries in astrophysics and beyond.
