paragraphs: Simulation-based inference uses simulated relationships between parameters and observations to estimate which parameter values are plausible given observed data. Generative models offer a route to efficient posterior estimation, but the paper argues that simply merging heterogeneous inputs loses important differences between parameters and observations. FUSE addresses how these inputs interact and how posterior samples are generated.

Its dual-track architecture maintains distinct representations for the different input types while allowing them to exchange information dynamically. During sampling, a Feynman-Kac steering strategy uses intermediate observation likelihoods to guide generative trajectories. This introduces observation-based guidance along the generation process, helping improve sample quality rather than relying only on the model’s initial conditioning.

On standard simulation-based inference benchmarks, FUSE outperforms leading baselines and produces posterior distributions closely matching reference MCMC results. In an exoplanet orbital-estimation task, it also resolves complex parameter degeneracies that challenge existing methods. These findings indicate potential for scientific problems where multiple parameter combinations can explain similar observations.
summary.tldr: FUSE combines distinct input-processing tracks with likelihood-guided generation to improve simulation-based posterior estimation.

title: FUSE: FK-Steered Multi-Modal Flow Matching for Efficient Simulation-Based Posterior Estimation

abstract: Autonomous AI agents powered by large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable of running a full cycle of scientific research, yet we still lack reliable ways to verify that their discoveries are correct. Because novel findings demand costly real-world validation, existing benchmarks fall back on LLM-as-judge scoring of generated papers or single leaderboard metrics, both coarse proxies for scientific reasoning. We introduce FIRE-BENCH (Full-cycle Insight Rediscovery Evaluation), which instead asks agents to rediscover established, verifiable findings from recent, high-impact machine learning research. Given only a high-level research question from a published study, an agent must independently design experiments, run them, and draw evidence-backed conclusions, scored against the study’s documented findings. Across state-of-the-art agents with frontier backbones such as gpt-5, even the strongest reaches limited rediscovery success ($<$50 F1), with high run-to-run variance and recurring failures in experimental design, execution, and evidence-based reasoning. Beyond diagnosing current systems, FIRE-BENCH shows that open-ended discovery can be evaluated rigorously and verifiably, laying a foundation for building reliable environments that improve agents.

paragraphs: Evaluating an AI agent’s scientific discoveries is difficult because verifying genuinely new findings can require costly real-world work. FIRE-Bench takes a different route: it asks agents to independently rediscover established findings from machine-learning studies. Those documented results provide a reference for checking whether the agent’s conclusions are supported, rather than relying only on the apparent quality of a generated paper.

Each task supplies a high-level research question. The agent must design experiments, execute them, and derive conclusions from the evidence it obtains. Its findings are then scored against those documented in the source study. This setup evaluates the research cycle as a connected process, including the decisions that determine which evidence gets collected.

Among the evaluated frontier agents, even the strongest achieves a rediscovery F1 score below 50. Performance varies substantially between runs, with repeated problems in experimental design, execution, and evidence-based reasoning. The benchmark therefore supplies both a verifiable evaluation approach and a way to identify where current scientific agents fail.
summary.tldr: FIRE-Bench evaluates scientific agents through verifiable rediscovery tasks and finds limited, inconsistent success across the agents tested.

title: FIRE-Bench: Evaluating AI Agents on the Rediscovery of Scientific Insights

abstract: Existing EEG models are limited by electrode heterogeneity and rigid "channel-first" architectures that treat sensors as independent features. We propose Brain Signal Rendering (BSR), which reinterprets EEG as a physical projection of neural activity and transforms raw signals into structured spatiotemporal tensors (termed Spectrum Videos), enabling the transfer of rich priors from video foundation models. By utilizing VideoMAE for self-supervised pre-training, BSR learns robust, layout-agnostic spatiotemporal representations that preserve neural topology. We further employ subject-level few-shot learning and introduce cross-montage fine-tuning to rigorously evaluate generalization across subjects and electrode configurations. Experiments show that VideoMAE model integrated with the BSR framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art spectrum based methods, providing a scalable and data-efficient foundation for generalizable EEG modeling. Our code is available at https://github.com/yanweifu-sii/BSR-VideoMAE.

paragraphs: EEG models must cope with differences between people and between electrode arrangements. Architectures that treat each sensor as an independent input feature can tie learned representations closely to a particular layout. Brain Signal Rendering addresses this problem by representing EEG as a physical projection of neural activity with spatial and temporal structure.

The framework transforms raw signals into structured tensors called Spectrum Videos. This representation enables the use of a video foundation model, VideoMAE, for self-supervised pretraining. The intended benefit is to transfer useful knowledge about patterns across space and time while preserving neural topology and learning representations that are less dependent on the electrode layout.

The authors evaluate adaptation with few examples at the subject level and introduce cross-montage fine-tuning to study changes in electrode configuration. VideoMAE combined with Brain Signal Rendering significantly outperforms the spectrum-based methods used for comparison. These findings support the representation as a data-efficient route toward EEG models that generalize across people and sensor arrangements, with the evaluation explicitly addressing both sources of variation.
summary.tldr: Brain Signal Rendering converts EEG into Spectrum Videos so video pretraining can support generalization across subjects and electrode layouts.

title: Harnessing Spectrum Video for Subject-Level Few-Shot and Cross-Montage EEG Generalization

abstract: We study adaptive querying for learning user-dependent quantities of interest, such as responses to held-out items and psychometric indicators, within tight question budgets. Classical Bayesian design and computerized adaptive testing typically rely on restrictive parametric assumptions or expensive posterior approximations, limiting their use in heterogeneous, high-dimensional, and cold-start settings. We introduce a persona-induced latent variable model that represents a user’s state through membership in a finite dictionary of AI personas, each offering response distributions produced by a large language model. This yields expressive priors with closed-form posterior updates and efficient finite-mixture predictions, enabling scalable Bayesian design for sequential item selection. Experiments on synthetic data and WorldValuesBench demonstrate that persona-based posteriors deliver accurate probabilistic predictions and an interpretable adaptive elicitation pipeline.

paragraphs: When only a few questions can be asked, each question should help reveal something useful about the respondent. This paper studies adaptive questioning for predicting unasked responses and user-dependent indicators. It targets settings where users differ substantially, the information space is large, or little is initially known about a new user.

The proposed model represents uncertainty about a user through a finite collection of AI personas. Each persona supplies response probabilities generated by a language model. As the user answers questions, the system updates the probabilities associated with those personas. This construction allows closed-form posterior updates and predictions formed by mixing the persona-specific response distributions.

Those efficient updates support sequential question selection through Bayesian design: observations inform which question to ask next. Experiments on synthetic data and WorldValuesBench report accurate probabilistic predictions and an interpretable elicitation process. The finite persona dictionary is central to the approach, supplying both its expressive starting assumptions about users and its computationally manageable representation of uncertainty.
summary.tldr: A finite dictionary of language-model-generated personas enables efficient Bayesian question selection and accurate user-response predictions.

title: Adaptive Querying with AI Persona Priors

abstract: Scaling large models requires optimization strategies that ensure rapid convergence grounded in stability. Maximal Update Parametrization ($\boldsymbol{\mu}$P) provides a theoretical safeguard for width-invariant $\Theta(1)$ activation control, whereas emerging optimizers like Muon are only "half-aligned" with these constraints: they control updates but allow weights to drift. To address this limitation, we introduce the Spectral Sphere Optimizer (SSO), which enforces strict module-wise spectral constraints on both weights and their updates. By deriving the steepest descent direction on the spectral sphere, SSO realizes a fully $\boldsymbol{\mu}$P-aligned optimization process. To enable large-scale training, we implement SSO as an efficient parallel algorithm within Megatron. Through extensive pretraining on diverse architectures, including Dense 1.7B, MoE 8B-A1B, and 200-layer DeepNet models, SSO consistently outperforms AdamW and Muon. Furthermore, we observe significant practical stability benefits, including improved MoE router load balancing, suppressed outliers, and strictly bounded activations.

paragraphs: Stable training depends on controlling how model computations change as parameters are updated. Maximal Update Parametrization, or μP, provides a theoretical basis for keeping activation scale controlled across model widths. This paper argues that optimizers such as Muon only partly match that framework because they constrain updates while allowing the weights themselves to drift.

The authors derive a steepest-descent direction on this constrained space, producing an optimization process they describe as fully aligned with μP. They also implement the method as a parallel algorithm within Megatron to support large-scale training.

Pretraining experiments cover a dense 1.7-billion-parameter model, an 8-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 1 billion active parameters, and 200-layer DeepNet models. SSO consistently outperforms AdamW and Muon in these evaluations. Reported stability benefits include better expert-router load balancing, fewer outliers, and strictly bounded activations, connecting the mathematical constraints to observed training behavior.
summary.tldr: SSO constrains both model weights and updates to improve optimization performance and stability in large-model pretraining.

title: Controlled LLM Training on Spectral Sphere

abstract: Autonomous image-editing agents powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs) improve transparency and controllability by translating high-level instructions into tool-mediated edit sequences, but training such agents with reinforcement learning often relies on dense proxy rewards (e.g., incremental image-quality score gains) to compensate for sparse human feedback. When these proxies overvalue small local changes, the resulting optimization signal can be dominated by numerically measurable yet perceptually negligible edits, biasing policy gradients toward proxy artifacts rather than meaningful progress. We propose B-Spar, a reward-centric Reinforcement Learning framework for perceptually aligned image retouching under sparse feedback that combines prior-guided trajectory sampling to reduce inefficient exploration, Bayesian reward modeling to densify sparse binary feedback into a stable training signal, and anchor-regularized policy optimization to steer updates toward high-reward regions while preventing early mode collapse. Experiments on public benchmarks demonstrate that B-Spar improves perceptual quality and metric alignment with stable training and competitive inference efficiency over strong prompt-based and training-based baselines. Notably, it outperforms AIGC-based baselines by over 95% in perceptual quality, achieving an improvement of approximately 33.5% over the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Image-editing agents can translate broad instructions into sequences of tool operations, making their actions easier to control and inspect. Training them is harder when human feedback is sparse. Dense substitute rewards can favor tiny, numerically detectable edits that barely change perceived quality, directing learning toward the scoring mechanism instead of meaningful visual improvement.

B-Spar combines three mechanisms to address this problem. Prior-guided trajectory sampling reduces inefficient exploration of editing sequences. Bayesian reward modeling turns sparse binary feedback into a denser, more stable training signal. Anchor-regularized policy optimization then guides updates toward high-reward behavior while preventing the policy from collapsing too early into a narrow set of choices.

On public benchmarks, the authors report better perceptual quality and metric alignment, stable training, and competitive inference efficiency against strong prompt-based and training-based alternatives. They report perceptual-quality improvements exceeding 95% over AIGC-based baselines and approximately 33.5% over the state of the art. The findings support improving the reward signal itself as a route to more perceptually meaningful retouching.
summary.tldr: B-Spar combines Bayesian reward modeling, guided exploration, and regularized updates to train image-retouching agents from sparse feedback.

title: B-Spar: Bayesian Sparse-Reward Modeling for RL-based Image Editing

abstract: Unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specified data, but its efficacy is typically assessed with task-level metrics like accuracy and perplexity. We show that these metrics can be misleading, as models can appear to forget while their original behavior is easily restored through minimal fine-tuning. This reversibility suggests that information is merely suppressed, not genuinely erased. To address this critical evaluation gap, we introduce a representation-level analysis framework. Our toolkit comprises PCA similarity and shift, centered kernel alignment (CKA), and Fisher information, complemented by a summary metric, the mean PCA distance, to measure representational drift. Applying this framework across multiple unlearning methods, data domains, and LLMs, we identify four distinct forgetting regimes based on their reversibility and catastrophicity. We compare recovery strategies and show that relearning efficiency relies on the data source. We also find that irreversible, non-catastrophic forgetting is exceptionally challenging. By probing unlearning limits, we identify a case of seemingly irreversible, targeted forgetting, offering insights for more robust erasure algorithms. Overall, our findings expose a gap in current evaluation and establish a representation-level foundation for trustworthy unlearning.

paragraphs: A model can perform poorly on information designated for removal yet quickly recover its earlier behavior after minimal fine-tuning. This paper shows why accuracy and perplexity alone can give a misleading picture of unlearning. Such reversibility suggests that targeted information may be suppressed rather than erased.

The authors introduce a framework for examining changes in internal representations. It combines PCA-based similarity and shift, centered kernel alignment, and Fisher information, with mean PCA distance summarizing representational drift. Applied across unlearning methods, data domains, and language models, the framework identifies four forgetting regimes based on reversibility and whether forgetting causes catastrophic damage.

The authors identify one case of seemingly irreversible targeted forgetting, preserving uncertainty about true erasure. Overall, the results motivate evaluating both recoverability and internal change when judging whether unlearning has achieved its intended effect.
summary.tldr: Representation-level analysis shows that apparent unlearning can be readily reversible, exposing gaps in evaluations based only on task performance.

title: Unlearning Isn’t Deletion: Investigating Reversibility of Machine Unlearning in LLMs

abstract: In this work, we extend distributional reinforcement learning (RL) to develop a risk-sensitive multi-objective RL framework, with applications to domains such as finance and robotics. We achieve this by adopting vector-risk measures and approximating them via Knothe-Rosenblatt (KR) quantile regression. This approach directly extends the IQN framework to the multi-objective setting, aligns with the axiomatic definition of vector-risk measures, and guarantees that critics converge under the distributional Bellman operator. To mitigate the artificial ordering imposed by the KR map, we employ a transformer architecture without positional encoding, and introduce MO-TQC for training stability. We demonstrate improved performance on MO-Gymnasium benchmarks and use our framework to study risk-sensitive policies in multi-objective tasks.

This approach directly extends the IQN framework to the multi-objective setting, aligns with the axiomatic definition of vector-risk measures, and guarantees that critics converge under the distributional Bellman operator. To mitigate the artificial ordering imposed by the KR map, we employ a transformer architecture without positional encoding, and introduce MO-TQC for training stability. We demonstrate improved performance on MO-Gymnasium benchmarks and use our framework to study risk-sensitive policies in multi-objective tasks.

paragraphs: Multi-objective reinforcement learning must account for several goals at once, while risk-sensitive learning also considers uncertainty in outcomes. This paper brings those requirements together through distributional reinforcement learning. Its framework uses vector-risk measures to represent risk across multiple objectives, with finance and robotics identified as potential application domains.

The method approximates these measures using Knothe-Rosenblatt quantile regression, extending the IQN framework to multiple objectives. The construction aligns with the axiomatic definition of vector-risk measures, and the paper establishes critic convergence under the distributional Bellman operator. This gives the proposed representation a theoretical connection to both risk measurement and the update rule used to learn outcome distributions.

They also introduce MO-TQC to improve training stability. Experiments report improved performance on MO-Gymnasium benchmarks and examine risk-sensitive policies in multi-objective tasks. The contribution provides a way to study preferences over uncertain outcomes when several objectives must be considered together.
summary.tldr: The paper extends distributional reinforcement learning to multiple objectives using quantile regression and vector-valued risk measures.

title: Knothe-Rosenblatt Quantile Regression for Risk-sensitive Multi-objective Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In multi-view clustering (MVC), conventional anchor learning based models implicitly assume a uniform distribution of anchors across clusters, which could lead to inferior representation, especially when clusters vary significantly in size, as larger clusters require more anchors so as to adequately capture their intrinsic structural complexity. To alleviate this, we design a method termed FCFMVC that explicitly encourages proportional anchor allocation. To be specific, we transfer anchor allocation to discrete sample-cluster learning via bipartite graph bridge, and then backpropagate cluster state consisting of size and dispersion degree to guide anchor assignment. This allows the model to integrate cluster cardinality awareness and structural compactness directly into anchor distribution. On the other hand, we regard anchors as pseudo-samples, introduce an anchor-cluster indicator matrix on each view, and directly constrain the number of anchors assigned to each cluster within a tolerance margin. These two paths are further coupled through anchor-sample label alignment, and collaboratively facilitate anchor generation from fine-grained (anchor-level) to coarse-grained (cluster-level) structures. Besides, the entire optimization operation with linear time and space cost makes FCFMVC well-scalable to large-scale tasks. Experiments on datasets with diverse scales confirm the effectiveness of our FCFMVC.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups samples using several representations of the same data. Anchor-based methods summarize those samples through representative points, but conventional approaches implicitly distribute anchors uniformly across clusters. The paper argues that this can underrepresent larger clusters, which may need more anchors to capture their internal structure.

FCFMVC encourages anchor allocation to reflect cluster proportions through two connected paths. One uses a bipartite graph to connect anchor allocation with discrete sample assignments, then feeds cluster size and dispersion back into anchor assignment. The other treats anchors as pseudo-samples and directly constrains how many belong to each cluster within a tolerance margin.

Alignment between anchor and sample labels couples the two paths, connecting detailed anchor decisions with broader cluster organization. Here, the allocation concern centers on cluster size and structure. The authors report linear time and space costs for the optimization, supporting scalability, and experiments across datasets of different sizes demonstrate effectiveness. The approach makes representational resources responsive to unequal cluster needs.
summary.tldr: FCFMVC allocates clustering anchors according to cluster size and structure, improving representation while retaining linear time and space costs.

title: Fine-to-Coarse Fairness-Informed Multi-View Clustering

abstract: Missing data is a common challenge in spatiotemporal systems, arising in applications such as air quality monitoring and urban traffic management. Traditional machine learning approaches, like recurrent and graph neural networks, rely on iterative propagation, which tends to accumulate errors over time and space. Recent diffusion-based methods mitigate error propagation but require iterative sampling and often depend on problem-agnostic Gaussian priors, limiting both efficiency and effectiveness. To address these limitations, we propose GiFlow, a Graph-Informed Flow Matching framework for spatiotemporal imputation. GiFlow replaces the typical Gaussian prior with a graph-informed prior constructed via spatiotemporal filtering of observable signals, which better aligns the source distribution to the target and thereby simplifies the generation trajectory. The flow field is parameterized by a hybrid vector field model that integrates spatial attention, temporal attention, and spatiotemporal propagation, enabling joint modeling of spatial and temporal dependencies. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed GiFlow outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches in spatiotemporal imputation. The code is available at https://github.com/zepengzhang/GiFlow.

paragraphs: GiFlow recovers missing observations in systems whose measurements vary across both space and time, such as traffic or air-quality monitoring. The paper describes two obstacles in existing approaches: repeated propagation can accumulate errors, while diffusion methods require iterative sampling and often start from Gaussian distributions unrelated to the particular problem.

GiFlow changes the starting distribution. It filters observable signals across space and time to construct a graph-informed prior that better matches the distribution of the data being reconstructed. This closer starting point simplifies the generation trajectory. A hybrid vector-field model then combines spatial attention, temporal attention, and spatiotemporal propagation to represent how reconstruction should proceed.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report that GiFlow outperforms state-of-the-art imputation methods. The contribution connects the choice of a generative starting distribution with the structure already available in the observations. Using that structure both in the prior and in the learned flow allows spatial and temporal relationships to inform recovery throughout the framework.
summary.tldr: GiFlow reconstructs missing spatiotemporal data using flow matching that starts from a graph-informed prior derived from observed signals.

title: Spatiotemporal Imputation with Graph-Informed Flow Matching

abstract: The ability to use tools is fundamental for large language model (LLM) agents. Given a task, existing systems use LLMs to plan and generate tool calls, which are executed by real-world tools to complete the task. However, tool calls are prone to errors because they are generated primarily from the intrinsic capabilities of LLMs. Moreover, while it is useful to let LLMs iteratively refine the tool-call sequence using execution results from real tools, this process can be expensive and may cause unsafe side effects. To improve LLM tool calls and address issues caused by using real tools for refinement, we introduce Gecko, a stateful simulation environment that provides informative feedback for refining LLM tool calls before real execution. Specifically, Gecko combines rules and LLMs to check the validity of tool names and arguments, synthesize schema-conforming and state-consistent responses, and judge task completion against the user objective. These three types of feedback allow LLMs to refine their tool calls in simulation, forming a simple yet effective test-time scaling method named GATS. On BFCLv3 and $\tau^2$-bench, GATS consistently improves the performance of various LLMs, including GPT-4o, GPT-5, and Gemini-3.0-pro.

paragraphs: Language-model agents can make mistakes when choosing tools or supplying arguments. Letting them discover those mistakes through real execution can be costly and can produce unwanted side effects. Gecko provides a simulation environment in which agents can revise their proposed tool calls before using the actual tools.

The simulator combines rules and language models to supply three kinds of feedback. It checks whether tool names and arguments are valid, generates responses that obey the tool schema and the current simulated state, and evaluates whether the sequence accomplishes the user’s objective. Maintaining state matters because a sequence of calls must remain coherent as earlier actions change the situation faced by later ones.

Using this feedback for iterative refinement yields GATS, a test-time scaling method that spends additional computation on simulated practice. On BFCLv3 and τ²-bench, GATS consistently improves multiple language models, including GPT-4o, GPT-5, and Gemini-3.0-pro. These results support stateful simulation as a useful source of corrective feedback for agent tool use before real execution.
summary.tldr: Gecko lets agents refine tool-call sequences using stateful simulated feedback, improving benchmark performance before real execution.

title: Gecko: A Simulation Environment with Stateful Feedback for Refining Agent Tool Calls

abstract: Open-vocabulary mobile manipulation (OVMM) requires long-horizon navigation in unseen environments and object-centric manipulation. Most existing methods treat navigation and manipulation as separate stages, which can yield navigation endpoints that are poor for manipulation or manipulation-friendly poses that are globally inefficient. We address this mismatch with 3D Interaction Chains (3D-IC), a unified framework that couples multi-stage navigation and manipulation planning. 3D-IC maintains a shared 3D feature map for both skills, generates stage-aligned interaction waypoints, and links them into candidate multi-stage chains. A hierarchical policy then scores these chains by jointly considering feasibility (via VLM reasoning over waypoint-centric 3D features) and transition cost, selecting the best trade-off between success and path efficiency. The robot executes the next waypoint and replans as new observations arrive. Experiments in simulation and on a real Stretch 3 robot demonstrate consistent gains in both task success and trajectory efficiency.

paragraphs: A mobile robot can reach an object yet stop somewhere that makes manipulation awkward. Conversely, a pose that suits manipulation may require an inefficient route. This paper addresses that coordination problem in open-vocabulary mobile manipulation, where robots must navigate unfamiliar environments and interact with objects over extended sequences of actions.

The proposed 3D Interaction Chains framework gives navigation and manipulation a shared 3D feature map. It generates interaction waypoints aligned with task stages and connects them into candidate chains. A hierarchical policy scores those chains using both feasibility, assessed through vision-language reasoning about waypoint-centered features, and the cost of moving between stages.

The robot executes the next selected waypoint and replans when new observations arrive. This keeps immediate action tied to a multistage plan while allowing that plan to change with new information. Experiments in simulation and on a Stretch 3 robot report consistent improvements in task success and trajectory efficiency. The findings support planning movement and object interaction together when their requirements affect one another.
summary.tldr: 3D Interaction Chains jointly plans navigation and manipulation to improve robot task success and path efficiency.

title: Joint Navigation and Manipulation Planning with 3D Interaction Chains

abstract: Post-training with explicit reasoning traces is common to improve the reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). However, acquiring high-quality reasoning traces is often costly and time-consuming. Hence, the self-improvement paradigm has emerged, enabling MLLMs to self-generate reasoning traces for training without external supervision. Despite its effectiveness, we reveal two shortcomings in the self-improvement training of MLLMs: 1) data imbalance, where simple samples are over-trained, but the challenging yet crucial samples are under-trained; 2) language prior bias, where MLLMs overly rely on linguistic priors while neglecting the visual cues. To this end, we propose VISTA, a VIsion-aware Self-improvement Training framework for enhancing the multimodal Reasoning of MLLMs. Specifically, VISTA first introduces a prefix resampling strategy to reuse the partial correct reasoning traces for efficient data collection, and then designs a vision-aware attention score to quantify the model’s focus on visual information. Extensive experiments show that VISTA can be applied to various post-training scenarios, i.e., supervised fine-tuning and preference learning, and effectively enhances the multimodal reasoning performance across various MLLMs and tasks, e.g., bringing up to +13.66% average performance gains for Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct.

paragraphs: Multimodal models can generate their own reasoning traces for further training, avoiding the cost of externally produced traces. The paper identifies two weaknesses in this process. Easy samples receive too much training attention while difficult ones receive too little, and models can rely heavily on language-based expectations while neglecting the visual evidence.

summary.tldr: VISTA improves multimodal self-training by reusing partially correct reasoning and measuring visual attention, with reported gains across models and post-training settings.

title: Learn to Think: Improving Multimodal Reasoning through Vision-Aware Self-Improvement Training

abstract: The rapid evolution of generative AI, from GANs to modern diffusion models, has resulted in increasingly subtle discriminative clues. These fine-grained signals are often overshadowed by dominant, high-fidelity image content (e.g., the main subject), limiting the reliability of existing detectors that predominantly rely on global representations. To address this challenge, we propose the Peak-Guided Calibration (PGC) framework. PGC introduces a novel strategy that aggregates salient features via a peak-focusing mechanism. Specifically, by employing a peak-sensitive aggregation that accentuates the most discriminative local clues, PGC leverages these critical signals to calibrate the global decision. This approach recovers subtle patterns that would otherwise be submerged in the global context. Furthermore, to better simulate real-world threats, we introduce the CommGen15 dataset, a challenging benchmark comprising samples from 15 commercial models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PGC achieves state-of-the-art performance. Specifically, it improves mean accuracy by +12.3% on our CommGen15 dataset, and sets new records on standard benchmarks, including GenImage (+2.1%), AIGI (+3.5%), and UniversalFakeDetect (+1.7%). Code is available at https://github.com/xiaoyu6868/PGC.

paragraphs: Detecting generated images becomes harder when the relevant clues are subtle and the dominant image content looks convincing. This paper argues that global image representations can overshadow small discriminative signals. Peak-Guided Calibration addresses that problem by giving particularly informative local features a stronger role in the final decision.

PGC uses peak-sensitive aggregation to emphasize local clues that best distinguish generated images. Those aggregated signals then calibrate the detector's global decision. The method therefore connects local evidence with image-level judgment, aiming to recover patterns that would otherwise be submerged by the main subject or other high-fidelity content.

The researchers also introduce CommGen15, containing samples from 15 commercial generative models, to provide a challenging evaluation setting. They report a 12.3% improvement in mean accuracy on this dataset and gains of 2.1% on GenImage, 3.5% on AIGI, and 1.7% on UniversalFakeDetect. These state-of-the-art reported results support the usefulness of emphasizing subtle local signals across the evaluated benchmarks, alongside the contribution of a new commercial-model benchmark.
summary.tldr: PGC strengthens generated-image detection by using discriminative local feature peaks to calibrate global decisions.

title: PGC: Peak-Guided Calibration for Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection

abstract: In the authorship verification problem, we are given examples of the writingof a single author and are asked to determine if given long texts were or werenot written by this author. We present a new learning-based method foradducing the �depth of difference� between two example sets and offer evidencethat this method solves the authorship verification problem with very highaccuracy. The underlying idea is to test the rate of degradation of theaccuracy of learned models as the best features are iteratively dropped fromthe learning process.

We present a new learning-based method foradducing the �depth of difference� between two example sets and offer evidencethat this method solves the authorship verification problem with very highaccuracy. The underlying idea is to test the rate of degradation of theaccuracy of learned models as the best features are iteratively dropped fromthe learning process.

paragraphs: The paper studies authorship verification: given writing from one known author, determine whether a long text was written by that person. This framing makes the available examples of a single author's writing central to the task. The proposed learning method measures how deeply two sets of examples differ.

Its key procedure repeatedly removes the strongest features from the learning process and tracks how quickly the accuracy of learned models declines. The rate of degradation provides information beyond the accuracy obtained with all features present. It makes the persistence of a learned distinction under feature removal part of the evidence used to assess the two example sets.

The authors present evidence that this approach achieves very high accuracy on the authorship verification problem. The stated finding supports examining the behavior of learned models as their best features disappear. The contribution is therefore both an authorship verification method and a particular way of probing the depth of differences between example collections.
summary.tldr: The method verifies authorship by measuring how model accuracy deteriorates as the strongest distinguishing features are repeatedly removed.

title: Authorship verification as a one-class classification problem

abstract: Divide-and-conquer is key to building sophisticated learning machines: hard problems are solved by composing a network of modules that solve simpler problems (LeCun et al., 1998; Rohde, 2002; Bradley, 2009). Many such existing systems rely on learning algorithms which are based on simple parametric gradient descent where the parametrization must be predetermined, or more specialized per-application algorithms which are usually ad-hoc and complicated. We present a novel approach for training generic modular networks that uses two existing techniques: the error propagation strategy of backpropagation and more recent research on descent in spaces of functions (Mason et al., 1999; Scholkopf & Smola, 2001). Combining these two methods of optimization gives a simple algorithm for training heterogeneous networks of functional modules using simple gradient propagation mechanics and established learning algorithms. The resulting separation of concerns between learning individual modules and error propagation mechanics eases implementation, enables a larger class of modular learning strategies, and allows per-module control of complexity/regularization. We derive and demonstrate this functional backpropagation and contrast it with traditional gradient descent in parameter space, observing that in our example domain the method is significantly more robust to local optima.

paragraphs: Modular learning systems solve complex problems by connecting components that handle simpler ones. Training such systems can require either a predetermined parameterization or specialized learning procedures. This paper proposes a more general training approach that combines backpropagation's way of distributing error with optimization performed in spaces of functions.

The resulting functional backpropagation separates two responsibilities: passing error information through the network and learning each individual module. Modules can use established learning algorithms while participating in a shared error-propagation scheme. This supports networks containing different kinds of functional components and allows their complexity or regularization to be controlled separately.

The authors derive the approach, demonstrate it, and compare it with conventional gradient descent over parameters. In their example domain, functional backpropagation is significantly more robust to local optima. This empirical result supports the method in that setting, while the broader methodological contribution is an implementation structure that makes additional modular learning strategies possible without requiring a single uniform learning procedure for every component.
summary.tldr: Functional backpropagation combines error propagation with learning in function spaces, supporting heterogeneous modules and showing greater robustness to local optima in an example domain.

title: Boosted Backpropagation Learning for Training Deep Modular Networks

abstract: In this paper, we address the scalability issue plaguing graph-based semi-supervised learning viaa small number of anchor points which adequately cover the entire point cloud. Critically, these anchor points enable nonparametric regression that predicts the label for each data point as a locally weighted average of the labels on anchor points. Because conventional graph construction is inefficient in large scale, we propose to construct a tractable large graph by couplinganchor-based label prediction and adjacency matrix design. Contrary to the Nystrom approximation of adjacency matrices which results in indefinite graph Laplacians and in turn leads to potential non-convex optimization over graphs, the proposed graph construction approach based on a unique idea called AnchorGraph provides nonnegative adjacency matrices to guarantee positive semidefinite graph Laplacians. Our approach scales linearly with the data size and in practice usually produces a large sparse graph. Experiments on large datasets demonstrate the significant accuracy improvement and scalability of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Graph-based semi-supervised learning becomes expensive when constructing connections among a large collection of data points. This paper uses a small set of anchor points that adequately cover the data. Each point's label is predicted through a locally weighted average of anchor labels, giving the anchors a central role in representing the larger dataset.

The proposed AnchorGraph method designs the graph adjacency matrix together with this anchor-based prediction rule. It produces nonnegative adjacency matrices and guarantees positive semidefinite graph Laplacians. This addresses the abstract's concern that the compared Nystrom approximation can produce indefinite Laplacians and potentially make graph optimization non-convex.

The approach scales linearly with dataset size and usually produces sparse graphs in practice. Experiments on large datasets report substantial accuracy improvements and demonstrate scalability. The significance is that computational efficiency and the graph's mathematical properties are addressed together: the anchors support both tractable label prediction and a graph construction with the stated positive-semidefiniteness guarantee.
summary.tldr: AnchorGraph uses representative anchor points to build scalable semi-supervised learning graphs with guaranteed positive semidefinite Laplacians.

title: Large Graph Construction for Scalable Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: We study the task of online boosting, which aims to combine online weak learners into an online strong learner. While boosting in the batch setting has a sound theoretical foundation, not much theory is known for the online setting. In this paper, we propose an online boosting algorithm and we provide a theoretical guarantee. In addition, we also perform experiments on real-world datasets and the results show that our algorithm compares favorably with existing algorithms.
originalAbstract: We study the task of online boosting, which aims to combine online weak learners into an online strong learner. While boosting in the batch setting has a sound theoretical foundation, not much theory is known for the online setting. In this paper, we propose an online boosting algorithm and we provide a theoretical guarantee. In addition, we also perform experiments on real-world datasets and the results show that our algorithm compares favorably with existing algorithms.

paragraphs: Boosting aims to combine weak learners into a stronger learner. This paper considers the online version of that task, in which the component learners and their combination operate as learning proceeds. The motivation is a gap in theoretical understanding: batch boosting already has a sound foundation, while the online setting has received less theoretical support.

The authors propose an online boosting algorithm and establish a theoretical guarantee for it. The contribution therefore goes beyond introducing another combination procedure: it supplies formal justification within the online setting itself. That matters because the paper's stated goal is to understand how weak online learners can support a strong online learner, rather than relying only on the established theory for batch learning.

The paper also evaluates the algorithm on real-world datasets and reports favorable comparisons with existing algorithms. These experiments provide practical evidence alongside the theoretical result. Together, the two parts support the proposed method as an online boosting approach with both formal backing and encouraging observed performance.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces an online boosting algorithm with a theoretical guarantee and favorable results on real-world datasets.

title: An Online Boosting Algorithm with Theoretical Justifications

abstract: The last decade has seen substantial work on the use of non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) and its probabilistic counterparts for audio source separation. Although able to capture audio spectral structure well, these models neglect the non-stationarity and temporal dynamics that are important properties of audio. The recently proposed non-negative factorial hidden Markov model (N-FHMM) introduces a temporal dimension and improves source separation performance. However, the factorial nature of this model makes the complexity of inference exponential in the number of sound sources. Here, we present a Bayesian variant of the N-FHMM suited to an efficient variational inference algorithm, whose complexity is linear in the number of sound sources. Our algorithm performs comparably to exact inference in the original NFHMM but is significantly faster. In typical configurations of the N-FHMM, our method achieves around a 30x increase in speed.

The recently proposed non-negative factorial hidden Markov model (N-FHMM) introduces a temporal dimension and improves source separation performance. However, the factorial nature of this model makes the complexity of inference exponential in the number of sound sources. Here, we present a Bayesian variant of the N-FHMM suited to an efficient variational inference algorithm, whose complexity is linear in the number of sound sources. paragraphs: Audio source separation benefits from modeling both spectral patterns and how sounds change over time. Non-negative matrix factorization captures spectral structure, but neglects temporal dynamics. Non-negative factorial hidden Markov models add that temporal dimension and improve separation, at the cost of inference complexity that grows exponentially with the number of sources.

The paper introduces a Bayesian variant of this temporal model designed for efficient variational inference. The proposed algorithm's complexity grows linearly with the number of sound sources. This addresses the computational burden of the factorial structure while retaining a model that represents temporal behavior.

The authors report separation performance comparable to exact inference in the original model, with substantially faster computation. Typical model configurations show roughly a thirtyfold speed increase. That figure describes the reported configurations rather than every possible use. The results show that approximate inference in the Bayesian variant can preserve comparable separation performance while making multi-source temporal modeling much more computationally manageable.
summary.tldr: Variational inference makes a Bayesian temporal audio-separation model scale linearly in source count, with comparable performance and roughly 30× speedups in typical configurations.
